findings.title: POST endpoint returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new AccountLink object, which is a resource-creation operation. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §6.3.2), successful creation of a new resource should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Using 200 conflates creation with retrieval or update operations and prevents clients and tooling from distinguishing between these semantics automatically. While Stripe uses this convention broadly across its API, it remains a deviation from standard REST semantics.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 specifies 201 Created as the appropriate status code when a new resource has been created as a result of a POST request.
findings.patchSummary: Change 200 response to 201 Created for resource creation semantics

findings.title: `account` field typed as plain string without format or pattern — cross-resource reference untyped
findings.narration: The `account` field is described as 'the identifier of the account to create an account link for' but is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Account resource, and client-side validation cannot verify the field holds a plausible identifier rather than an arbitrary string. At minimum, a `pattern` such as `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` should be added.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and make client-side pre-validation impossible.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `account` field to reflect Stripe account ID format

findings.title: Deprecated `collect` parameter not marked with `deprecated: true`
findings.narration: The `collect` field's description states 'The collect parameter is deprecated. Use `collection_options` instead.' However, the schema property does not include `deprecated: true`. Without this machine-readable marker, OpenAPI tooling (SDKs, documentation generators, linters) cannot automatically surface the deprecation to consumers. The prose-only deprecation notice is invisible to automated tooling and will likely be ignored by developers relying on generated clients.
findings.rationale: OpenAPI 3.x supports a `deprecated: true` boolean on schema properties. Documenting deprecation only in prose means automated tooling cannot surface the warning to API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add `deprecated: true` to the `collect` property to enable tooling-level deprecation warnings

findings.title: `refresh_url` and `return_url` should have format: uri and conditional-required rule not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `refresh_url` and `return_url` fields are described as URLs where users are redirected, but are typed as plain `type: string` without `format: uri`. Additionally, the description for `refresh_url` implies it is functionally required when the account link can expire (which is always), yet it is not listed in the schema's `required` array and no machine-readable `if/then` or `dependencies` rule encodes when these fields must be present. Adding `format: uri` enables at-a-glance validation hints and downstream validation in many frameworks.
findings.rationale: URL fields without `format: uri` miss built-in validation in many OpenAPI-aware tools. Conditional requirements described only in prose cannot be enforced by schema validators.
findings.patchSummary: Add `format: uri` to `refresh_url` and `return_url` fields

findings.title: account field typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `account` field in the request body is described as 'The identifier of the account to create an Account Session for.' This is clearly a reference to a Stripe Account resource (IDs typically follow the pattern `acct_*`), but it is typed as a bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref` to a typed schema. Code-generation tools cannot infer the relationship between this field and the Account resource, making it impossible to build type-safe clients or validate ID format at the schema level.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed codegen and miss input validation. A pattern like `^acct_` or a dedicated format would encode the relationship.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to account field to encode Stripe Account ID format

findings.title: No description on individual component feature boolean fields
findings.narration: The `components` object contains dozens of nested boolean feature flags (e.g., `disable_stripe_user_authentication`, `external_account_collection`, `instant_payouts`, `capture_payments`, `dispute_management`, etc.) that have no `description` at all. These flags control significant capability grants on the embedded component (e.g., allowing external account collection on behalf of a connected account). Without descriptions, API consumers cannot understand the security and business implications of enabling each flag, especially sensitive ones like `disable_stripe_user_authentication` and `external_account_collection` which could expose connected accounts to risk if misused.
findings.rationale: Missing descriptions on security-relevant boolean feature flags leaves integrators without guidance on the implications of enabling them, increasing the risk of misconfiguration.

patchOps.value: Disables Stripe user authentication for this embedded component. When true, the platform takes responsibility for authenticating users before granting access.
Allows the embedded component to collect external account (bank account or debit card) information from the connected account.

findings.patchSummary: Add descriptions to sensitive feature flag boolean fields in components

findings.title: Missing request body example for complex nested components schema
findings.narration: The request body schema contains a deeply nested `components` object with over 20 distinct embedded component types, each with their own feature flag sets. There is no example provided at the request body, media-type, or schema level. For an endpoint of this complexity — where a developer must choose among `payments`, `payouts`, `issuing_card`, `financial_account`, etc. and configure features per component — at least one concrete example is essential for discoverability and correct integration.
findings.rationale: Complex, deeply nested request bodies without examples force developers to reverse-engineer the schema, significantly increasing integration friction and risk of misconfiguration.
findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the request body for the complex components schema

findings.title: components object has no minimum-one-component constraint encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `components` field is required in the request body but its schema allows an empty object (all component keys are optional). Submitting an AccountSession with no components enabled would be semantically meaningless — the session token would grant no embedded component access. The constraint that at least one component key must be present (and enabled) appears to be a business rule enforced only server-side, with nothing in the schema to guide clients. This should be encoded using `minProperties: 1` on the `components` object to give clients early feedback.
findings.rationale: Without a minProperties constraint on the components object, clients can submit an empty components dictionary and only discover the error at runtime from the server, rather than at schema-validation time.
findings.patchSummary: Add minProperties: 1 to components to enforce at least one component is configured

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (min/max not encoded)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties. This means client-side validators and code generators cannot enforce the documented range or inject the default value automatically. A caller passing `limit=0` or `limit=9999` would receive a server-side error with no prior schema-level warning.
findings.rationale: Documented range constraints that exist only in prose and not in the schema cannot be enforced by validators or leveraged by codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema that contains no properties and `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests conventionally have no body, and most HTTP clients and proxies discard or reject bodies on GET. Declaring an empty, closed request body adds confusion for consumers and may cause issues with certain HTTP middleware. All necessary parameters are already expressed as query parameters; the requestBody block should be removed.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 §4.3.1 states GET requests SHOULD NOT have a body. An empty closed schema in a requestBody on GET is semantically misleading.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Sensitive fields (tax_id, id_number, ssn_last_4) not marked writeOnly
findings.narration: Several fields in the request body carry highly sensitive PII or financial identifiers: `company.tax_id`, `individual.id_number`, `individual.id_number_secondary`, and `individual.ssn_last_4`. None of these are marked `writeOnly: true`. Without the `writeOnly` annotation, code generators and documentation tools may render these fields in response schemas, potentially encouraging clients to log or display them. Marking them writeOnly signals that the values are accepted on input but never echoed back, which is the actual Stripe behavior and an important security hint.
findings.rationale: Sensitive identifiers should be marked writeOnly to prevent accidental exposure in generated clients, docs, and logs.
findings.patchSummary: Mark tax_id, id_number, id_number_secondary, ssn_last_4 as writeOnly

findings.title: Conditional-required relationship between `individual` and `business_type` expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The description for the `individual` field states: 'This field is null unless `business_type` is set to `individual`.' This conditional dependency — that `individual` is only meaningful/applicable when `business_type === 'individual'` — is documented in prose but not encoded in the schema. Similarly, the `company` field is relevant for business types other than `individual`. These conditional rules cannot be validated automatically by tooling without JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependencies` constructs. While the full `if/then` encoding across business_type branches would be complex, at minimum the prose-only constraint is a documentation gap that generators and validators cannot act on.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules expressed only as prose descriptions cannot be enforced by validators or leveraged by codegen tools; they should be encoded as schema constraints.
findings.patchSummary: Encode business_type/individual/company conditional relationship using JSON Schema if/then

findings.title: `bank_account.account_number` not marked writeOnly
findings.narration: The `bank_account` object inline variant includes `account_number`, which is a sensitive banking credential. Like the identity numbers above, it lacks `writeOnly: true`. Bank account numbers should never be echoed back by an API, and the writeOnly marker is the standard way to communicate this to SDK generators and documentation systems, preventing clients from inadvertently caching or displaying the value.
findings.rationale: Bank account numbers are sensitive credentials that should be annotated writeOnly to prevent them from appearing in response schema tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Mark bank_account.account_number as writeOnly

findings.title: Missing operation-level `summary` field
findings.narration: The operation has a detailed `description` (HTML) but no `summary` field. The `summary` is displayed prominently in API reference UIs (Redoc, Swagger UI) as the one-line title for the endpoint in navigation and endpoint lists. Without it, tooling falls back to the operationId ('PostAccounts') or leaves the entry untitled, reducing discoverability for developers browsing the reference.
findings.rationale: A missing summary reduces API reference usability; tooling uses summary as the primary human-readable label for the operation.
findings.patchSummary: Add summary: 'Create an account' to the operation

findings.title: Request body defined on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content on a GET request. HTTP semantics (RFC 9110) strongly discourage request bodies on GET operations because intermediaries (proxies, caches) may ignore or strip them. While the body schema is empty (`properties: {}`), its mere presence is misleading to API consumers and codegen tooling, which may generate client code that attempts to send a body with a GET request. The `requestBody` block should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per RFC 9110 best practices; an empty body schema adds noise and may confuse codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/accounts/{account}

findings.title: Account path parameter lacks ID format hint
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `acct_` followed by alphanumerics). Without a `pattern` constraint or at minimum a `description` documenting the expected format, codegen tools and API consumers have no machine-readable way to validate the identifier before sending the request. Adding a pattern such as `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would close this gap.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings with no format or pattern guidance prevent typed codegen and offer no client-side validation.

patchOps.value: The identifier of the Stripe account to retrieve. Should be an `acct_`-prefixed ID.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to the account path parameter

findings.title: Sensitive identity fields lack writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The request body contains highly sensitive personal identity fields such as `individual.id_number`, `individual.id_number_secondary`, `individual.ssn_last_4`, `company.tax_id`, and `company.vat_id`. None of these fields are marked `writeOnly: true`. Without this marker, code-generation tools and documentation renderers may surface these fields as readable properties, potentially misleading consumers into expecting these values back in responses. More critically, tooling that auto-generates client models may inadvertently log or persist values returned from the API when these fields should only travel in one direction.
findings.rationale: Credential and government-issued ID fields should be marked writeOnly to signal they are submit-only and never returned in responses, which is a standard PII protection pattern.
findings.patchSummary: Mark id_number, id_number_secondary, ssn_last_4, tax_id, vat_id as writeOnly

findings.title: Conditional-required relationship between individual and business_type encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `individual` field description states it is null unless `business_type` is set to `individual`, and several other fields (`company`, `individual`) are only meaningful for specific `business_type` values. This conditional-required relationship is documented purely in prose descriptions but is not encoded in the schema using `if/then/else` or `dependencies`. Consumers and validators cannot enforce this constraint programmatically, increasing the chance of malformed requests that will fail at runtime rather than being caught by client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements noted only in description text should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints (if/then or dependencies) so validators can enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Encode business_type/individual and business_type/company conditional constraints using JSON Schema if/then

findings.title: payout schedule fields monthly_anchor and weekly_anchor are conditionally required by interval but only in prose
findings.narration: Within `settings.payouts.schedule`, the `monthly_anchor` field is only relevant when `interval` is `monthly`, and `weekly_anchor` is only relevant when `interval` is `weekly`. Similarly `monthly_payout_days` and `weekly_payout_days` have implicit applicability conditions. These cross-field constraints are entirely absent from the schema and are not even documented in field-level descriptions. Consumers cannot know which sub-fields are applicable for a given `interval` value without reading external documentation. This is a classic case where `if/then/else` or `oneOf` should constrain the allowed sub-fields based on the chosen interval.
findings.rationale: Fields that are only valid in combination with specific sibling field values should have those constraints expressed in schema, not left implicit.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then constraints in transfer_schedule_specs tying anchor fields to their respective interval values

findings.title: No 4xx error response definitions beyond the generic default
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a catch-all `default` error response. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `403`, or `404` response definitions. For an account-update endpoint that accepts highly conditional inputs (business_type constraints, account_link lifecycle restrictions, controller-type restrictions), callers have no schema-level understanding of what specific error shapes to expect for validation failures, authorization failures, or not-found conditions. The `default` schema is cyclic-referenced and provides no discriminating information per status code.
findings.rationale: Explicit 400/401/403/404 responses aid client error handling and are standard practice; relying solely on a default catch-all obscures the error contract.

value.description: Bad request — invalid or missing parameters.
Unauthorized — authentication credentials missing or invalid.
Forbidden — caller does not have permission to update this account.
Not found — no account with the specified ID.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400, 401, 403, 404 response definitions alongside the existing default

findings.title: Account ID path parameter lacks format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK generators cannot produce typed, validated references, and developers cannot distinguish this from a free-form string. Adding a regex pattern like `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]{16,}$` (or equivalent) would enable early client-side validation and improve codegen relationships.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and enable silent misuse.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to account path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format

findings.title: Successful delete returns 200 instead of semantically correct 204
findings.narration: The operation returns HTTP 200 on success, but it references a cyclic schema (a deleted-account confirmation object). While Stripe's API conventionally returns a deletion confirmation object with `deleted: true`, if the response body is effectively just a tombstone, HTTP 204 No Content would be more semantically appropriate for a DELETE. However, since Stripe does return a body (the deleted object marker), this is acceptable — but the response description 'Successful response.' is too sparse. It should at minimum indicate that a deletion confirmation object (with `id` and `deleted: true`) is returned, so consumers understand why a DELETE yields a body rather than 204.
findings.rationale: Sparse response descriptions on non-trivial delete responses leave consumers guessing about the shape and meaning of the returned body.

patchOps.value: Successful deletion. Returns a deletion confirmation object with `id` and `deleted: true`.

findings.patchSummary: Improve 200 response description to clarify deletion confirmation object shape

findings.title: Response should be 201 Created, not 200 OK for resource creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new external bank account resource. Per HTTP semantics, successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created rather than 200 OK. Using 200 misrepresents the nature of the operation to API consumers, tooling, and proxies that rely on status codes to distinguish creation from update or query operations.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 specifies 201 for successful resource creation. Returning 200 for a POST that creates a resource is a well-known HTTP semantic violation.
findings.patchSummary: Change 200 OK to 201 Created for resource creation response

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `bank_account` and `external_account` not encoded as schema constraint
findings.narration: The request body exposes two overlapping fields: `bank_account` (which accepts either a token string or a full bank account object) and `external_account` (which also accepts a token string for an external account). The description of `external_account` says 'Please refer to full documentation instead', implying these are alternative ways to supply the same data. There is no JSON Schema `oneOf` or `not` constraint preventing a caller from supplying both simultaneously. This conditional-required / mutual-exclusion rule exists only in prose documentation (the external_account description) and is not machine-enforceable. Validation libraries and SDK generators cannot surface this constraint to callers.
findings.rationale: Field-level mutual exclusion rules expressed only in prose descriptions should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints (oneOf, not, if/then) so they are enforceable by validators and legible to code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusion of `bank_account` and `external_account` as oneOf constraint

findings.title: `account_number` field lacks writeOnly flag — sensitive financial data exposed in responses
findings.narration: The `account_number` property inside the `bank_account` object parameter is typed as a plain string with no `writeOnly: true` annotation. Bank account numbers are sensitive financial credentials. Without `writeOnly: true`, code generators and documentation tools may include this field in response schemas or in serialization/deserialization logic, increasing the risk of accidental exposure. Stripe itself masks account numbers in responses, so the schema should reflect that this field is only meaningful on write.
findings.rationale: Credential and sensitive financial fields should carry writeOnly:true to signal to clients, code generators, and documentation tools that the value is never returned in responses.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly:true to account_number to mark it as a write-only credential field

findings.title: `account` path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern — resource ID relationship untyped
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is a Stripe Account resource identifier (typically prefixed `acct_`) but is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint and no `pattern` or `format` hint. Code generators cannot infer the relationship to the Account resource, and callers receive no machine-readable signal about the expected ID format. Adding a pattern such as `^acct_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` or a custom `format: account-id` would allow validation at the client and make the cross-resource reference explicit.
findings.rationale: Resource ID path parameters should carry a pattern or format to enable client-side validation and typed cross-resource references in generated SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `account` path parameter to encode the acct_ ID format

findings.title: GET request includes an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type, but its schema is an empty object (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a body at all — RFC 7231 discourages it, many HTTP clients and proxies strip or reject bodies on GET requests, and no fields are actually documented to be sent. This empty request body definition is noise that may confuse client generators into emitting incorrect code.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 §4.3.1 states that a payload body in a GET request has no defined semantics. An empty, non-functional request body schema should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty GET request body — it has no defined semantics and confuses codegen tools.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks maxLength and format constraints
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with no `maxLength`, `pattern`, or `format`. Stripe external account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ba_` for bank accounts). Without a constraint, validation tooling and client generators cannot enforce correctness. The `account` parameter correctly defines `maxLength: 5000`, so parity is expected here too. At minimum, a `maxLength` should be added; a `pattern` matching the Stripe ID prefix would be even better.
findings.rationale: Uncontrained string path parameters allow arbitrarily long values and prevent client/server-side validation. Consistency with the sibling `account` parameter is also broken.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength: 5000 (and optionally a pattern) to the `id` path parameter schema.

findings.title: Card-specific fields present in bank account update schema
findings.narration: The request body schema includes fields that are clearly card-specific: `exp_month`, `exp_year`, `name` (described as 'Cardholder name'), `address_city`, `address_country`, `address_line1`, `address_line2`, `address_state`, and `address_zip` (described as 'Billing address country, if provided when creating card'). This endpoint is documented exclusively for updating bank accounts, not cards. The presence of these card fields—likely copied from a shared external-account update schema—creates confusion for API consumers and codegen tools, implying that fields like `exp_month` or `name` are applicable to bank account updates when they are not. This is a design/clarity problem because the schema does not accurately represent the contract of this specific endpoint.
findings.rationale: Fields inapplicable to the resource type pollute the schema, mislead consumers, and generate incorrect client code. The descriptions for these fields explicitly reference cards, not bank accounts.
findings.patchSummary: Remove card-specific fields (exp_month, exp_year, name, address_*) from the bank account update schema

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks maxLength and pattern constraints
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter has `maxLength: 5000` defined, but the `id` path parameter (representing the bank account ID, typically prefixed `ba_`) has no `maxLength` or `pattern` constraint at all. Without these constraints, client-side validation cannot catch obviously malformed IDs, and generated SDK code has no type information beyond bare `string`. A pattern like `^ba_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and a reasonable maxLength (e.g. 5000 consistent with other parameters) would improve safety and documentation.
findings.rationale: Inconsistent parameter constraints reduce the quality of generated client code and miss an opportunity to validate input early. The sibling `account` parameter already has maxLength set.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength: 5000 to `id` path parameter schema for consistency with `account`

findings.title: Missing operationId summary field
findings.narration: The operation has a detailed `description` but no `summary` field. The `summary` is the short human-readable label displayed in API reference UIs and used by codegen tools as the method label. Without it, tools fall back to the `operationId` (`PostAccountsAccountBankAccountsId`), which is verbose and not human-friendly. A concise summary like 'Update a bank account' would significantly improve discoverability.
findings.rationale: The OpenAPI `summary` field is the primary UI label for an operation. Its absence forces tooling to use the raw operationId as display text.
findings.patchSummary: Add summary 'Update a bank account' to the operation

findings.title: Path parameter `account` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot produce a typed resource reference, and clients have no machine-readable guidance to distinguish this from arbitrary free-text. The `id` parameter has the same issue — it references an external account ID but carries no pattern or format.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent typed codegen relationships and offer no validation signal to consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `account` path parameter for typed resource reference.

findings.title: DELETE returns 200 instead of semantically preferred 204 for deletion
findings.narration: The operation responds with HTTP 200 on successful deletion. RESTful convention and common API design practice recommend HTTP 204 (No Content) when a DELETE operation produces no meaningful response body, or 200 only when a representation of the deleted resource is returned. Here the response schema is a cyclic ref (deleted-object marker), which typically carries minimal payload. Using 200 is not wrong per se, but the absence of a 204 definition and the reliance on a cyclic/opaque schema means clients cannot distinguish 'deleted with body' from a generic success. This is a design clarity issue worth calling out.
findings.rationale: HTTP DELETE semantics are better expressed with 204 when no body is returned, or 200 with a well-defined deleted-resource schema. Opaque cyclic ref as the 200 body reduces client clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Consider documenting whether 200 returns a deleted-object body or switch to 204 for no-content deletes.

findings.title: account path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot build a typed cross-resource relationship, and client-side validation is impossible. A regex pattern such as `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would provide meaningful constraints and improve both documentation and SDK generation quality.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent code generators from building typed relationships and prevent client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to account path parameter to reflect Stripe account ID format.

findings.title: List endpoint has has_more flag but no pagination cursor parameters
findings.narration: The response schema includes a `has_more` boolean and a `url` field, clearly indicating this is a paginated list resource. However, the operation defines no pagination parameters (e.g., `starting_after`, `ending_before`, or `limit`). Consumers cannot traverse pages beyond the first without knowing these parameters exist, and the API contract is incomplete. Stripe typically supports cursor-based pagination on list endpoints, and these parameters should be documented here.
findings.rationale: A list endpoint that signals pagination via has_more but provides no pagination query parameters leaves API consumers unable to navigate beyond the first page based on the spec alone.

value.name: starting_after
value.description: A cursor for use in pagination. `starting_after` is an object ID that defines your place in the list.

value.name: ending_before
value.description: A cursor for use in pagination. `ending_before` is an object ID that defines your place in the list.

value.name: limit
value.description: A limit on the number of objects to be returned. Limit can range between 1 and 100.

findings.patchSummary: Add starting_after, ending_before, and limit pagination parameters to the list capabilities endpoint.

findings.title: Empty request body unnecessarily declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are non-standard per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110), and many proxies, gateways, and HTTP clients will strip or reject a body on GET requests. Stripe uses this pattern for its form-encoded expansion parameters, but since all parameters here are already represented as query parameters, the empty body definition adds noise and could confuse consumers or code generators.
findings.rationale: An empty, body-less request body on a GET endpoint contradicts HTTP semantics and provides no value since all parameters are already query/path parameters.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: GET operation includes a request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content. While the schema is empty and `required` is false, including a request body on a GET operation is semantically incorrect per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). Many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks strip or reject request bodies on GET requests, making this a potentially broken pattern in practice. The request body definition should be removed entirely from this operation.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 states GET requests SHOULD NOT have a message body. Including one — even empty — misleads API consumers and may cause client or proxy incompatibilities.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `capability` lacks maxLength or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter has a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but the `capability` path parameter has only `type: string` with no `maxLength`, `pattern`, or `enum` constraint. Stripe capability identifiers are well-known values (e.g. `card_payments`, `transfers`). Without constraints, generated clients and validators accept arbitrarily long or malformed strings, and documentation gives no indication of valid values. At minimum a `maxLength` should be added to match the convention applied to `account`, and ideally an `enum` or `pattern` should describe valid capability names.
findings.rationale: Missing constraints on a string path parameter weaken input validation hints for clients and codegen tools, and is inconsistent with the sibling `account` parameter's treatment.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength: 5000 to the `capability` path parameter schema.

findings.title: Path parameter `capability` lacks format constraint or enumeration
findings.narration: The `capability` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with no `maxLength`, `pattern`, or `enum`. Stripe capability identifiers follow a well-known set (e.g. `card_payments`, `transfers`, `us_bank_account_ach_payments`). Without any constraint, client code cannot validate the value before sending the request, and codegen tools treat it as a free-form string, offering no type safety or discoverability. At minimum, a `maxLength` should be applied (consistent with the `account` parameter), and ideally an `enum` or `pattern` should restrict the values to known capability keys.
findings.rationale: A completely unconstrained path parameter degrades API usability and prevents clients from catching invalid values early.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength:5000 to capability path parameter schema to match account parameter.

findings.title: GET endpoint includes a redundant empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema that contains no properties and sets `additionalProperties: false`. A GET request should carry no body at all — HTTP semantics discourage bodies on GET requests, many intermediaries strip them, and some clients (e.g. fetch, curl defaults) will ignore or reject them. Including this empty body block is noise at best and actively misleading to SDK generators and documentation tooling at worst.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per HTTP semantics; an empty, closed schema body serves no purpose and may confuse code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (min/max not encoded in schema)
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` query parameter clearly states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` keyword. This means validation tools and generated SDKs cannot enforce the documented range, nor will clients see a useful default value. Any integer — including 0, -1, or 9999 — would pass schema validation, forcing the server to silently clamp or reject values that appear valid per the spec.
findings.rationale: Documented range constraints (1–100) and default (10) should be encoded in the schema so validators and code generators can enforce them.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Response `url` field lacks `format: uri` constraint
findings.narration: The `url` property in the `ExternalAccountList` response schema is described as 'The URL where this list can be accessed' and carries a `maxLength: 5000`, but is typed only as `type: string` without `format: uri`. Adding `format: uri` enables SDK generators to use a typed URL type in generated code and allows validators to reject clearly malformed values. This is a low-effort, high-clarity improvement.
findings.rationale: A property explicitly described as a URL should carry format: uri to help code generators and validators.
findings.patchSummary: Add format:uri to the response url property

findings.title: account_number field missing writeOnly flag — sensitive banking data exposed in logs/responses
findings.narration: The `account_number` field within the `bank_account` object parameter contains a full bank account number. Without `writeOnly: true`, OpenAPI tooling (documentation generators, mock servers, logging middleware) will treat this field as readable in responses, potentially exposing it in logs, SDK-generated response types, or developer tooling. Bank account numbers are highly sensitive PII. The field should be marked `writeOnly: true` to signal that this value is write-only and should never appear in response payloads.
findings.rationale: Bank account numbers are sensitive credentials/PII. `writeOnly: true` is the standard OpenAPI mechanism to prevent codegen and documentation tools from surfacing them as readable fields.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to bank_account.account_number to protect sensitive banking data

findings.title: routing_number field missing writeOnly flag — sensitive banking data
findings.narration: Similar to `account_number`, the `routing_number` field in the `bank_account` object is sensitive financial data that should be marked `writeOnly: true`. Routing numbers in combination with account numbers can be used for ACH fraud. Without this flag, documentation generators and SDK tooling will not distinguish this write-only credential from readable response fields.
findings.rationale: Routing numbers are sensitive financial identifiers; marking them writeOnly prevents accidental exposure through code generation and API documentation tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to bank_account.routing_number to protect sensitive banking data

findings.title: Conditional mutual-exclusion between bank_account and external_account not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The request body exposes two distinct ways to supply an external account: `bank_account` (an object or token string) and `external_account` (a token string). The descriptions suggest these are alternatives, but neither `oneOf`, `not`, `dependentSchemas`, nor any other JSON Schema constraint encodes the mutual-exclusion rule. Callers could supply both fields simultaneously without any schema-level rejection, and clients reading the spec cannot determine whether both, one, or neither is required. The spec description for `external_account` even says 'Please refer to full documentation instead', implying this is an either/or choice. This conditional requirement exists only in prose and should be encoded formally.
findings.rationale: Conditional field relationships expressed only in prose are a high-leverage schema gap; they cannot be enforced by validators or communicated to code generators without explicit JSON Schema constructs.
findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf constraint to enforce mutual exclusion between bank_account and external_account

findings.title: external_account field typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or resource-ID hint
findings.narration: The `external_account` field accepts a Stripe token (e.g., `btok_...`) but is declared as a bare `type: string` with no `pattern`, no `format`, and no description of expected prefix conventions. Code generation tools and client validators cannot derive any structural constraint for this field. While `x-stripeBypassValidation: true` suppresses Stripe's internal validation, the absence of even a pattern leaves API consumers with no machine-readable guidance. Adding a regex pattern such as `^(btok|tok)_` would at minimum document the expected shape.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and prevent client-side pre-validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern to external_account string field to document expected Stripe token format

findings.title: GET operation includes a superfluous empty request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema that has no properties and `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests must not include a body per RFC 9110 §9.3.1 — intermediaries (proxies, CDNs) are explicitly permitted to discard or reject a body on a GET. Including an empty, locked-down body schema in a GET operation is semantically incorrect and can confuse client generators into emitting code that sends a body with the request.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body per HTTP semantics. Even an empty body schema causes confusion in generated clients and violates RFC 9110.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `account` lacks a pattern or format constraint
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a tighter `maxLength`, the schema provides no structural validation guidance to consumers and codegen tools cannot infer the resource relationship. The `id` parameter has the same issue — it has no `maxLength` at all and no format or pattern hint, even though external account IDs follow the `ba_` or `card_` prefix patterns.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern hints prevent typed codegen relationships and make validation weaker than necessary.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern to `account` and maxLength to `id` path parameters.

findings.title: Request body mixes bank account and card fields without schema discrimination
findings.narration: The request body schema conflates fields that apply exclusively to bank accounts (account_holder_name, account_holder_type, account_type, documents) with fields that apply exclusively to cards (address_city, address_country, address_line1, address_line2, address_state, address_zip, exp_month, exp_year, name). There is no `oneOf` / `discriminator` separating these two resource types. A consumer using this schema has no machine-readable way to know which fields are valid for which external account type. This is especially problematic for codegen tools and SDK authors: they will generate a single flat object where bank-account-only fields appear valid for card updates and vice versa, potentially leading to silent no-ops or unexpected API errors.
findings.rationale: Mixing two semantically distinct resource update shapes into one undiscriminated schema prevents type-safe usage and produces misleading documentation. A oneOf or conditional schema (if/then/else on a discriminating property) would encode the constraint machine-readably.

account_holder_name.description: The name of the person or business that owns the bank account.

account_holder_type.description: The type of entity that holds the account.

default_for_currency.description: When set to true, this becomes the default external account for its currency.

documents.description: Documents that may be submitted to satisfy various informational requests.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

findings.patchSummary: Split flat schema into oneOf BankAccountUpdateParams / CardUpdateParams

findings.title: exp_month and exp_year typed as string instead of integer
findings.narration: The fields `exp_month` and `exp_year` are described as 'Two digit number' and 'Four digit number' respectively, but both are declared as `type: string` with a `maxLength` constraint rather than `type: integer`. Using `string` for numeric values prevents range validation (e.g. `minimum: 1, maximum: 12` for month), causes type confusion in generated clients, and forces downstream consumers to parse and validate the values themselves. The descriptions explicitly say 'number', making the `string` type a direct contradiction.
findings.rationale: Numeric card expiry fields should be typed as integer to enable proper range constraints and type-safe codegen. The field descriptions say 'number' but the type says string — this is a type mismatch.

value.description: Two digit number representing the card's expiration month.
Four digit number representing the card's expiration year.

findings.patchSummary: Change exp_month and exp_year from string to integer with range constraints

findings.title: documents.bank_account_ownership_verification.files items type as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `documents.bank_account_ownership_verification.files` array contains items of `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 500`, but these strings are clearly Stripe file object IDs (format: `file_...`). Without a `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a File ID type, codegen tools treat these as arbitrary strings, losing the typed relationship to the File resource. A `pattern` such as `^file_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or a dedicated `format: stripe-file-id` would make the relationship explicit.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID references typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and give no validation hint to API consumers.

value.description: The ID of a file uploaded via the Stripe Files API.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to file ID strings in documents.files array

findings.title: Missing operation-level summary
findings.narration: The operation has a detailed `description` but no `summary` field. The `summary` is what most API tooling (Redoc, Swagger UI, SDK generators) uses as the short human-readable label for the operation in navigation, method docstrings, and changelog entries. Without it, tooling falls back to the `operationId` or the first sentence of the description, both of which are suboptimal for discoverability. A concise summary such as 'Update an external account' would improve usability significantly.
findings.rationale: A missing summary degrades discoverability in API tooling that relies on it for navigation and generated docstrings.

patchOps.value: Update an external account (bank account or card) for a connected account

findings.patchSummary: Add a concise summary field to the operation

findings.title: Path parameter 'account' lacks format/pattern constraint for account ID
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client codegen tools cannot validate the ID format at the client side, and the constraint is uselessly loose — a 5000-character arbitrary string would pass validation. Similarly, the `id` parameter for the external account has no constraints at all.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern/format provide no validation signal to consumers or codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to account param and maxLength to id param.

findings.title: DELETE returns 200 instead of semantically appropriate 204
findings.narration: The operation returns HTTP 200 on successful deletion. REST conventions and Stripe's own pattern for deletions typically return a deleted-object confirmation object — which does justify a 200 with a body (rather than 204). However, the 200 response schema is a cyclic `$ref` placeholder, so the actual shape of the deletion confirmation object (e.g., `{id, object, deleted: true}`) is not documented in a human or machine-readable way for this operation. Consumers cannot understand what they receive on success. While cyclic refs are noted as intentional, the effective result is a completely opaque success response.
findings.rationale: An opaque 200 response schema means clients cannot parse or validate the deletion confirmation envelope without external documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Consider inlining a deletion confirmation schema (id, object, deleted) for the 200 response.

findings.title: Path parameter 'account' typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, SDK code generators and API consumers have no machine-readable indication that this is a cross-resource reference to an Account object. Adding a pattern such as `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would catch obviously malformed inputs at the client layer and improve generated SDK type fidelity.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow malformed IDs to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'account' path parameter to reflect Stripe acct_ ID format

findings.title: POST returns 200 instead of semantically correct 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new login link resource, yet the success response is documented as HTTP 200. Per HTTP semantics and REST best practices, a POST that creates a new resource should return 201 Created. The current 200 status code is misleading to consumers and API clients that branch on status codes to determine whether a resource was created or simply retrieved. Stripe uses 200 broadly across its API, but for a creation endpoint the mismatch is a notable design inconsistency.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status for resource creation via POST. Using 200 conflates creation with retrieval, reducing semantic clarity for clients.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response from 200 to 201 to reflect resource creation semantics

findings.title: GET request body is semantically incorrect
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. GET requests must not carry a request body per HTTP/1.1 semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and HTTP/2 semantics. While some frameworks accept it, many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will silently drop or reject a body on GET requests. Since the body schema is empty (`properties: {}`), the intent appears to be to leave room for future additions or it was added by template. This should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody violates RFC 7231 semantics. The body schema is empty (no properties), confirming it carries no useful information.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/accounts/{account}/people

findings.title: Missing minimum/maximum constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` query parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` keywords enforcing this. Clients relying on schema validation will not catch out-of-range values, and SDK generators will not surface these constraints as typed validations. The default value of 10 is also missing, meaning clients unaware of the description will not know the default behaviour.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but not encoded in schema are high-leverage issues: SDKs, validators, and documentation generators all miss them.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Response `url` field lacks a `format: uri` and pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `url` field in the 200 response schema is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`, but no `format: uri` or `pattern`. The description states it is 'The URL where this list can be accessed', making it clearly a URI. Without `format: uri`, SDK generators cannot produce typed URL fields, and validators cannot check that the value is a well-formed URL. This is a low-effort, high-signal fix.
findings.rationale: A field documented as a URL should carry format:uri so code generators and validators can treat it correctly.
findings.patchSummary: Add format:uri to the url property in the 200 response schema

findings.title: Sensitive PII fields (id_number, ssn_last_4) lack writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The fields `id_number`, `id_number_secondary`, and `ssn_last_4` carry highly sensitive personal identifiers — government-issued ID numbers and Social Security number digits. Although these are request body fields, OpenAPI 3.x allows `writeOnly: true` to signal that a field must not be returned in responses. Without this marker, code generators and documentation tools will not warn consumers that these values should never be read back, increasing the risk of inadvertent logging, caching, or exposure of PII. Stripe's own documentation acknowledges that PII tokens should be used in place of raw values wherever possible, but the schema itself provides no mechanical guard.
findings.rationale: Sensitive credential/identity fields should carry `writeOnly: true` per OpenAPI 3.x §10.6 to prevent unintentional read-back and to help downstream tooling enforce data minimization.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to id_number, id_number_secondary, and ssn_last_4 fields

findings.title: nationality field missing ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `nationality` field description explicitly states it must be a two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code or the special value "XX". However, the schema only enforces `maxLength: 5000` and `type: string`, which would accept any arbitrary string of up to 5000 characters. The expected format should be encoded as a `pattern` (e.g. `^[A-Z]{2}$` with an additional allowance for "XX") and a tighter `maxLength: 2` so that validation tools and client generators can enforce the constraint rather than relying solely on prose documentation. The same applies to the `country` sub-fields across all address objects, but `nationality` is the most explicit case.
findings.rationale: A field whose description precisely defines its valid values (ISO 2-letter codes or XX) should encode that constraint in the schema via pattern and maxLength so validators enforce it automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten nationality to maxLength:2 + pattern for ISO alpha-2 / XX

findings.title: gender field is a free-form string despite description implying an enum
findings.narration: The `gender` field description states 'International regulations require either "male" or "female"', clearly implying the only accepted values are those two strings. Yet the schema declares `type: string` with no `enum`, no `pattern`, and no `maxLength`. A client sending any arbitrary string (e.g. "unknown", "m") would pass schema validation. The allowed values should be encoded as `enum: ["male", "female"]` so that validation tools and generated clients enforce the documented constraint. If Stripe needs to accept other values in non-regulated contexts, the description should clarify this and an `anyOf` pattern can be used.
findings.rationale: A description that lists the only permitted values constitutes a conditional-required/field-value constraint that belongs in the schema, not just in prose.
findings.patchSummary: Add enum:["male","female"] to gender field to match its prose constraint

findings.title: POST creating a resource returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new Person resource under the given account, which is a canonical resource-creation action. The HTTP specification and REST conventions indicate that successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, optionally with a Location header pointing to the new resource. The spec declares only a 200 response. While Stripe is known to use 200 uniformly across its API for historical reasons, from a correctness and documentation standpoint this deviates from expected semantics and can confuse clients that check status codes to determine whether a resource was created vs. merely updated. This is a low-severity note since it is a consistent Stripe-wide pattern.
findings.rationale: POST endpoints that create resources should return 201 per RFC 9110 §15.3.2 to distinguish creation from update; 200 is semantically ambiguous for new resource creation.

value.description: Person created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response alongside existing 200 for resource creation semantics

findings.title: Path parameter 'account' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format`, codegen tools cannot produce a typed reference, and client-side validation cannot catch malformed IDs early. Adding a pattern such as `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would make the constraint machine-readable and improve DX.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters typed as plain strings without a pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and miss an easy validation opportunity.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'account' path parameter schema

findings.title: Path parameter 'person' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `person` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe person IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `person_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format`, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship between this parameter and the Person resource, and callers receive no early validation signal when passing an incorrect ID type.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters typed as plain strings without a pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and miss an easy validation opportunity.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'person' path parameter schema

findings.title: GET operation includes a superfluous empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 notes that a payload body on a GET has no defined semantics). Many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks will drop or reject a body on a GET request, making this declaration both misleading and potentially harmful to consumers relying on the spec for code generation.
findings.rationale: A GET request body with no allowed properties violates HTTP semantics and may confuse codegen tools into generating clients that send empty bodies, which intermediaries may strip or reject.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Sensitive PII fields (id_number, ssn_last_4) lack writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The fields `id_number`, `id_number_secondary`, and `ssn_last_4` capture highly sensitive government-issued identity numbers and Social Security number fragments. None of them are marked `writeOnly: true` in the schema. Without this marker, code-generation tools may include these fields in response models and serialisation round-trips, increasing the risk of accidental logging or echoing of PII in client applications. Stripe never returns raw ID numbers in responses, so `writeOnly` accurately models the API contract and signals to consumers that these values should be treated as write-only secrets.
findings.rationale: Sensitive credential/PII fields should carry writeOnly:true so code generators and documentation tools correctly exclude them from response object models.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly:true to id_number, id_number_secondary, and ssn_last_4 fields

findings.title: nationality field accepts unconstrained string instead of ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 pattern
findings.narration: The `nationality` description states it must be a two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (or "XX"), but the schema only specifies `type: string` with `maxLength: 5000`. There is no `pattern` or `enum` constraint encoding this rule. Clients sending invalid values (e.g., a full country name) will discover the constraint only at runtime via a server error. Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^[A-Z]{2}$`) or an `enum` would allow client-side validation and improve generated SDK type safety.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but absent from the schema cannot be validated client-side and are invisible to code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern ^[A-Z]{2}$|^XX$ and maxLength:2 to nationality field

findings.title: us_cfpb_data contains sensitive demographic PII with no writeOnly or privacy annotation
findings.narration: The `us_cfpb_data` object captures race, ethnicity, and self-identified gender — among the most sensitive categories of personal data under GDPR, CCPA, and other privacy frameworks. The schema provides no indication that this data is write-only or subject to special handling. While this may be intentionally readable (for compliance audit purposes), the absence of any `writeOnly` marker or description note advising consumers about data sensitivity is a risk gap. At minimum, `self_identified_gender`, `race`, and `ethnicity` sub-fields should carry `writeOnly: true` if they are not returned in responses, or the description should explicitly state the retention and read-back policy.
findings.rationale: Special-category PII under GDPR/CCPA requires explicit handling signals. Absence of writeOnly or sensitivity annotation increases risk of accidental exposure.

patchOps.value: Demographic data related to the person, collected for CFPB compliance. Contains special-category personal data (race, ethnicity, gender). Treat as sensitive; do not log or expose unnecessarily.

findings.patchSummary: Enhance us_cfpb_data description to flag special-category PII sensitivity

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body contains a large, deeply nested schema covering address variants (standard, kana, kanji), date of birth, relationship roles, document uploads, verification, and demographic data. There are no `examples` or `example` annotations anywhere in the request body schema. For an operation of this complexity, the absence of at least one representative example makes it significantly harder for API consumers to understand how to construct a valid request, and prevents documentation renderers from showing a populated payload. A minimal example covering at least the most common fields (name, dob, relationship) would substantially improve usability.
findings.rationale: Complex multi-field update endpoints benefit greatly from request body examples; their absence is a clarity gap that increases integration time.
findings.patchSummary: Add representative example to request body for the update person operation

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'person' path parameter to reflect Stripe person ID format

findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema that has no properties (`properties: {}`) and `additionalProperties: false`. For a GET endpoint this is semantically incorrect — HTTP GET requests must not carry a body per RFC 9110, and including an empty, closed body schema misleads client generators into potentially serializing an empty form body or blocking the request.
findings.rationale: GET requests MUST NOT include a message body (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). An empty `requestBody` on a GET is noise at best and a code-gen hazard at worst.
