findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` query parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10.' However, the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties — these constraints exist only in prose. Client-side validators and code generators cannot enforce or document the valid range, leaving consumers to discover the allowed range through API errors.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but not encoded in the schema cannot be validated automatically. Missing `minimum`, `maximum`, and `default` reduces generated SDK quality.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: account path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Stripe account IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g. `acct_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a tighter `maxLength` reflecting realistic ID lengths, codegen tools cannot produce typed or validated references, and spec consumers have no machine-readable indication this is a resource identifier.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as unformatted strings prevent typed cross-resource relationships and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and tighten maxLength on account path parameter

findings.title: Sensitive PII fields (id_number, id_number_secondary, ssn_last_4) lack writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The fields `id_number`, `id_number_secondary`, and `ssn_last_4` accept government-issued identification numbers and Social Security Number digits. These are highly sensitive PII values. The schema does not mark them as `writeOnly: true`, meaning code-generation tools may include them in serialized response objects and documentation may not signal to consumers that these values are never returned in API responses. Marking them `writeOnly` is a standard OpenAPI 3.x mechanism to communicate this intent and reduce the risk of accidental logging or display of PII.
findings.rationale: Missing writeOnly on credential/PII fields is a risk finding; consumers and codegen tools may incorrectly treat these as readable response fields.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to id_number, id_number_secondary, and ssn_last_4 fields

findings.title: nationality field missing ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 pattern constraint despite documented format
findings.narration: The `nationality` field description states it accepts a two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code or the special value "XX". However, the schema only specifies `maxLength: 5000` and `type: string`, with no `pattern` constraint to enforce the expected format. This means any arbitrary string up to 5000 characters is accepted by schema validators, defeating the intent of the documented constraint. A pattern such as `^[A-Z]{2}$` (with allowance for "XX") would encode the rule formally and enable client-side validation.
findings.rationale: A prose-documented format constraint that is not encoded in the schema is a high-leverage finding; validators cannot enforce it and clients cannot rely on it.

value.description: The country where the person is a national. Two-letter country code ([ISO 3166-1 alpha-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1_alpha-2)), or "XX" if unavailable.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and correct maxLength for nationality to enforce ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 format

findings.title: POST returning HTTP 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new person resource and returns HTTP 200. REST convention and OpenAPI best practices indicate that a successful POST that creates a new resource should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. While Stripe consistently uses 200 across its API (a known design choice), it means clients relying on standard HTTP semantics to detect whether a resource was created vs. updated cannot distinguish the two cases from the status code alone. This is worth flagging as a design finding for the aggregator to track as a cross-cutting pattern.
findings.rationale: POST creating a new resource should return 201; returning 200 deviates from HTTP semantics and can confuse clients.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 for resource creation semantics

findings.title: Missing examples on complex request body with sensitive PII fields
findings.narration: The request body is complex, containing PII-sensitive fields (id_number, ssn_last_4), Japan-specific address variations, demographic data (us_cfpb_data), and nested verification documents. There are no examples provided at either the schema level or the media-type level. Examples are particularly valuable here to guide integrators on how to submit partial payloads (e.g., only relationship fields), how to use person tokens instead of raw PII, and what a minimal valid request looks like. Without examples, developers must infer the correct shape purely from field descriptions.
findings.rationale: Complex schemas with security-sensitive fields benefit greatly from examples to guide safe integration; their absence is a clarity gap.

with_pii_token.summary: Person creation using a Stripe.js PII token instead of raw ID number

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating minimal and PII-token-based person creation

findings.title: Path parameters `account` and `person` lack ID format/pattern constraints
findings.narration: Both `account` and `person` path parameters are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_...`) and person IDs follow `person_...`. Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client-side validation and SDK codegen cannot enforce correct resource ID shapes, increasing the risk of misrouted requests and unhelpful error messages. Adding a regex pattern (e.g., `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) would make the contract explicit and allow early rejection of malformed inputs.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no pattern/format are a documented anti-pattern in this review rubric and reduce the utility of the spec for codegen and validation tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID prefix patterns to `account` and `person` path parameters.

findings.title: GET operation includes an unnecessary empty request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`). RFC 7231 discourages request bodies on GET requests, and many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks drop or reject them. The presence of this body definition — even if never populated — can confuse SDK generators into emitting code that sends an unnecessary empty body, or cause issues with strict HTTP intermediaries. It should be removed entirely for a semantically clean GET.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty body definition adds noise and can cause codegen/tooling confusion.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Sensitive PII fields (id_number, ssn_last_4) lack writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The request body fields `id_number`, `id_number_secondary`, and `ssn_last_4` carry highly sensitive government-issued identity numbers (SSN, national ID, etc.). These fields are not marked `writeOnly: true`, which means documentation generators and SDK builders will treat them as readable response properties as well. Marking them `writeOnly: true` explicitly signals to tooling and consumers that these values are accepted on write but never echoed back, reducing accidental logging or caching of PII.
findings.rationale: Fields carrying government ID numbers, SSNs, or secondary ID numbers are classic `writeOnly` candidates. Omitting the flag increases risk of accidental PII exposure in generated clients and logs.
findings.patchSummary: Mark id_number, id_number_secondary, ssn_last_4 as writeOnly to prevent PII leakage in generated SDKs

findings.title: nationality field should enforce ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 pattern or maxLength 2
findings.narration: The `nationality` field description explicitly states it should be a two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (or the special value "XX"). However, the schema only sets `maxLength: 5000`, which gives no meaningful constraint. A `pattern` of `^[A-Z]{2}$` (with "XX" being valid) or at minimum `maxLength: 2` should be added so validators and code generators can enforce the documented invariant at the schema level rather than relying solely on prose.
findings.rationale: Documented format constraints that exist only in prose and not in schema are a missed validation opportunity and a source of integration bugs.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to nationality field to enforce ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 as documented

findings.title: person_token and direct PII fields are simultaneously accepted with no mutual-exclusion constraint
findings.narration: The description for `person_token` says it is used to 'securely provide details to the person', implying it is an alternative to submitting raw PII fields like `id_number`, `ssn_last_4`, `first_name`, `dob`, etc. directly. There is no schema-level constraint (e.g. `not`, `oneOf`, or `dependencies`) encoding this mutual exclusivity. Consumers cannot tell from the schema alone whether providing both `person_token` and `id_number` is valid, redundant, or an error. This conditional relationship lives only in prose and linked documentation.
findings.rationale: Conditional field relationships documented only in prose are a well-known API usability and correctness risk; the rule should be encoded in JSON Schema to be machine-enforceable.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual-exclusion between person_token and direct PII fields using JSON Schema not/dependencies

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body contains deeply nested objects (address, dob, verification, documents, us_cfpb_data, relationship, etc.) but no `examples` or `example` field is present at the media-type level or on individual properties. This makes it harder for API consumers, documentation generators, and test tools to understand valid payloads, especially for less obvious structures like `us_cfpb_data` (US CFPB demographic data) or `additional_tos_acceptances`.
findings.rationale: Complex multi-level request bodies without examples are a common source of integration confusion. Adding at least one top-level example significantly improves developer experience.

basic_update.summary: Update a person's name and date of birth

findings.patchSummary: Add at least one example to the request body to aid developer understanding of nested payload structure

findings.title: Path parameters typed as unconstrained strings with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Both `account` and `person` path parameters are typed as plain `string` with only a loose `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe account IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `acct_...`) and person IDs follow `person_...`. Without a `pattern` or `format`, codegen tools cannot build typed relationships, client SDKs cannot perform lightweight validation before sending the request, and documentation is less informative. Adding a regex pattern (e.g., `^acct_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` and `^person_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) would encode the real constraint directly in the schema.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain string with no format or pattern lose type-safety in codegen and prevent client-side pre-validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-format patterns and tighter maxLength to account and person path parameters.

findings.title: Reason field accepts arbitrary string instead of enforcing enum values
findings.narration: The `reason` field description explicitly states it can only be `fraud`, `terms_of_service`, or `other`, but the schema declares it as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. This means clients submitting invalid values like `'spam'` or `'abuse'` will only discover the constraint at runtime via an API error, rather than at the schema/codegen level. The allowed values should be encoded as an `enum` array so tooling can validate requests before they are sent and generate appropriate UI controls or typed enumerations.
findings.rationale: A constraint documented only in prose is not enforceable by validators or code generators. The enum is small and stable; encoding it in the schema eliminates a class of client bugs.
findings.patchSummary: Add enum constraint to reason field to enforce allowed values at schema level

findings.title: Account path parameter typed as unconstrained string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is a Stripe account ID (prefixed `acct_`) but is declared only as `type: string` with a `maxLength: 5000`. No `pattern` (e.g. `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or `format` hint is provided. This is a cross-resource reference typed as a plain string with no structural constraint, which prevents codegen tools from building a typed relationship to the Account resource and allows structurally invalid IDs to be passed without client-side feedback.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry enough schema information for tools to identify them as typed references. A pattern covering the known ID prefix eliminates a class of trivial client mistakes.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern to account path param to reflect Stripe acct_ ID format and tighten maxLength

findings.title: Missing minimum/maximum constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states that 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` encoded. This means clients can send `limit=0` or `limit=9999` without any schema-level validation hint, and the documented default of 10 is invisible to tooling. Validators and SDK generators cannot enforce the stated business rule without these constraints.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but not encoded in schema are a high-leverage issue; codegen tools cannot enforce them and clients may send invalid values.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty requestBody on a GET operation is extraneous
findings.narration: A GET request body with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false`, no properties) is defined but serves no purpose. HTTP GET semantics discourage request bodies, and many HTTP clients and intermediaries will drop or reject them. Its presence adds noise, may confuse SDK generators into expecting a body parameter, and signals a copy-paste artefact from a write-operation template.
findings.rationale: GET with a mandatory-form request body is contrary to HTTP semantics and will mislead SDK generators and documentation tools.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/apple_pay/domains

findings.title: Missing description on `domain_name` filter parameter
findings.narration: The `domain_name` query parameter has no `description` field at all. Because it is the primary filter for this list endpoint, its absence leaves consumers guessing whether it performs an exact match, a prefix search, or a substring match. All other parameters on this operation include descriptions; this one is conspicuously undocumented.
findings.rationale: A filter parameter with no description on a list endpoint is a clarity gap that affects how developers use the API.

patchOps.value: Filter results to only include domains whose domain name matches this value.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to domain_name query parameter

findings.title: domain_name field has no format, pattern, or maxLength constraint
findings.narration: The `domain_name` field in the request body is typed as a plain `string` with no `maxLength`, no `pattern`, and no `format`. Domain names have well-known structural constraints (e.g., RFC 1035: labels ≤63 chars, total ≤253 chars, alphanumeric + hyphens only). Without these constraints, clients receive no machine-readable guidance, and the API accepts obviously invalid inputs at the schema-validation layer before the server needs to reject them. Adding at least a `maxLength` and ideally a `pattern` (e.g., `^[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9\-\.]{1,251}[a-zA-Z0-9]$`) would improve both validation and codegen quality.
findings.rationale: Missing structural constraints on a resource identifier field reduces schema utility for client validation and code generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength:253 and a domain-name pattern to domain_name

findings.title: POST create endpoint returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new Apple Pay domain registration, which is a resource-creation operation. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource creation should respond with HTTP 201 Created. The spec currently only defines a 200 response. While Stripe's API historically returns 200 for creation endpoints, this is a deviation from standard REST semantics that surprises integrators and prevents HTTP middleware (e.g., caches, API gateways) from correctly identifying creation events. Documenting a 201 response (even if the server currently returns 200) or at minimum noting the non-standard choice in the description would clarify intent.
findings.rationale: Using 200 for resource creation deviates from RFC 9110 semantics; 201 is the correct status for created resources.
findings.patchSummary: Consider documenting 201 as the creation response status per HTTP semantics

findings.title: No description or example on domain_name property
findings.narration: The `domain_name` property in the request body schema has no `description` and no `example`. Callers have no schema-level guidance on what format is expected (FQDN? with or without subdomain? with or without trailing dot?), nor do they have an example to copy. This is particularly important for Apple Pay domain registration, where the exact domain format may affect verification outcome. Adding a short description (e.g., 'The fully qualified domain name to register for Apple Pay, e.g. shop.example.com') and an example value would materially improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: Required fields without descriptions or examples reduce clarity and increase integration errors.

patchOps.value: The fully qualified domain name to register with Apple Pay (e.g. shop.example.com).

findings.patchSummary: Add description and example to domain_name request body property

findings.title: Path parameter 'domain' has no format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The path parameter `domain` is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Apple Pay domain identifiers in Stripe follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `apwc_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, clients and code-generation tools cannot distinguish this identifier from a raw domain name string, leading to potential misuse or confusion. Adding a pattern like `^apwc_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would enable proper validation at the SDK and gateway layer.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern provide no machine-readable type relationship, hindering code generation and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'domain' path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET operation
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared on this GET operation with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per RFC 7231; many HTTP intermediaries, proxies, and clients will drop or reject a body on GET requests. The presence of this empty requestBody is at best noise and at worst will confuse code generators into emitting a body-bearing GET call. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET operations must not include a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). An empty body definition is misleading and can cause code-gen artifacts.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation — GET requests must not have a body

findings.title: charge parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern — cross-resource reference not encoded
findings.narration: The `charge` query parameter is described as 'the charge specified by this charge ID', meaning it holds a reference to a Charge resource. It is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. No `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^ch_`), and no `$ref` to a typed ID schema. Codegen tools and API clients cannot infer the relationship to the Charge resource, and input validation cannot check that the value looks like a valid charge ID. At minimum, a `pattern` such as `^ch_[0-9a-zA-Z]+$` should be added; ideally a shared `$ref` to a typed ChargeId schema.
findings.rationale: Fields named after resource IDs should encode the relationship; plain string with only maxLength provides no type-safety for codegen or validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `charge` parameter to encode the Charge resource ID format.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description of the `limit` parameter explicitly states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` keywords. Clients and validators cannot enforce this range without reading the prose, and auto-generated SDKs will accept out-of-range values silently. The schema should include `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, and `default: 10` to match the documented behaviour.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints that exist only in prose rather than in machine-readable schema keywords are high-severity because validators and codegen tools cannot act on them.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1, maximum: 100, default: 10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty form-encoded request body on a GET operation is unusual and noisy
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content carrying an empty object schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are technically allowed by HTTP but are discouraged by many proxies, gateways, and clients; several HTTP client libraries strip the body from GET requests silently. More importantly, the body is entirely empty — no properties are defined — so it provides no utility. All parameters are already expressed as query parameters. The requestBody declaration adds noise, may confuse SDK generators, and could cause interoperability problems.
findings.rationale: An empty request body on a GET operation is semantically vacuous and risks interoperability problems with proxies and clients that strip bodies from GET requests.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/application_fees operation.

findings.title: GET operation includes an unnecessary empty request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). While some frameworks tolerate this, many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will reject or ignore a body on a GET request. Codegen tools may also generate incorrect client code that attempts to send a body. The `requestBody` should be removed entirely from this operation.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate HTTP semantics and cause interoperability issues with clients, proxies, and code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Path parameters `fee` and `id` lack format or pattern constraints
findings.narration: Both `fee` and `id` path parameters are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe resource IDs follow well-known prefixed formats (e.g., `fee_` for application fees, `fr_` for fee refunds). Without a `pattern` or documented `format`, API clients and validators cannot distinguish a misplaced ID from a valid one, leading to confusing downstream errors. Adding a regex pattern (e.g., `^fee_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for `fee` and `^fr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for `id`) would enable early client-side validation and improve generated SDK type fidelity.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow accidental ID swaps.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to fee and id path parameters

findings.title: Path parameters `fee` and `id` typed as plain strings with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The path parameters `fee` (an application fee ID) and `id` (a refund ID) are typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe resource IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `fee_*`, `fr_*`). Without a `pattern` or at least a descriptive `format`, codegen tools cannot distinguish these from arbitrary strings, produce no typed wrappers, and cannot validate that callers are passing the correct resource-ID type. This is a cross-resource reference typed as a plain string.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings prevent SDK generators from creating typed wrappers and give no machine-readable hint about expected ID format.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to fee and id path parameters to indicate Stripe ID format.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx response definitions beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` error response. Common, predictable error conditions for this endpoint — such as `404 Not Found` (fee or refund does not exist), `400 Bad Request` (invalid metadata), or `401 Unauthorized` — are not individually documented. Consumers relying on the spec to understand which specific error codes to handle are forced to treat all errors as opaque. The `default` catch-all is useful as a fallback but should not be the sole error contract for an update operation.
findings.rationale: Omitting explicit 4xx status codes reduces clarity for API consumers and prevents SDK generators from producing typed error-handling code for predictable failure modes.

value.description: Bad request — e.g. invalid metadata keys or values.
The specified application fee or refund was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the existing default error response.

findings.title: Path ID parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter for the application fee resource is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe application fee IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `fee_...`). Without a `pattern` (e.g., `^fee_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at least a descriptive `format`, codegen tools and validators cannot distinguish this ID from an arbitrary string, weakening type safety and making it harder to detect routing errors.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent typed relationship modeling in generated clients and validators.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to the `id` path parameter to reflect Stripe's fee ID format.

findings.title: Empty form-encoded request body on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, but the schema is an empty object (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`), and the body is marked `required: false`. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). Many HTTP clients, intermediaries, and proxies discard or reject GET bodies. This empty requestBody adds noise, may confuse codegen tools, and should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET operations must not include a request body; it violates HTTP semantics and is silently ignored or rejected by many clients and proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: Empty operation description
findings.narration: The operation's `description` field is an empty string. There is no explanation of what this endpoint does — that it creates a refund for an application fee, what side effects it has, what the `directive` field means, or any constraints on the `amount`. Consumers reading the spec cannot understand the semantics without consulting external documentation.
findings.rationale: An empty description leaves clients without any context about the operation's purpose, behavior, or field semantics, reducing the spec's usefulness as standalone documentation.

patchOps.value: Refunds an application fee that has previously been collected but not yet refunded. Funds will be refunded to the Stripe account from which the fee was originally collected. You can optionally refund only part of an application fee by specifying an `amount`. If `amount` is omitted, the default is the full fee amount.

findings.patchSummary: Add meaningful description explaining the refund semantics and `amount` optionality.

findings.title: `directive` field is undocumented and has no description
findings.narration: The `directive` property in the request body has no `description` field at all. Its name is ambiguous — it is unclear whether this controls refund behavior, maps to an internal enum, or is a freeform string. Consumers cannot determine valid values or the effect of setting this field without reading external documentation.
findings.rationale: A field with no description and an opaque name such as `directive` is a clarity risk; codegen tools and API consumers will have no guidance on how or when to use it.

patchOps.value: An optional string that controls special refund behavior. Consult Stripe documentation for valid values.

findings.patchSummary: Add a description to the `directive` request body property.

findings.title: `amount` field missing constraints and description
findings.narration: The `amount` field accepts any integer with no minimum (e.g., 0 or negative values), no maximum relative to the original fee, and no description explaining that it represents the amount to refund in the smallest currency unit. Without a `minimum: 1` constraint and a description, clients can trivially submit nonsensical values and receive confusing errors from the server.
findings.rationale: Missing minimum constraint allows zero or negative integers which are semantically invalid for a refund amount. Missing description leaves the currency unit and relationship to the original fee amount unexplained.

patchOps.value: A positive integer, in the smallest currency unit, representing how much of this fee to refund. Can refund only up to the remaining unrefunded amount of the fee.

findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1 and a description to the `amount` field.

findings.title: Request body present on GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though HTTP GET requests must not carry a body per RFC 9110. Although the schema is an empty object (`properties: {}`), its presence is semantically incorrect and may confuse client generators, proxies, or middleware that reject body-carrying GET requests. The body should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP semantics. Including one, even an empty one, is incorrect and may cause compatibility issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Missing minimum/maximum constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. Clients and validators have no machine-readable enforcement of this range, making it possible to send values outside the documented bounds without schema-level rejection. Adding `minimum: 1` and `maximum: 100` encodes this constraint in the schema where validators and code generators can consume it.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints cannot be enforced by JSON Schema validators or SDK generators. Missing min/max on a limit parameter is a well-known high-impact omission.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 and maximum: 100 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: Response `url` field lacks format annotation
findings.narration: The `url` property in the `FeeRefundList` response schema is typed as `string` with a `maxLength` but no `format: uri`. Since the description explicitly states it is the URL where the list can be accessed, adding `format: uri` aligns the schema with its semantic meaning and enables client-side validation and typed representations in generated SDKs.
findings.rationale: A field semantically representing a URL should carry format: uri so tooling and validators can enforce its structure.
findings.patchSummary: Add format: uri to the url property in the FeeRefundList response schema.

findings.title: Refund amount field lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `amount` field is described as 'a positive integer' representing cents, but the schema has no `minimum` constraint to enforce the positivity requirement. A client could submit `amount: 0` or a negative integer and only discover the error at runtime. Adding `minimum: 1` encodes the documented invariant in the schema, enabling client-side validation and clearer codegen.
findings.rationale: Described constraint (positive integer) is not machine-encoded; clients and validators cannot enforce it without hitting the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 to amount field to enforce 'positive integer' constraint

findings.title: Missing `application_fee` resource-ID cross-reference on path parameter
findings.narration: The path parameter `id` references an application fee resource ID but is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. There is no `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^fee_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`), or description indicating the resource type it identifies. Codegen tools and SDK generators cannot infer a typed relationship to the application fee resource from this definition. Adding a description noting this is an application fee ID and optionally a pattern would improve discoverability and type safety.
findings.rationale: Resource-ID path parameters typed as bare strings without format, pattern, or description prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships.

patchOps.value: The identifier of the application fee to be refunded.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to path param `id` to clarify it is an application fee ID

findings.title: GET endpoint carries an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests must not include a message body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). Including a requestBody on a GET operation confuses HTTP clients, proxies, and generated SDKs, some of which will reject or ignore bodies on GET requests entirely. The body conveys no information here and should be removed.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 prohibits GET message bodies. The body schema is empty and adds no value while potentially breaking tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty GET request body

findings.title: scope.user field conditional requirement not machine-encoded
findings.narration: The `scope` parameter schema has a `type` enum with values `account` and `user`, and a `user` sub-field. The description states 'Requests originating from UI extensions can only access account-scoped secrets or secrets scoped to their own user', strongly implying that when `scope.type` is `user`, the `scope.user` field becomes required. This conditional constraint exists only in prose. JSON Schema `if/then` or `oneOf` constructs should encode this so validators, code generators, and documentation tools can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional required fields described only in prose cannot be validated programmatically; they should be encoded in the schema.
findings.patchSummary: Encode conditional requirement: scope.user required when scope.type is 'user'

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter clearly states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema specifies only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values. Without these constraints, clients can pass 0 or negative integers, or arbitrarily large values, and validation tools cannot catch them. The prose constraint should be encoded in the schema.
findings.rationale: Numeric constraints described in prose but absent from the schema cannot be enforced at validation time.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Secret payload transmitted as plaintext string without writeOnly marking
findings.narration: The `payload` field contains the plaintext secret value, yet it is not marked `writeOnly: true`. Without this flag, documentation generators, SDK generators, and logging middleware may treat the field as readable in responses, potentially exposing the secret value. OpenAPI 3.x provides `writeOnly` precisely to signal that a field is write-only and should never appear in responses. This is particularly important for secrets management endpoints where accidental exposure carries serious security implications.
findings.rationale: Sensitive credential fields should be marked writeOnly to prevent documentation tools and code generators from treating them as response-readable values.
findings.patchSummary: Mark payload field as writeOnly to prevent secret leakage via docs/codegen.

findings.title: scope.user field lacks description of when it is required
findings.narration: The `scope` object has a `type` enum of `account` or `user`, and a sibling `user` field. The description of the parent `scope` field mentions user-scoped secrets, but nowhere in the schema is it indicated that `user` is required when `scope.type` equals `user`. This conditional requirement exists only in prose (implied), not in the schema. Clients consuming this API via generated SDKs or schema validation will not know that omitting `user` when `type=user` is invalid, potentially causing runtime errors that could have been caught at schema validation time.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements that live only in prose (or are merely implied) should be encoded as JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependencies` to enable automated validation.

patchOps.value: The ID of the user to scope the secret to. Required when `type` is `user`; must be omitted when `type` is `account`.

findings.patchSummary: Encode conditional requirement: user field required when scope.type=user.

findings.title: POST creating/replacing a resource returns 200 instead of 201 for net-new secrets
findings.narration: The endpoint is documented as 'Create or replace a secret'. When a secret is created for the first time (rather than replaced), HTTP semantics prescribe a 201 Created response. Returning only 200 OK conflates creation and update, making it impossible for clients to distinguish whether a resource was newly created or an existing one was overwritten. While upsert endpoints sometimes deliberately use 200, the description explicitly calls out 'create' as a distinct operation type, and lacking a 201 path removes a useful semantic signal.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 Created is the correct status for resource creation; upsert endpoints should ideally return 201 on creation and 200 on replacement to allow clients to distinguish the two outcomes.

value.description: Secret successfully created.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 response for net-new secret creation to distinguish from 200 upsert.

findings.title: No example provided for the request body containing a sensitive payload field
findings.narration: The request body schema contains a `payload` field for storing plaintext secrets, a `scope` object, and an optional `expires_at`. Despite this being a security-sensitive and somewhat complex body, no examples are provided. Examples are especially important here to illustrate correct scoping (account vs. user), proper handling of `expires_at` as a Unix timestamp, and valid `name` conventions. Without examples, API consumers are more likely to misuse the endpoint, e.g., sending ISO-8601 dates instead of Unix timestamps for `expires_at`.
findings.rationale: Complex or security-sensitive request bodies benefit greatly from examples to prevent misuse, especially when fields like expires_at use non-obvious formats.

user_scoped_with_expiry.summary: Create a user-scoped secret with expiry

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating account-scoped and user-scoped secrets.

findings.title: DELETE semantic performed via POST with non-RESTful path suffix
findings.narration: This operation deletes a resource but uses HTTP POST on a path ending in `/delete` rather than HTTP DELETE on the resource path (e.g., `DELETE /v1/apps/secrets/{name}`). While Stripe's form-encoded API convention has historically used POST for mutations, this pattern is especially confusing for a destructive action because it breaks HTTP semantics: DELETE implies idempotency and cacheability contracts that POST does not. Clients and intermediaries (reverse proxies, audit logs) that inspect HTTP methods to classify requests as destructive cannot correctly identify this call. A `204 No Content` or `200` with the deleted object on `DELETE /v1/apps/secrets/{name}` would be more idiomatic and self-documenting.
findings.rationale: HTTP DELETE is the standard method for deletion. Using POST /…/delete prevents correct semantic classification by clients and middleware.
findings.patchSummary: Consider replacing POST /v1/apps/secrets/delete with DELETE /v1/apps/secrets/{name}.

findings.title: scope.user field lacks conditional-required encoding — rule expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `scope` object has a `type` field that can be `account` or `user`, and the description mentions scoping to a user. However, the `user` field (which should be required when `scope.type` is `user`) is not marked required anywhere — not even conditionally. This rule is implied by the description ('secrets scoped to their own user') but is not encoded in the schema using `if/then`, `oneOf`, or similar JSON Schema constructs. As a result, clients and validators cannot know that omitting `user` when `type` is `user` is an error, and code generators cannot model the relationship.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements documented only in prose are a high-leverage defect: they cannot be enforced by validators or understood by codegen tools.

value.description: Specifies the scoping of the secret. Requests originating from UI extensions can only access account-scoped secrets or secrets scoped to their own user.
value.title: scope_param

findings.patchSummary: Add if/then to require scope.user when scope.type is 'user'.

findings.title: Missing examples on request body for a non-trivial nested scope parameter
findings.narration: The request body contains a nested `scope` object with enum-driven behaviour, but no request body examples are provided. Without examples, consumers must infer how to construct the `scope` object for each type (`account` vs `user`) from the description alone. Adding at least two examples — one for `account` scope and one for `user` scope — would significantly improve developer experience and reduce integration errors.
findings.rationale: Complex nested objects with conditional semantics benefit strongly from concrete examples; absence makes integration harder.

account-scope.summary: Delete a secret scoped to the account

user-scope.summary: Delete a secret scoped to a specific user

findings.patchSummary: Add examples for account-scoped and user-scoped deletion requests.

findings.title: Conditional-required field 'scope.user' not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `scope` parameter description states that requests can be scoped to a specific user, implying `scope.user` is required when `scope.type` is `user`. However, this conditional requirement is expressed only in prose. The schema marks only `type` as required and leaves `user` as an optional string with no constraints. A JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependentRequired` construct should encode this rule so validators and code generators can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields documented only in prose are a high-leverage finding category: tooling cannot enforce the rule, leading to runtime errors that the schema should have caught at request validation time.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then to require `scope.user` when `scope.type` is `user`

findings.title: Secret name potentially sensitive value exposed in query string
findings.narration: The `name` parameter is transmitted as a URL query string parameter. Secret names in a secret store can themselves be sensitive or reveal information about the secrets being stored (e.g., `stripe_live_api_key`, `database_password`). Transmitting them in the query string means they appear in server access logs, browser history, and HTTP intermediary logs. A POST body or a path-encoded approach would be safer, but at minimum the spec should document this risk. As a GET request for a lookup this is a design trade-off, but the risk should be acknowledged.
findings.rationale: Sensitive identifiers in URLs are a risk finding; secret names in a secret-store endpoint may reveal the nature of secrets being accessed to anyone with log access.

patchOps.value: A name for the secret that's unique within the scope. **Note:** this value is transmitted as a URL query parameter and will appear in server access logs.

findings.patchSummary: Add log-exposure warning to `name` parameter description

findings.title: Empty requestBody on a GET operation is unnecessary
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type whose schema has no properties (`properties: {}`) and forbids additional properties (`additionalProperties: false`). This body can never carry any data and is semantically meaningless on a GET request (RFC 7231 discourages GET request bodies). Its presence may confuse SDK generators into emitting code that sends a body with GET requests, which some HTTP clients and proxies reject.
findings.rationale: An empty, non-functional requestBody on a GET operation is a design noise issue that can cause code-generation and interoperability problems.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, no-op requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: GET request carries an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, but the schema is an empty object (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests must not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1); many HTTP clients and intermediaries will strip or reject a body on a GET request. This body definition serves no purpose and may cause client-generation tools to emit incorrect code (e.g. setting a `Content-Type` header on a body-less request).
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 explicitly states a GET request has no defined semantics for a message body. The empty body adds noise and potential incompatibilities.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically incorrect requestBody from the GET /v1/balance operation.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema for the parameter only specifies `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` keywords. This means API clients and validators cannot enforce or discover the valid range without reading the prose description. Code generators will also not produce range-validated inputs, leading to runtime 400 errors that could have been caught client-side.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints stated in prose but not encoded in JSON Schema are a high-leverage finding; they cannot be enforced by validators or surfaced by SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: `type` filter should be an enum, not a free-form string
findings.narration: The `type` query parameter description enumerates roughly 50 specific accepted values (e.g., `charge`, `refund`, `payout`, `transfer`, etc.), but the schema is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Using a free-form string means SDK generators cannot produce type-safe enumerations, validation cannot be performed client-side, and documentation tools cannot display the permitted values as a structured list. The full enumeration should be expressed as a JSON Schema `enum` array.
findings.rationale: A field whose valid values are exhaustively listed in prose but not encoded as `enum` in schema prevents client-side validation and typed SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Replace free-form string with enum of documented valid `type` values

findings.title: Description references deprecated path, creating confusion about canonical endpoint
findings.narration: The operation description says: "Note that this endpoint was previously called 'Balance history' and used the path `/v1/balance/history`." However, this operation IS served at `/v1/balance/history`, so the note is self-contradictory and appears to be a copy-paste from the sibling endpoint at `/v1/balance_transactions`. The note implies the current path is the new canonical one, but readers hitting this endpoint will be confused about which path to use. The description should either be corrected to name the old path accurately or removed from this operation.
findings.rationale: A description that contradicts or misidentifies the endpoint it documents is a clarity bug; it likely indicates a copy-paste error from the canonical /v1/balance_transactions endpoint.

patchOps.value:
Returns a list of transactions that have contributed to the Stripe account balance (e.g., charges, transfers, and so forth). The transactions are returned in sorted order, with the most recent transactions appearing first.

Note that this endpoint is the legacy path /v1/balance/history. The canonical path is /v1/balance_transactions.

findings.patchSummary: Correct self-referential deprecation note to clarify legacy vs. canonical path

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint for balance transaction IDs
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000 but no `pattern` or `format` hint indicating it should match Stripe's balance transaction ID prefix (e.g., `txn_`). Stripe balance transaction IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern, and codegen tools or API clients cannot build a typed relationship or perform basic format validation without this information. Adding a pattern such as `^txn_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would enable client-side validation and improve documentation clarity.
findings.rationale: A cross-resource ID typed as a plain string with no format/pattern means codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship or enforce correct ID formats.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path param to reflect Stripe balance transaction ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests conventionally do not carry a body; including one here is semantically incorrect per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that a GET body has no defined semantics) and may confuse SDK generators, proxies, or API gateways that strip or reject GET bodies. The `requestBody` block should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: A GET endpoint with a request body contradicts HTTP semantics and can break SDK generators or intermediary proxies that discard GET bodies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET endpoint; GET requests should not carry a body.

findings.title: GET request carries an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type, but the schema is an empty object (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 notes that a payload body on a GET has no defined semantics). Many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks will either reject or silently drop a GET body. The `expand` parameter is already correctly represented as a query parameter, so the request body serves no purpose and should be removed.
findings.rationale: GET + request body violates HTTP semantics and causes interoperability issues with intermediaries and some clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty GET request body

findings.title: Conditional fields in payout schedule not encoded as schema constraints
findings.narration: The `payments.payouts.schedule` object has three fields: `interval`, `monthly_payout_days`, and `weekly_payout_days`. Based on standard Stripe API semantics and the enum values of `interval` (`daily`, `manual`, `monthly`, `weekly`), `monthly_payout_days` is only meaningful when `interval` is `monthly`, and `weekly_payout_days` is only meaningful when `interval` is `weekly`. These conditional-required / conditional-allowed relationships exist only implicitly through field naming; there are no `if/then/else` or `oneOf`/`not` constraints encoding them. Consumers relying on schema validation alone cannot detect invalid combinations like providing `monthly_payout_days` with `interval: weekly`.
findings.rationale: Conditional field relationships expressed only in naming conventions should be encoded as schema constraints so validators and codegen tools can enforce them.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then/else constraints to encode monthly/weekly_payout_days conditional requirements.

findings.title: Missing descriptions on nested schedule and settlement_timing fields
findings.narration: Several nested fields within `payments.payouts.schedule` (e.g., `interval`, `monthly_payout_days`, `weekly_payout_days`) and `payments.settlement_timing.delay_days_override` have no `description` property. Without descriptions, consumers have no guidance on what values are valid, their units (e.g., is `delay_days_override` in days? business days?), or the semantics of each interval type. This is especially important for an update endpoint where partial application of settings could have financial consequences.
findings.rationale: Fields with financial or scheduling implications should carry descriptions explaining valid values, units, and usage context.

patchOps.value: The frequency at which payouts are made. One of 'daily', 'manual', 'monthly', or 'weekly'.
Day(s) of the month on which payouts are made. Required when interval is 'monthly'.
Day(s) of the week on which payouts are made. Required when interval is 'weekly'.
Overrides the default settlement delay in calendar days. Pass an empty string to reset to the default.

findings.patchSummary: Add descriptions to interval, monthly_payout_days, weekly_payout_days, and delay_days_override.

findings.title: minimum_balance_by_currency uses open additionalProperties with no key constraints
findings.narration: The `payments.payouts.minimum_balance_by_currency` object uses `additionalProperties` typed as integer or empty-string, allowing any arbitrary currency code as a key. There is no description explaining that keys must be valid ISO 4217 currency codes, no `pattern` or `minLength`/`maxLength` on key names (OpenAPI 3.1 supports `propertyNames`), and no example showing a sample currency mapping. This leaves the schema effectively unconstrained and opaque to consumers.
findings.rationale: Currency-keyed maps should document that keys are ISO 4217 codes and ideally enforce this via propertyNames or a description with example.

patchOps.value: A map of ISO 4217 currency codes to minimum balance amounts (in the smallest currency unit). Pass an empty string value to clear the minimum for a given currency.

findings.patchSummary: Add description and example to minimum_balance_by_currency clarifying ISO 4217 key requirement.

findings.title: The `limit` parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. This means a client can pass `limit=0` or `limit=99999` and the constraint is enforced only server-side with no API-contract-level feedback. Tooling for client generation, validation middleware, and documentation renderers cannot surface this range to consumers.
findings.rationale: Undeclared numeric constraints cause generated clients to accept out-of-range values and documentation to omit the effective bounds, increasing integration errors.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: The `type` parameter should use an enum schema rather than free-form string
findings.narration: The `type` query parameter accepts one of a closed, well-known set of approximately 50 transaction type values, all of which are enumerated in the description prose. However, the schema is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. This means the contract does not enforce the closed set of valid values, losing the ability for generated clients to use typed enumerations, for validators to reject unknown values at the boundary, and for documentation tools to present a dropdown of options. The full enum list is already present in the description, making it trivial to migrate it to a schema-level enum.
findings.rationale: A closed vocabulary of string values documented in prose but not encoded as a schema enum prevents type-safe client generation and boundary validation.
findings.patchSummary: Replace free-form string schema on `type` parameter with an enum of valid transaction types

findings.title: Empty `requestBody` on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared on this GET operation with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests must not have a meaningful body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). Having a body declaration — even with `required: false` — confuses generated clients, some of which will attempt to serialize the body, and indicates a templating artifact rather than intentional design. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: A body on a GET endpoint violates HTTP semantics and causes code-generator and documentation confusion.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint for balance transaction IDs
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe balance transaction IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `txn_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client-side validation and codegen tools cannot distinguish this from any arbitrary string, missing an opportunity to catch obviously invalid IDs early and to generate typed client code that expresses the relationship to the balance transaction resource.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to id path parameter to match Stripe txn_ prefix format

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema is included on this GET operation. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that a payload body on a GET has no defined semantics). Including an empty body definition is misleading, may confuse some HTTP clients or proxies, and adds noise to generated SDKs. The `requestBody` block should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body per HTTP semantics; an empty body definition is misleading and may cause issues with some HTTP clients and code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only specifies `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values encoded. This means clients and validators cannot enforce the documented constraints programmatically, and codegen tools will produce unconstrained integer fields.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but not in schema cannot be machine-validated or surfaced in generated SDKs, leading to runtime errors when out-of-range values are submitted.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum=1, maximum=100, default=10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: meter filter parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `meter` query parameter is described as filtering to alerts associated with a given meter (a resource ID), but its schema is a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. There is no `pattern` (e.g. `^mtr_`) or `format` hint to communicate that this is a meter resource identifier rather than an arbitrary string. Codegen tools cannot build a typed foreign-key relationship from this.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent codegen tools from surfacing typed relationships and make it harder for API consumers to understand what value is expected.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern hint for meter resource ID format to the meter parameter schema

findings.title: Empty form-encoded request body on GET operation is unusual
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` containing an empty properties object, even though this is a GET list endpoint. GET requests with request bodies are semantically discouraged by HTTP specifications and many intermediaries (proxies, gateways) may strip or reject them. All inputs for this operation are already expressed as query parameters, making the request body redundant and potentially confusing to consumers.
findings.rationale: GET with a request body violates conventional HTTP semantics and may cause interoperability issues. The empty body provides no value and could mislead API consumers or codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty GET request body; all inputs are query parameters

findings.title: POST creates a resource but returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new billing alert, which is a resource-creation action. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource creation should respond with 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 200 makes it ambiguous to API consumers whether a new resource was created or an existing one was updated/retrieved. Many client libraries and API gateways also key on 201 to perform post-creation logic such as reading the Location header.
findings.rationale: HTTP semantics dictate 201 Created for successful POST resource creation. 200 implies the resource already existed or no creation occurred.
findings.patchSummary: Rename 200 response to 201 Created for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: Conditional requirement 'usage_threshold required when alert_type=usage_threshold' not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The request body has `alert_type` as a required field with the only allowed value being `usage_threshold`. However, the `usage_threshold` object — which is the configuration for that alert type — is not listed as required in the top-level schema. The relationship between `alert_type` and `usage_threshold` is implicit: if `alert_type` is `usage_threshold`, then `usage_threshold` must be provided. This conditional-required constraint exists only by implication and is not machine-readable. It should be encoded using JSON Schema `if/then` or `oneOf` constructs so validators and codegen tools can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements left as implicit coupling create runtime errors that could be caught at schema validation time. JSON Schema supports if/then for this pattern.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then to require usage_threshold object when alert_type=usage_threshold.

findings.title: usage_threshold.filters[].customer typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` field inside the `filters` array items is typed as a plain `string` with only `maxLength: 5000`. This field is clearly a reference to a Stripe Customer resource (IDs follow the `cus_*` prefix pattern), but there is no `pattern`, no `format`, and no `$ref` to communicate this. Codegen tools will treat it as an arbitrary string rather than a typed foreign key reference. At minimum, a pattern like `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` would communicate the resource relationship and enable client-side pre-validation.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or $ref break typed codegen and provide no guidance to API consumers on valid values.

patchOps.value: The ID of the customer to filter by. Must be a valid Stripe customer ID (e.g. cus_xxxxx). Required when type is 'customer'.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to customer field to identify it as a Stripe Customer resource ID.

findings.title: usage_threshold.filters[].customer conditional requirement not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `filters` array item has `type` as required and an enum of `["customer"]`, with `customer` (the customer ID string) as a sibling property. When `type` is `customer`, the `customer` field is presumably required — yet this is not expressed in the schema. The constraint is left purely implicit, meaning validators will not flag a filter item with `type: customer` and no `customer` value. An `if/then` or `dependencies` construct would make this machine-enforceable.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements left only to implicit coupling cannot be validated by schema validators or codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then to filter items requiring customer field when type=customer.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint for billing alert ID
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Billing alert IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `alrt_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK generators and validators have no way to enforce or document the expected identifier shape. This can lead to silent misuse — e.g., passing a charge ID or customer ID where a billing alert ID is expected — with errors only surfacing at runtime.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID typed as plain string without pattern/format is a well-known codegen and validation gap per the review guidelines.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter to enforce billing alert ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET operation
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests semantically must not include a body; many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will discard or reject a body on GET requests. This empty body definition is at best misleading and at worst will cause tooling to generate unnecessary body-serialization logic for a no-op payload. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests carrying a request body violate HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). Even when marked optional and empty, the declaration is misleading and harmful to codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect empty requestBody from GET operation.

findings.title: No explicit 404 response defined for missing billing alert
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a generic `default` error response. The most predictable and actionable error for a resource-fetch-by-ID endpoint is a `404 Not Found` — when the requested billing alert does not exist or belongs to a different account. Relying solely on `default` for this case means API consumers cannot easily distinguish a not-found condition from other errors (rate limits, auth failures, server errors) without inspecting the error body at runtime. Explicitly documenting `404` improves client code clarity and generated SDK error handling.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses on a GET-by-ID endpoint is a common design gap; `404` is the canonical response for a non-existent resource and should be explicitly enumerated.

value.description: The requested billing alert was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 404 response for billing alert not found.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe billing alert IDs have a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `alrt_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, SDK generators and validators cannot validate or type the reference correctly, and clients may pass arbitrary strings silently.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format so generated clients can validate input before making a network call.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter to reflect known Stripe alert ID format.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Billing alert IDs in Stripe follow a predictable prefix pattern (e.g., `alrt_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK code generators and validators have no way to distinguish this ID from an arbitrary string. Adding a regex pattern such as `^alrt_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` would make the constraint machine-readable and improve both documentation clarity and generated client safety.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent typed relationship building in codegen tools and offer no input validation guidance.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error responses defined beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error response. Callers have no machine-readable indication of specific HTTP error semantics — for instance, `404 Not Found` when the alert ID does not exist, `400 Bad Request` for invalid input, or `409 Conflict` if the alert is already archived. Relying solely on a `default` bucket makes it impossible for tooling or client libraries to branch on specific error codes, reducing the usability of auto-generated SDKs and documentation.
findings.rationale: Specific 4xx response codes allow tooling and consumers to handle known error conditions explicitly; a lone `default` provides no discriminability.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint

Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client-side validation and codegen tools cannot distinguish this ID from an arbitrary free-form string. A regex such as `^balrt_[0-9a-zA-Z]+$` or a documented example would substantially improve usability and catch obvious misuse early.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without pattern or format are a documented anti-pattern that prevents typed relationship generation in codegen tools.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response codes defined
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` and a catch-all `default` error response. For an action endpoint like deactivation, specific HTTP error codes such as `404` (alert not found), `400` (bad request / already deactivated), and `403` (insufficient permissions) are highly likely and actionable by API consumers. Relying solely on `default` means clients cannot distinguish between recoverable and non-recoverable error states without inspecting the response body. Documenting at least `404` and `400` as distinct responses improves both clarity and client resilience.
findings.rationale: Missing 4xx response definitions is a documented per-operation design finding. An action endpoint acting on a resource identified by ID should at minimum document 404.

findings.title: Exactly-one-of rule between `customer` and `customer_account` encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The two query parameters `customer` and `customer_account` both identify the same logical entity (the customer whose balance is retrieved) but are both marked `required: false` with no schema-level constraint enforcing that exactly one must be supplied. The description text for each parameter implies mutual exclusivity or at least that one of them is required, yet neither the parameter-level schemas nor any enclosing schema uses `oneOf`, `not`, or `if/then/else` to formalise that rule. Client SDKs generated from this spec can call the endpoint with neither parameter, or with both, and pass validation.
findings.rationale: A conditional-required field relationship expressed only in prose is a high-severity issue because code-generation and validation tools cannot enforce it automatically.

patchOps.value: The customer whose credit balance summary you're retrieving. Exactly one of `customer` or `customer_account` must be provided.
