findings.patchSummary: Clarify mutual-exclusivity/exactly-one rule in descriptions (full encoding requires a wrapper schema)

findings.title: Conditional field rule inside `filter` expressed only in prose: `applicability_scope` vs `credit_grant` depends on `type`
findings.narration: The `filter` parameter schema has a discriminator field `type` whose value (`applicability_scope` or `credit_grant`) determines which sibling field should be present. When `type` is `applicability_scope`, the `applicability_scope` sub-object is expected; when `type` is `credit_grant`, the `credit_grant` string ID is expected. Neither rule is encoded in the schema — both `applicability_scope` and `credit_grant` are optional properties with no `oneOf`/`if-then` guard. A client could send `type: credit_grant` with the `applicability_scope` object (or neither), and the schema would pass validation.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements driven by a discriminator field must be encoded in the schema to be machine-enforceable; prose alone is insufficient for SDK generation and linting.
findings.patchSummary: Encode `type` discriminator as oneOf branches requiring the matching sibling field

findings.title: `customer` and `credit_grant` filter field are plain strings with no format or pattern hinting at resource ID type
findings.narration: The `customer` query parameter and the `credit_grant` field inside the `filter` schema are both typed as bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. These are well-known Stripe resource identifiers (`cus_…` and `cgrt_…` prefixes respectively). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a `format` annotation (e.g. `format: "stripe-resource-id"` or a regex), SDK generators cannot build a typed cross-resource reference and validation tools cannot catch a misplaced ID.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no pattern or format prevent code-generation tools from building typed cross-resource relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add resource-ID patterns to `customer` and `customer_account` parameters

findings.title: Response `url` pattern does not match the endpoint's own path
findings.narration: The `url` field in the 200 response schema has `pattern: "^/v1/billing/credit_grants"`, but the endpoint is `/v1/billing/credit_balance_transactions`. This looks like a copy-paste error from a related credit_grants list endpoint. Consumers relying on this pattern for validation or code generation will be misled about the canonical URL of this list resource.
findings.rationale: Pattern mismatch between the described URL and the actual resource path indicates a copy-paste bug that could confuse SDK generators and API clients.
findings.patchSummary: Fix url pattern to match the actual endpoint path instead of credit_grants.

findings.title: `credit_grant` and `customer`/`customer_account` filter parameters lack ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `credit_grant`, `customer`, and `customer_account` query parameters are typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. These are clearly resource ID references (Stripe IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern, e.g. `cgrt_…`, `cus_…`, `acct_…`). Without a `pattern` constraint or documented `format`, codegen tools cannot build typed cross-resource references, and clients cannot validate inputs before sending. At minimum, a `pattern` like `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` should be applied to `customer` to communicate the expected shape.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings without pattern/format prevent typed codegen relationships and remove client-side validation opportunities.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID patterns to credit_grant and customer filter params for typed codegen and validation.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states "Limit can range between 1 and 100", but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum`. This means the prose documents a constraint that is not machine-readable or enforced at the schema level. Clients and validators cannot catch out-of-range values without parsing the prose description.
findings.rationale: Numeric range constraints documented only in prose should be encoded as minimum/maximum in the JSON Schema to be enforceable and machine-readable.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1 and maximum:100 to the limit parameter schema to match its prose description.

findings.title: GET endpoint includes an unnecessary empty request body
findings.narration: This GET operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema containing no properties. GET requests should never carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 discourages it, and many HTTP clients/proxies strip or reject bodies on GET requests). An empty, optional request body on a read endpoint is dead weight and can confuse clients and code generators.
findings.rationale: GET requests are not expected to carry a body. An empty request body adds noise, may confuse codegen tools, and signals a copy-paste issue from a POST/PUT template.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path ID parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter for this credit balance transaction lookup is typed as `type: string` with only a loose `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe resource IDs for billing credit balance transactions follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cbtxn_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, tooling cannot validate the identifier format, and documentation consumers receive no signal about the expected shape of the ID. A regex pattern like `^cbtxn_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at least a realistic `maxLength` (Stripe IDs are typically under 255 characters) would dramatically improve both safety and clarity.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters typed as unconstrained strings miss an opportunity for format validation and hinder typed client generation. The maxLength of 5000 is far beyond any real Stripe ID.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten id parameter: reduce maxLength to 255 and add a pattern for cbtxn_ prefix.

findings.title: customer and customer_account cross-field constraint expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The parameters `customer` and `customer_account` both serve as filters to narrow results to a specific customer identity, but through different identifier types (customer ID vs. account ID). The descriptions imply they represent mutually exclusive ways to identify the same customer context, yet no schema-level constraint (e.g., a `oneOf`, `not`, or parameter-level note about mutual exclusivity) is present. If passing both simultaneously is invalid or has undefined behavior, API consumers and code generators have no machine-readable signal to enforce the constraint. This is a classic 'field relationship rule in prose only' pattern.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required or mutually-exclusive field relationships that exist only in description text cannot be validated by tools or SDKs, increasing the risk of erroneous API calls.

patchOps.value: Only return credit grants for this customer. Mutually exclusive with `customer_account`; pass at most one of the two.
Only return credit grants for this account representing the customer. Mutually exclusive with `customer`; pass at most one of the two.

findings.patchSummary: Document mutual exclusivity of customer vs customer_account in both parameter descriptions.

findings.title: customer and customer_account typed as plain string without ID format or pattern
findings.narration: Both `customer` (a Stripe customer ID, typically prefixed `cus_`) and `customer_account` (a Stripe account ID, typically prefixed `acct_`) are declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a typed ID schema is present. Code generation tools treat these as arbitrary strings, losing the semantic relationship to the Customer and Account resources. Adding a pattern (e.g., `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for customer) would both document intent and enable client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent SDK generators from building typed references and allow invalid IDs to pass client-side validation silently.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer and customer_account parameter schemas.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` fields. Consumers relying on the schema alone (e.g., auto-generated forms, validators) will not enforce these bounds, potentially sending out-of-range values that the server will reject. The constraint exists only in prose.
findings.rationale: Numeric bounds stated in prose but absent from schema allow client tools to send invalid values without validation feedback.
findings.patchSummary: Encode limit's minimum (1), maximum (100), and default (10) in schema.

findings.title: POST returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This operation creates a new credit grant resource, which is a canonical resource-creation action. By REST convention and HTTP semantics, a successful creation should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 200 is misleading to clients, API consumers, and code generators, which typically use the response status code to determine whether a resource was created versus merely updated or fetched. Stripe's own newer APIs (e.g. Payment Intents) sometimes exhibit this same pattern, but it remains a design deficiency worth noting.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 specifies 201 Created for successful POST requests that result in a new resource. Using 200 reduces the semantic clarity of the API.

value.description: Credit grant created.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response alongside existing 200 to reflect resource creation semantics

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `customer` and `customer_account` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The request body exposes two fields — `customer` (ID of the customer) and `customer_account` (ID of the account representing the customer) — that are semantically alternative ways to identify the recipient. In practice, callers should supply exactly one of these, but neither field is marked `required`, and the schema imposes no `oneOf`, `not`, or `if/then/else` constraint to enforce mutual exclusivity or require at least one. This means the schema silently accepts requests that supply both fields or neither field, pushing validation into server-side logic without surfacing the rule to tooling, documentation generators, or clients.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually-exclusive relationships expressed only in prose (or implied by field names) should be encoded as JSON Schema `oneOf` or `dependencies` so validators and codegen tools can enforce them.
findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf constraint to require exactly one of `customer` or `customer_account`

findings.title: `customer` and `customer_account` ID fields lack type format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` field (described as 'ID of the customer') and `customer_account` field (described as 'ID of the account representing the customer') are typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_*`) and account IDs follow `acct_*`. Without a `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a typed ID schema, code generators cannot build a typed relationship between this field and the Customer or Account resource, and validators cannot catch obviously malformed IDs at the schema layer.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain string without pattern or format prevent typed codegen relationships and early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to `customer` and `customer_account` to express Stripe ID format

findings.title: `priority` field lacks minimum/maximum constraints despite prose bounds
findings.narration: The `priority` field description states explicitly: 'The highest priority is 0 and the lowest is 100.' However, the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum: 0` or `maximum: 100` constraint. Any integer outside this range would pass schema validation and fail only at the server side. Encoding the range in the schema makes the valid range discoverable by tooling, documentation generators, and client-side validators without a server round-trip.
findings.rationale: Numeric bounds stated in prose should be encoded as JSON Schema `minimum`/`maximum` to enable client-side validation and improve tooling support.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:0 and maximum:100 to `priority` to match prose-stated bounds

findings.title: expires_at accepts empty string to clear value — conditional semantics undocumented in schema
findings.narration: The `expires_at` field uses an `anyOf` of an integer (unix-time) and an empty-string literal (`""`). The description says "If set to empty, the billing credits never expire", but the schema does not encode what "set to empty" means formally (i.e., this is a Stripe convention for unsetting a nullable timestamp via form-encoded bodies). Consumers relying on code generation will see this as a union of integer and a string whose only valid value is `""`, without understanding the semantic. A `description` annotation directly on each branch (or a top-level note explaining the Stripe "clear" convention) would prevent misuse.
findings.rationale: Conditional field semantics expressed only in prose rather than encoded in schema comments or branch-level descriptions reduce clarity for codegen and API consumers.

patchOps.value: Pass an empty string to remove the expiration, making the credits never expire.

findings.patchSummary: Add branch-level description to the empty-string variant of expires_at to clarify its 'clear' semantics.

findings.title: No 4xx response codes defined — only 200 and default
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error response. While `default` technically covers all error status codes, best practice (and many tooling expectations) require explicit 4xx entries — at minimum `400` (bad request / validation) and `404` (credit grant not found). Without explicit entries, documentation renderers and client SDKs cannot describe the distinct error shapes or HTTP semantics for common failure modes such as passing an invalid `expires_at` value or referencing a non-existent credit grant ID.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses reduces clarity for consumers and limits the usefulness of generated client code and documentation.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions to improve documentation and client SDK clarity.

findings.title: Conditional field 'cancel' required when type='cancel' but not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `cancel` object field is semantically required whenever `type` is set to `'cancel'`, yet this relationship is expressed only implicitly (the field name mirrors the only enum value). There is no JSON Schema `if/then`, `oneOf`, or `dependencies` construct to enforce that `cancel` must be present when `type` equals `'cancel'`. Consumers relying on schema validation alone will not receive a validation error if they omit the `cancel` object, leading to a runtime API error instead of a client-side schema violation. The description of `type` also hints at future values ('Time period cancellation is not supported yet'), making this coupling more important to document formally now.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required field relationships expressed only in prose (or inferred from naming) should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints to enable codegen, validation, and documentation tools to surface them.

findings.title: Missing 'identifier' required constraint inside 'cancel' object
findings.narration: The `cancel` object has a single property `identifier`, which is the event identifier to cancel. The description implies this is the mechanism by which a specific event is targeted, yet `identifier` is not marked as `required` within the `cancel` object. Submitting a `cancel` object without `identifier` would either silently fail or return a runtime API error. Clients and codegen tools have no schema-level signal that `identifier` must be provided.
findings.rationale: A nested object with a single meaningful field that drives the operation's behaviour should enforce that field as required, or the schema provides no useful constraint.
findings.patchSummary: Mark 'identifier' as required inside the 'cancel' object schema

findings.title: No request body example provided for a non-trivial multi-field POST
findings.narration: The request body schema has multiple fields with a conditional relationship between `type` and `cancel`, yet no example is provided in the schema or encoding. Developers looking at this operation in generated documentation or tooling have no concrete illustration of what a valid payload looks like. An example showing `event_name`, `type: 'cancel'`, and a `cancel.identifier` would greatly reduce integration friction and clarify the conditional relationship at a glance.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies with conditional field requirements benefit from at least one inline example to guide consumers and validate tooling.

findings.title: POST returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new billing meter event (a new resource), but the success response is defined as HTTP 200. Per HTTP semantics and REST conventions, a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created. Using 200 conflates creation with retrieval/update responses, making it harder for clients to distinguish between different operation outcomes. This is a particularly important signal for idempotency-aware clients and intermediate infrastructure.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 §6.3.2 specifies 201 Created for successful resource creation. POST endpoints that create resources should use 201.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response from 200 to 201 Created for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: timestamp constraints (35-day past / 5-minute future window) not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `timestamp` field description states it must be "within the past 35 calendar days or up to 5 minutes in the future", but the schema has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints to enforce this. This means client-side validation tools, SDK generators, and API gateways cannot enforce these bounds automatically. Callers will only discover the constraint at runtime via a server error, which is a poor developer experience and a source of hard-to-debug bugs. While dynamic bounds (relative to 'now') cannot be fully expressed in static JSON Schema, a prose note alongside a relative-constraint marker or at minimum a documentation example would help; ideally, the server's documented constraint should at least be surfaced as a format note in the schema rather than exclusively in the description string.
findings.rationale: Operational constraints expressed only in prose description rather than schema keywords cause silent validation failures in generated clients and SDKs.

patchOps.value: Dynamic range: must be within the past 35 calendar days or up to 5 minutes in the future relative to the server's current time. Static min/max cannot be encoded here.

findings.patchSummary: Add x-constraint-note to timestamp field to surface its dynamic range constraint to tooling.

findings.title: identifier field should declare UUID-like format or pattern
findings.narration: The description of `identifier` states 'We recommend using UUID-like identifiers', but the schema only constrains `maxLength: 100` with `type: string`. There is no `format: uuid` or `pattern` to guide SDK generators or validation tooling. As a result, generated client code cannot enforce the recommended format, leading to accidental misuse. Even if the server accepts non-UUID values, providing a pattern or format helps developers understand the expected structure and enables linting tools to flag obvious mismatches early.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource and idempotency key fields typed as plain string without format/pattern prevent codegen tools from building properly typed or validated client code.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern to the identifier field to encode its recommended UUID-like format constraint.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema defines only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. This means client tooling and validators cannot enforce the documented range, allowing callers to send values like 0 or 999 without schema-level rejection.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints should encode documented business rules so validators and code-generation tools can enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Superfluous empty request body on GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema that has no properties and `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests with a body are semantically unusual (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers strip or reject bodies on GET requests. The empty body carries no information and may cause interoperability issues.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty body definition adds noise and potential client-compatibility issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/billing/meters operation

findings.title: POST resource-creation endpoint returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new billing meter resource, which is a canonical resource-creation operation. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110), a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 200 obscures the fact that a new resource was created and makes it harder for clients to distinguish creation from update operations. The `default` error response is defined, but the success response uses the wrong status code.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for successful resource creation. Using 200 for POST-based creation violates HTTP semantics and reduces API clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response from 200 to 201 Created for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: Missing request body examples for complex nested schema
findings.narration: The request body contains several nested objects (`customer_mapping`, `default_aggregation`, `value_settings`) with non-obvious field relationships and enum constraints. There are no examples provided at the schema or media-type level. Without examples, API consumers and code-generation tools must infer correct usage from field descriptions alone. An example showing a minimal valid request (with all required fields) and optionally a more complete request (with `customer_mapping` and `value_settings`) would significantly improve usability.
findings.rationale: Complex nested request schemas with enum constraints and multiple required fields benefit greatly from concrete examples for developer comprehension and codegen tooling.

findings.title: Conditional relationship between `value_settings` and `default_aggregation.formula` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `value_settings` object, which specifies the event payload key for numeric value extraction, is logically only meaningful when `default_aggregation.formula` is `sum` or `last` (since `count` does not use a value field). This conditional requirement is not expressed in the schema — neither as a `oneOf`/`if-then-else` construct nor in any description text. Clients using `count` formula could supply `value_settings` unnecessarily, or conversely, omit it when using `sum`, and the schema provides no guidance. This field-relationship rule should be encoded or at minimum documented in descriptions.
findings.rationale: Conditional field relationships that exist only implicitly in business logic but are absent from schema or descriptions create integration errors and unclear validation behavior.

findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Billing meter IDs in Stripe follow a predictable prefix pattern (e.g., `mtr_*`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a documented `format`, codegen tools and API clients cannot validate or type the relationship between this path parameter and the billing meter resource. This also makes it harder to catch accidental use of IDs from other resource types (e.g., customer IDs, invoice IDs) passed to this endpoint.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without format/pattern constraints reduce type safety and make generated SDKs weaker.

GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks will silently discard or reject a body on a GET request. The presence of this empty body, even marked `required: false`, is misleading and may cause interoperability problems with strict HTTP implementations. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate HTTP semantics and can cause interoperability issues with proxies, gateways, and client libraries.

Adding a pattern such as `^mtr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow early validation and improve codegen fidelity.

The catch-all `default` entry documents that errors exist but does not guide client developers on which specific error codes to handle or what discriminated schema to expect per status code. Enumerating at least `400` and `404` would significantly improve API usability and allow clients to implement targeted error-handling logic without reading external documentation.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx response definitions reduce clarity for API consumers and prevent tools from generating typed error handlers.

findings.title: Missing example on expand parameter
findings.narration: The `expand` array parameter has no example illustrating which fields can be expanded. For Stripe's API, the `expand` mechanism is non-obvious to new consumers — without an example, callers cannot easily discover valid expansion paths for billing meter objects (e.g., `['event_name']`). findings.patchSummary: Add example value for the expand array property on the deactivate request body.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint for meter IDs
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe meter IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `mtr_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `format`, codegen tools and validators cannot enforce or communicate the expected shape of the identifier, increasing the risk of callers passing incorrect resource IDs (e.g., a price ID instead of a meter ID) without receiving a clear client-side validation error.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as unadorned strings make it impossible for generated SDKs to create typed relationships or validate ID format at the client layer.

patchOps.value: The unique identifier of the billing meter to deactivate. Must be a valid meter ID (e.g., mtr_...).

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to the `id` path parameter to communicate expected meter ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body on GET list endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body; HTTP semantics for GET do not define body semantics, many proxies and HTTP clients strip it, and it provides no value here since all query parameters are already declared as query/path parameters. The body should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a request body are semantically incorrect per RFC 9110. Including it creates confusion for consumers and SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty request body from the GET operation

findings.title: customer parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` query parameter is a required reference to a customer resource (Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern, e.g. `cus_...`). It is typed as a plain `type: string` with only `maxLength: 5000`, providing no machine-readable indication that this is a resource identifier. Adding a `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]{16,}$`) or at least a descriptive `format` such as `customer-id` would allow codegen tools to build typed relationships and enable basic validation at the client side before a round-trip to the API.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with no format or pattern prevent tooling from inferring cross-resource relationships and allow clearly invalid values to pass client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the customer parameter to identify it as a typed resource ID

findings.title: value_grouping_window boundary constraints expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `value_grouping_window` states that when `hour` is chosen, `start_time`/`end_time` must align with hour boundaries, and when `day` is chosen they must align with UTC day boundaries. These conditional constraints are documented only in the parameter description as prose. This is a machine-unenforceable rule that could be at least partially encoded via schema annotations or an `if/then` in the request schema. At minimum, this cross-parameter relationship should be flagged so API client authors know that misaligned timestamps will result in API errors, and ideally the spec should encode it formally.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required or conditional-constraint rules expressed only in prose cannot be validated by tooling and will silently pass schema validation with invalid combinations.

patchOps.value: When 'hour', start_time and end_time must align with hour boundaries. When 'day', they must align with UTC midnight boundaries. These constraints cannot be fully expressed in JSON Schema but should be validated server-side and documented prominently.

findings.patchSummary: Annotate value_grouping_window with a machine-readable constraint note for the boundary alignment rules

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values. Clients and validation tools have no way to enforce this constraint without relying solely on the prose description. Values outside [1, 100] will only be rejected at runtime by the server rather than caught early in SDK validation layers.
findings.rationale: Missing minimum/maximum on a bounded integer parameter means client-side validators and code generators cannot enforce the documented constraint.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, and default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Missing minimum/maximum constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties. This means client-side validation cannot enforce the documented range, and code generators cannot surface these constraints in generated SDKs.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints (1–100, default 10) must be encoded in the schema to be machine-enforceable and usable by validators and code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 constraints to `limit` schema

findings.title: POST /v1/billing_portal/configurations returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new billing portal configuration — a resource creation operation. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110), a successful POST that creates a new resource should return 201 Created, not 200 OK. The response currently declares only `200`. While Stripe has historically used 200 for creation endpoints, this deviates from standard REST semantics and can confuse client code generators and API consumers who expect 201 on creation.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the standard status code for successful resource creation via POST. Using 200 conflates creation with retrieval and breaks conventional REST client expectations.

value.description: Configuration created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response alongside existing 200 to align with HTTP creation semantics.

findings.title: Typo in default_return_url description: 'overriden' should be 'overridden'
findings.narration: The description for `default_return_url` contains a typo: 'overriden' should be 'overridden' (double 'd'). While minor, this reduces the perceived quality of the API documentation and may cause confusion for developers reading it carefully.
findings.rationale: Typos in public API documentation reduce developer confidence and documentation quality.

patchOps.value: The default URL to redirect customers to when they click on the portal's link to return to your website. This can be [overridden](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customer_portal/sessions/create#create_portal_session-return_url) when creating the session.

findings.patchSummary: Fix typo: 'overriden' → 'overridden' in default_return_url description.

findings.title: features.subscription_update.products[].product typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `product` field inside `features.subscription_update.products[]` is a reference to a Stripe Product resource ID (e.g., `prod_XXXX`), but is declared only as `type: string` with a `maxLength` constraint and no `format`, `pattern`, or semantic annotation. Code generation tools cannot infer the cross-resource relationship, making it impossible to build typed SDK wrappers. The same concern applies to `features.payment_method_update.payment_method_configuration`, which references a PaymentMethodConfiguration ID.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent code generators from building typed cross-resource references, degrading SDK quality.

patchOps.value: The Stripe Product ID (e.g., prod_XXXX) to associate with this portal subscription update option.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to product ID field to signal it is a cross-resource reference.

findings.title: No examples provided for the complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body for this endpoint is deeply nested (features with sub-features like subscription_cancel, subscription_update with products and schedule_at_period_end conditions, etc.). There are no `examples` or `example` annotations anywhere in the request schema. Without examples, developers must reverse-engineer the full request structure from schema alone, significantly increasing integration friction for a non-trivial endpoint.
findings.rationale: Complex nested request bodies without examples are harder to integrate correctly. Examples serve as both documentation and as input to mock servers and code generators.

basic_configuration.summary: Minimal configuration with invoice history enabled

full_configuration.summary: Configuration with subscription update and cancel features

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating minimal and full portal configuration payloads.

findings.title: GET operation includes an empty request body definition
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. HTTP GET requests should not carry a request body — many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will ignore or reject a body on GET requests. Having this definition is semantically incorrect and can confuse code-generation tools into emitting a body parameter for what should be a pure read-only retrieval.
findings.rationale: Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110), GET requests MUST NOT include a message body that affects server behavior. An empty request body definition adds noise and contradicts the read-only nature of this operation.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Path parameter `configuration` lacks a format or pattern hint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `configuration` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe billing portal configuration IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `bpc_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK generators and validators cannot distinguish this ID from arbitrary strings, reducing type safety and making it harder to catch obviously wrong values early.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string with no pattern or format are a known low-leverage issue for codegen and validation toolchains. A pattern like `^bpc_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode the constraint explicitly.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to configuration path parameter schema

findings.title: Typo in `default_return_url` description: 'overriden' should be 'overridden'
findings.narration: The description for `default_return_url` contains a spelling error: 'overriden' should be 'overridden'. While minor, this appears in customer-facing documentation and API reference pages.
findings.rationale: Typo in a published API description field; low severity but worth correcting for professionalism.

patchOps.value: The default URL to redirect customers to when they click on the portal's link to return to your website. This can be [overridden](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customer_portal/sessions/create#create_portal_session-return_url) when creating the session.

findings.patchSummary: Fix typo: 'overriden' → 'overridden' in default_return_url description

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain `string` without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that are clearly Stripe resource identifiers — `configuration` (path param), `features.subscription_update.products[].product` and `features.subscription_update.products[].prices[]`, and `features.payment_method_update.payment_method_configuration` — are declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^(prod_|price_|pmc_)[A-Za-z0-9]+$`), or description is provided. This prevents codegen tools from building typed cross-resource relationships and makes validation looser than necessary.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as bare strings without pattern or format make it impossible for client generators to produce typed resource references.

patchOps.value: The ID of the billing portal configuration to update (e.g. bpc_...).
The Stripe product ID (e.g. prod_...) to allow updates for.

findings.patchSummary: Add descriptions/patterns to resource ID fields (configuration, product, prices, payment_method_configuration)

findings.title: No 4xx client-error response definitions
findings.narration: The operation defines a `200` success response and a `default` catch-all error response, but no explicit 4xx responses (e.g. 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found) are declared. For an update operation on a resource identified by path parameter `{configuration}`, a 404 when the configuration does not exist and a 400 for invalid input are both common and important for API consumers to handle correctly. The `default` response covers these technically, but clients cannot distinguish error types at the schema level without explicit status codes.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses prevent API consumers and generated clients from applying status-code-specific error handling logic.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.
Configuration not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default catch-all

findings.title: Missing 'required' constraint on 'customer' field — conditional requirement documented only in prose
findings.narration: The 'customer' field has no 'required' marker at the schema level. The API documentation implies a customer identifier is needed to create a portal session, yet neither 'customer' nor 'customer_account' is marked required in the schema. The description for each field gives no hint that exactly one of the two must be supplied. This means code-generation and validation tooling will treat both as fully optional, allowing requests to be sent with neither field populated — which the API will likely reject at runtime. The conditional 'exactly one of customer or customer_account' rule must be expressed as a JSON Schema oneOf or dependencies block to be machine-readable.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships encoded only in prose (or not at all) are a high-severity gap: validators and SDKs cannot enforce the constraint, leading to avoidable runtime errors.

customer.description: The ID of an existing customer. Exactly one of `customer` or `customer_account` must be provided.

customer_account.description: The ID of an existing account. Exactly one of `customer` or `customer_account` must be provided.

findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf constraint requiring exactly one of 'customer' or 'customer_account' in the request schema.

findings.title: flow_data.type enum does not encode which sub-object is conditionally required
findings.narration: The 'flow_data' object has a discriminator field 'type' whose value determines which of the sub-objects ('subscription_cancel', 'subscription_update', 'subscription_update_confirm') must also be present. For example, when type='subscription_cancel', the 'subscription_cancel' sub-object is required; when type='payment_method_update', none of the sub-objects may be needed. None of this conditional logic is expressed in the schema — all sub-objects are optional regardless of 'type'. This forces API consumers to read external documentation to understand the constraint, and validation tools will silently pass malformed requests.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields described only by enum semantics and docs, not by schema, are a high-severity design gap. They cannot be enforced by standard validators or code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf to flow_data schema encoding which sub-object is required per type value.

findings.title: Resource ID fields ('customer', 'customer_account', 'configuration', 'on_behalf_of') typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that clearly reference Stripe resource IDs — 'customer' (cus_…), 'customer_account' (acct_…), 'configuration' (bpc_…), 'on_behalf_of' (acct_…) — are typed as plain 'type: string' with only a generic 'maxLength: 5000'. There is no 'format', no 'pattern', and no $ref to a typed ID schema. Code-generation tools are therefore unable to produce strongly typed resource-ID wrappers or validate the ID prefix, making it easy to accidentally pass an ID of the wrong resource type.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as bare string with no format or pattern prevent code generators from building typed relationships and prevent validators from catching wrong-type IDs.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer, customer_account, and on_behalf_of fields to enable basic type validation.

findings.title: Successful response returns 200 instead of 201 for a resource-creating POST
findings.narration: This operation creates a new billing portal session, which is a resource-creation action. By HTTP semantics and REST convention, such operations should return HTTP 201 Created, ideally with a Location header pointing to the new resource. The spec declares only a 200 OK response. While Stripe consistently uses 200 across its API, this diverges from RFC 9110 and may confuse consumers or HTTP-level tooling that interprets 201 as the expected success code for POST-creates.
findings.rationale: POST operations that create resources should return 201 per HTTP semantics. Using 200 is a design inconsistency, though common in Stripe's API.

value.description: Portal session created.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 response definition to align with HTTP semantics for resource creation.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` annotations. Without these constraints, client-side validation tools and SDK generators cannot enforce the documented range, and consumers cannot discover the default value programmatically. A request with `limit=0` or `limit=999` would pass schema validation even though it violates the documented contract.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints (min/max/default) belong in the schema, not solely in prose, so tooling can enforce and surface them.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `customer` parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern — ID relationship untyped
findings.narration: The `customer` query parameter references a Stripe Customer ID (e.g. `cus_xxxx`) but is defined only as `type: string` with `maxLength: 5000`. No `format`, `pattern`, or structured reference indicates it is a resource identifier. Code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Customer resource, and SDK consumers get no hint that this must be a valid Customer ID prefix string rather than arbitrary text.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters should carry a pattern or format hint so codegen and validators can distinguish them from freeform strings.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern `^cus_` to the `customer` parameter schema to mark it as a Customer ID.

findings.title: `payment_intent` parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern — ID relationship untyped
findings.narration: The `payment_intent` query parameter references a Stripe PaymentIntent ID (e.g. `pi_xxxx`) but is defined only as `type: string` with `maxLength: 5000`. As with `customer`, this prevents codegen tools from building a typed relationship to the PaymentIntent resource and gives API consumers no machine-readable hint that the value must be a PaymentIntent ID.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters should carry a pattern or format hint so codegen and validators can distinguish them from freeform strings.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern `^pi_` to the `payment_intent` parameter schema to mark it as a PaymentIntent ID.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). HTTP GET semantics explicitly discourage request bodies, and many HTTP clients and intermediaries will ignore or reject a body on a GET request. Having a body definition here causes confusion for SDK generators (which may generate a body parameter for what should be a purely query-parameter-driven call) and incorrectly implies the body is a valid input channel.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a semantically meaningful request body per RFC 9110. An empty, closed-schema body definition adds noise and may confuse code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: card.cvc and card.number lack writeOnly marking — sensitive PAN/CVV exposed in codegen
findings.narration: The inline card object schema includes `number` (a full PAN) and `cvc` fields with no `writeOnly: true` annotation. OpenAPI's `writeOnly` keyword signals to code generators, documentation tools, and logging middleware that these fields must never be serialized in responses or logged. Without it, generated SDKs may inadvertently reflect these fields back, and documentation portals will not flag them as input-only sensitive values. PCI-DSS explicitly prohibits storage of CVV data, and exposure in tooling increases that risk.
findings.rationale: Sensitive card credential fields (PAN, CVC) must be marked writeOnly:true to prevent inadvertent serialization/logging by generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Mark card.number and card.cvc as writeOnly:true to protect sensitive credential fields.

findings.title: No operation-level summary field — discovery and documentation tools show only a deprecation notice
findings.narration: The operation has only a `description` field (which is a deprecation notice pointing users elsewhere) and no `summary` field. OpenAPI tooling such as Swagger UI, Redoc, and API gateway portals use `summary` as the primary short label in navigation lists and route tables. Without it, developers see no meaningful label for this endpoint in generated documentation, making the API harder to navigate even if just to understand what to avoid. A concise summary like 'Create a charge (deprecated — use Payment Intents)' would serve discovery without implying recommendation.
findings.rationale: Missing summary degrades documentation usability; all operations should have a concise summary for tooling and navigation.

patchOps.value: Create a charge (deprecated — use Payment Intents API instead)

findings.patchSummary: Add a summary field clearly marking the endpoint as deprecated.

findings.title: application_fee field has no description — purpose and mutual exclusivity with application_fee_amount undocumented
findings.narration: The `application_fee` property is present in the schema with `type: integer` but carries no `description` at all, while `application_fee_amount` has a full description covering its semantics. These are two similarly named fields and it is unclear from the schema alone whether they are mutually exclusive, whether one is legacy, or under what conditions each applies. Prose-only rules about which field to use are a high-severity clarity issue that also hides a likely conditional-required constraint from machine-readable tooling.
findings.rationale: Undocumented field alongside a near-duplicate named field creates ambiguity; conditional or mutual-exclusion rules should be in both prose descriptions and schema constraints.

patchOps.value: A fee in cents that will be applied to the charge and transferred to the application owner's Stripe account. Deprecated in favor of `application_fee_amount`. Mutually exclusive with `application_fee_amount`.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to application_fee clarifying its relationship to application_fee_amount.

findings.title: customer field typed as plain string with no format or pattern — cross-resource ID relationship not machine-readable
findings.narration: The `customer` field accepts a Stripe Customer ID (e.g. `cus_...`) but is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_`), or `$ref` to a Customer schema is provided. Code generation tools cannot infer the relationship between this field and the Customer resource, so generated SDKs treat it as an opaque string rather than a typed foreign key. This hinders SDK ergonomics and makes validation tooling unable to catch obviously wrong ID prefixes at request-building time. The same pattern applies to `on_behalf_of` and `destination.account`.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format so codegen tools can model cross-resource relationships and validate ID prefixes.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer and on_behalf_of to encode cross-resource relationships.

findings.title: Empty request body on GET search endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content and an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics, and all search parameters are already declared as query parameters. The presence of this request body is misleading to clients, SDK generators, and spec validators, and may cause interoperability issues with some HTTP clients and proxies that strip or reject bodies on GET requests.
findings.rationale: GET with a body is discouraged by RFC 9110 and breaks many HTTP intermediaries. All inputs for this operation are query parameters; the body serves no purpose.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/charges/search operation

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (min/max not encoded)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states "Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10", but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values. Clients and validation tools rely on schema constraints for input validation; without them, any integer (including 0 or 99999) passes schema validation, contrary to the documented behaviour.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are a high-leverage anti-pattern. Encoding minimum, maximum, and default into the schema allows client-side and server-side validation tools to enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Missing example on the `query` parameter
findings.narration: The `query` parameter is a free-form search query string referencing an external query language. Without a concrete example (e.g. `amount>5000 AND currency:usd`), consumers of the spec — especially developers new to Stripe Search Query Language — get no immediate guidance on valid syntax. An example would significantly improve usability of generated docs and SDK stubs.
findings.rationale: Complex free-form string parameters benefit greatly from examples; this one references a non-trivial external DSL, making an example especially valuable.
findings.patchSummary: Add an example value to the `query` parameter

findings.title: GET operation includes an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content (though the schema is empty and `required: false`). GET requests should not have a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). Many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks silently drop or reject bodies on GET requests, making this a misleading and potentially broken construct. The body carries no information here — it should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests MUST NOT include a body per HTTP/1.1 semantics. An empty, optional form body is a spec noise issue that can confuse client generators and middleware.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/charges/{charge}

findings.title: Path parameter `charge` lacks a format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `charge` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe charge IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ch_` followed by alphanumeric characters). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot produce typed helpers or client-side validation, and the maximum length of 5000 is far too permissive for what is always a short identifier. Adding a pattern like `^ch_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would tighten the contract and help clients fail fast on obviously invalid inputs.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without a pattern or format prevent client generators from establishing a typed relationship and allow nonsensical values to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint and tighten maxLength on `charge` path parameter

findings.title: customer field typed as plain string with no format or pattern — cross-resource reference untyped
findings.narration: The `customer` field in the request body is described as 'The ID of an existing customer' but is modeled as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Codegen tools and SDK generators cannot infer that this is a reference to a Customer resource. Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at least a `format: uri-reference` conveys the semantic intent and enables typed relationship generation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships between resources.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to customer field to signal it is a Customer resource ID

findings.title: Conditional-constraint for customer update encoded only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: The `customer` field description states 'This field may only be updated if there is no existing associated customer with this charge.' This is a meaningful conditional business rule that is invisible to validators and codegen tools — it exists only as prose. While it is admittedly a server-side state check that cannot be fully encoded in OpenAPI, at minimum the description should explicitly document the 422/400 error clients will receive if violated, and a note in the field-level description should reference the error code. Ideally, a `x-stripe-constraint` extension or a clear `x-validation` annotation would surface this to SDK generators.
findings.rationale: Conditional rules in prose only are invisible to client-side validation and SDK generators, increasing likelihood of avoidable API errors.

patchOps.value: The ID of an existing customer that will be associated with this request. This field may only be updated if there is no existing associated customer with this charge. Attempting to set this field when a customer is already associated will result in an error.

findings.patchSummary: Annotate customer field with immutability constraint and add x-constraint extension

findings.title: Conditional-constraint for transfer_group encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `transfer_group` field description says it 'may only be provided if it has not been set'. This is another write-once / immutable-after-set rule expressed solely in prose. Clients that send a `transfer_group` value on a charge that already has one set will receive an error, but nothing in the schema signals this. An `x-constraint` extension or equivalent annotation would expose this to SDK generators and API documentation tools.
findings.rationale: Immutability rules expressed only in description prose cannot be validated client-side and are invisible to codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add x-constraint extension to transfer_group to signal write-once semantics

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error fallback. Explicit 4xx response codes (400 for bad request, 404 for charge not found, 402 for request failed, 422 for unprocessable entity) are absent. While Stripe uses the `default` catch-all in many places, the absence of typed 4xx responses means client code generators cannot produce differentiated error-handling logic for expected failure modes such as 'charge not found' or 'customer already set'. At minimum, a `404` and a `402` response should be explicitly enumerated.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses prevent SDK generators from producing typed error handlers and leave API consumers without documented failure modes.

value.description: Charge not found.
Request failed (e.g. immutable field update attempted).

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 404 and 402 response definitions to the operation

findings.title: transfer_group conditional-required constraint expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `transfer_group` field description states 'may only be provided if it has not been set', implying a conditional constraint that is not encoded in the schema. This is a business rule embedded in prose that code generators, validators, and SDK builders cannot enforce automatically. While encoding the full idempotency constraint of 'field not already set on server' in JSON Schema is not fully possible, the intent to restrict this to first-time-set-only semantics should at minimum be noted via `x-` extensions or the constraint should be surfaced as clearly as possible in machine-readable form.
findings.rationale: Prose-only conditional constraints cannot be enforced by validators or code generators, increasing the risk of misuse.

patchOps.value: may only be set if not already assigned to the charge; subsequent capture attempts with a different value will be rejected

findings.patchSummary: Add x-constraint extension to transfer_group to surface conditional-set-once rule machine-readably

findings.title: charge path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `charge` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe charge IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `ch_*`). Without a `pattern` or at least a note that this should be a charge ID, code generators produce generic string inputs, and client-side validation cannot catch obviously malformed IDs before the API call is made. Adding a pattern such as `^ch_[0-9a-zA-Z]+$` would allow clients to validate the parameter before making the call.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID references typed as plain string with no pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and client-side validators from catching malformed IDs.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to charge path parameter to document expected Stripe charge ID format

findings.title: application_fee and application_fee_amount co-presence constraint not encoded
findings.narration: Both `application_fee` and `application_fee_amount` are present in the request body schema with no indication of their relationship. In the Stripe API, `application_fee` is the legacy field and `application_fee_amount` is the current preferred field; they are mutually exclusive. This mutual exclusion is not documented in either field's description and is not encoded in the schema (e.g. via a `not` / `oneOf` / `dependencies` constraint). Clients generating valid requests by combining both fields could receive unexpected or ambiguous behavior, and the schema provides no guidance to prevent this.
findings.rationale: Mutually exclusive fields that are not encoded as schema constraints rely solely on runtime rejection, with no design-time or client-side enforcement.

patchOps.value: An application fee to add on to this charge. Deprecated — use `application_fee_amount` instead. Mutually exclusive with `application_fee_amount`.
An application fee amount to add on to this charge, which must be less than or equal to the original amount. Mutually exclusive with `application_fee`.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify mutual exclusion between application_fee (deprecated) and application_fee_amount in field descriptions

findings.title: Path parameter 'charge' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `charge` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe charge IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ch_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship between this parameter and the Charge resource, and clients receive no validation guidance about the expected identifier format.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters should carry a pattern or format so tooling can validate inputs and generate typed client code.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'charge' path parameter to match Stripe charge ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body on GET operation is unnecessary
findings.narration: A GET operation should not have a request body at all per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110). Including an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` request body — even one with no properties and `required: false` — is misleading. Some HTTP intermediaries and clients will reject or ignore a body on GET requests, and its presence suggests a copy-paste artifact from a POST/PUT template. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP semantics; its presence is misleading and may cause issues with some clients and proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody block from this GET operation.

findings.title: Operation description is empty
findings.narration: The `description` field for this operation is an empty string. Developers relying on generated documentation, SDKs, or API explorers will receive no explanation of what this operation does, what the dispute update lifecycle is, or under what conditions evidence submission is triggered. For a complex operation like dispute evidence management — where submitting evidence is irreversible and time-sensitive — the absence of a description is a meaningful gap.
findings.rationale: An empty description provides no context about the operation's purpose, side effects, or business rules, leaving API consumers without essential documentation.

patchOps.value: Updates the dispute associated with the specified charge. You can submit evidence to respond to the dispute by providing the `evidence` hash. Setting `submit` to `true` (the default) immediately sends all staged evidence to the card network for review; setting it to `false` stages the evidence without submitting. The combined character count of all evidence fields is limited to 150,000.

findings.patchSummary: Add a meaningful description explaining dispute update semantics and evidence submission behaviour.

findings.title: File-reference fields typed as plain `string` without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several evidence fields — `cancellation_policy`, `customer_communication`, `customer_signature`, `duplicate_charge_documentation`, `receipt`, `refund_policy`, `service_documentation`, `shipping_documentation`, `uncategorized_file` — appear to represent Stripe File object IDs (prefixed `file_…`) but are declared as `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no description hinting at the expected value. Codegen tools and client authors cannot distinguish these from free-text fields. The same applies to `duplicate_charge_id`, which is a Charge ID (`ch_…`), and to `prior_undisputed_transactions[].charge`.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings without a pattern or description prevent code generators from producing typed relationships and prevent validators from catching obviously wrong values.

patchOps.value: A file ID (prefixed `file_`) uploaded via the Files API representing the cancellation policy.
The ID of the charge (prefixed `ch_`) that is a duplicate of the disputed charge.

findings.title: Missing examples on a complex, deeply-nested request body
findings.narration: The request body contains a deeply-nested `evidence` object including the `enhanced_evidence.visa_compelling_evidence_3` sub-tree, which has non-obvious semantics (prior undisputed transactions, disputed transaction fingerprints, merchandise vs. services classification). No `example` or `examples` is provided at the request body, schema, or property level. API consumers attempting to construct a valid dispute response payload — particularly for Visa Compelling Evidence 3.0 — have no reference to follow and must rely entirely on external documentation.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas without examples significantly increase integration effort and error rates, especially for compliance-critical flows like dispute evidence submission.

evidence.uncategorized_text: Customer confirmed receipt via email on 2024-03-18.

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples for basic evidence submission and Visa CE3 flows.

findings.title: Empty operation description
findings.narration: The `description` field for `PostChargesChargeDisputeClose` is an empty string. This leaves API consumers without any explanation of what closing a dispute means, what preconditions apply (e.g., what dispute states allow closure), what the side-effects are, or what the returned dispute object represents after the action. Stripe's dispute close action is consequential and irreversible, so documentation is especially important.
findings.rationale: An empty description on a non-trivial, stateful action reduces developer confidence and increases support burden.

patchOps.value: Closing the dispute for a charge indicates that you do not have evidence to submit and are essentially dismissing the dispute, acknowledging it as lost. The status of the dispute will change from `needs_response` to `lost`. Once a dispute is closed, it cannot be reopened.

findings.patchSummary: Add a meaningful description explaining the semantics and consequences of closing a dispute.

findings.title: Charge path parameter typed as unconstrained string — missing format or pattern
findings.narration: The `charge` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe charge IDs have a well-known prefix and structure (e.g., `ch_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Charge resource, and validation tooling cannot catch obviously invalid IDs early. A `maxLength` of 5000 is also implausibly large for an ID that is typically ~30 characters.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields without a pattern or format prevent typed SDK generation and allow large garbage values through client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Constrain the charge path parameter with a realistic maxLength and a Stripe charge ID pattern.

findings.title: Missing operation summary
findings.narration: The operation has no `summary` field. The `operationId` (`PostChargesChargeDisputeClose`) is machine-readable but not human-friendly. In tools like Swagger UI, ReDoc, and Postman, the summary is the primary label shown in navigation and collection listings. Without it, users must decode the operationId or read the (currently empty) description to understand what this endpoint does.
findings.rationale: A missing summary degrades discoverability in documentation tools and requires consumers to infer intent from the operationId.
findings.patchSummary: Add a human-readable summary: 'Close a dispute'.

findings.title: payment_intent field typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `payment_intent` field in the request body references a PaymentIntent resource by ID but is declared as a plain `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^pi_`), and no `$ref`. Codegen tools cannot infer the typed relationship between this field and the PaymentIntent resource, making it harder to build strongly-typed SDKs or validate IDs before sending the request.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern are a known high-leverage issue; they prevent codegen from building typed relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern ^pi_ to payment_intent to indicate it must be a PaymentIntent ID.

findings.title: Prose describes conditional requirement (charge OR payment_intent) not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The operation description states: 'you must specify either a Charge or a PaymentIntent object.' The charge is supplied via path parameter, but the description implies that for some call paths a `payment_intent` body field may be the primary identifier. The mutual exclusivity / conditional requirement between the path param `charge` and the body field `payment_intent` is documented only in prose. This condition should be encoded as a JSON Schema `oneOf` or similar constraint so validators and code generators can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields documented only in prose are a high-severity pattern; the rule cannot be machine-validated without schema encoding.
findings.patchSummary: Encode the charge-vs-payment_intent mutual-exclusion rule in schema (oneOf/not) rather than only prose.

findings.title: Missing examples on request body for a financially sensitive operation
findings.narration: This endpoint performs a financial mutation — creating a refund — yet the request body schema contains no `examples` or `example` values. Developers integrating this endpoint must infer correct payloads entirely from descriptions. Adding at least one example (e.g. a partial refund with a reason) would significantly reduce integration errors for a money-movement operation.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on complex or financially sensitive request bodies are a medium-severity clarity issue.

partial_refund.summary: Partial refund for a fraudulent charge

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples for partial and full refund scenarios.

findings.title: Path parameter `charge` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `charge` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or description hinting at its expected structure (e.g., `ch_[a-zA-Z0-9]+`). Stripe charge IDs have a well-known prefix pattern (`ch_`). Without a constraint, client code generators and validators cannot enforce that the value is a valid charge ID rather than an arbitrary string. This makes it harder to catch mistakes early (e.g., accidentally passing a customer ID or a raw UUID).
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format reduce codegen quality and allow invalid IDs to reach the API, causing avoidable runtime errors.
