findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to `charge` path parameter to convey expected ID format.

findings.title: Request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary and misleading
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a body; RFC 7231 discourages it, many HTTP clients and intermediaries strip or reject it, and it is semantically misleading to document one here. All parameters for this operation are already conveyed via path and query parameters. The presence of a `requestBody` — even an empty one — may confuse code generators into producing clients that attempt to send a body with GET calls.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not use a request body per HTTP semantics; an empty requestBody entry adds noise, may confuse codegen tools, and can break some HTTP clients/proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation; all params are query/path based.

findings.title: `limit` parameter has no minimum/maximum constraints documented in schema
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` — it has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` fields encoded. This means client-side validators and code generators cannot enforce the stated range. A client sending `limit=0` or `limit=500` will only discover the constraint at the Stripe API level at runtime, rather than being caught locally. The stated prose constraint should be lifted into the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints stated only in prose are invisible to validators and codegen; they must be encoded in the schema to be enforceable client-side.
findings.patchSummary: Encode minimum (1), maximum (100), and default (10) on the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Summary misleads: 'Create customer balance refund' does not reflect general refund creation
findings.narration: The operation's `summary` is 'Create customer balance refund', which implies this endpoint is exclusively for customer-balance refunds. However, the full description and request body make clear this is a general-purpose refund creation endpoint for any charge, regardless of payment method. The `origin: 'customer_balance'` field is just one optional variant. A consumer reading only the summary would have an inaccurate model of this endpoint's scope, potentially causing them to use the wrong endpoint for standard refund creation.
findings.rationale: Misleading summary reduces API discoverability and will cause confusion for developers scanning endpoint lists.

patchOps.value: Create a refund for a charge

findings.patchSummary: Replace misleading 'customer balance' summary with general refund creation description

findings.title: Conditional field `currency` should be required when `origin` is `customer_balance`
findings.narration: The `description` for the operation's context and Stripe documentation indicate that `currency` is required when `origin` is `customer_balance` (i.e., refunding to a customer balance). This conditional requirement is not encoded in the schema — there is no `if/then` or `dependencies` structure to enforce it. API consumers and code generators have no machine-readable signal that omitting `currency` when using the customer-balance origin will result in a server error. The rule lives only in external documentation, not in the spec.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields should be expressed as JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependencies`, not left implicit or in external prose.
findings.patchSummary: Encode that `currency` is required when `origin` is `customer_balance` using if/then

findings.title: Resource ID fields `charge` (path), `customer`, and `payment_intent` typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: The path parameter `charge`, and body fields `customer` and `payment_intent` are all cross-resource identifier references typed only as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`. Stripe IDs follow well-known prefix conventions (`ch_`, `cus_`, `pi_`). Without a pattern or format, code generators cannot create typed relationships between resources, and validation tools cannot catch obviously wrong values such as passing a customer ID where a charge ID is expected. This is particularly relevant for `payment_intent`, which is documented as an alternative target for the refund — yet it lives in the body of an endpoint whose path already carries a charge ID, creating an implicit mutual-exclusion constraint that is undocumented in the schema.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields used as cross-resource references should carry a pattern or format to enable typed codegen and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add Stripe-prefix patterns to charge path param, customer, and payment_intent body fields

findings.title: Response should be 201 Created for resource creation, not 200 OK
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new refund resource (POST to a collection resource `/v1/charges/{charge}/refunds`) and returns HTTP 200. Per REST conventions and HTTP semantics, a successful resource creation should respond with 201 Created, accompanied by a `Location` header pointing to the newly created resource. Using 200 conflates creation with retrieval and makes it harder for clients to distinguish between a newly created refund and an existing one being returned, especially in retry/idempotency scenarios common on payment APIs.
findings.rationale: POST endpoints that create new resources should return 201 Created per HTTP/REST conventions (RFC 9110 §15.3.2).

value.description: Refund created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response alongside 200 to properly signal resource creation

findings.title: Path parameter 'charge' typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The 'charge' path parameter represents a Stripe charge resource ID (typically prefixed 'ch_...') but is declared as a bare `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`. Codegen tools and client SDKs have no signal that this is a resource identifier rather than an arbitrary string. Adding a pattern constraint (e.g. `^ch_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at least a descriptive `format` improves documentation quality and enables client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships.

findings.title: Path parameter 'refund' typed as plain string with no format or pattern

As with the 'charge' parameter, this loses type information useful to both human readers and machine codegen tooling. Adding a pattern like `^re_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and a short description would make the contract explicit.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests carrying a body violate HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 discourages it, and many intermediaries/servers strip or reject it). The body adds noise to the spec, misleads consumers, and may cause issues with HTTP clients that refuse to send bodies on GET requests. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body; it contradicts HTTP semantics and confuses consumers and codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty request body from GET operation

findings.title: Path parameters 'charge' and 'refund' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Both `charge` (e.g. `ch_xxx`) and `refund` (e.g. `re_xxx`) are Stripe resource IDs with well-known prefixes and fixed formats, yet they are declared as bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no description. Codegen tools cannot build typed cross-resource relationships from these declarations, and clients get no validation hint (e.g. the expected `ch_` or `re_` prefix). Adding at least a `description` and ideally a `pattern` (e.g. `^re_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) would enable consumers to validate inputs before making a network call and allow documentation generators to link these to their respective resource types.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or description prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and give clients no input-validation guidance.

patchOps.value: The identifier of the charge whose refund will be updated (e.g. ch_xxx).
The identifier of the refund to update (e.g. re_xxx).

findings.patchSummary: Add description and pattern constraints to 'charge' and 'refund' path parameters.

findings.title: Missing description on 'metadata' request body property
findings.narration: The `metadata` field in the request body accepts either a key-value string map or an empty string (to clear existing metadata), but there is no `description` on the property to explain this dual-mode behavior. The `anyOf` branching — object vs empty string — is a non-obvious pattern that warrants explicit documentation so API consumers understand they can pass an empty string to unset all metadata. Without this description, integrators may be confused by the schema or rely on separate documentation sources.
findings.rationale: Non-obvious anyOf semantics (object to set vs empty string to clear) should be documented inline on the field; missing descriptions reduce clarity for code generators and documentation tools.

patchOps.value: Set of key-value pairs that you can attach to the refund. This can be useful for storing additional information about the object in a structured format. Pass an empty string to clear all existing metadata.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to 'metadata' property explaining object-vs-empty-string semantics.

findings.title: Cross-resource filter IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: The parameters `customer`, `customer_account`, `payment_intent`, `payment_link`, and `subscription` are all resource ID filters typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe IDs follow well-known prefixes (e.g., `cus_`, `pi_`, `plink_`, `sub_`) and a consistent alphanumeric pattern. Without a `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a named ID schema, codegen tools cannot model the typed relationship between the filter and the referenced resource, reducing type safety and discoverability in generated SDKs.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields named after first-class Stripe objects should encode their identity via a pattern or format so consumers and codegen tools understand the relational semantics.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-format patterns to customer, payment_intent, payment_link, and subscription filter params

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema is simply `{ "type": "integer" }` — no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` is encoded. This means API clients and validators cannot enforce the documented constraint without reading prose, and codegen tools will produce an unconstrained integer type. A value of 0 or 10000 would pass schema validation but fail at the API layer, causing a confusing runtime error.
findings.rationale: Documented numeric constraints (range 1–100, default 10) belong in the schema, not only in the description, to enable client-side validation and accurate SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Presence of a request body on a GET endpoint is incorrect HTTP semantics
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though the schema inside it is an empty object (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests must not carry a body per RFC 9110 §9.3.1; many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks will ignore or reject a body on GET. While the body is empty and marked `required: false`, its presence signals incorrect HTTP semantics and can confuse codegen tools into generating HTTP clients that attach a form body to every GET call.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per HTTP specification; even an empty optional body is a semantic error that misleads client generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Multiple conditional-required fields encoded only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: Several fields have conditional requirements described only in human-readable descriptions rather than machine-readable JSON Schema constraints. Key examples: (1) `success_url` description says 'not allowed if ui_mode is embedded or custom', but no `not` or `if/then/else` schema encodes this. (2) `cancel_url` description says 'not allowed if ui_mode is embedded or custom'. (3) `return_url` description says 'required if ui_mode is embedded or custom'. (4) `after_expiration` description says 'can't set if ui_mode is custom'. (5) `customer_update` description says 'can only be provided when customer is provided'. (6) `currency` description says 'required in setup mode when payment_method_types is not set'. (7) `payment_method_collection` description says 'can only be set in subscription mode'. (8) `customer_creation` description says 'can only be set in payment and setup mode'. These relationships should be expressed with JSON Schema `if/then/else`, `oneOf`, or `dependentRequired` so validators and code-generation tools can enforce them automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional requirements expressed only in prose are invisible to validators and SDK generators, leading to silent errors at runtime and degraded developer experience.
findings.patchSummary: Encode conditional field relationships as JSON Schema if/then/else or dependentRequired

findings.title: Missing `ui_mode` values: spec description references 'embedded' and 'custom' but enum only lists 'elements', 'embedded_page', 'hosted_page'
findings.narration: The `ui_mode` field description throughout the request body repeatedly references values 'embedded' and 'custom' (e.g., 'not allowed if ui_mode is embedded or custom', 'can only be set when creating embedded or custom sessions'), but the actual enum for `ui_mode` only contains ['elements', 'embedded_page', 'hosted_page']. This is a clear copy-paste / documentation mismatch — either the descriptions are outdated and reference old values, or the enum is missing 'embedded' and 'custom' as valid values. Either way the spec is internally inconsistent and will mislead API consumers.
findings.rationale: A discrepancy between the enum values and the prose descriptions of those same values constitutes a clarity and correctness bug that will cause consumer confusion and potential integration errors.
findings.patchSummary: Reconcile ui_mode enum values with the 'embedded' and 'custom' values referenced in field descriptions

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that represent references to other Stripe resources are typed as plain `type: string` without any `format`, `pattern`, or structured reference: `customer` (Customer ID, e.g., cus_xxx), `customer_account` (Account ID, e.g., acct_xxx), `payment_method_configuration` (pmc_xxx), and within nested objects `automatic_tax.liability.account`, `invoice_creation.invoice_data.issuer.account`, `subscription_data.invoice_settings.issuer.account`, `payment_intent_data.on_behalf_of`, `payment_intent_data.transfer_data.destination`, `setup_intent_data.on_behalf_of`, `subscription_data.on_behalf_of`, `subscription_data.transfer_data.destination`. Without format hints or ID prefix patterns, code-generation tools cannot build typed relationships to related resources.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as unqualified strings prevent SDK generators from constructing typed relationships and prevent validators from catching mismatched ID types.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID prefix patterns or x-stripe-resource-type annotations to resource reference string fields

findings.title: Missing examples on a highly complex request body
findings.narration: The request body has no `examples` or `example` defined at the media-type level, despite having one of the most complex schemas in the Stripe API — dozens of nested objects, conditional modes (payment/setup/subscription), multiple UI modes, and 40+ payment method options. Without at least one illustrative example (e.g., a minimal payment-mode session and a subscription-mode session), developers must infer the minimal required payload from the schema alone, which is extremely difficult given the conditional requirements embedded only in prose.
findings.rationale: Complex schemas without examples increase integration time and error rates. OpenAPI supports examples at both the media-type and property level; neither is used here.
findings.patchSummary: Add at least two examples (payment mode and subscription mode) to the request body

findings.title: GET request includes an explicit empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content (an empty schema with `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests must not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1); many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will reject or silently drop a body on a GET. The presence of this block, even marked `required: false`, signals incorrect design and may confuse client generators into emitting a body-sending call.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per RFC 9110; including one—even optional—violates HTTP semantics and harms interoperability.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `session` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `session` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 66` constraint. Stripe session IDs have a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cs_test_` or `cs_live_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client code generators cannot validate the ID before sending the request, and documentation readers have no guidance on what constitutes a valid session ID. Adding a regex pattern (e.g., `^cs_(test|live)_[A-Za-z0-9]{1,58}$`) or at minimum a description note plus a `minLength` would materially improve usability and catch obvious mistakes early.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters typed only as plain strings with no pattern, format, or minLength prevent client-side validation and make codegen relationships opaque.

findings.title: Conditional field constraint encoded only in prose: `collected_information` session-type restriction
findings.narration: The description for `collected_information` states it 'Can only be set when updating `embedded` or `custom` sessions.' This is a conditional requirement that should be enforced in the schema (e.g., via `if`/`then` or a `description` note alongside a server-side validation pattern), but it exists only as prose. Client SDK generators and validators cannot enforce or communicate this constraint programmatically, leading to potential runtime 400 errors that could have been surfaced at design/generation time.
findings.rationale: Field relationships expressed only in prose are a high-leverage pattern that should be encoded in schema constraints to enable validation and code generation.

findings.patchSummary: Strengthen description to clarify error behavior; ideally encode constraint in schema.

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions on a write endpoint
findings.narration: This POST operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error catch-all. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `403`, or `404` response definitions. For a write endpoint that has documented constraints (e.g., session type restrictions, max 5 shipping options), the absence of specific 4xx responses means API consumers and generated clients have no structured information about validation error shapes, authentication failures, or resource-not-found scenarios. The `default` handler is too coarse to guide client error handling.
findings.rationale: Write endpoints should document at minimum 400 (validation) and 404 (resource not found) to enable proper client error handling and SDK generation.

value.description: Bad request. Returned when request parameters are invalid or the session cannot be updated in its current state.
The specified session was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the existing default catch-all.

findings.title: `line_items` array: mutually exclusive `price` vs `price_data` rule is prose-only
findings.narration: The `line_items` description states that to add a new line item you must specify 'one of `price` or `price_data`'. However, the `line_item_params` schema does not encode this mutual exclusivity — both `price` and `price_data` are optional properties with no `oneOf` or `not` constraint preventing them from being submitted simultaneously. Client code generators and validators will allow payloads that include both fields, leading to server-side errors that could have been caught earlier.
findings.rationale: A 'exactly one of' rule expressed in prose should be encoded as a schema constraint (e.g., oneOf) so validators and SDK generators can enforce it.

findings.title: Missing example on the complex `line_items` request body field
findings.narration: The `line_items` property has a complex nested structure covering add, update, remove, retain, and reorder operations — all described only in prose. There is no `example` or `examples` attached to the field or the enclosing request body schema. Complex array fields with multiple mutation modes (by presence/absence of `id`, `price`, `price_data`) are exactly the kind of fields that benefit most from concrete examples, reducing integration time and mistakes for API consumers.
findings.rationale: Complex fields with multiple conditional usage modes should include examples to reduce integration friction and risk of misuse.

findings.title: session path parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `session` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe session IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cs_live_...` or `cs_test_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot validate or type-narrow this ID, and client SDKs cannot distinguish it from an arbitrary string. Adding a pattern such as `^cs_(test|live)_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` would encode the invariant in the schema and enable automated validation.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs with a known prefix/format should carry a `pattern` or `format` so codegen tools can build typed references and client-side validation is possible.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to session path parameter to encode known ID format

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error responses defined
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` catch-all error response. It does not enumerate specific 4xx responses such as `400 Bad Request` (e.g. session not in `open` status) or `404 Not Found` (session ID does not exist). The `default` bucket is useful but hides the shape of common, predictable error conditions from consumers and documentation generators. At minimum, a `400` covering the 'session not in open status' business-rule violation and a `404` for unknown session IDs should be explicitly modeled.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx definitions obscure predictable failure modes from API consumers and tooling, reducing discoverability and forcing clients to rely only on the generic default.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 does not prohibit it, but many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks strip or reject bodies on GET requests). Because this body carries no properties and is not required, it adds noise without value and may cause interoperability problems. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies are semantically undefined and frequently discarded by intermediaries; an empty one serves no purpose.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically incorrect request body from the GET operation.

findings.title: Missing description and pattern on the `session` path parameter
findings.narration: The `session` path parameter lacks both a `description` and a `pattern` (or `format`) constraint. Stripe session IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cs_live_...` or `cs_test_...`). Without a description, callers have no documentation of what kind of value to supply. Without a pattern or format hint, SDK generators and validators cannot enforce the expected shape, increasing the chance of malformed requests making it to the API.
findings.rationale: Path parameters identifying resources should include a description and, where the ID format is known, a pattern or format to aid validation and codegen.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it accepts values between 1 and 100, but the schema has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means the schema does not enforce the documented range; clients relying on schema-level validation (e.g., generated validators or mock servers) will accept out-of-range values without complaint.
findings.rationale: Prose-documented numeric bounds should be encoded as schema constraints so tooling can enforce them automatically.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)

The description prose states the range is 1–100 with a default of 10, but these constraints are not encoded in the schema. Clients and code-generation tools reading the schema alone will not enforce or communicate these bounds, potentially sending out-of-range values that the server rejects.
findings.rationale: Constraint information documented only in prose is a high-severity gap; machine-readable schemas should encode minimum, maximum, and default so SDKs and validators can enforce them.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is defined for this GET operation, containing an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema with no properties. GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients and intermediaries silently drop GET bodies. This declaration may confuse SDK generators into emitting code that sends a body with the request, or may cause certain HTTP clients to error. The requestBody should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET with a request body is semantically incorrect and can cause interoperability problems with proxies and HTTP clients that discard GET bodies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields 'amount' and 'metric_tons' expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The request schema description for `amount` says "Either this or `metric_tons` must be specified" and vice versa, but the schema itself does not encode this constraint. JSON Schema provides `oneOf` (or `dependencies`/`if-then-else`) to enforce exactly-one-of semantics. As-is, a client SDK or validator cannot determine that exactly one of the two must be present, and a request supplying both (or neither) will only fail at runtime on Stripe's servers rather than being caught client-side by schema validation.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required constraints left in prose are a high-leverage pattern: they prevent code-generation tools and validators from enforcing the rule automatically, leading to silent client bugs.
findings.patchSummary: Encode the amount/metric_tons exactly-one-of constraint as a JSON Schema oneOf instead of prose.

findings.title: POST creating a resource returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new Climate order and immediately processes payment, making it a resource-creation operation. The HTTP standard (RFC 9110 §15.3.2) assigns 201 Created to responses where a new resource has been created. Returning 200 instead conflates creation with retrieval semantics, confuses clients that branch on status codes, and diverges from REST conventions that most OpenAPI tooling and SDK generators rely on to infer operation type.
findings.rationale: Using 201 for resource creation is a well-established HTTP convention. Mislabeling it as 200 misleads consumers and code-gen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Change the success response code from 200 to 201 Created for this resource-creation endpoint.

findings.title: Product ID field typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or $ref
findings.narration: The `product` field is described as "Unique identifier of the Climate product" and is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe product IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `climsku_...`). Without a `pattern` or a `$ref` to a typed identifier schema, code-generation tools cannot build a typed cross-resource relationship, and clients can accidentally pass arbitrary strings. At minimum, a `pattern` matching the known Climate product ID format (or a `format: "climate-product-id"` custom format) should be added.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent codegen tools from creating typed relationships and prevent client-side format validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the 'product' field to reflect the Climate product ID format.

findings.title: GET operation includes an unnecessary empty requestBody
findings.narration: This GET operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not include a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will ignore or reject a body on GET requests. The presence of this field may confuse consumers and codegen tools into thinking a body is expected or allowed.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 defines GET as a safe, idempotent method with no defined semantics for a message body. Declaring an empty requestBody on a GET is misleading and against HTTP conventions.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/climate/orders/{order}

findings.title: Path parameter `order` lacks a format or pattern hint for resource ID validation
findings.narration: The `order` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe order IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `clord_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, clients and validators cannot detect obviously wrong IDs before making a round trip to the API, and codegen tools cannot create typed resource references. A pattern such as `^clord_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would improve discoverability and early error detection.
findings.rationale: A resource ID field typed as plain string with no pattern or format prevents codegen tools from building typed relationships and allows obviously invalid values through client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID pattern constraint to `order` path parameter schema

findings.title: Path parameter 'order' typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `order` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but Climate order IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `climateord_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `format`, codegen tools cannot build a typed reference to the Climate order resource, and validation tooling will accept any arbitrary string up to 5000 characters as a valid order ID. Adding a regex pattern anchoring to the known ID prefix would tighten validation and improve generated SDK ergonomics.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as bare strings without pattern/format prevent typed relationship generation in codegen and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'order' path parameter to reflect known Climate order ID format.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error responses documented (e.g. 404, 400)
findings.narration: The operation only declares a `200` success response and a `default` catch-all error response. For an action endpoint like cancel, specific error conditions are highly probable and important to document: `404` when the order ID does not exist, `400` when the order is outside the 24-hour cancellation window or already cancelled, and potentially `409` for conflict states. Relying solely on `default` for all error cases forces API consumers to inspect the error body at runtime rather than handling anticipated failure modes by HTTP status code. OpenAPI consumers (gateway policies, SDK error handling, mocking tools) all benefit from explicit status codes.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses on action endpoints reduce discoverability of known failure modes and degrade SDK/gateway integration quality.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values encoded. Clients and code-generation tools cannot enforce or discover these constraints from the schema alone — they are buried in prose. A value of 0 or 101 would pass schema validation but be rejected at runtime.
findings.rationale: Machine-readable constraints prevent invalid requests and enable better client-side validation and documentation generation.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false, properties: {}`). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual — RFC 9110 permits it but many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways drop or reject GET bodies. Since all parameters for this list endpoint are properly modeled as query parameters, the empty request body serves no purpose and may confuse consumers or code-generation tooling into emitting a body-construction call for a GET request.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not carry a request body. The empty body adds noise and may cause interoperability issues.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint

GET requests MUST NOT include a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). While some servers and clients tolerate this, many proxies and HTTP frameworks will reject or strip a body on GET requests. Including the body definition in the spec is misleading and may cause codegen tools to emit incorrect client code that attempts to send a request body.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a body per HTTP semantics. Declaring an empty request body on a GET creates semantic confusion and potential client/proxy incompatibility.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation to conform to HTTP semantics.

Without a `description` or `pattern`, consumers and codegen tools cannot validate IDs before sending requests, and documentation readers have no indication of what constitutes a valid product ID. Adding a description and a regex pattern (e.g., `^climsku_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) would meaningfully improve usability and catch client-side errors early.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with a schema that has no properties and `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that GET has no defined semantics for a message body). Including an empty, closed-schema body confuses HTTP clients and intermediate proxies, and some clients will reject or drop it. It adds no value and should be removed.
findings.rationale: A requestBody with zero properties on a GET endpoint violates HTTP semantics and creates client-side confusion. It should be removed entirely.

findings.title: Path parameter `supplier` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `supplier` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000 but no `format`, `pattern`, or minimum length. Stripe supplier IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `climsup_...`). Without a pattern or at least a `minLength`, clients and code generators cannot validate the ID before sending the request, and the generous upper bound of 5000 characters offers no practical input validation.
findings.rationale: A typed resource ID without format/pattern prevents codegen tools from building typed relationships and allows clearly invalid values to be submitted.
findings.patchSummary: Add minLength and pattern to the `supplier` path parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). While Stripe's API conventionally includes this as a spec artifact for tooling uniformity, the presence of `required: false` does not mitigate the semantic confusion it introduces. Tooling that strictly follows HTTP semantics may warn or error on this.
findings.rationale: A non-null request body on a GET operation violates HTTP semantics and may confuse code generators or HTTP clients that disallow bodies on GET.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `confirmation_token` typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `confirmation_token` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe confirmation token IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `ctoken_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot establish a typed reference to the ConfirmationToken resource, and client SDKs cannot validate the ID format at the boundary. Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^ctoken_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at minimum an `example` would make the contract more precise and catch misrouted IDs early.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as bare strings without pattern or format lose type safety in generated clients and cannot be validated client-side.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and example to confirmation_token path parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests must not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1); many HTTP/2 intermediaries, proxies, and client libraries will ignore or reject a body on a GET. The Stripe API appears to include this pattern across all GET operations for tooling uniformity, but it is semantically incorrect and may confuse consumers or code generators that validate HTTP semantics strictly. The `requestBody` field should be removed from this operation.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 prohibits semantically meaningful request bodies on GET; an empty form-urlencoded body is misleading and may break strict HTTP clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect empty requestBody from GET operation

Sending a body with a GET request is technically allowed by HTTP but is unusual, semantically wrong, and breaks many HTTP clients, proxies, and caching intermediaries that strip or reject GET bodies. Because the schema has no properties at all, the body carries no information and should simply be removed.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body. An empty, closed schema provides no value and creates interoperability risk with clients and intermediaries.

findings.title: Missing minimum/maximum constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter explicitly states "Limit can range between 1 and 100", but the schema (`type: integer`) has no `minimum: 1` or `maximum: 100` constraints. This means any consumer relying on the schema (code generators, validators, mock servers) will accept values outside the documented range, potentially causing API errors at runtime that could have been caught earlier by schema validation.
findings.rationale: Prose-documented numeric constraints should be encoded as JSON Schema keywords so they are machine-enforceable.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 and maximum: 100 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Country path parameter lacks format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `country` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Country codes are well-defined ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 values (2 uppercase letters). The extremely permissive `maxLength: 5000` is also misleading — it allows strings orders of magnitude longer than any valid country code. Adding a `pattern` (e.g. `^[A-Z]{2}$`) and tightening `maxLength` to 2 would make client validation explicit, enable better tooling, and serve as inline documentation.
findings.rationale: A string with maxLength:5000 for a 2-character country code provides virtually no validation signal. Pattern constraints enable codegen tools to produce properly validated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten country path param to ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 pattern and maxLength:2

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is redundant noise
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual (RFC 7231 discourages it), and since the body schema is empty and `required: false`, it carries zero information. Most HTTP clients and proxies ignore or strip GET bodies. Removing the `requestBody` entirely cleans up the contract and avoids confusing generated clients that may attempt to send an empty form body.
findings.rationale: Empty GET request bodies are semantically incorrect per HTTP semantics and can confuse SDK generators and intermediaries. The body here is both empty and not required, making it pure noise.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty, not-required requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. Clients and generated SDKs have no machine-readable way to enforce the documented bounds, and no default value is encoded in the schema.
findings.rationale: Missing numeric constraints mean clients can send out-of-range values (e.g., 0 or 999) without client-side validation catching it. The default should also be encoded so code-generation tools can fill it in correctly.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, and default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `amount_off`/`percent_off` and conditional `currency` requirement expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The schema description states that either `percent_off` OR `amount_off`+`currency` must be provided, and that `currency` is required when `amount_off` is passed. Similarly, `duration_in_months` is described as required only when `duration` is `repeating`. None of these conditional-required relationships are encoded in the JSON Schema — they live only in field descriptions. This means client-side validators and code-generation tools cannot enforce these constraints, and callers will only learn about them at runtime via API errors.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields documented only in prose are a high-severity design issue; they should be encoded using `oneOf`/`if-then-else`/`required` so validators and SDK generators can surface them early.
findings.patchSummary: Encode amount_off+currency vs percent_off mutual exclusion and currency conditional-required as oneOf schema rules

findings.title: `duration_in_months` conditional requirement not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The description for `duration_in_months` states it is "Required only if `duration` is `repeating`". This conditional dependency is purely prose-based. A JSON Schema `if`/`then` or `dependencies` construct should encode: when `duration` equals `repeating`, `duration_in_months` is required; conversely, when `duration` is not `repeating`, `duration_in_months` should arguably be disallowed. Without this, generators and validators cannot warn callers who omit `duration_in_months` when setting `duration: repeating`.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships documented only in description text leave validators and SDK generators unable to enforce the constraint before the API call is made.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then to require duration_in_months when duration is 'repeating'

findings.title: `percent_off` lacks minimum/maximum constraints despite prose description
findings.narration: The description for `percent_off` states it must be "a positive float larger than 0, and smaller or equal to 100". However, the schema for this field only declares `type: number` with no `minimum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, or `maximum` constraints. Clients and validators cannot enforce the 0 < percent_off ≤ 100 range without making a live API call.
findings.rationale: Numeric constraints documented only in field descriptions are not enforceable by JSON Schema validators or code generators; they should be expressed as schema keywords.
findings.patchSummary: Add exclusiveMinimum: 0 and maximum: 100 to percent_off field

findings.title: POST create endpoint returns HTTP 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new coupon resource and documents only a 200 response. REST conventions (and HTTP RFC 9110 §15.3.2) call for a 201 Created response when a new resource has been created, optionally with a `Location` header pointing to the new resource. Returning 200 is not incorrect per se, but it is semantically imprecise and can confuse HTTP clients and middlewares that use status codes to detect resource creation.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the standard status code for successful resource creation; using 200 reduces semantic clarity for clients relying on status codes.
findings.patchSummary: Consider returning 201 Created for successful coupon resource creation

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints

This means client-side validation cannot enforce the documented range, and code generators cannot surface the default or bounds. An API consumer could inadvertently send `limit=0` or `limit=999` and receive a server-side error rather than being guided by the schema itself.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints (min, max, default) belong in the schema, not only in prose. Codegen tools and validators rely on schema constraints to produce correct client code and input validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

Without a `pattern` or structured `format`, codegen tools see an opaque string rather than a typed resource relationship, and clients receive no schema-level guidance that an invoice ID (not an arbitrary string) is required.

findings.title: Unnecessary empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests with a body are semantically ambiguous (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that a GET message body has no defined semantics), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will strip or reject it. Having this body defined in the spec may mislead consumers or codegen tools into sending a body with the GET request, which can cause unexpected behavior.

findings.title: Conditional-required fields encoded only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: The description for `amount` states 'One of `amount`, `lines`, or `shipping_cost` must be provided.' Similarly, the descriptions for `lines` and `shipping_cost` repeat this constraint. This mutual-exclusivity / at-least-one rule exists only in prose; there is no JSON Schema `oneOf`, `anyOf`, or `if/then/else` block encoding it. Consumers generating client code or request validation logic cannot mechanically enforce this constraint — they must read the description text and hand-code the check.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required field relationships expressed only in prose cannot be machine-validated and are a high-leverage clarity and design gap per the review guidance.

findings.title: Post-payment amount allocation constraint (refunds + credit + out-of-band = post_payment_amount) not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The operation description states: 'The sum of refunds, customer balance credits, and outside of Stripe credits must equal the `post_payment_amount`.' This is a critical business invariant linking `refund_amount`, `refunds`, `credit_amount`, and `out_of_band_amount`. None of these fields carry schema-level constraints, cross-field validation hints, or even individual `minimum: 0` bounds. A client or code-gen tool has no way to represent or enforce this constraint from the schema alone; it is purely narrative.
findings.rationale: A field-relationship rule stated in prose that should be encoded structurally is a high-severity design finding per the review guidance.

patchOps.value: NOTE: The sum of refund_amount (or refunds), credit_amount, and out_of_band_amount must equal the post_payment_amount. This constraint cannot be fully expressed in JSON Schema; enforce it server-side.

findings.title: `invoice` field typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `invoice` field holds an invoice resource ID (a cross-resource reference) but is declared only as `type: string, maxLength: 5000`. There is no `pattern` (e.g. `^in_`) or `format` hint. Code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Invoice resource, and validation tooling cannot distinguish a mistyped ID from a valid one. The same issue applies to `lines[].invoice_line_item` (plain string referencing a line-item resource) and `refunds[].refund` (referencing a Refund resource).
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed client codegen and weaken validation; this is a design finding per the review guidance.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and x-stripeResource hint to invoice field (and analogously to invoice_line_item and refund sub-fields).

findings.title: Missing examples on a complex, multi-variant request body
findings.narration: The request body has a complex schema with three alternative provision modes (amount, lines, shipping_cost), several optional monetary allocation fields, and nested line-item and refund structures. No `examples` or `example` is provided on the request body or on any of the complex sub-schemas. This makes it significantly harder for API consumers to understand correct usage, especially the allocation rules and the line-item `type` field which drives conditional requirements.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on complex request bodies reduce clarity and make integration harder; this is a medium-severity clarity finding per the review guidance.

findings.title: Conditional-required constraint 'one of amount, lines, or shipping_cost' encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The descriptions for `amount`, `lines`, and `shipping_cost` each state 'One of `amount`, `lines`, or `shipping_cost` must be provided.' This mutual-exclusivity/at-least-one constraint is expressed only in natural-language documentation. No machine-readable schema construct (e.g., `oneOf`, `anyOf`, `not`, or OpenAPI-level `dependentRequired`) encodes this rule. Clients and validators cannot automatically enforce it, and code-generation tools will treat all three fields as fully independent optionals, potentially allowing calls with none of them.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships expressed only in prose are a well-known high-leverage design gap; they should be encoded in JSON Schema so validators and SDK generators can enforce them.

findings.title: Resource ID field `invoice` typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `invoice` parameter is named like a resource ID and references an Invoice object, but its schema is bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. There is no `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^in_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`), or `$ref` to a typed schema. Code-generation tools cannot infer the relationship between this parameter and the Invoice resource, and consumers have no machine-readable hint about the expected ID format.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed-relationship inference in codegen and provide no validation hint to callers.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `invoice` parameter schema to indicate it is a Stripe Invoice ID

findings.title: Complex nested query parameters (lines, refunds) lack request/response examples
findings.narration: The `lines` and `refunds` parameters have deeply nested object schemas with multiple required sub-fields and conditional sub-structures (e.g., `tax_amounts`, `payment_record_refund`). No examples are provided anywhere on these parameters or on the 200 response body. For complex preview operations — where the exact shape of the input directly determines what the preview contains — examples are especially important for both human understanding and documentation tooling.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on complex request parameter schemas reduce clarity and make it harder for integrators to understand how to construct valid requests.
findings.patchSummary: Add example values to the complex `lines` and `refunds` nested query parameters

findings.title: `refunds[].type` field has no `required` constraint despite being a discriminator
findings.narration: The `refunds` array item schema has a `type` property that acts as a discriminator between `payment_record_refund` and `refund` sub-types, but `type` is not listed in the item's `required` array (the item object has no `required` field at all). This means validators will accept a refund item object with no `type` field, making it impossible to determine which sub-structure applies. By contrast, the `lines` array item schema correctly marks `type` as required.
findings.rationale: A discriminator/union-type field not marked as required leaves the schema open to ambiguous or invalid inputs that validators cannot catch.
findings.patchSummary: Add `required: [type]` to refunds array item schema to enforce discriminator field presence

findings.title: Conditional-required constraint 'one of amount, lines, or shipping_cost' encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The descriptions of `amount`, `lines`, and `shipping_cost` each state 'One of `amount`, `lines`, or `shipping_cost` must be provided.' This mutually-exclusive-but-at-least-one requirement is a structural constraint that should be expressed in the schema (e.g., via `oneOf` or `anyOf` at the parameter level, or ideally through a request body schema). As a GET endpoint with query parameters, full JSON Schema composition isn't directly applicable per the OpenAPI parameter model, but the prose-only constraint means client SDK generators and validators cannot enforce it automatically. At minimum, adding a clear note in the operation description with an explicit enumeration, and ideally migrating to a request body for such complex constraint semantics, would be appropriate.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields expressed only in prose are a high-leverage finding: tooling cannot enforce the constraint, leading to runtime errors that could be caught at validation time.

findings.title: Complex nested objects passed as GET query parameters — HTTP semantic mismatch
findings.narration: This operation accepts deeply-nested, complex objects (e.g., `lines` with nested `tax_amounts`, `refunds` with nested `payment_record_refund`, `shipping_cost`) as GET query parameters. Passing structured arrays of objects with deepObject serialization in a GET request is fragile: URL length limits (commonly 2048–8192 chars depending on client/server) can be easily exceeded, many HTTP clients and proxies do not fully support deepObject serialization for deeply nested structures, and it makes caching semantics awkward. This pattern strongly suggests the operation was designed as a POST preview endpoint and retrofitted to GET. A POST to `/v1/credit_notes/preview/lines` with a JSON request body would be semantically cleaner and more robust for this use case.
findings.rationale: Using GET with deeply-nested query parameters violates practical HTTP constraints and is a design risk for clients sending large line-item arrays.
findings.patchSummary: Consider POST with a JSON request body for this preview endpoint to avoid URL length and serialization limits.

findings.title: Missing `minimum` and `maximum` constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema has no `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10` annotations. Without these, client-side and server-side validators cannot enforce the stated range, and SDK generators cannot provide default values.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints stated in prose but not encoded are not enforceable by tooling; minimum/maximum/default are standard JSON Schema keywords.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: `invoice` parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `invoice` query parameter is described as 'ID of the invoice' and is the only required parameter, yet its schema is simply `type: string, maxLength: 5000`. Stripe invoice IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `in_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a format hint, SDK generators treat this as a generic string rather than a typed resource reference, losing the relationship to the Invoice resource. A `pattern: "^in_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$"` or an `x-stripeResource` annotation would improve developer experience and code generation quality.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed cross-resource relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the invoice parameter schema to mark it as a typed resource ID.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter's description states it 'can range between 1 and 100', but the schema has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints — it is just `type: integer`. Without these constraints, client-side validation and code-generation tools cannot enforce the documented range, meaning callers can pass 0, -5, or 999 without a schema-level rejection.
findings.rationale: Prose-documented constraints that are not encoded in the schema are a high-severity design issue because clients and SDKs cannot enforce them without reading the description.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `url` field in list response has no format or pattern to identify it as a URL
findings.narration: The `url` property in the `CreditNoteLinesList` response schema is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength`, but no `format: uri` or pattern constraint. Consumers and documentation generators cannot distinguish it from a generic string, and IDE autocompletion tools miss the semantic signal. Adding `format: uri` costs nothing and aligns with OpenAPI best practice.
findings.rationale: A field semantically representing a URI should carry `format: uri` so tooling can apply proper validation and rendering.
findings.patchSummary: Add `format: uri` to the `url` property in the CreditNoteLinesList response schema.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false`, no properties). GET requests with a body are discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 9110), many HTTP clients and proxies drop or reject them, and the body here is entirely empty — it carries no useful information. The `requestBody` block should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody is an HTTP anti-pattern. Empty request bodies on GET endpoints add noise and may break clients or intermediate proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Unnecessary empty requestBody on GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET endpoint includes a `requestBody` field with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). Many HTTP clients, proxies, and load balancers will silently drop or reject request bodies on GET requests. Having it in the spec misleads consumers and code generators into thinking a body is relevant here.
findings.rationale: GET requests MUST NOT use a request body for conveying resource-specific data. An empty body schema adds noise and may confuse client generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/credit_notes/{id}

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000, which is extremely permissive. Stripe credit note IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cn_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` constraint, clients cannot validate inputs before sending them, and documentation consumers have no hint of the expected format. This also means codegen tools cannot produce typed resource-reference accessors.
findings.rationale: Resource identifier fields with known patterns should declare a `pattern` to enable client-side validation and improve developer experience.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter for credit note IDs

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `customer` and `customer_account` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The request body accepts both `customer` (existing Customer ID) and `customer_account` (existing Account ID), but the spec does not constrain that exactly one of these must be supplied — nor does any description prose indicate the mutual-exclusivity rule. A caller could omit both or supply both, and the schema would not catch it. The constraint (provide exactly one of `customer` or `customer_account`) should be expressed as a JSON Schema `oneOf` or via `required` inside each branch of an `if/then/else` or `oneOf`, rather than left purely to runtime validation.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules that live only in prose (or implicitly in runtime behaviour) are a high-leverage gap: codegen tools cannot enforce them, and callers cannot discover them without reading docs carefully.

customer.description: The ID of an existing customer for which to create the Customer Session.

customer_account.description: The ID of an existing Account for which to create the Customer Session.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusivity of `customer` vs `customer_account` as oneOf branches

findings.title: Resource ID fields `customer` and `customer_account` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Both `customer` (a Stripe Customer ID, e.g. `cus_...`) and `customer_account` (a Stripe Account ID, e.g. `acct_...`) are typed as plain `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no indication of the expected Stripe object-ID prefix. Codegen and client SDK tools cannot infer a typed relationship to the Customer or Account resources. Adding a `pattern` constraint (e.g. `^cus_[0-9A-Za-z]+$`) and/or an `x-stripeResource` extension would enable typed cross-resource references.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings without constraints or cross-resource hints make codegen tools produce loose string fields instead of typed references, degrading SDK quality.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to customer and customer_account ID fields

findings.title: No examples on the complex `components` request body object
findings.narration: The `components` field is the most complex part of the request body — it contains nested objects for five different UI components, each with multiple features and enum options. No `examples` or `example` values are provided at the property level or at the request body level, making it difficult for developers to understand how to configure a typical session (e.g. enabling just the payment element with default features). Adding at least one illustrative example would significantly improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas without examples force developers to reverse-engineer acceptable payloads from the schema alone, increasing integration friction.
findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating common component configurations

findings.title: Missing min/max constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter's description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties to enforce or document this machine-readably. Clients relying on the schema alone (e.g., generated SDKs or validators) will not enforce the documented range, allowing invalid values like 0 or 200 to pass schema validation silently.
findings.rationale: Constraint rules described only in prose and not encoded in the schema cannot be enforced by validators or used by code-generation tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: GET endpoint carries a (vacuous) request body
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, albeit an empty object schema with `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests with bodies are semantically undefined in HTTP (RFC 9110) and many proxies, gateways, and HTTP clients will strip or reject them. Even as a no-op, advertising a request body on a GET discourages correct client behaviour and may confuse code-generation tools that emit body-sending logic for the request.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 notes that GET requests have no defined semantics for a request body. OpenAPI tooling may incorrectly generate body-sending code when requestBody is present on a GET operation.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the vacuous requestBody from the GET /v1/customers operation

findings.title: `test_clock` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `test_clock` parameter is described as an ID that filters customers to those associated with a specific test clock resource, yet its schema is a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. No `format`, `pattern`, or cross-reference indicates this is a resource identifier (e.g., a `tclk_…` prefixed ID). Code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to the test clock resource, and API consumers have no machine-readable hint about expected value format.
findings.rationale: Resource-ID fields typed only as plain strings prevent codegen from expressing cross-resource relationships and leave clients without format guidance.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern hint (^tclk_) to test_clock parameter schema to signal it is a resource ID

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that reference other Stripe resources are typed as plain `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`: `payment_method` (references a PaymentMethod), `source` (references a Source/Card/BankAccount), `test_clock` (references a TestClock), and `invoice_settings.default_payment_method` (references a PaymentMethod). Without any structural hint, codegen tools and documentation generators cannot express these as typed resource relationships, making it harder to validate input, build typed SDKs, or cross-link resource docs. Each should at minimum carry a `pattern` such as `^pm_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for payment methods, or a `description` note is insufficient alone — a `format: stripe-object-id` extension or similar convention should be applied consistently.
findings.rationale: Fields named like resource IDs without format/pattern/x-type annotations prevent codegen from building typed relationships, a high-impact gap per review rules.
findings.patchSummary: Add patterns to resource-ID string fields so codegen can express typed relationships

findings.title: invoice_prefix constraint described in prose only — not encoded as schema pattern
findings.narration: The `invoice_prefix` field description says it 'Must be 3–12 uppercase letters or numbers', but the schema only sets `maxLength: 5000` with no `minLength`, `maxLength` tightened to 12, or `pattern` enforcing the format. This means any client submitting a lowercase or out-of-range value will only discover the constraint at runtime via an API error rather than at schema-validation time. The constraint should be encoded as `minLength: 3`, `maxLength: 12`, and `pattern: '^[A-Z0-9]{3,12}$'`.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints that can be expressed as JSON Schema properties should be encoded structurally; this is a high-leverage correctness gap for client-side validation and documentation accuracy.
findings.patchSummary: Encode invoice_prefix length and character constraints as schema properties instead of prose only

findings.title: Overlapping and ambiguous name fields: 'name', 'individual_name', and 'business_name' relationship not encoded
findings.narration: The request body exposes three distinct name-related fields: `name` ('The customer's full name or business name'), `individual_name` ('The customer's full name'), and `business_name` ('The customer's business name'). The intended relationship between these fields — whether they are mutually exclusive, whether `individual_name`/`business_name` supersede `name`, or whether exactly one of the latter two should be used — is not encoded in the schema. This creates ambiguity for API consumers who may populate all three fields without knowing the precedence rules. If `individual_name` and `business_name` are mutually exclusive or conditionally required, that constraint must be expressed using `oneOf`, `not`, or `dependencies`; at minimum the `name` field description should clarify its relationship to the newer fields.
findings.rationale: Field relationships expressed only in documentation (or not at all) rather than schema constraints are a high-leverage finding per review rules.

findings.title: Missing examples on complex request body
findings.narration: This endpoint accepts a rich, multi-field request body covering address, shipping, tax IDs, invoice settings, and cash balance — yet no `example` or `examples` are provided at the request body or schema level. Developers integrating this endpoint for the first time have no reference payload to validate their understanding of the shape, particularly for the nested objects like `invoice_settings`, `shipping`, and `tax_id_data`. Adding even one representative example (e.g., creating a customer with an address, email, and one tax ID) would significantly reduce integration friction.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on complex request bodies with many nested objects impede developer experience and integration accuracy; medium severity per review calibration.
