findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a body according to HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and most HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks silently drop or reject a body on GET. All relevant inputs (query, limit, page, expand) are already correctly declared as query parameters, so the request body declaration is entirely spurious and may confuse code generators into emitting incorrect client code.
findings.rationale: GET requests carrying a body violate HTTP semantics and cause client/proxy interoperability issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove spurious empty requestBody from GET /v1/customers/search

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (min/max not encoded)
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states "Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10", but the schema only specifies `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` value. This means validation tools, SDK generators, and documentation renderers cannot enforce or display these bounds; client libraries will silently accept out-of-range values. The documented constraint should be encoded directly in the schema.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are a high-leverage finding category; documented min/max/default must be encoded in the schema to enable validation and correct codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Response schema missing `required` entries for `next_page` and `total_count`
findings.narration: The 200 response schema's `required` array omits `next_page` and `total_count`, yet both fields are documented without any indication they are optional or conditional. Consumers cannot safely rely on their presence without explicit inclusion in `required`. At minimum, `next_page` is critical for pagination correctness — if it is always returned (even as null), it should be marked required. If it can be absent, a `nullable: true` with an explicit note is the right pattern but it should still be in `required` since it is always included in the payload (even as null per the existing `nullable: true`).
findings.rationale: Fields already marked `nullable: true` are still always present in the response payload; they belong in `required` to ensure type-safe deserialization in SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add next_page and total_count to the required array of the 200 response schema

findings.title: GET operation includes a request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content. While the schema is empty (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`), the presence of a request body on a GET operation is contrary to HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 discourages message bodies on GET) and will confuse many HTTP clients, proxies, and OpenAPI tooling. The body carries no data and serves no purpose; it should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty, non-functional body on a GET endpoint is misleading and can cause client-side issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically incorrect request body from the GET operation.

findings.title: Customer path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_XXXXXXXXXX`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the customer resource, and client-side validation cannot catch malformed IDs early. Adding a pattern such as `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,255}$` would make the contract self-documenting and enable stronger validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format/ref prevent typed relationships in codegen and weaken validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the customer path parameter to reflect Stripe's ID format.

findings.title: Card CVC and account number fields lack writeOnly flag
findings.narration: The `card.cvc` field (card verification value) and `bank_account.account_number` field are sensitive payment credentials submitted in the request body. Neither field is marked `writeOnly: true` in the schema. Without `writeOnly`, code-generation tools may include these fields in response deserialization models, and documentation tools will not flag them as input-only sensitive data. This is a security hygiene issue: tools that generate client SDKs or mock responses may inadvertently expose or round-trip these values.
findings.rationale: Sensitive credential fields should be marked writeOnly to prevent codegen tools from exposing them in response models and to signal to API consumers that these values are never returned.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to card.cvc and bank_account.account_number fields

findings.title: invoice_prefix pattern constraint described in prose but not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The description for `invoice_prefix` states "Must be 3–12 uppercase letters or numbers" but the schema only has `maxLength: 5000` with no `minLength`, no `maxLength` reflecting the 12-character limit, and no `pattern` to enforce uppercase alphanumeric characters. This means any string up to 5000 characters passes schema validation, and the actual constraint is invisible to validators, code generators, and client developers unless they read the prose description carefully. A `pattern: "^[A-Z0-9]{3,12}$"` and corrected `minLength`/`maxLength` would encode this rule properly.
findings.rationale: Constraints expressed only in prose are ignored by validators and code generators. The rule 'must be 3–12 uppercase letters or numbers' is a high-leverage machine-enforceable constraint.
findings.patchSummary: Encode invoice_prefix constraint (3–12 uppercase alphanumeric) as minLength, maxLength, and pattern

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields reference Stripe resource IDs — `default_alipay_account`, `default_bank_account`, `default_card`, `default_source`, and `invoice_settings.default_payment_method` — but are typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe resource IDs have well-known prefixes (e.g. `ba_`, `card_`, `pm_`, `aliacc_`) and predictable formats. Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `format` (e.g. `format: stripe-id`), codegen tools cannot model typed relationships between resources, and client-side validation is impossible. At minimum, a pattern or `x-stripeResourceId` extension should be used to distinguish these from arbitrary strings.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow any string to be submitted where a specific resource reference is expected.
findings.patchSummary: Add x-stripeResourceType extension to resource ID fields to enable typed cross-resource relationships

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body schema is complex, containing nested objects for `address`, `bank_account`, `card`, `cash_balance`, `invoice_settings`, `shipping`, and `tax`, along with multiple `anyOf` unions that use empty-string sentinels for clearing fields. There are no examples at the operation level, request body level, or on individual complex properties. Without examples, consumers must infer from the schema alone how to construct a valid update payload — particularly for the anyOf/empty-string-clearing pattern, which is a non-obvious Stripe convention. Adding at least one representative example would significantly improve usability.
findings.rationale: Complex schemas with non-obvious patterns like empty-string clearing of optional fields greatly benefit from examples; their absence forces developers to reverse-engineer intent from schema alone.

Adding a pattern like `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]{1,}$` would encode the relationship and allow immediate validation.
findings.rationale: A cross-resource ID typed as a bare string with no pattern or format prevents typed relationship modeling in generated SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to customer path parameter to encode Stripe ID format.

findings.title: DELETE returns 200 instead of semantically correct 204 for a deletion response
findings.narration: The operation returns HTTP 200 with a response body. For a permanent deletion that cannot be undone, HTTP 204 No Content is the more idiomatic REST choice when no meaningful body is returned, or if Stripe intentionally returns a deleted-object confirmation body, the description should clearly state what the shape is. The cyclic schema reference prevents any inspection of the actual response shape, so it is ambiguous whether the 200 body is substantive (e.g. `{ deleted: true, id: ... }`) or vestigial. If a body is intentionally returned, this is acceptable, but the response description 'Successful response.' is too sparse to communicate intent and should at minimum note what object is returned.
findings.rationale: REST semantics recommend 204 for delete operations with empty bodies; if 200 is used, the response body purpose must be clearly described.

patchOps.value: Successful response. Returns a confirmation object with `id` and `deleted: true` upon successful customer deletion.

findings.patchSummary: Improve 200 response description to clarify the deleted-object confirmation body.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints encoded. This means validation tools and generated clients cannot enforce the documented constraint, and the default is not machine-readable.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but not encoded in the schema cannot be enforced by validators or surfaced in generated SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: invoice filter parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `invoice` query parameter is documented as filtering transactions related to a specific invoice, but its schema is `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint and no `pattern` (e.g. `^in_`) or other indicator that it is a resource ID. Codegen tools and client SDKs cannot infer it represents an Invoice resource reference.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships to referenced resources.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to invoice parameter to mark it as an Invoice resource ID

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema is included on this GET operation. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). While Stripe does use form-encoded bodies on some GET endpoints for historical reasons, an explicitly empty body schema with `required: false` serves no purpose and may confuse consumers and intermediaries.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate HTTP semantics and can cause issues with proxies, caches, and generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Missing `writeOnly` or format hint on `amount` — sign convention undocumented
findings.narration: The `amount` field description says it applies to the customer's credit balance, but it does not clarify whether negative values are accepted (to debit) or only positive values (to credit). The Stripe API in practice accepts negative integers to represent debits. Without a `minimum`/`maximum` constraint or explicit prose on sign convention, SDK generators and API consumers have no machine-readable signal about the valid range. This is a clarity and risk issue: a consumer might assume only positive values are valid and fail to apply negative adjustments.
findings.rationale: Constraint information (valid sign, min/max) should be encoded in the schema, not left implicit, to avoid integration errors.

patchOps.value: The integer amount in **cents (or local equivalent)** to apply to the customer's credit balance. A positive value credits the customer, a negative value debits the customer. Cannot be zero.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify that `amount` can be negative (debit) or positive (credit) and must be non-zero.

findings.title: `customer` path parameter typed as plain string with no pattern or format
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is a reference to a Customer resource (Stripe customer IDs follow the pattern `cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+`), but it is declared as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. No `pattern` or `format` is provided. Codegen tools cannot infer the relationship to the Customer resource, and client-side validation cannot reject obviously malformed IDs before making a network call. Adding a `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) would close this gap.
findings.rationale: Resource-ID path parameters typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent codegen from building typed client relationships and inhibit early validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `customer` path parameter to reflect Stripe's ID format.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx response definitions (e.g. 400, 402, 404)
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` and a catch-all `default` error response. While the `default` technically covers all error status codes, the absence of explicit 4xx entries (400 Bad Request for validation failures, 404 for unknown customer, 402 for card errors) means documentation tooling cannot surface per-status semantics, and API gateway routing rules cannot distinguish error classes. For a write operation that creates a financial record, at minimum a 400 and 404 should be enumerated explicitly.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx definitions improve generated documentation accuracy and allow gateway/middleware to apply per-status policies.

value.description: Bad request — validation error (e.g. missing required field, invalid currency).
Customer not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the catch-all default.

findings.title: Path parameter 'customer' missing format/pattern — plain string with no ID constraint
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, SDK/codegen tools treat this as a free-form string, losing the typed relationship to the Customer resource. The `transaction` parameter has the same issue — balance transaction IDs follow the `cbtxn_...` pattern and carry no constraint at all (not even a maxLength).
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters that encode a cross-resource reference should carry a `pattern` or at minimum a `format` annotation so codegen can build typed relationships and client-side validation can pre-screen obvious bad values.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to 'customer' and 'transaction' path params to encode resource-ID relationships.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per RFC 9110; many HTTP clients, proxies, and load balancers drop or reject GET bodies. While Stripe uses this pattern across its spec (likely for the `expand` parameter), the `expand` array is already correctly modeled as a query parameter here, so the empty body serves no purpose and adds noise. It may confuse client generators into adding body-serialization logic for a GET call.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 states GET requests have no defined semantics for a message body. An empty, additionalProperties-false schema that contributes nothing to the API surface should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, no-op requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter 'customer' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot establish a typed relationship to the Customer resource, and clients cannot validate the ID format client-side before making the request. This reduces tooling value and increases the risk of passing an ID from the wrong resource type.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent code-gen tools from building typed relationships and allow silent misuse.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'customer' path parameter schema

findings.title: Path parameter 'transaction' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `transaction` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe customer balance transaction IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cbtxn_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot establish a typed relationship to the CustomerBalanceTransaction resource, and no client-side validation of the ID format is possible.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent code-gen tools from building typed relationships and allow silent misuse.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'transaction' path parameter schema

findings.title: GET list endpoint carries an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though the schema is empty (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`) and the body is marked `required: false`. GET requests with a body are semantically incorrect per RFC 9110; many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will strip or reject GET bodies. The body adds no value here and may confuse code-generators and SDK authors into thinking a form payload is expected.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 states that a GET request has no defined semantics for a request body. Having one — even empty and optional — violates HTTP semantics and can cause interoperability problems.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically incorrect requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` query parameter states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema (`type: integer`) carries no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. Without these constraints, clients sending `limit=0` or `limit=999` will not receive schema-level validation feedback, and code generators cannot enforce the documented bounds. The prose documents the rule but the schema does not encode it.
findings.rationale: A conditional or bounded rule described in prose but absent from the schema cannot be validated by tooling, increasing the chance of invalid requests reaching the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 and maximum: 100 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: customer path parameter lacks resource ID format/pattern hint
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, code generators treat this as any arbitrary string, losing the ability to build typed cross-resource references. Other Stripe list endpoints that accept customer IDs typically constrain the shape further.
findings.rationale: A resource ID typed as a bare string without pattern or format prevents code-generation tools from building typed relationships and makes it harder for API consumers to identify the correct ID format.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the customer path parameter to reflect Stripe's cus_ prefix format.

findings.title: Description documents credit card creation; endpoint path and operationId indicate bank account creation
findings.narration: The operation's `description` reads: 'When you create a new credit card, you must specify a customer or recipient on which to create it.' However, the path is `/v1/customers/{customer}/bank_accounts` and the operationId is `PostCustomersCustomerBankAccounts`. This is a classic copy-paste bug — the description documents the card-creation endpoint, not the bank-account endpoint. The summary also says 'Create a card', compounding the confusion. Consumers reading the spec will be misled about what resource this endpoint creates, what validation rules apply, and what response to expect.
findings.rationale: A description that documents the wrong resource is a clarity defect that can mislead SDK consumers, documentation generators, and developers integrating the API.

patchOps.value:
When you create a new bank account source for a customer, you must specify the customer on which to create it.

If the customer has no default source, then the new bank account will become the default. However, if the customer already has a default, then it will not change. To change the default, you should update the customer to have a new default_source.

findings.patchSummary: Fix copy-paste description and summary that document card creation instead of bank account creation

findings.title: card.cvc field is missing writeOnly flag — exposes sensitive PAN-adjacent data in schema
findings.narration: The `card` object in the request body includes a `cvc` field and a `number` field (full card number), neither of which is marked `writeOnly: true`. While these are request-only fields, OpenAPI's `writeOnly` keyword exists precisely to signal that a field must never appear in a response. Without it, code generators may include these fields in bidirectional model definitions, potentially causing accidental serialization of sensitive card data in logs, client caches, or response objects. The card `number` field (PAN) is particularly sensitive.
findings.rationale: PCI-DSS and general security best practices require that full PANs and CVCs are never returned. The writeOnly flag encodes this constraint in the schema so tooling enforces it.
findings.patchSummary: Mark card number, CVC, and bank account_number as writeOnly to prevent exposure in generated model serialization

findings.title: No examples provided for complex anyOf request body fields
findings.narration: The request body contains several complex fields (`bank_account`, `card`) that use `anyOf` to accept either a plain string token or a structured object. There are no `examples` or `example` annotations on these fields or on the request body itself. Without examples, developers cannot easily distinguish how to pass a Stripe.js token versus raw bank/card details, and tooling like Postman or Stoplight cannot auto-generate meaningful try-it-out requests. An example for each branch of the `anyOf` (token string vs. object) would substantially improve usability.
findings.rationale: Complex anyOf schemas without examples are a common source of integration confusion and increase support burden.

token.summary: Using a Stripe.js bank account token

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating token-based and raw bank account detail submission

findings.title: customer path parameter typed as unconstrained string — should have an ID pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or explicit format, code generators and validators cannot distinguish a valid customer ID from arbitrary strings, and cannot surface early errors. A `pattern` such as `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,255}$` would encode the relationship and allow client-side pre-validation.
findings.rationale: ID fields lacking a pattern or format lose the ability to participate in typed codegen relationships and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add Stripe customer ID pattern constraint and reduce maxLength from 5000 to a reasonable bound

findings.title: Description references wrong resource context ('sources stored on a Customer')
findings.narration: The operation description says 'you can see the 10 most recent sources stored on a Customer directly on the object, but you can also retrieve details about a specific bank account stored on the Stripe account.' The phrase 'stored on the Stripe account' appears to be a copy-paste error — this endpoint retrieves a bank account stored on a *Customer*, not on the Stripe account (which is the Connect usage). The description conflates two distinct resources and misleads the reader about what this endpoint does.
findings.rationale: Inaccurate description creates confusion about whether the retrieved bank account belongs to the customer or the platform account. Developers may misuse the endpoint.

patchOps.value: Retrieves a specific bank account stored on a Customer. By default, the 10 most recent bank accounts are included on the Customer object, but this endpoint lets you fetch the details of any bank account by its ID.

findings.patchSummary: Fix description to correctly reference the customer-owned bank account, not the Stripe account.

findings.title: Path parameter 'customer' lacks format/pattern for typed resource ID
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint, but it represents a Stripe Customer ID (format: `cus_XXXX`). Without a `pattern` or documented format, code-generation tools cannot establish a typed relationship between this parameter and the Customer resource, and client SDKs will treat it as an arbitrary string. The same applies to the `id` parameter, which should reference a bank account ID (format: `ba_XXXX`).
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent codegen tools from creating typed cross-resource relationships and omit validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID patterns to customer and id path parameters to encode the resource type relationship.

findings.title: Empty requestBody on a GET operation is superfluous
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1); many HTTP clients and intermediaries will drop or reject bodies on GET requests. The presence of this empty request body is confusing and technically incorrect.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 discourages request bodies on GET; the body here carries no fields at all, making it both semantically wrong and functionally useless.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Request body mixes bank account and card fields — no schema discrimination
findings.narration: The endpoint is named `bank_accounts/{id}` and the description says 'Update a specified source', yet the request body schema contains fields that are clearly card-specific (`exp_month`, `exp_year`, `address_city`, `address_country`, `address_line1`, `address_line2`, `address_state`, `address_zip`, `name` as 'Cardholder name') alongside bank-account-specific fields (`account_holder_name`, `account_holder_type`). There is no `oneOf`/`discriminator` to separate these two shapes; all fields are presented as a flat optional bag. This makes it impossible for API consumers or code-generation tools to know which fields are valid for a bank account vs. a card, and which combinations are mutually exclusive. The description also says 'Update a specified source' rather than 'Update a bank account', confirming this is a shared handler whose schema was never split per resource type.
findings.rationale: Mixed schemas without discrimination cause incorrect client usage, break code-generation, and obscure which fields apply to bank accounts versus cards.

patchOps.value: Update a specified bank account for a given customer. Bank account fields: account_holder_name, account_holder_type, metadata, expand. Card fields (exp_month, exp_year, address_*, name, owner) are not applicable to bank accounts and should be removed from this schema or separated via oneOf.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify that card fields do not apply to bank_accounts and recommend oneOf discrimination

findings.title: Description refers to 'source' not 'bank account' — likely copy-paste from a generic source endpoint
findings.narration: The operation description reads 'Update a specified source for a given customer.' This is almost certainly copy-pasted from the generic `/v1/customers/{customer}/sources/{id}` endpoint. The URL specifically scopes this operation to bank accounts, so the description should say 'Update a specified bank account for a given customer.' As written, it misleads consumers about the resource being operated on.
findings.rationale: Misleading descriptions reduce developer trust and can cause incorrect integration; this is a classic copy-paste bug.

patchOps.value: Update a specified bank account for a given customer.

findings.patchSummary: Fix description to reference 'bank account' instead of 'source'

findings.title: customer and id path parameters typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter holds a Stripe customer ID (prefixed `cus_...`) and `id` holds a bank account ID (prefixed `ba_...`). Both are typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint and no `pattern` or `format`. Code-generation tools and client SDKs cannot derive the typed relationship between these parameters and the corresponding Stripe resource objects. Adding a `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for `customer`, `^ba_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for `id`) would enable input validation and improve generated SDK types.
findings.rationale: Resource-ID fields typed as plain strings prevent typed relationship inference in codegen and client validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add patterns to customer and id path parameters to reflect Stripe resource ID prefixes

findings.title: Description documents 'source' but path and operationId target 'bank_accounts'
findings.narration: The operation's description reads 'Delete a specified source for a given customer', but the endpoint path is `/v1/customers/{customer}/bank_accounts/{id}` and the operationId is `DeleteCustomersCustomerBankAccountsId`. This is a classic copy-paste bug where the description was borrowed from a sibling 'sources' endpoint. Consumers relying on the description to understand the resource being deleted will be misled into thinking this operates on generic sources rather than specifically on bank accounts.
findings.rationale: Mismatched description creates documentation confusion and may cause incorrect client code generation or SDK documentation.

patchOps.value: Delete a specified bank account for a given customer.

findings.patchSummary: Correct description from 'source' to 'bank account' to match the actual resource.

findings.title: Path parameter 'customer' typed as plain string with no format or pattern — cross-resource ID relationship not encoded
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint, with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a Customer ID schema. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix format (e.g., `cus_...`). Without a pattern or typed reference, codegen tools cannot establish the typed relationship between this parameter and the Customer resource, and validation tooling cannot reject obviously malformed IDs at the schema level.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent codegen from building typed relationships and weaken request validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the 'customer' parameter to encode the Stripe Customer ID format.

findings.title: Path parameter `customer` typed as unconstrained string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship between this parameter and the Customer resource, and callers receive no machine-readable hint about valid values. The same concern applies to the `id` parameter which references a bank account resource (typically `ba_...`).
findings.rationale: Resource-ID fields typed as plain strings without format, pattern, or $ref prevent codegen tools from modeling cross-resource relationships and offer no validation hint to API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-format patterns and tighten maxLength on customer and id path parameters

findings.title: `amounts` array lacks item count constraint (must be exactly 2 integers)
findings.narration: The description for `amounts` explicitly states "Two positive integers", but the schema imposes no `minItems`, `maxItems`, or `minimum` constraints on the array or its items. A consumer sending one amount, three amounts, or negative integers will only discover the error at runtime from the Stripe API. Encoding the cardinality and value constraints directly in the schema would allow client-side validation and accurate documentation generation.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints ('Two positive integers') that are not encoded in the schema are a high-leverage finding — they should be expressed as JSON Schema keywords so validators and codegen tools can enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Encode minItems:2, maxItems:2, and minimum:1 on amounts array per its own description

findings.title: No example provided for the `amounts` request body field
findings.narration: The `amounts` field is the key verification input and its format (two positive cent values) is non-obvious to new integrators. No example is present on the field or on the request body schema. Adding a concrete example (e.g. `[32, 45]`) would materially improve developer experience and reduce integration errors.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on non-trivial, semantically critical request fields reduce clarity and increase the chance of incorrect integration.
findings.patchSummary: Add example [32, 45] to the amounts field to illustrate cent-value microdeposit amounts

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter schema is declared as `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints, despite the description explicitly stating 'Limit can range between 1 and 100'. A client or codegen tool inspecting the schema alone would have no way to enforce these bounds without reading the prose, potentially leading to API errors or unexpected behavior when out-of-range values are submitted.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented only in prose (not encoded in the schema) are high-severity because they cannot be enforced by validators or surfaced by SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 constraints to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `customer` path parameter is a plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot establish a typed reference to the Customer resource and cannot validate the ID format client-side. This is a recurring Stripe API pattern worth flagging on write-path endpoints, but is particularly notable here since the endpoint is scoped entirely to a single customer.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and make input validation weaker.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `customer` path parameter to reflect the Stripe customer ID format.

findings.title: Raw card number (PAN) submitted in request body — `writeOnly` not set and no masking hint
findings.narration: The `card` object schema includes a `number` field (the full PAN) and a `cvc` field. Neither field is marked `writeOnly: true`, and neither carries a `format` or description hint that these values are never returned. Without `writeOnly`, code-generation tools may include these fields in deserialization paths, increasing the risk of inadvertently logging or caching raw card data. The PAN and CVC are among the most sensitive pieces of cardholder data under PCI DSS; their schema definitions should explicitly signal write-only semantics.
findings.rationale: PCI DSS and general security hygiene require that raw card numbers and CVCs never be read back from the API. `writeOnly: true` is the OpenAPI-idiomatic way to encode this, and its absence misleads generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Mark card `number` and `cvc` fields as writeOnly to prevent round-trip exposure in generated clients.

findings.title: `bank_account.account_number` missing `writeOnly` flag
findings.narration: Similarly, the inline bank account object includes `account_number` without `writeOnly: true`. Bank account numbers are sensitive financial identifiers; Stripe's own API masks them on retrieval (returning only the last 4 digits). The schema should reflect this write-only nature so generated clients do not attempt to read back the full value.
findings.rationale: Account numbers are sensitive and masked on retrieval by Stripe. `writeOnly: true` encodes this contract for code generators and validators.
findings.patchSummary: Mark bank_account `account_number` as writeOnly to reflect masked-on-retrieval semantics.

findings.title: `source` field description is a placeholder — no actionable documentation
findings.narration: The `source` field carries the description "Please refer to full documentation instead." with a link to the bare `https://api.stripe.com` domain. This provides no information to developers about what `source` accepts, how it relates to `card`, `bank_account`, or `alipay_account`, whether it is a token ID, or when it should be used over the other payment source fields. This is a copy-paste/placeholder description that must be replaced with a real explanation of the field's accepted values and relationship to the other payment source properties.
findings.rationale: A description that only says 'see the docs' gives zero value to SDK users or anyone reading the spec offline. It also hides potentially important conditional-required relationships between `source` and the other payment source fields.

patchOps.value: A payment source token (e.g. `tok_visa`) returned by Stripe.js or the Stripe mobile SDKs. Use this field as a shorthand alternative to supplying a full `card` or `bank_account` object. Exactly one of `source`, `card`, `bank_account`, or `alipay_account` should be provided.

findings.patchSummary: Replace placeholder `source` description with a meaningful explanation of accepted values and mutual-exclusivity with other source fields.

findings.title: Mutually-exclusive payment source fields not encoded in schema — prose-only constraint
findings.narration: The request body exposes four distinct ways to specify a payment source: `card`, `bank_account`, `alipay_account`, and `source`. There is no schema-level constraint enforcing that exactly one (or at most one) of these is provided. The mutual exclusivity is implied by context but never stated, even in prose. Submitting multiple source fields simultaneously would be ambiguous or erroneous. This should be modelled as a `oneOf` over the four alternatives, or at minimum documented with a prose warning; ideally a JSON Schema `oneOf` or `not` constraint should enforce it so validators can catch violations.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually-exclusive field relationships left only as implicit context are a high-leverage source of integration bugs. OpenAPI's `oneOf` exists precisely to encode this constraint.

patchOps.value: A payment source token. Exactly one of `source`, `card`, `bank_account`, or `alipay_account` must be provided.

findings.patchSummary: Document (and ideally encode via oneOf) the mutual-exclusivity of source, card, bank_account, and alipay_account.

findings.title: Path parameter `customer` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Customer resource, and client-side validation cannot catch obviously malformed IDs before the request is sent.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string without pattern/format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and reduce early validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `customer` path parameter to match Stripe customer ID format.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter (representing a card ID) is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe card IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `card_...`). Adding a pattern would improve documentation clarity, enable better client-side validation, and help codegen tools recognize this as a typed card resource reference.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields without pattern/format lose the semantic type information that codegen and validation tooling depend on.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter to match Stripe card ID format.

findings.title: exp_month and exp_year typed as string instead of integer
findings.narration: The fields `exp_month` and `exp_year` are described as numeric values ('Two digit number' and 'Four digit number' respectively) but are declared as `type: string` with a `maxLength` constraint. This is a type mismatch: numeric months and years should be `type: integer` with appropriate `minimum`/`maximum` constraints (e.g., `minimum: 1, maximum: 12` for `exp_month`, and `minimum: 2000, maximum: 2100` for `exp_year`). Using string types for these fields can lead to type confusion in codegen tools, client validation gaps, and unexpected serialization behavior.
findings.rationale: Expressing numeric values as strings is a type confusion issue. Integer constraints allow proper validation at the schema level rather than relying on server-side rejection.

This is a copy-paste issue where the description was reused from a more generic `sources` endpoint. Consumers reading the description may be confused about what resource is actually being updated, and automated documentation tools will generate misleading prose. The description should be updated to accurately reflect that this endpoint updates a card.

Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot establish typed relationships to the underlying resources, and client-side validation cannot pre-validate ID format before making the request. Adding a regex pattern such as `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and `^card_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow downstream tooling to build typed references.

findings.title: Empty request body included on a GET operation
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema is declared on this GET operation. HTTP/1.1 (RFC 7231) does not prohibit a body on GET, but it is semantically undefined, ignored by most intermediaries and proxies, and actively misleading to API consumers and tooling. Stripe's own pattern for GET operations uses query parameters exclusively. The empty body object carries no useful information and adds noise.
findings.rationale: Including a requestBody on a GET operation contradicts HTTP semantics and confuses codegen tools and documentation renderers; it should be removed.

GET requests with a request body are outside normal HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 does not prohibit it, but many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers silently discard or reject GET bodies). All parameters for this operation are already expressed as query/path parameters. The empty body serves no purpose and may confuse consumers or cause interoperability issues.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies are semantically meaningless per HTTP conventions and many clients/proxies will discard them. Advertising one in the spec creates confusion without providing value.

findings.title: url field in list response lacks pattern constraint

findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. In Stripe's API, customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength` reflecting the actual ID length, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship between this parameter and the Customer resource. The `maxLength: 5000` is almost certainly inherited from a generic string constraint rather than intentionally set for this field.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern constraints prevent codegen tools from building typed cross-resource relationships and allow unrealistically large inputs.

findings.title: Path parameter `transaction` lacks any length or format constraint

Unlike the `customer` parameter it does not even carry the generic `maxLength: 5000`. This is inconsistent with the sibling parameter and provides no guidance to consumers about the shape of a valid cash balance transaction ID.
findings.rationale: Missing constraints on ID parameters offer no validation signal to API consumers or codegen tools, reducing type safety and documentation quality.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET operation
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema is present on this GET operation. GET requests must not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1); intermediaries including proxies and CDNs may strip or reject it. Even in Stripe's convention of allowing form-encoded query parameters, these should be declared as `in: query` parameters, not as a request body. The presence of an empty request body may confuse client generators into emitting unnecessary body-handling code.
findings.rationale: GET operations must not have a request body per HTTP semantics; this can confuse HTTP clients, proxies, and SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation.

findings.title: Empty operation description provides no documentation
findings.narration: The `description` field for this GET operation is an empty string. Consumers of this API have no inline documentation explaining what a customer discount is, what the response represents, when it might be absent, or any edge cases (e.g., the discount could be null if the customer has no active discount). Given that Stripe's API surface is large and this is a read-only sub-resource endpoint, a meaningful description is important for developer experience and generated SDK documentation.
findings.rationale: An empty description is a clarity issue; developers relying on auto-generated docs or SDK tooling get no guidance on the resource semantics.

findings.title: Request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary and misleading
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is defined on this GET operation with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`). HTTP GET requests MUST NOT include a request body per RFC 7231, and several HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will either reject or silently drop it. While Stripe's API pattern appears to use form-encoded bodies on GET requests for `expand`, the `expand` parameter is already correctly declared as a query parameter here, making the empty request body doubly redundant. Its presence is misleading and may confuse code generators and API clients.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies violate HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and several intermediaries drop them; an empty body here adds noise with no benefit.

Without a `pattern` or at minimum a narrower `maxLength`, the schema gives no guidance to clients or validators about what constitutes a valid customer ID. Code generation tools also cannot build a typed relationship between this parameter and a Customer resource. A pattern such as `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]{1,255}$` would meaningfully constrain the value and signal the cross-resource reference.

findings.title: DELETE response should be 204 No Content or return a typed deleted object, not a 200 with a cyclic schema
findings.narration: This endpoint removes the currently applied discount on a customer. According to REST semantics, a successful DELETE that returns no meaningful body should use 204 No Content. If Stripe intentionally returns a deleted-discount confirmation object (as it does in several other delete endpoints), the 200 response schema should reference a concrete `deleted_discount` shape rather than the opaque cyclic marker. As specified, consumers cannot determine what, if anything, is returned on success.
findings.rationale: Unclear response semantics (200 vs 204, and a cyclic/opaque schema) prevent clients from handling the response correctly and reduce API discoverability.
findings.patchSummary: Clarify 200 response shape with a concrete deleted_discount schema or switch to 204.

findings.title: POST used for a retrieve/upsert operation that is effectively idempotent
findings.narration: The operation description explicitly states 'we will return the same funding instructions each time' — meaning once created, subsequent calls always return the same resource. This is effectively a safe, idempotent retrieval operation disguised as a POST. While GET cannot carry a body, using POST for what is semantically a 'get or create' pattern that never mutates on repeat calls is a design smell. HTTP semantics suggest this should either be a GET with query parameters, or if a body is unavoidable, at least be documented as idempotent via the `x-idempotent` or similar vendor extension so clients and caching layers can treat it appropriately.
findings.rationale: POST implies non-idempotent state mutation; the operation description contradicts that by guaranteeing the same result on every invocation. This misleads client developers about side-effect expectations.
findings.patchSummary: Mark operation as idempotent via vendor extension to clarify repeat-call semantics.

findings.title: customer path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_XXXX`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools and validators cannot build a typed reference to the Customer resource, and client SDKs cannot validate the value before sending the request. Adding a `pattern` such as `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would make the constraint machine-readable and improve SDK ergonomics.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed only as plain strings without pattern or format lose type-relationship information, per the review guidelines.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to customer path parameter to encode the Stripe customer ID format.

findings.title: bank_transfer.type and bank_transfer.eu_bank_transfer conditional relationship not machine-encoded
findings.narration: The `bank_transfer` object requires a `type` field (one of `eu_bank_transfer`, `gb_bank_transfer`, etc.) and separately accepts an `eu_bank_transfer` sub-object. The natural semantic is that `eu_bank_transfer` is required when `type == 'eu_bank_transfer'` and must not be present otherwise. This conditional relationship is entirely implicit — the schema neither uses `if/then/else` nor `oneOf` to enforce it. As a result, a client could submit `type: gb_bank_transfer` alongside a populated `eu_bank_transfer` object and only receive a runtime error from the server. Similarly, a client submitting `type: eu_bank_transfer` without the required `country` sub-object will only fail server-side.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields documented only implicitly (by proximity and naming) should be encoded as JSON Schema if/then or oneOf, per the review guidelines on field-relationship rules in prose.

Codegen tools and client SDKs cannot infer that these are Stripe resource identifiers, preventing typed relationship mapping and reducing the utility of generated clients. Adding a `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) or a recognized `format` (e.g. `format: "stripe-customer-id"`) encodes the domain constraint in the schema rather than leaving it implicit.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and omit useful validation.

findings.title: No explicit 404 response defined for unknown customer or payment_method
findings.narration: The operation retrieves a specific PaymentMethod for a specific Customer via path parameters. When either the customer or the payment method does not exist (or the payment method does not belong to the customer), the API will naturally return a 404. This case is entirely absent from the `responses` object — only a `200` and a generic `default` error response are declared. Consumers cannot distinguish a 404 (not found / wrong ownership) from a 400 (bad request) or 401 (unauthorized) without explicit response codes. The `default` bucket is a catch-all that does not communicate intent. A dedicated `404` entry should be added.
findings.rationale: Omitting a 404 for a resource-fetch-by-ID endpoint leaves clients unable to handle the most common non-success path correctly.

This means clients and validators will accept values like 0, -1, or 10000 without complaint, and the server must silently clamp or reject them. Encoding the constraint in the schema aligns documentation with enforcement and enables client-side validation.

findings.title: Card `number` and `cvc` fields missing `writeOnly` marker
findings.narration: The inline `card` object schema includes `number` (full PAN) and `cvc` fields typed as plain strings with no `writeOnly: true` annotation. According to OpenAPI 3.x, `writeOnly: true` signals to code generators, documentation tools, and API gateways that these fields must never be included in responses or logs. Without it, generated SDKs may inadvertently echo these values, and documentation tools will not visually distinguish them as input-only sensitive credentials. This is a direct PCI-DSS concern: raw card numbers flowing through an API should always be marked to prevent accidental exposure.
findings.rationale: Raw PAN and CVC are the most sensitive card data possible. `writeOnly: true` is the OpenAPI mechanism to prevent them from appearing in response schemas or generated response models.
findings.patchSummary: Mark card `number` and `cvc` as writeOnly to prevent echoing in responses/codegen.

findings.title: Bank account `account_number` field missing `writeOnly` marker
findings.narration: Similarly, the inline `bank_account` object schema contains `account_number` as a plain string with no `writeOnly: true`. Bank account numbers are sensitive financial identifiers that should never appear in serialised responses. Marking them `writeOnly` ensures code generators do not include them in response types and documentation tools flag them as input-only, reducing the risk of unintentional data leakage.
findings.rationale: Bank account numbers are sensitive PII/financial data. `writeOnly: true` prevents codegen tools from including the field in response models.
findings.patchSummary: Mark bank account `account_number` as writeOnly.

findings.title: Exactly-one-of constraint between source fields expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The request body accepts `alipay_account`, `bank_account`, `card`, and `source` as mutually alternative ways to provide a payment source, but the schema allows all four to be submitted simultaneously with no validation rule preventing it. The API semantics clearly require exactly one (or at most one) of these to be provided, but this constraint lives only in human-readable documentation outside this spec. Encoding the mutual exclusivity as a JSON Schema `oneOf` or a combination of `not` + `dependencies` would allow client-side validators and SDK generators to enforce the constraint automatically and surface it clearly in generated documentation.
findings.rationale: Conditional required/exclusive field relationships must be encoded in the schema, not left as implicit documentation, to enable automated validation and clear SDK generation.

findings.narration: The `id` path parameter represents a source or payment-method ID (e.g., `src_...`, `card_...`, `ba_...`) but is typed only as `type: string` with a `maxLength`. Without a `pattern` or description of valid prefixes, codegen tools treat it as an arbitrary string, losing the semantic link to the underlying resource type. A description or pattern documenting the accepted ID prefixes would significantly improve usability.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships.

patchOps.value: The ID of the source to retrieve. Accepts IDs with prefixes such as `src_`, `card_`, or `ba_`.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to 'id' path parameter documenting accepted Stripe source ID prefixes.

findings.title: GET request body is unnecessary and misleading
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared for this GET operation containing an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema with `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients and proxies will silently drop it. The presence of this empty request body adds noise to generated clients and documentation without providing any value.
findings.rationale: GET operations should not have request bodies; this violates HTTP semantics and can confuse client generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation to conform to HTTP semantics.

findings.title: exp_month and exp_year typed as string instead of integer
findings.narration: The fields `exp_month` and `exp_year` are described as numeric values ('Two digit number' and 'Four digit number' respectively) but are declared as `type: string` with `maxLength: 5000`. This is a type confusion issue: card expiration month and year are numeric values and should be typed as `integer` with appropriate `minimum`/`maximum` constraints (e.g., month: 1–12, year: four-digit positive integer). Using `string` allows invalid inputs like 'abc' to pass schema validation and forces API consumers and codegen tools to treat them as strings rather than integers, which is semantically incorrect.
findings.rationale: String type for a field explicitly described as a number is a type mismatch that weakens validation and misleads consumers and code generators.

value.description: Two digit number representing the card's expiration month.
Four digit number representing the card's expiration year.

findings.patchSummary: Change exp_month and exp_year from string to integer with min/max constraints

findings.title: customer and id path parameters lack format or pattern hinting at resource ID type
findings.narration: The `customer` and `id` path parameters are typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. These are clearly Stripe resource identifiers (customer IDs typically start with `cus_`, source/card IDs with `src_` or `card_`). Without a `pattern` or at least a descriptive `format`, codegen tools cannot infer these are typed resource references and may generate overly generic code. Additionally, `maxLength: 5000` is far too permissive for what are fixed-prefix identifiers typically under 64 characters. This makes the schema a weak validator and obscures the cross-resource relationship.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings with no pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow wildly invalid values through schema validation.

patchOps.value: The identifier of the customer whose source is being updated. Typically prefixed with `cus_`.
The identifier of the source or card to update. Typically prefixed with `src_` or `card_`.

findings.patchSummary: Add descriptions and tighten maxLength on customer and id path parameters

findings.title: Mixed bank-account and card fields in a single schema without conditional constraints encoded
findings.narration: The request body mixes fields that apply exclusively to bank accounts (`account_holder_name`, `account_holder_type`) with fields that apply exclusively to cards (`address_city`, `address_country`, `address_line1`, `address_line2`, `address_state`, `address_zip`, `exp_month`, `exp_year`, `name`) and fields that apply to Sources (`owner`). The schema provides no `oneOf`/`if-then-else` or `dependencies` to enforce which fields are valid depending on the source type. Prose documentation (not present here) is the only guide. This means a client could submit `exp_month` alongside `account_holder_type` without schema validation raising an error, and codegen tools see a flat, unconditionally optional bag of unrelated fields.
findings.rationale: Conditional field applicability expressed only in prose (or not at all) instead of schema constraints is a high-leverage design finding — it weakens both validation and client SDK generation.

patchOps.value: Update fields for a customer source. Fields `account_holder_name` and `account_holder_type` apply only to bank account sources. Fields `address_*`, `exp_month`, `exp_year`, and `name` apply only to card sources. The `owner` field applies to Source objects. Ideally, use a `oneOf` or `if/then/else` to enforce mutual exclusivity per source type.

findings.patchSummary: Add schema-level description noting conditional field applicability per source type

findings.title: No example provided for the complex request body
findings.narration: The request body schema contains numerous optional fields spanning multiple source types (bank account, card, Source) with no example illustrating a representative update. Consumers and documentation generators have no concrete reference for how to form a valid request, making this operation harder to integrate correctly. At minimum, two examples should be provided: one for updating a card, one for updating a bank account source.
findings.rationale: Complex multi-type request bodies without examples increase integration friction and documentation gaps.
findings.patchSummary: Add examples for card and bank account source update requests

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter representing the source ID is typed as a bare `type: string` with no `maxLength`, `pattern`, or format hint. Source IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix convention (e.g., `src_`, `card_`, `ba_`). Without a pattern or at least a maxLength, codegen tools cannot validate or type this relationship properly, and clients may send garbage values that only fail server-side.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without constraints prevent codegen from building typed relationships and allow silent validation gaps.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength:5000 to `id` path parameter schema, matching `customer` param convention.

findings.title: DELETE operation returns 200 instead of 204 for deletion
findings.narration: This endpoint deletes a customer source and returns HTTP 200 with a response body. While Stripe's API pattern typically returns a deleted-object envelope (with `deleted: true`) on 200, the more idiomatic and widely understood REST convention for a successful deletion with no meaningful body would be 204 No Content. However, since Stripe intentionally returns a body confirming deletion, the real concern is that the response schema is fully cyclic (`$ref: '#cyclic'`) and cannot be inspected. Consumers have no way to know the shape of the deletion confirmation object from the spec alone, making the 200 response effectively opaque.
findings.rationale: A 200 response with an anyOf of two cyclic refs provides no usable schema information to clients or codegen tools. At minimum, an inline or referenced schema should be resolvable.
findings.patchSummary: No mechanical patch possible; cyclic refs should be replaced with resolvable $refs to deleted-object schemas.

findings.title: Path parameter `customer` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Based on Stripe's naming conventions, this field references a Customer resource and should carry a `pattern` (e.g., `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at minimum a description clarifying the expected ID format. Without this, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Customer resource, and callers have no machine-readable hint about the expected identifier format.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed relationships in generated clients.

patchOps.value: The ID of the customer whose bank account source is being verified. Must begin with `cus_`.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to `customer` path parameter for typed resource reference.

findings.title: `amounts` array items missing minimum/maximum value constraints
findings.narration: The `amounts` field is described as 'Two positive integers, in cents', yet the schema has no `minimum` constraint on array items (they could be zero or negative), no `maxItems`/`minItems` constraints enforcing exactly two values, and no upper bound. The description encodes business rules ('two positive integers') that should be machine-readable. A caller could submit an empty array, a single value, or three values without any schema-level rejection.
findings.rationale: Business rules stated only in prose (exactly two items, must be positive) should be encoded as `minItems`, `maxItems`, and `minimum` to enable validation at the client and gateway levels.
findings.patchSummary: Encode `amounts` array constraints (minItems:2, maxItems:2, items minimum:1) in schema.

findings.title: Missing example on `amounts` request field
findings.narration: The `amounts` field represents microdeposit cent values (e.g., `[32, 45]`) and is central to the verification flow, yet there is no example provided in the schema or at the media-type level. An example would substantially improve developer experience for this security-sensitive verification action, where wrong input results in failed verification and potential account lockout.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on critical, non-obvious fields reduce developer ergonomics and increase integration errors.
findings.patchSummary: Add example [32, 45] to the `amounts` property to illustrate microdeposit cent values.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter is simply `{ "type": "integer" }` — no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` are encoded. This means API clients and generated SDKs have no machine-readable enforcement of these constraints. A caller could send `limit=0` or `limit=9999` without any schema-level warning.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented only in prose cannot be validated by tooling. The minimum, maximum, and default values should be encoded directly in the schema.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary
findings.narration: This GET operation declares a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema that contains no properties (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers strip or reject bodies on GET requests. Having an empty, closed request body object on a read-only list endpoint is misleading and may cause issues with strict clients.
findings.rationale: GET semantics do not support a request body. The empty body definition adds confusion with no benefit and should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: customer path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe customer IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_XXXXXXXXXX`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Customer resource, and input validation is limited. Cross-referencing path parameters to their resource type is a recommended practice for strongly-typed SDK generation.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters should carry at minimum a pattern constraint so tooling and callers can validate the expected format.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to customer path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format

findings.title: Conditional mutual-exclusion rules for trial fields encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The descriptions for `trial_end`, `trial_from_plan`, and `trial_period_days` contain important mutual-exclusion and conditional-required rules that exist only in prose: (1) `trial_from_plan` says 'Setting this flag to `true` together with `trial_end` is not allowed'; (2) `trial_period_days` says it always overwrites any trials from a subscribed plan. These constraints should be encoded in JSON Schema using `not` / `if-then-else` / `dependencies` so validators and code generators can enforce them automatically rather than relying on developers reading the description text.
findings.rationale: Machine-readable constraints enable client-side validation, better SDK generation, and clearer contract enforcement. Prose-only rules are invisible to tooling.

value.description: trial_end must not be set when trial_from_plan is true

findings.patchSummary: Encode trial_from_plan + trial_end mutual-exclusion as JSON Schema if/then/not

findings.title: `payment_behavior` enum includes `pending_if_incomplete` which is invalid on create
findings.narration: The description for `payment_behavior` explicitly states: '`pending_if_incomplete` is only used with updates and cannot be passed when creating a Subscription.' Despite this, the enum lists `pending_if_incomplete` as a valid value. Accepting an invalid value at the schema level and then rejecting it at runtime creates a confusing developer experience; the value should be removed from the enum or a separate schema used for the create vs update operation.
findings.rationale: Including a value in the enum that the API will always reject at runtime for this specific operation creates misleading documentation and forces clients to rely on runtime errors rather than spec validation.
findings.patchSummary: Remove pending_if_incomplete from payment_behavior enum on the create endpoint

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain `string` without pattern or format
findings.narration: Several fields clearly reference Stripe resource IDs but are declared as bare `type: string` with no `pattern`, `format`, or `$ref`: `customer` (path parameter), `default_payment_method`, `default_source`, `transfer_data.destination`, `automatic_tax.liability.account`, `invoice_settings.issuer.account`, and various `coupon`, `discount`, `promotion_code`, `price`, `product` fields inside nested objects. Stripe IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `cus_`, `pm_`, `src_`, `acct_`). Without any constraint, codegen tools treat these as arbitrary strings and cannot build typed resource relationships.
findings.rationale: Typed resource ID fields improve SDK ergonomics, enable cross-reference validation in tooling, and reduce integration errors from passing wrong ID types.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID patterns to customer path param and key resource ID string fields

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body
findings.narration: This operation has an exceptionally large and deeply nested request body with many interacting fields (items with price_data, payment_settings with per-payment-method options, trial settings, etc.) but provides zero examples. Developers integrating this endpoint face significant cognitive overhead without at least one representative example showing a minimal subscription creation and one showing a more complete use case such as a metered subscription with a trial period.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies without examples significantly increase integration time and error rates. OpenAPI supports both operation-level and field-level examples.

subscription_with_trial.summary: Create a subscription with a trial period

findings.patchSummary: Add minimal and trial-with-items request body examples to the operation

Codegen tools cannot infer these are resource identifiers or validate their structure. Adding a pattern constraint (e.g. `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) and/or a vendor `x-stripeResource` annotation would make the relationship explicit and allow client generators to build typed wrappers.
findings.rationale: Untyped resource ID strings prevent code generators from building typed relationships and miss basic input validation.
