findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema is defined on this GET operation. The HTTP specification strongly discourages GET requests carrying a body, and many HTTP clients and proxies silently strip or reject GET bodies. This declaration adds noise to generated clients, may confuse SDK generators into emitting body-sending code, and signals a design inconsistency. The `requestBody` block should be removed entirely from this operation.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1) and mislead codegen tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Cryptic operationId with internal implementation detail exposed
findings.narration: The operationId `GetCustomersCustomerSubscriptionsSubscriptionExposedId` leaks the internal naming artifact `ExposedId` (likely reflecting an internal `subscription_exposed_id` field name). Public SDK consumers and documentation readers will see this as a confusing, overly verbose identifier. A cleaner id like `GetCustomerSubscription` or `RetrieveCustomerSubscription` would align with the human-readable `summary` already present and produce better method names in generated SDKs.
findings.rationale: OperationIds that expose internal naming artifacts produce awkward SDK method names and confuse API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Rename operationId to RetrieveCustomerSubscription to remove internal artifact

findings.title: Conditional field relationship between `trial_end` and `trial_from_plan` encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `trial_from_plan` states: 'Setting this flag to `true` together with `trial_end` is not allowed.' This mutual-exclusion constraint is expressed only in natural language. Client code generators, validation libraries, and SDK authors cannot mechanically derive or enforce the constraint from the schema alone. The relationship should be encoded as a JSON Schema `not` / `dependencies` construct or as a top-level `if/then/else` or by annotating both fields with a shared `x-mutuallyExclusive` extension at minimum.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually-exclusive field rules expressed only in prose are a well-known failure mode. Codegen tools and validators ignore prose, so the constraint is invisible to automated tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add a JSON Schema `dependencies` rule to enforce that `trial_end` and `trial_from_plan=true` are mutually exclusive.

findings.title: `days_until_due` conditional requirement on `collection_method` is prose-only
findings.narration: The description for `days_until_due` states: 'Valid only for subscriptions where `collection_method` is set to `send_invoice`.' This is a conditional-required / conditional-valid constraint that lives solely in prose. When `collection_method` is `charge_automatically` (the default), passing `days_until_due` is silently invalid or ignored. Without a machine-readable encoding (e.g., `if collection_method=charge_automatically then not required days_until_due`, or an `x-requires` annotation), automated validators and SDK builders cannot surface this constraint.
findings.rationale: Conditional field validity expressed only in descriptions is invisible to schema validators and codegen tools, leading to silent API errors for integrators.
findings.patchSummary: Encode `days_until_due` as valid only when `collection_method=send_invoice` using `if/then`.

findings.title: Resource-ID fields typed as plain `string` with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that clearly reference other Stripe resources are typed as bare `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`: `customer` (path param), `subscription_exposed_id` (path param), `default_payment_method`, `default_source` (anyOf branch), `items[].id`, `add_invoice_items[].price`, `add_invoice_items[].price_data.product`, `items[].price`, `items[].price_data.product`, `transfer_data.destination`, `automatic_tax.liability.account`, `invoice_settings.issuer.account`. Without at least a `pattern` (e.g., `^(cus|sub|pm|src|prod|price)_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) or a named format, codegen tools cannot distinguish these from arbitrary strings, which prevents building typed, navigable client SDKs.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings prevent codegen tools from building typed client relationships and make spec-driven mocking imprecise.
findings.patchSummary: Add `x-stripeResource` (or pattern/format) annotations to resource-ID string fields so codegen can build typed references.

findings.title: No 4xx error response definitions beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The responses block contains only a `200` success and a `default` error catch-all. For an update endpoint with this many business-rule constraints (mutual exclusions, conditional requirements, resource ownership checks, platform-only fields, payment failures returning 402), the absence of explicit 4xx definitions (400 for invalid params, 402 for payment errors, 404 for unknown customer/subscription, 422 for unprocessable entity) means integrators have no machine-readable signal about expected failure modes. This is particularly important because the `payment_behavior` enum itself lists `error_if_incomplete`, which the docs note returns HTTP 402.
findings.rationale: Without explicit 4xx response definitions, clients cannot programmatically distinguish error classes, and documentation generation tools emit a single generic error bucket.

value.description: Bad request – invalid or missing parameters.

Not found – customer or subscription does not exist.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400, 402, and 404 response definitions to replace the single catch-all `default`.

findings.title: Conditional field constraints expressed only in prose, not schema
findings.narration: Both `invoice_now` and `prorate` have descriptions stating they 'Can be set to `true` if `at_period_end` is not set to `true`'. However, `at_period_end` is not even present in the request schema (it appears to be missing from the properties entirely), and the mutual-exclusion rule between these fields and `at_period_end` is expressed only in natural language. Clients and code-generation tools have no machine-readable signal about this constraint. The rule should be encoded as JSON Schema `if/then/else` or `not`/`dependencies` constructs, or at minimum `at_period_end` should be added as a property so the constraint can be co-located.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually-exclusive field rules buried in prose are a high-leverage anti-pattern. SDKs and validators cannot enforce them, leading to runtime errors for developers.

findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. In Stripe's API, customer identifiers follow the pattern `cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+`. Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Customer resource, and client libraries treat it as a free-form string. Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) and/or a description noting the expected format would improve clarity and enable type-safe SDK generation.

While `default` technically covers all error codes, the absence of explicit entries means documentation tools render no specific error guidance, and consumers cannot differentiate between, for example, a 404 (subscription not found) and a 400 (invalid parameter). At minimum, `400` and `404` are common enough in cancel/delete flows to warrant explicit entries.

Returning 200 conflates creation with update/read operations and prevents clients and intermediaries from distinguishing creation events from other successful operations.

patchOps.value: The ID of the customer to attach the tax ID to. Must match the pattern `cus_XXXXXX`.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to customer path parameter to encode Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Request body `value` field has no constraints on format or length
findings.narration: The `value` field representing the tax ID value (e.g. a VAT number, EIN, etc.) is declared only as `type: string` with no `maxLength`, `pattern`, or format hint. Since over 100 different tax ID types are supported, each with different structural requirements, at minimum a `maxLength` should be provided to prevent excessively large payloads. Without any constraint, clients receive no guidance and servers are exposed to trivially oversized inputs.
findings.rationale: Unconstrained string fields on write endpoints increase risk of oversized inputs and provide no validation guidance to API consumers or their tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength to the `value` field in the request schema.

findings.title: Path parameter 'customer' lacks format/pattern hint for typed resource ID
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship back to the Customer resource, and client-side validation cannot reject obviously malformed IDs before the round-trip. The same issue applies to the `id` parameter (tax ID, e.g., `txi_...`), which has no `maxLength` constraint at all.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from inferring typed relationships and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to 'customer' and 'id' path parameters to encode typed resource ID expectations.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically incorrect per RFC 9110 — intermediaries (proxies, caches) may strip or reject bodies on GET requests. Even if Stripe's server accepts it, advertising a request body on a read-only GET endpoint is misleading and may confuse client generators into serializing an empty form body. The body should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate HTTP semantics and can cause intermediary incompatibilities; an empty body adds no value.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: Path parameter `customer` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Given that Stripe customer IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_...`), the absence of a `pattern` or `format` hint means codegen tools cannot produce a typed relationship back to the Customer resource. The `id` parameter (the tax_id) has the same issue — no `maxLength`, no pattern, just a bare string.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed resource relationships and offer no input validation hint to API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to customer and id path parameters to hint at Stripe ID formats.

findings.title: DELETE operation returns 200 instead of 204 for deletion confirmation
findings.narration: The operation returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body on successful deletion. While this is a common Stripe pattern (returning a deleted confirmation object), it deviates from REST convention where a DELETE with no meaningful body to return should use 204 No Content. Since Stripe does return a deletion confirmation payload (`{ id, object, deleted: true }`), the 200 is arguably acceptable, but the response schema is cyclic/opaque, preventing consumers from knowing the shape of the deleted confirmation object. This limits discoverability and documentation quality.
findings.rationale: Returning 200 with a deletion confirmation object is a known Stripe pattern, but the response schema being cyclic means consumers have no schema-level knowledge of what is returned upon deletion.
findings.patchSummary: No patch possible as response schema is a cyclic reference; consider resolving the schema.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it 'can range between 1 and 100', but the schema definition only specifies `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means API clients and generated SDKs receive no machine-readable validation hint, and documentation generators will omit the valid range. Callers could accidentally pass 0 or 1000 without any indication from the schema that this is invalid.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints should encode the same rules stated in prose descriptions; a `minimum: 1, maximum: 100` would enable client-side validation and code generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: `charge` and `payment_intent` filter IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `charge` parameter (expected to be a Stripe charge ID like `ch_...`) and `payment_intent` parameter (expected to be `pi_...`) are both typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. Stripe IDs follow predictable prefix patterns, and the absence of a `pattern` or at least a note on `format` means codegen tools cannot build typed relationships, and validators cannot catch malformed IDs before a round-trip to the server occurs. At a minimum a `pattern` like `^ch_[a-zA-Z0-9]{8,}$` for charge and `^pi_[a-zA-Z0-9]{8,}$` for payment_intent would improve API ergonomics.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain strings prevent typed client generation and miss cheap input validation opportunities.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to charge and payment_intent query parameter schemas

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 9110) because intermediaries (proxies, CDNs) may strip or ignore the body, and many HTTP client libraries disallow or warn on GET bodies. The empty body conveys no information and should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: HTTP GET requests should not have a request body; this confuses clients, may break intermediaries, and violates common HTTP conventions.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/disputes operation

findings.title: GET request body is semantically incorrect
findings.narration: This GET operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content. While the schema is empty and `required: false`, including a request body on a GET endpoint is semantically incorrect per HTTP specifications (RFC 7231) and OpenAPI semantics. Many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will ignore or reject a body on GET requests. The body here appears to be a boilerplate artifact and carries no useful information.
findings.rationale: GET requests MUST NOT have a request body per HTTP semantics. Its presence here is misleading to consumers and may break certain client implementations.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect requestBody from GET /v1/disputes/{dispute}

findings.title: Dispute path parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `dispute` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe dispute IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `dp_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code generators and validators cannot enforce the expected ID format, making it impossible to detect obviously invalid inputs at the client or gateway level before a network round-trip.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID references typed as bare strings without pattern or format make typed SDK generation and input validation harder and less safe.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to the `dispute` path parameter schema

findings.title: File-reference fields typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several evidence fields — `cancellation_policy`, `customer_communication`, `customer_signature`, `duplicate_charge_documentation`, `receipt`, `refund_policy`, `service_documentation`, `shipping_documentation`, `uncategorized_file` — represent file upload IDs (Stripe File objects, e.g. `file_...`) but are typed as bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no description clarifying that a File object ID is expected. Code-generation tools and API consumers cannot distinguish these from free-text fields. This forces developers to read prose documentation to understand the expected value type, increasing integration error rates. Adding a `format` (e.g. `format: "stripe-file-id"`) or at least a `description` and `pattern` (e.g. `^file_`) would make the contract machine-readable.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as undecorated strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and increase integration errors.

patchOps.value: A file ID (e.g. file_...) representing the cancellation policy document.
A file ID (e.g. file_...) for any additional supporting documentation.

findings.patchSummary: Add descriptions/format hints to file-reference fields to distinguish them from free-text strings.

findings.title: Conditional-required relationship between `submit` and staged evidence only described in prose
findings.narration: The `submit` field's description explains that setting it to `false` stages evidence without submitting it to the bank, and that a subsequent request with `submit: true` is needed to actually submit. This conditional workflow — where omitting `submit` defaults to `true` — is documented only in the description string. The default value of `true` is also not declared in the schema (`default: true` is absent), so clients and validators cannot automatically apply it. The description also implies the operation is the mechanism for both staging and submitting, a two-phase pattern that warrants explicit default declaration and potentially a note in the field's description about the irreversibility of submission.
findings.rationale: Prose-only conditional field relationships and missing `default` declarations prevent automated validation and tooling from correctly representing the field's behavior.
findings.patchSummary: Add `default: true` to `submit` field to make the implicit default machine-readable.

findings.title: Missing `format: email` and `format: ipv4` on customer PII fields
findings.narration: The fields `customer_email_address` (both at top-level evidence and nested within `enhanced_evidence`) and `customer_purchase_ip` (similarly present at multiple levels) are typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. `customer_email_address` should carry `format: email` and `customer_purchase_ip` should carry `format: ipv4` (or `ipv4`/`ipv6` via `oneOf`). Without format declarations, clients cannot perform client-side validation, API documentation generators cannot signal expected input shapes, and codegen tools produce generic string fields. This is especially notable given the security sensitivity of these PII fields.
findings.rationale: Well-known string formats such as email addresses and IP addresses should use the `format` keyword so validators and code generators can enforce correct structure.
findings.patchSummary: Add `format: email` and `format: ip` to customer_email_address and customer_purchase_ip fields.

findings.title: No request body examples on a highly complex, multi-field evidence submission operation
findings.narration: This operation has one of the most complex request bodies in typical Stripe usage — developers submitting dispute evidence must understand which fields to populate for each dispute category (fraud, duplicate charge, subscription cancellation, etc.). The description explicitly references an external guide for field selection, yet the spec provides zero examples in the `requestBody` content. Without concrete examples showing at least two or three representative scenarios (e.g. a fraud dispute with `customer_communication` + `customer_signature`, and a duplicate charge dispute with `duplicate_charge_id` + `duplicate_charge_documentation`), developers must rely entirely on prose documentation and experimentation, increasing the risk of incomplete or incorrect evidence submissions.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies with many context-dependent optional fields benefit significantly from examples to guide correct usage and reduce integration errors.

duplicate_charge.summary: Responding to a duplicate charge dispute

evidence.duplicate_charge_explanation: The original charge was refunded on 2024-01-15.

findings.patchSummary: Add representative examples for fraud and duplicate charge dispute responses to the request body.

findings.title: Path parameter `dispute` lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `dispute` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe dispute IDs follow a well-known prefixed format (e.g. `dp_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot establish a typed cross-resource reference, and clients have no way to validate an ID before sending the request. The maxLength of 5000 is also extremely permissive for what is effectively a short identifier.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent typed SDK generation and offer no client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID pattern and reduce maxLength on `dispute` path parameter

findings.title: Irreversible state-changing action has no explicit 4xx error responses documented
findings.narration: This endpoint closes a dispute permanently — an irreversible operation that changes status from `needs_response` to `lost`. Despite this severity, the only documented responses are `200` and `default` (a generic error catch-all). At minimum, `400` (invalid state, e.g. dispute already closed or not in `needs_response`), `404` (dispute not found), and `422` (unprocessable) should be explicitly listed. Consumers relying on generated SDK clients cannot distinguish between a not-found error, an invalid-state error, or an authorization failure without explicit response codes. The `default` catch-all is not a substitute for explicit error documentation on destructive endpoints.
findings.rationale: Irreversible write operations should document distinct 4xx codes so clients can implement appropriate error handling and recovery logic.

value.description: Bad request — e.g. dispute is not in `needs_response` state.
Dispute not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions for this irreversible action

findings.title: customer parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The required `customer` query parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but it represents a Stripe Customer resource ID (e.g. `cus_xxxxx`). Without a `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at minimum a note-worthy format hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship between this parameter and the Customer resource, and clients receive no early validation feedback when an obviously wrong ID format is supplied.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings without pattern or format prevent typed codegen relationships and give no client-side format validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to customer parameter schema to signal it is a Customer ID.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties. This means the documented constraints exist only in prose, not in the machine-readable schema. Clients and validators cannot enforce the 1–100 range automatically, and SDK generators will not produce default-value code.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but not encoded in schema are invisible to validators and SDK generators, increasing the chance of out-of-range requests reaching the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema to match prose description.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary and semantically incorrect
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a request body violate HTTP semantics per RFC 7231 §4.3.1 — GET has no defined semantics for a body and many intermediaries (proxies, CDNs) will strip it. The body is also effectively unusable since `additionalProperties: false` with no properties means no payload is accepted. This should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies are semantically undefined in HTTP and many intermediaries strip them. An empty, closed schema body provides no value and may confuse SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically invalid empty GET request body.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type, but the schema is an empty object with `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 notes that GET has no defined request body semantics). Including an empty form-encoded body declaration pollutes generated clients, which may emit unexpected Content-Type headers or attempt to serialize an empty body.
findings.rationale: GET operations must not define a request body. The empty requestBody block is dead weight and can confuse code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` has no format, pattern, or type constraint beyond maxLength
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Entitlement IDs in Stripe follow a structured prefix pattern (e.g., `ent_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `format`, code generators and validators cannot verify that callers are supplying a valid entitlement ID rather than an arbitrary string. Consumers using this schema for validation will silently accept malformed IDs, leading to confusing downstream 404/400 errors.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain string without pattern or format lose typed-relationship semantics and prevent client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `id` path parameter reflecting the entitlement ID format.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values encoded. Client validation tools and SDK generators rely on schema constraints, not prose descriptions, to enforce these bounds. A client sending `limit=0` or `limit=999` would only be rejected at the server layer, with no prior tooling warning.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented only in prose descriptions cannot be used by validators or code generators; they must be encoded as schema properties.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: POST endpoint returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This operation creates a new entitlements feature resource, but the success response is documented as HTTP 200 rather than HTTP 201 (Created). Per RFC 9110 and REST conventions, a successful POST that creates a new resource should return 201 Created, optionally with a Location header pointing to the newly created resource. Using 200 here is semantically misleading to clients and tooling that distinguish between 200 (OK) and 201 (Created) to determine whether a resource was newly instantiated.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status for resource creation POST operations per RFC 9110 §15.3.2. Returning 200 conflates creation with general success, reducing API semantics clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: Missing explicit 4xx error response definitions (e.g., 400, 422)
findings.narration: The operation defines only a 200 success response and a catch-all `default` error response. For a resource creation endpoint that accepts required parameters (`lookup_key` and `name`) and likely enforces uniqueness on `lookup_key`, callers would benefit from explicit 400 (Bad Request) and 422 (Unprocessable Entity) response definitions. The `default` bucket masks what kinds of client errors are expected and prevents code generators and documentation tools from surfacing actionable guidance. Explicit 4xx entries significantly improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: A catch-all `default` provides no semantic signal about expected client error types. Documenting 400/422 responses lets clients handle validation and conflict errors predictably.

value.description: Bad request. Invalid or missing required parameters.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 (and optionally 422) response definitions alongside the catch-all default.

findings.title: lookup_key uniqueness constraint documented nowhere in schema
findings.narration: The `lookup_key` field is described as 'A unique key you provide as your own system identifier.' This uniqueness constraint is expressed only in prose. Callers submitting a duplicate `lookup_key` would likely receive a conflict error at runtime (e.g., 409 Conflict), but the schema and response definitions give no hint of this constraint or outcome. The missing conflict response (409) and lack of any `x-` extension or schema description indicating the uniqueness enforcement behavior leaves clients under-informed about a likely failure mode. At minimum, a 409 response should be documented, and the description should clarify the conflict behavior.
findings.rationale: Runtime uniqueness constraints that can cause predictable errors (duplicate key) should be reflected in both the schema description and a corresponding 409 response definition.

patchOps.value: A unique key you provide as your own system identifier. This may be up to 80 characters. Must be unique across all features; submitting a duplicate key will result in a conflict error.

value.description: Conflict. A feature with the provided lookup_key already exists.

findings.patchSummary: Document uniqueness constraint in lookup_key description and add 409 Conflict response.

findings.title: Permanent deactivation via `active: false` is irreversible but not documented as such
findings.narration: The operation description says a feature can be 'permanently deactivated', and the `active` field description notes inactive features 'cannot be attached to new products'. However, there is no indication in the schema or description whether setting `active: false` is truly permanent (i.e., `active` cannot be set back to `true` once false). If this is indeed a one-way operation for deactivation, the `active` field description should explicitly state 'once set to false, this cannot be reversed' or similar. If it can be reversed, the word 'permanently' in the operation description is misleading and should be removed. This is a clarity issue that could cause API consumers to either accidentally deactivate a feature or to be unnecessarily afraid to set it inactive.
findings.rationale: The word 'permanently' in the description conflicts with the field accepting a boolean that ostensibly could be toggled. Misleading documentation on irreversibility can lead to operational mistakes.

patchOps.value: Update a feature's metadata or deactivate it. Note: once a feature is deactivated (active set to false), it cannot be reactivated.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify whether deactivation is permanent and reflect that accurately in the description.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` has no format or pattern constraint for feature ID validation
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe feature IDs typically follow a structured format (e.g., a prefix like `feat_` followed by an alphanumeric string). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, API clients and code generators cannot validate or construct IDs correctly, and documentation consumers have no hint of the expected format. Adding a `pattern` regex (e.g., `^feat_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at minimum a descriptive example would significantly improve usability and reduce integration errors from malformed IDs.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain unconstrained strings prevent client-side validation and yield poor codegen output. A pattern or example communicates the expected format.
findings.patchSummary: Add an example (and ideally a pattern) to the `id` path parameter to clarify the expected feature ID format.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive resource ID fields documented only in prose, not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The request body accepts `customer`, `issuing_card`, and `verification_session` as resource selectors, but exactly one of these should be provided — the ephemeral key is scoped to a single resource. This constraint exists only implicitly (each field's description says 'the ID of …'), not as a JSON Schema `oneOf` or similar construct. Additionally, `nonce` is documented as associated with `issuing_card` specifically ('used for creating ephemeral keys for Issuing Cards'), implying it is only valid (or required) when `issuing_card` is set. Neither the conditional-required relationship between `nonce` and `issuing_card` nor the mutual exclusivity of the three resource ID fields is machine-readable. Code generators, validators, and SDK builders cannot enforce these rules automatically, increasing the risk of invalid requests being constructed by consumers.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules expressed only in prose should be encoded as JSON Schema `oneOf`/`dependencies`/`if-then` to enable automated validation and correct codegen.

customer.description: The ID of the Customer you'd like to modify using the resulting ephemeral key.

issuing_card.description: The ID of the Issuing Card you'd like to access using the resulting ephemeral key.

nonce.description: A single-use token, created by Stripe.js, used for creating ephemeral keys for Issuing Cards without exchanging sensitive information.

verification_session.description: The ID of the Identity VerificationSession you'd like to access using the resulting ephemeral key.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusivity of resource ID fields and nonce-issuing_card dependency as oneOf in the request schema.

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The fields `customer`, `issuing_card`, and `verification_session` are all cross-resource reference IDs (to Stripe Customer, Issuing Card, and Identity VerificationSession objects respectively), but each is typed as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` is provided. Stripe IDs have well-known prefix patterns (e.g. `cus_*`, `ic_*`, `vs_*`), and without a `pattern` constraint, code generators cannot produce typed foreign-key relationships. This also makes it harder for client-side validators to catch mismatched ID types early.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and miss early validation of ID prefix mismatches.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to customer, issuing_card, and verification_session to encode Stripe ID prefix expectations.

findings.title: Missing example on request body for a multi-variant operation
findings.narration: The operation supports three distinct usage modes (Customer ephemeral key, Issuing Card ephemeral key with optional nonce, and VerificationSession ephemeral key), but no examples are provided on the request body schema or its properties. Given the mutual exclusivity of the resource fields and the special-purpose `nonce` field, concrete examples are particularly valuable here to guide integrators toward correct usage. Without examples, developers reading the spec must infer correct combinations from descriptions alone.
findings.rationale: Complex multi-variant request bodies benefit significantly from examples to communicate correct field combinations to consumers.

issuing_card_key.summary: Ephemeral key for an Issuing Card

issuing_card_key_with_nonce.summary: Ephemeral key for an Issuing Card using a Stripe.js nonce

verification_session_key.summary: Ephemeral key for an Identity VerificationSession

findings.patchSummary: Add examples illustrating each of the three resource ID variants and the nonce usage.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive `type` and `types` parameters encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description for the `types` parameter states 'You may pass either `type` or `types`, but not both.' This mutual exclusion constraint is documented only in prose and is not encoded in the OpenAPI schema. Clients, code generators, and validators have no machine-readable signal to enforce the constraint. A proper encoding would use `oneOf` at the parameter level or a note using `not` / `dependencies` in a combined schema, making the relationship exploitable by tooling.
findings.rationale: Prose-only conditional-required (or exclusive) field rules are a high-leverage finding class because tooling cannot enforce them and callers regularly violate them without client-side validation.

patchOps.value: A string containing a specific event name, or group of events using * as a wildcard. The list will be filtered to include only events with a matching event property. Mutually exclusive with `types`; pass one or the other but not both.

An array of up to 20 strings containing specific event names. The list will be filtered to include only events with a matching event property. Mutually exclusive with `type`; pass one or the other but not both.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify prose and note that enforcement via schema (oneOf/not) should be added.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for the parameter is `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` annotations. Validators, generated SDKs, and documentation tools cannot surface or enforce these bounds automatically, meaning clients can accidentally send out-of-range values (e.g. 0 or 500) and only learn of the error at runtime.
findings.rationale: Constraints stated in prose but not encoded as schema keywords are a medium-severity design gap that prevents automated client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: `types` array missing `maxItems` constraint
findings.narration: The description for the `types` parameter says 'An array of up to 20 strings', but the schema for the array has no `maxItems` keyword. Tooling and generated validators cannot enforce this upper bound automatically, so clients may send more than 20 items without any client-side indication of the error.
findings.rationale: Array length constraints described only in prose cannot be machine-enforced; adding maxItems closes the gap.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxItems:20 to the `types` array schema to match the prose constraint.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false`, no properties). GET requests must not have a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). While some HTTP stacks permit it, including a body definition on a GET operation is semantically incorrect and will confuse client code generators, which may attempt to serialize and send a body with the request.
findings.rationale: HTTP GET requests are defined as body-less. Declaring a requestBody on GET is a semantic violation that misleads codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/events/{id} operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks pattern or format constraining event ID format
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe event IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `evt_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `example`, consumers have no machine-readable hint about the expected format. This limits validation in generated SDKs and API gateways, which could allow obviously invalid IDs to make round trips to Stripe before failing.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with known prefixes should carry a pattern or example to enable early client-side validation and improve codegen type safety.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and example to the `id` path parameter to constrain valid Stripe event ID values.

findings.title: limit parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and total number of supported payout currencies', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum: 1` or `maximum` constraint. Without these encoded in the schema, clients and validation tools cannot enforce the documented bounds, and any integer (including 0 or negative values) would pass schema validation.
findings.rationale: Missing numeric constraints that are explicitly described in prose should be encoded in the schema to enable automated validation and accurate client-side documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 constraint to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Deprecated endpoint lacks deprecation flag
findings.narration: The operation description explicitly marks the ExchangeRate API as deprecated and directs users to the FX Quotes API instead. However, the operation does not set OpenAPI's `deprecated: true` field. Without this flag, tooling (SDK generators, API explorers, linters) cannot automatically surface the deprecation to consumers — it is only visible to someone reading the prose description.
findings.rationale: OpenAPI 3.x provides a first-class `deprecated` boolean on operations. Using it ensures all tooling (code generators, portals, linters) communicates the deprecation status without relying solely on prose.
findings.patchSummary: Add deprecated: true to mark the operation as deprecated in tooling

findings.title: ending_before cursor description references a generic placeholder instead of a currency code
findings.narration: The description for `ending_before` says 'your subsequent call can include `ending_before=obj_bar`', which uses a generic object-ID placeholder (`obj_bar`) inconsistent with the actual cursor semantics. The `starting_after` parameter correctly uses `X` as a currency code placeholder. The `ending_before` description copy-pastes from a generic list-parameter template without adapting it to currency codes, which is confusing to API consumers.
findings.rationale: Misleading placeholder values in parameter descriptions can cause developer confusion about the expected value format. This is a copy-paste inconsistency that should use a currency code placeholder like the sibling parameter does.

patchOps.value: A cursor for use in pagination. `ending_before` is the currency that defines your place in the list. For instance, if you make a list request and receive 100 objects, ending with the exchange rate for currency X, your subsequent call can include `ending_before=X` in order to fetch the previous page of the list.

findings.patchSummary: Fix ending_before description to use a currency code placeholder instead of obj_bar

findings.title: rate_id path parameter lacks format/pattern constraint for currency code
findings.narration: The `rate_id` path parameter represents a currency code (e.g. 'usd', 'eur') but is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. Currency codes follow ISO 4217 format (3 uppercase or lowercase letters). Without a `pattern` or `format` constraint, clients receive no machine-readable hint about the expected format, leading to poor DX and potential unnecessary API calls with obviously invalid values.
findings.rationale: A field named like a resource identifier typed as plain string with no pattern or format is a known high-leverage finding. Currency codes are well-defined by ISO 4217.
findings.patchSummary: Add ISO 4217 pattern constraint to rate_id path parameter

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema containing no properties. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1); many proxies, CDNs, and HTTP clients strip or reject bodies on GET requests. This empty body definition adds noise, may confuse SDK generators, and violates HTTP conventions.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty form-encoded body on a GET endpoint is an anti-pattern that can break intermediaries and confuse tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty request body from GET /v1/exchange_rates/{rate_id}

findings.title: No deprecation marker on a self-described deprecated operation
findings.narration: The operation description explicitly states it is deprecated and directs users to the FX Quotes API instead. However, the operation is missing the OpenAPI `deprecated: true` field. Without this machine-readable marker, code generators, documentation renderers, and linters cannot surface the deprecation automatically. Developers relying on generated SDKs or tooling may not notice the deprecation notice buried in the HTML description.
findings.rationale: OpenAPI 3.x provides a `deprecated` boolean at the operation level precisely for this purpose. A prose-only deprecation notice does not propagate to generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Add deprecated: true to the operation to match prose deprecation notice

findings.title: Request body mixes bank-account and card fields without conditional constraints
findings.narration: The request body schema contains fields applicable only to bank accounts (`account_holder_name`, `account_holder_type`, `account_type`, `documents`) alongside fields applicable only to cards (`address_city`, `address_country`, `address_line1`, `address_line2`, `address_state`, `address_zip`, `exp_month`, `exp_year`, `name`). The operation description explicitly states it updates bank accounts, yet card-specific fields are present with no `oneOf`/`if-then-else` or `not` constraint to signal mutual exclusivity. Consumers generating clients or validating payloads have no machine-readable indication that `exp_month`/`exp_year` are irrelevant for bank accounts and that `account_holder_type` is irrelevant for cards. This is a design flaw: the conditional-required and mutually-exclusive field relationships exist only in implicit understanding and Stripe's external docs, not in the schema.
findings.rationale: Field-applicability rules that are only implied by context (bank vs. card external account) should be encoded as `oneOf` or `if/then` discriminator branches in the schema so that client generators and validators can enforce them correctly.
findings.patchSummary: Split flat schema into oneOf bank-account vs. card update branches to encode mutual exclusivity

findings.title: Card numeric fields `exp_month` and `exp_year` are typed as string instead of integer
findings.narration: `exp_month` is described as "Two digit number" and `exp_year` as "Four digit number", yet both are typed as `type: string`. This is a type confusion issue: consumers generating typed clients will produce string fields where integer or pattern-validated fields are semantically correct. At a minimum these should be `type: integer` (or `type: string` with `pattern: "^[0-9]{2}$"` / `"^[0-9]{4}$"`), consistent with the description. The current schema does not help clients detect that passing `"ab"` for `exp_month` is invalid.
findings.rationale: Fields described as numbers should be typed as integers or constrained with a numeric pattern so that validators and code generators produce correct types.

value.description: Two digit number representing the card's expiration month.
Four digit number representing the card's expiration year.

findings.patchSummary: Add numeric patterns to exp_month (2 digits) and exp_year (4 digits) to match their descriptions

findings.title: Operation description documents only bank-account updates but endpoint also handles cards
findings.narration: The `description` field exclusively describes updating bank accounts (mentions "bank account", `account.controller.requirement_collection`, Custom accounts) but the request schema also includes card-specific fields (`exp_month`, `exp_year`, `name`, address fields). This is a partial copy-paste documentation issue: a developer reading the description would not know this endpoint also handles card external accounts, nor what constraints apply when updating a card. The description should explicitly document both resource types and their respective editable fields.
findings.rationale: When a description covers only one of two resource types handled by the endpoint, developers building against the API will have an incomplete and potentially misleading picture of the operation's behavior.

patchOps.value:
Updates an external account (bank account or card) belonging to a connected account.

For bank accounts, you can update the metadata, account holder name, account holder type, account type, and optionally set it as the default for its currency. You can only update bank accounts when account.controller.requirement_collection is application, which includes Custom accounts. You can re-enable a disabled bank account by performing an update call without providing any arguments or changes.

For cards, you can update the cardholder name, billing address, and expiration date.

findings.patchSummary: Expand description to cover both bank account and card update scenarios

findings.title: Missing examples on complex request body and polymorphic response
findings.narration: The request body has no `examples` or `example` at the media-type or property level, and the 200 response schema is a cyclic reference with no examples either. Given that this endpoint handles two distinct resource types (bank account vs. card) with mutually exclusive fields, the absence of examples makes it significantly harder for API consumers to understand which fields to send in each scenario. At minimum, two examples should be provided: one for updating a bank account and one for updating a card.
findings.rationale: Complex endpoints with multiple resource types and many optional fields benefit greatly from examples that illustrate the distinct usage paths; without them, developers must rely on external documentation.

update_bank_account.summary: Update a bank account's holder name and set as default

update_card.summary: Update a card's expiration date and billing address

findings.patchSummary: Add bank-account and card update examples to the request body media type

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (minimum/maximum not encoded)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it 'can range between 1 and 100', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means client-side validators and code generators cannot enforce the documented bounds, and callers may send values outside the valid range without any schema-level warning.
findings.rationale: Prose-documented constraints should be encoded in JSON Schema so tooling and generated clients can validate inputs automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: `file` filter parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `file` query parameter is documented as 'Only return links for the given file' and clearly represents a Stripe file object ID (typically prefixed `file_`). However, its schema is a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. There is no `pattern` to validate the ID format, and no semantic hint (e.g. `format: stripe-file-id`) that code-generation tools could use to build a typed relationship to the `file` resource.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields without patterns or format hints produce weakly-typed client code and give no runtime hint about expected value shape.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern `^file_` to the `file` parameter schema to document Stripe ID format

findings.title: GET request body is semantically unnecessary and may confuse tooling
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). HTTP GET requests should not carry a request body per RFC 9110; some HTTP clients and API gateways drop or reject GET bodies. All filter parameters for this list endpoint are already expressed as query parameters, making this body entirely redundant. Its presence may cause generated clients to emit a request body for a GET call, potentially breaking in proxies or servers that strictly follow HTTP semantics.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies violate HTTP conventions and can cause interoperability issues with proxies, gateways, and generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty GET requestBody; all parameters are already expressed as query params

findings.title: file field typed as plain string with no format or pattern — cross-resource ID relationship not encoded
findings.narration: The `file` field accepts a Stripe File object ID (e.g. `file_abc123`) but is declared as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` is used to signal that this is a foreign-key reference to the File resource. Code-generation tools cannot infer a typed relationship from this, and API consumers cannot distinguish it from an arbitrary string payload.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent SDK generators and documentation tools from expressing typed relationships. A pattern constraint (e.g. `^file_`) or a format annotation would meaningfully improve consumer tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `file` field to express it as a File resource ID reference

findings.title: POST /v1/file_links returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new file link object (the description and operationId both confirm creation semantics). HTTP convention calls for a `201 Created` response when a new resource is successfully created. Returning `200 OK` misrepresents the outcome and conflicts with RESTful semantics, potentially confusing clients that branch on response status codes.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 and standard REST conventions specify 201 for resource creation. 200 is appropriate for updates or actions that don't produce a new resource. Using 200 here is a semantic mismatch.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 to reflect resource creation semantics

findings.title: expires_at conditional constraint encoded only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: The description for `expires_at` says 'The link isn't usable after this future timestamp,' which implies the value must be a future Unix timestamp. This temporal constraint (value must be > now) is expressed only in prose and cannot be validated by schema-level tooling. While JSON Schema cannot express 'greater than current time', at minimum a `minimum` value or an `exclusiveMinimum: 0` can be added to rule out obviously invalid (past-epoch or negative) values, and the prose constraint should be prominently flagged for server-side validation.
findings.rationale: Constraints expressed only in descriptions are invisible to validators and code generators. Even a partial schema constraint (non-negative, non-zero) is better than nothing.
findings.patchSummary: Add exclusiveMinimum: 0 to expires_at to partially encode the future-timestamp constraint in schema

findings.title: Path parameter `link` lacks format/pattern constraint for file link ID
findings.narration: The `link` path parameter is typed as a bare `type: string` with no `maxLength`, `pattern`, or `format`. Stripe file link IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `link_...`). Without a constraint, code generators and validators cannot distinguish valid IDs from arbitrary strings, which degrades client SDK ergonomics and may allow obviously malformed inputs to reach the API layer before being rejected.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings without pattern/format miss the opportunity for early validation and clear codegen typing.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength and pattern constraint to `link` path parameter.

findings.title: Empty request body defined for a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per RFC 7231 §4.3.1; many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will drop or reject a body on a GET request. This is likely a copy-paste artefact from a POST/PATCH template. Removing the `requestBody` entirely removes the misleading hint that callers should or may supply a body.
findings.rationale: A request body on a GET endpoint contradicts HTTP semantics and confuses clients/tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter 'link' lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `link` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `maxLength`. Stripe file link IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `link_...`). Without any constraint, client SDKs and code-gen tools cannot validate the ID before making the request, and documentation consumers have no clue what a valid value looks like. Adding a `pattern` such as `^link_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and a reasonable `maxLength` would make the contract self-documenting and safer.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings with no pattern/format/maxLength prevent SDK code-gen from building typed relationships and allow obviously invalid values to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength and pattern constraint to 'link' path parameter

findings.title: expires_at encoding style is deepObject but field is a scalar (anyOf string/integer)
findings.narration: The `encoding` block for `expires_at` specifies `style: deepObject, explode: true`. DeepObject encoding is intended for nested object structures (e.g., `field[key]=value`). However, `expires_at` is an `anyOf` of scalar types — either the string `"now"`, a Unix-time integer, or an empty string. Applying deepObject encoding to a scalar is semantically incorrect and may confuse client libraries or form-encoding middleware that attempt to serialize it as `expires_at[...]=...`. The encoding entry for `expires_at` should be removed or changed to `style: form, explode: false`.
findings.rationale: deepObject encoding applied to a non-object field is a schema contract error; client SDK generators may produce incorrect serialization for this field.
findings.patchSummary: Remove incorrect deepObject encoding for scalar field 'expires_at'

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default documented in schema)
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the JSON Schema for this parameter (`type: integer`) does not encode `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10`. This means client-side validators and SDK generators will not enforce the stated range, and the default value is invisible to tooling. A caller sending `limit=0` or `limit=500` will only learn about the constraint via a runtime error rather than at the schema validation stage.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints that should be machine-readable schema properties are a high-leverage issue — they prevent client-side validation and make SDK generation less reliable.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET list endpoint is unnecessary and misleading
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not have a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that a body on GET has no defined semantics). Listing an empty, non-expandable request body is misleading to consumers — it suggests a body is expected or allowed — and some HTTP clients and proxies may reject or silently discard GET bodies. This is a design smell consistent with Stripe's form-encoded POST pattern accidentally applied to a GET.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate HTTP best practices and can confuse tooling and intermediaries. An empty, closed schema adds no value and should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically incorrect request body from the GET /v1/files operation

findings.title: Response should be 201 Created, not 200 OK for resource creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new File resource. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource creation should respond with HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 200 implies the operation was processed without necessarily creating a new resource, which is semantically misleading for clients and SDK generators that rely on status codes to determine behavior.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for successful resource creation via POST. Using 200 is a semantic mismatch that can confuse clients.
findings.patchSummary: Change 200 response to 201 Created for resource creation semantics

findings.title: Conditional field relationship in file_link_data not schema-encoded
findings.narration: The `file_link_data` object has `create` as required, but `expires_at` and `metadata` are presumably only meaningful (or even permitted) when `create` is `true`. This conditional relationship exists in documentation prose elsewhere in Stripe's API but is not encoded here in the schema. Clients and validators cannot programmatically enforce the rule that `expires_at`/`metadata` should only be set when `create: true`. This should be expressed using `if/then` or `oneOf` JSON Schema constructs.
findings.rationale: Schema-level constraints are machine-readable and enforceable; prose-only conditionals are not. Missing encoding leads to invalid payloads passing validation.

patchOps.value: A Unix timestamp representing when the link expires. Only valid when `create` is `true`.
Metadata to attach to the file link. Only valid when `create` is `true`.

findings.patchSummary: Encode conditional constraint: expires_at and metadata only apply when create is true

findings.title: No example provided for multipart/form-data request body
findings.narration: The request body schema for multipart file upload is fairly complex — it requires a binary `file` field, a constrained `purpose` enum, and an optional nested `file_link_data` object. No `examples` or `example` is provided in the schema or encoding section. This makes it harder for developers integrating via API explorers, Postman, or codegen tools to understand how to correctly construct the request. An example with a sample purpose value and file_link_data usage would significantly aid discoverability.
findings.rationale: Complex multipart schemas with nested objects benefit greatly from concrete examples for developer tooling and documentation.

upload_with_file_link.summary: Upload a file and create a file link

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples for multipart file upload with and without file link

findings.title: Path parameter `file` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `file` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe file IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `file_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK code generators cannot build a typed relationship to the File resource, and validation tools cannot reject obviously malformed IDs early. Adding a pattern such as `^file_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would improve both tooling and defensive client validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings with no format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and reduce early validation coverage.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `file` path parameter to reflect Stripe's ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. HTTP GET requests with a request body are non-standard; RFC 9110 §9.3.1 discourages it. The body carries no properties at all, so it provides no utility. Its presence may confuse consumers and code generators, some of which will erroneously generate body-serialization code for a read-only endpoint.
findings.rationale: GET operations with empty, non-functional request bodies are semantically incorrect per HTTP standards and pollute generated client SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty, non-functional requestBody from GET /v1/files/{file}.

findings.title: account_holder[account] and account_holder[customer] mutual exclusion expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `account_holder` parameter description states that `account_holder[customer]` and `account_holder[account]` are mutually exclusive, but this constraint is expressed only as prose. There is no JSON Schema `oneOf`, `not`, or `dependencies` construct enforcing it. Consumers generating clients or validators from the spec cannot derive this rule programmatically, leading to potential misuse that only fails at runtime on Stripe's server.
findings.rationale: Conditional exclusion constraints documented only in prose cannot be enforced by tooling; they should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints.
findings.patchSummary: Encode account/customer mutual exclusion as JSON Schema `not` constraint instead of prose only.

findings.title: account_holder[account] and account_holder[customer] fields typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account_holder[account]` field is a cross-resource reference to a Stripe Account object ID, and `account_holder[customer]` references a Stripe Customer object ID, yet both are typed as bare `string` with only a `maxLength`. Stripe IDs follow well-known prefixes (`acct_` and `cus_` respectively). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, code generators cannot build typed relationships and client-side validation cannot reject obviously wrong values before the API call is made.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields without pattern/format lose typed relationship information valuable to codegen and validation tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add Stripe ID prefix patterns to account and customer fields in account_holder parameter.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties — only `type: integer`. This means clients and validators cannot enforce the documented bounds without reading the prose, and code generators will produce unconstrained integer fields. A value of 0 or 200 would pass schema validation but fail at the API layer.
findings.rationale: Documented numeric constraints should be encoded as JSON Schema keywords so validators and generators can enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, and default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: Path parameter `account` lacks format or pattern constraint

Financial Connections account IDs follow a well-known Stripe prefix pattern (e.g., `fca_...`). findings.title: ownership query parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern

findings.title: account path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints

findings.title: Account path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint

Financial Connections account IDs in Stripe follow a known prefix convention (e.g., `fca_`). findings.title: Missing example on the `features` request body field
findings.narration: The `features` array is the sole required field in the request body, yet it carries no `example` or `examples` annotation. Consumers integrating against this endpoint must infer valid values solely from the enum list in the items schema. Adding an example showing a realistic set of feature values (e.g., `["balance", "transactions"]`) would improve developer experience and allow documentation renderers to produce meaningful code samples.

findings.title: Missing example on 'features' request body field
findings.narration: The `features` array field in the request body currently has no example value. While the enum currently only contains `"transactions"`, it is marked with `x-stripeBypassValidation: true`, suggesting that additional values may be accepted at runtime. An example would clarify the intended usage for consumers and codegen tools.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on required request body fields reduces developer experience and makes it harder for documentation generators and SDK tooling to produce useful samples.
findings.patchSummary: Add example value to 'features' array field in request body schema.

findings.title: Account path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Based on Stripe's conventions, Financial Connections account IDs follow a structured prefix pattern (e.g., `fca_...`). Without a `pattern` constraint, codegen tools and validators cannot distinguish a valid account ID from an arbitrary string, and consumers receive no guidance on the expected format.
