findings.title: The `features` enum allows only `transactions` but uses `x-stripeBypassValidation`
findings.narration: The `features` array items declare a single enum value `["transactions"]` but also carry `x-stripeBypassValidation: true`. This extension signals that the validation is intentionally bypassed, implying additional undocumented values may be accepted at runtime. Consumers relying on the schema for client-side validation or code generation will believe only `transactions` is valid, while the server may silently accept other strings. Either the full set of valid feature values should be listed in the enum, or the bypass extension should be accompanied by a description that explains which additional values are permissible, reducing the mismatch between the declared contract and actual server behaviour.
findings.rationale: Schema should be the source of truth for valid values; a bypass extension without documentation of valid extras creates ambiguity for SDK generation and API consumers.

patchOps.value: The list of account features from which you would like to unsubscribe. Currently supported value: `transactions`. Additional values may be supported by the server.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify description of `features` to acknowledge the bypass and document known valid values.

findings.title: No `pattern` or `format` on the `account` path parameter to communicate expected ID shape
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Stripe Financial Connections account IDs have a well-known prefix (e.g. `fca_`). Without a `pattern` such as `^fca_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`, client code generators and validators cannot detect obviously malformed IDs before they reach the API, leading to avoidable round-trips and confusing error messages. Adding a pattern here would also help SDK consumers understand what kind of resource ID is expected, especially in a deep path like this where the parameter name `account` is not fully self-describing.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow malformed IDs to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern to the `account` path parameter to reflect expected Stripe Financial Connections account ID format.

findings.title: account_holder object lacks cross-field constraint: 'account' or 'customer' conditionally required by type
findings.narration: The `account_holder` object has a `type` enum with values `account` and `customer`, and sibling fields `account` and `customer`. Based on standard Financial Connections semantics, when `type` is `account` the `account` field is required, and when `type` is `customer` the `customer` field is required. This conditional-required relationship is documented only implicitly (by the field names and enum values) and is not encoded as JSON Schema `if/then`, `oneOf`, or `dependencies`. Additionally, the field `customer_account` has no description explaining when it applies versus `customer` or `account`, and no constraint prevents conflicting values from being submitted. Codegen tools and validators cannot enforce this logic from the current schema alone.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required field relationships expressed only through naming conventions and field presence rather than schema constraints lead to runtime errors and unclear API contracts for integrators.
findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf constraint to account_holder enforcing account/customer required by type value

findings.title: account_holder.customer and account_holder.account typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The fields `account_holder.account` and `account_holder.customer` are plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. These are clearly Stripe resource IDs (Stripe account ID prefixed `acct_`, customer ID prefixed `cus_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools treat them as arbitrary strings and cannot build typed cross-resource relationships. The field `customer_account` has the same issue and no description at all, making its purpose completely opaque. Adding patterns like `^acct_` and `^cus_` would at minimum let validators catch obviously wrong inputs early.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings with no pattern or format lose cross-resource relationship information that codegen and validation tooling relies on.

patchOps.value: The ID of a Stripe customer account to link. Used when the account holder is both a customer and a connected account.

findings.patchSummary: Add patterns to account/customer ID fields and description to customer_account

findings.title: Missing example on the request body for this non-trivial multi-field object
findings.narration: The request body contains several interrelated fields (`account_holder`, `permissions`, `filters`, `prefetch`) whose valid combinations are not obvious. There is no `example` or `examples` block on the request schema or any of its complex properties. Integrators learning the API or codegen tools that generate sample calls have no reference payload to work from. Adding even one canonical example (e.g., creating a session for a customer with balances and transactions permissions) would substantially improve discoverability.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies with conditional required fields and enumerated arrays benefit greatly from examples to reduce integration errors.
findings.patchSummary: Add a canonical request body example for session creation

findings.title: Path parameter `session` lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `session` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Financial Connections Session IDs follow a known Stripe prefix pattern (e.g. `fcsess_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDKs and code generators cannot validate that callers pass a Session ID rather than, say, an Account ID or arbitrary string. A regex pattern such as `^fcsess_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would catch accidental cross-resource ID substitution early and improve generated client typing.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID confusion is a common API misuse vector. Stripe resource IDs have predictable prefixes that can be encoded as a schema pattern, improving both safety and documentation clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `session` path param to enforce Stripe Session ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests MUST NOT include a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers silently drop or reject body content on GET requests. Including this empty body object is misleading and could cause interoperability issues with strict HTTP implementations. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 discourages request bodies on GET; tools like curl and many proxies may strip or reject them. An empty body schema adds noise with no benefit.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation — bodies on GET are semantically incorrect.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values encoded. This means clients and code-generation tools have no machine-readable enforcement of this constraint — a caller could pass `limit=0` or `limit=9999` without the schema signalling a violation. The prose description is the sole carrier of the constraint, which is insufficient for automated validation.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but absent from the schema cannot be enforced by validators or surfaced by documentation generators. Adding minimum, maximum, and default encodes the contract unambiguously.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: `account` parameter typed as plain string with no ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `account` query parameter references a Financial Connections Account ID (e.g. `fca_xxx`), yet its schema is simply `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. No `pattern` (e.g. `^fca_`) constrains it to the expected ID prefix, and there is no `format` or `$ref` linking it to the Account resource type. Code-generation tools will treat this as a free-form string and cannot infer the cross-resource relationship. A pattern or at minimum a tighter maxLength reflecting realistic ID lengths (Stripe IDs are typically under 100 chars) would significantly improve type safety.
findings.rationale: Stripe resource IDs have well-known prefixes. A plain `type: string` with maxLength:5000 provides no useful constraint for validation or codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern ^fca_ and tighten maxLength on account parameter

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a request body are semantically non-standard (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes GET bodies have no defined semantics) and many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will strip or reject them. The body carries no properties and is marked `required: false`, so its presence provides no value while potentially confusing consumers and generating dead code in client SDKs.
findings.rationale: GET bodies are semantically undefined per RFC 7231 and are frequently dropped by intermediaries. An empty, non-required body adds noise without benefit.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: GET request body is unnecessary and semantically incorrect
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type, even though it is a GET request retrieving a single resource by ID. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that a payload on GET has no defined semantics). The body schema is empty (`properties: {}`), making it entirely useless. Its presence may confuse client generators that produce code attempting to send a body with a GET request, and some HTTP clients or proxies will reject or strip it.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a request body violate HTTP semantics and can cause client-side code generation issues or proxy failures.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically incorrect GET requestBody.

findings.title: Path parameter `transaction` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `transaction` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Stripe transaction IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `txn_...`). Without a `pattern` constraint or at minimum a shorter `maxLength` reflecting realistic ID lengths, the schema provides no useful validation hint to consumers or codegen tools. A deliberately invalid or excessively long string could reach the backend before being rejected. At minimum, the `maxLength` of 5000 is far too permissive for what is effectively an opaque ID.
findings.rationale: ID fields should have meaningful constraints (pattern or realistic maxLength) to enable client-side validation and typed codegen relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `transaction` path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: GET list endpoint includes an empty requestBody
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. GET requests should not carry a body; HTTP semantics do not define meaning for bodies on GET requests, many intermediaries (proxies, CDNs) will strip them, and OpenAPI tooling often warns or errors when a GET operation includes a requestBody. All filter/pagination parameters for this endpoint are correctly placed in query parameters, so the requestBody serves no purpose and should be removed.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody violates HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). Intermediaries may discard the body, and OpenAPI generators often reject this pattern.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/forwarding/requests

findings.title: limit parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it must be between 1 and 100, but the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. Clients and validators have no machine-readable way to enforce this range, meaning invalid values like 0 or 10000 pass schema validation silently. The constraint should be encoded in the schema rather than only communicated in prose.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are a high-leverage finding: codegen tools, validators, and documentation renderers all ignore them. Schema-level min/max enforces the documented contract.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: payment_method field typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `payment_method` field references a PaymentMethod resource by ID (e.g. `pm_...`) but is declared as a bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Codegen tools cannot infer the typed relationship to the PaymentMethod resource, and clients receive no hint about the expected ID format. A `pattern` such as `^pm_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or a dedicated format annotation would communicate the constraint and enable typed SDK generation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and leave clients without schema-enforced validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to payment_method to signal PaymentMethod ID format

findings.title: url field sent as form body parameter but carries sensitive routing data
findings.narration: The `url` field is the destination endpoint for forwarded payment-method data. Although it travels in the POST body (not the URL path/query), it lacks any `format: uri` annotation and has no `pattern` to restrict valid schemes (e.g. `https://` only). An HTTP destination would silently allow forwarding sensitive card data over a non-TLS connection. Adding a `pattern` that enforces the `https://` scheme and a `format: uri` annotation would both document and partially enforce safe usage.
findings.rationale: Forwarding card data to an HTTP (non-TLS) URL is a critical security risk; the schema should enforce HTTPS-only destinations.
findings.patchSummary: Add format:uri and https-only pattern to url field to prevent plaintext forwarding

findings.title: request.body and request.headers lack descriptions and request object has no required fields declared
findings.narration: The nested `request` object—which carries the actual HTTP body and headers forwarded to the third party—has no description on its `body` or `headers` sub-fields, and the `request` object itself declares no `required` array. It is unclear whether `body` or `headers` are individually optional or mandatory, and callers have no guidance about which combinations are valid. A prose description on `body` and `headers` and a `required` constraint (at minimum on `headers` if headers are always expected) would eliminate this ambiguity.
findings.rationale: Missing descriptions and required constraints on a complex nested object that carries forwarded payment data leave integrators without critical documentation and allow schema-invalid payloads to pass client-side validation.

patchOps.value: The raw HTTP request body to forward to the destination URL. May be omitted if no body is required.
HTTP headers to include in the forwarded request. Each entry must contain a name and value.

findings.patchSummary: Add descriptions to request.body and request.headers sub-fields for clarity

findings.title: No request body example for a security-sensitive forwarding operation
findings.narration: This operation forwards raw payment-method credentials to a third-party endpoint, making the correct construction of the request body critical. Yet no `example` or `examples` block is provided on the request body schema. Without a concrete example, integrators must infer the correct payload shape from the field descriptions alone, increasing the risk of misconfiguration (e.g. omitting required `replacements` items or misformatting `request.headers`). An example showing a typical card-forwarding scenario would significantly reduce integration errors.
findings.rationale: Complex, security-sensitive request bodies benefit greatly from examples; their absence increases misconfiguration risk for integrators.
findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the forwarding request body

findings.title: GET operation includes a superfluous empty request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests must not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1); many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will ignore or reject a body on GET requests. Including an empty requestBody on a GET operation is misleading to client code generators and API consumers, who may believe a body is expected or optionally useful. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 does not forbid a body on GET, but it is semantically meaningless and widely unsupported in tooling. An empty body schema adds no value and introduces confusion.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks a format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe forwarding request IDs have a well-known prefix and structure (e.g., `fwdreq_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, client-side validation is almost nonexistent. Tooling cannot build typed references to this resource ID, and an accidentally submitted UUID or other format will only fail server-side. A pattern such as `^fwdreq_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` (or whatever the real prefix is) and a realistic max length would greatly improve client validation and code-generation quality.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no pattern/format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `id` path parameter to reflect Stripe's resource ID format.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter has neither `minimum`, `maximum`, nor `default` properties defined. This means client-side validation tools, SDK generators, and documentation renderers cannot enforce or display these constraints automatically. A client could inadvertently pass `limit=0` or `limit=999` without any schema-level rejection signal.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose should be encoded in the schema so they are machine-readable and enforceable by validation tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: verification_session parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `verification_session` query parameter description states it accepts a VerificationSession ID or a VerificationIntent ID, but its schema is a plain `type: string` with only `maxLength`. No `pattern` (e.g. `^(vs_|vi_)`) or cross-reference hint is provided. SDK and codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to either resource, and API consumers have no machine-readable way to distinguish which ID prefix is expected. The description even notes 'It is allowed to provide a VerificationIntent ID', which is a conditional rule buried in prose.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships; a pattern or at least an x- extension should signal the expected format.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix pattern and resource hint to verification_session parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers silently discard or reject bodies on GET requests. While Stripe's API may tolerate this as a transport artefact, documenting a request body on a GET endpoint is misleading to API consumers and contradicts standard HTTP semantics. All relevant parameters are already correctly defined as query parameters.
findings.rationale: Including a requestBody on a GET operation violates HTTP semantics and may confuse clients or be discarded by intermediaries.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Path parameter `report` typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `report` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe verification report IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `vr_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a descriptive `format`, code-generation tools cannot build a typed reference to this resource, and client-side validation cannot reject obviously malformed IDs before sending the request. Adding a pattern such as `^vr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would close this gap and make the relationship to the VerificationReport resource explicit.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent typed cross-resource references in generated SDKs and allow trivially invalid IDs to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `report` path parameter to encode the Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests must not carry a semantic body per RFC 9110 §9.3.1; many HTTP clients and intermediaries strip or reject GET bodies. Stripe appears to use this pattern across its API (likely a spec-generation artefact), but it is technically incorrect and can mislead consumers and tooling that validates request bodies. The `requestBody` block should be removed from this operation.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 forbids GET request bodies with semantic meaning. An empty-schema body is a spec artefact that confuses validators and client generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically empty requestBody from GET operation.

findings.title: limit parameter missing min/max constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties enforcing these constraints. Clients and validators have no machine-readable way to enforce the described range, and code generators will not produce correct validation logic.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints should be encoded in the schema, not left exclusively in prose descriptions, to enable automatic validation and accurate client SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, and default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: related_customer typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `related_customer` parameter is described as a Customer ID but its schema is a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. Stripe customer IDs follow a predictable prefix pattern (e.g., `cus_...`). Without a `format`, `pattern`, or semantic hint, code generators cannot model the relationship to the Customer resource, and API consumers have no machine-readable hint that this is a resource reference rather than an arbitrary string.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format so that codegen tools can build typed references and validators can catch obviously invalid inputs.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern '^cus_' to related_customer schema to indicate it is a Customer ID.

findings.title: related_customer_account typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `related_customer_account` parameter is described as 'The ID of the Account representing a customer' but has a bare `type: string` schema. Account IDs on Stripe follow a known pattern (e.g., `acct_...`). The absence of a `pattern` or `format` means codegen tools cannot model this as a typed reference to an Account resource.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format so tooling can generate typed references and perform basic input validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern '^acct_' to related_customer_account schema to indicate it is an Account ID.

findings.title: Empty request body included on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type whose schema has no properties. GET requests with request bodies are discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 7231) and many HTTP clients and intermediaries silently drop them. This empty body definition adds noise and may confuse client generators into emitting unnecessary body serialisation code for a read-only list endpoint.
findings.rationale: GET endpoints should not declare request bodies. Any Stripe-specific query parameters are already captured via `parameters`. The empty body should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Conditional-required fields ('type' vs 'verification_flow') expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The description of `type` states: 'You must provide a `type` if not passing `verification_flow`.' This means `type` and `verification_flow` are mutually constraining: exactly one of them must be supplied. This rule is expressed only in natural-language prose and is invisible to validators, code generators, and SDK builders. It should be encoded in the JSON Schema using a `oneOf` or `if/then/else` construct so tooling can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Machine-readable constraints enable automated validation and prevent runtime errors. Prose-only rules are routinely missed by consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusivity of 'type' and 'verification_flow' as schema oneOf

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or $ref
findings.narration: `related_customer` is described as 'Customer ID' and `related_customer_account` as 'The ID of the Account representing a customer.' Both are `type: string` with only `maxLength`, providing no machine-readable hint that these are references to Stripe resources. Similarly, `related_person.account` and `related_person.person` are bare strings. Without a `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_`, `^acct_`, `^person_`), or `$ref`, SDK generators cannot create typed resource relationships. This is a common Stripe API pattern but is nevertheless a design gap for consumers relying on code generation.
findings.rationale: Typed resource IDs enable codegen tools to build cross-resource relationships and allow validation of ID prefixes before network calls.
findings.patchSummary: Add patterns to related_customer and related_customer_account to encode Stripe ID prefixes

findings.title: POST creating a resource returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new VerificationSession resource and documents a single success response with HTTP status 200. REST convention and RFC 9110 recommend HTTP 201 Created for successful resource creation, optionally paired with a `Location` header pointing to the new resource. Using 200 conflates creation with retrieval and makes it harder for generic REST clients and frameworks to automatically handle the post-creation flow (e.g. following the Location header).
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 semantically signals resource creation; 200 is for successful reads or in-place updates. This affects REST client behavior and discoverability.

value.description: VerificationSession successfully created.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response definition alongside existing 200 for resource creation clarity

findings.title: Sensitive fields (email, phone) in provided_details lack writeOnly annotation
findings.narration: The `provided_details` object accepts `email` and `phone`, which are PII fields used for identity verification. Neither field has `writeOnly: true` set. In OpenAPI 3.x, `writeOnly` signals to documentation generators and SDK builders that a field should not be returned in responses (or at minimum that it is write-only on input). Without this annotation, consumers and generated models may inadvertently expose these values in logging, serialization, or response mirroring.
findings.rationale: PII fields should be marked writeOnly to guide SDK generators and documentation tools to treat them as input-only, reducing inadvertent exposure risk.
findings.patchSummary: Mark provided_details.email and .phone as writeOnly to flag PII fields for SDK generators

findings.title: client_secret returned in GET response is a sensitive credential not marked writeOnly
findings.narration: The operation description explicitly calls out that a `client_secret` field may be returned in the response when the session status is `requires_input`. Client secrets are sensitive credential-equivalent values; they should be marked `writeOnly: true` on any request body field, and ideally the response schema should call out that this field must be handled securely. While the response schema is a cyclic ref (not fully reviewable here), the description itself surfaces the risk: a `client_secret` traveling in a standard GET JSON response to any authenticated caller is a notable security surface. At minimum, the API description should note that the `client_secret` must not be logged, cached, or forwarded, and the field on the response schema should be annotated accordingly. The URL for the session is also returned, which is a one-time verification link that grants access to the end-user verification flow — equally sensitive.
findings.rationale: Credential-equivalent values like client_secret in responses should be documented with sensitivity warnings; missing annotation increases risk of accidental exposure via logging or caching.

patchOps.value:
Retrieves the details of a VerificationSession that was previously created.

When the session status is requires_input, you can use this method to retrieve a valid client_secret or url to allow re-submission.

Security note: The client_secret and url fields are sensitive. Do not log, cache, or forward these values. The url grants direct access to the verification flow for the end-user.

findings.patchSummary: Add security note to description about sensitive client_secret and url fields in response.

findings.title: Path parameter `session` lacks pattern constraint for verification session ID format
findings.narration: The `session` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe verification session IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `vs_...`). Without a `pattern` constraint, the schema provides no validation signal to clients or generated SDKs that this is a specific resource identifier type. Code-generation tools cannot infer a typed relationship to the VerificationSession resource, and validators will not catch obviously malformed IDs (e.g., an accidentally passed payment intent ID). Adding a regex pattern like `^vs_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would enable client-side validation, improve generated SDK types, and make the spec self-documenting about cross-resource references.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format lose type-safety benefits in codegen and client validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `session` path parameter to identify it as a VerificationSession ID.

findings.title: Missing writeOnly on sensitive PII fields (email, phone) in provided_details
findings.narration: The `provided_details` object accepts `email` and `phone` fields representing user PII. These fields lack `writeOnly: true`, meaning documentation tools and client generators will treat them as both readable and writable. In practice these should be write-only inputs — they are submitted to pre-populate the verification flow and should not appear in response objects. Without `writeOnly`, there is no schema-level signal to tooling that these are inbound-only values.
findings.rationale: PII fields that are submission-only should be marked writeOnly to guide code generators and security scanners.
findings.patchSummary: Mark provided_details.email and provided_details.phone as writeOnly to reflect their inbound-only nature.

findings.title: Conditional update restriction (status=requires_input) documented in prose only
findings.narration: The operation description explicitly states that updates to the verification check and options are only allowed when the session status is `requires_input`. This is a conditional constraint that governs when the request will succeed, yet it is expressed only in the operation description prose and is not encoded anywhere in the schema. There is no `x-stripe-condition` extension, no discriminator, and no server-side schema variant that captures this state guard. Consumers relying solely on the schema will not understand that the same endpoint behaves differently based on the resource's current state, and client-side validation tooling cannot enforce or surface the restriction.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required constraints documented only in prose cannot be enforced by validators or communicated to code generators; they should be encoded or at minimum flagged via a schema extension.

patchOps.value: Updates to `type` and `options` are only permitted when the session `status` is `requires_input`. Requests to update these fields when the session is in any other status will be rejected with a 400 error.

findings.patchSummary: Add x-stripe-condition extension to schema to machine-annotate the requires_input status guard.

findings.title: No 400/422 error response defined for invalid-state or validation failures
findings.narration: The operation's responses only define `200` (success) and `default` (catch-all error). Given that the operation explicitly restricts updates based on session status (`requires_input` only) and accepts a constrained `type` enum, a 400 or 422 response should be explicitly documented. The `default` bucket technically covers it, but without a named 400/422 entry, consumers cannot distinguish client-error behavior from server errors in generated code or documentation, reducing the usefulness of the spec for integration testing and SDK generation.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx response definitions allow SDK generators and documentation tools to properly model client-error flows distinct from server errors.

value.description: Bad request. Returned when the session is not in `requires_input` status or when invalid parameters are provided.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 response entry to surface client-error semantics alongside the catch-all default.

findings.title: Session path parameter lacks resource ID format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `session` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe verification session IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `vs_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the VerificationSession resource, and API consumers receive no early validation feedback if they accidentally pass an ID from a different resource type (e.g., a customer ID).
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as bare strings without pattern/format constraints prevent typed SDK generation and offer no client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to session path parameter to enforce VerificationSession ID format

findings.title: No 4xx error responses defined beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The operation only declares a `200` and a `default` response. Callers attempting to cancel a session that is not in `requires_input` status, or referencing a non-existent session, will encounter errors that are not explicitly documented. At minimum, a `400` (invalid state transition) and `404` (session not found) response should be declared. The current shape gives API consumers and SDK generators no structured way to distinguish these common failure modes from unexpected server errors.
findings.rationale: Specific 4xx responses improve discoverability and allow generated clients to handle known error cases explicitly rather than falling through to generic error handling.

value.description: Bad request — e.g., the session is not in `requires_input` status and cannot be canceled.
The specified VerificationSession was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions to document known error scenarios

findings.title: Resource ID 'session' typed as plain string without format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The path parameter `session` is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe VerificationSession IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `vs_...`). Without a `pattern` constraint or at least a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot build a typed reference to this resource, and client-side validation cannot reject obviously malformed IDs before making a network call. The `maxLength: 5000` is also unusually permissive for an ID that is expected to be a short opaque token.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields named after a resource (here 'session') typed as plain string with no format or pattern are a known high-leverage issue for codegen and client validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint for VerificationSession ID and tighten maxLength.

findings.title: payment.payment_intent and payment.payment_record conditional-required rule not schema-encoded
findings.narration: The `payment` query parameter object has a `type` field that acts as a discriminator between `payment_intent` and `payment_record`, but the relationship between `type` and the corresponding ID field (`payment_intent` or `payment_record`) is not encoded in the schema. When `type` is `payment_intent`, the `payment_intent` field should be required; when `type` is `payment_record`, the `payment_record` field should be required. This conditional-required constraint exists only implicitly and cannot be validated automatically by tooling.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required constraints expressed only through naming conventions rather than `oneOf`/`if-then-else` or `dependencies` allow invalid payloads (e.g. `type=payment_intent` with no `payment_intent` field) to pass schema validation silently.
findings.patchSummary: Encode oneOf discriminator so payment_intent or payment_record field is required based on type

findings.title: invoice query parameter ID field lacks format or pattern hinting resource type
findings.narration: The `invoice` query parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe invoice IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `in_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, codegen and validation tools treat this as an arbitrary string and cannot build a typed cross-resource reference. The same pattern applies to `payment.payment_intent` and `payment.payment_record` fields.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from creating typed relationships and allow obviously wrong values (e.g. a charge ID) to pass schema validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to invoice ID parameter to signal resource-type expectation

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema does not encode `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10`. Without these constraints, clients and validators cannot enforce the documented range, and server errors from out-of-range values are not preventable at the schema level.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but absent from the schema are not enforced by validators or surfaced in generated SDK documentation, leading to avoidable runtime errors.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty application/x-www-form-urlencoded request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. GET requests conventionally do not carry a body; RFC 9110 does not prohibit it, but many HTTP clients and intermediaries drop or ignore GET bodies. All filterable parameters are already expressed as query parameters. The empty request body adds noise and could confuse codegen tools into generating body-sending GET requests.
findings.rationale: An empty request body on a GET operation is an anti-pattern that may mislead generated clients and does not serve any functional purpose since all parameters are query params.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty request body from GET /v1/invoice_payments

findings.title: Request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` of type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with an empty schema. GET requests must not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will silently drop or reject a body on a GET request. The body here contains no properties and carries no value, so it should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET with a request body violates HTTP semantics and causes interoperability issues across HTTP clients, CDNs, and API gateways.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` query parameter states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema does not encode `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10`. Without these constraints, validators and SDK generators cannot enforce the stated range, and documentation tooling will not display the default. Prose-only constraints are a well-known source of client bugs.
findings.rationale: Constraints described only in prose are not machine-enforceable; schema-level minimum/maximum/default enable validation and accurate codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: status parameter missing description
findings.narration: The `status` filter parameter has no `description` field. While the enum values (`active`, `archived`) are self-explanatory in isolation, API consumers benefit from knowing what status filtering does (e.g., whether omitting the parameter returns both statuses or only active ones). This is a documentation clarity gap that affects developer experience and generated reference docs.
findings.rationale: Missing description leaves the semantics of omitting the parameter ambiguous and reduces the quality of generated documentation.

patchOps.value: Filter templates by status. If omitted, templates of all statuses are returned. Use `active` to return only live templates and `archived` to return only archived templates.

findings.patchSummary: Add a description to the status query parameter

findings.title: GET endpoint includes an empty request body definition
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though the schema has no properties and the body is not required. RFC 7231 discourages request bodies on GET requests, and many HTTP clients (proxies, frameworks) strip or reject bodies on GET. This is a design smell — the empty requestBody should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate common HTTP conventions and can cause interoperability issues with proxies and HTTP client libraries.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, superfluous requestBody from the GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `template` lacks description and format/pattern constraints
findings.narration: The `template` path parameter has no `description` field and no `format` or `pattern` constraint beyond a generous `maxLength: 5000`. For a resource ID that likely follows a structured prefix (e.g. `irt_...`), the absence of a pattern means consumers and code generators have no guidance on valid ID shapes. A description and a pattern (e.g. `^irt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) would improve clarity and reduce invalid request errors.
findings.rationale: Untyped, undescribed resource ID path parameters make codegen and API consumer tooling less useful and increase the chance of malformed requests reaching the server.

patchOps.value: The ID of the invoice rendering template to retrieve.

findings.patchSummary: Add a description (and ideally a pattern) to the `template` path parameter.

findings.title: Path parameter `template` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `template` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. This is a resource ID field (referencing an invoice rendering template), but it has no `pattern` (e.g., `^invrt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or `format` hint that would allow codegen tools to treat it as a typed resource reference. The maxLength of 5000 is also far too permissive for what is typically a short opaque ID string (Stripe IDs are typically under 100 characters). Without a pattern, clients cannot validate the ID format before sending the request, and generated SDKs cannot build a typed relationship to the template resource.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string with no pattern or format lose type-safety in codegen and provide no client-side validation feedback.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten template ID parameter: reduce maxLength and add pattern constraint.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error responses defined (only a catch-all `default`)
findings.narration: The responses object contains only `200` and `default`. The `default` entry covers all error cases, but there are no discrete 4xx response codes such as `400` (bad request / invalid parameters), `404` (template not found), or `409` (conflict — e.g., template already archived). Without explicit status codes, client code generators cannot produce typed error-handling branches, and API consumers cannot understand what error conditions to expect. At minimum, a `404` (template not found) and `400` (invalid request) should be enumerated separately since this is a state-mutation operation on an identified resource.
findings.rationale: State-mutating POST operations on a specific resource should enumerate 404 and 400 explicitly; a catch-all default is insufficient for client code generation and documentation clarity.

value.description: Bad request. Invalid parameters supplied.
The specified template was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the existing default.

findings.title: Path parameter `template` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `template` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a loose `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe invoice rendering template IDs follow a specific prefix pattern (e.g., `invrt_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDKs and code generators cannot distinguish this from an arbitrary string, nor can validation layers catch obviously malformed IDs before the request hits the server. Adding a regex pattern like `^invrt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would make the contract more precise and enable earlier client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent typed relationship building in codegen tools and offer no validation surface.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `template` path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Resource ID parameters typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer`, `customer_account`, `invoice`, `ending_before`, and `starting_after` parameters are all typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. These are Stripe object IDs (e.g., `cus_xxx`, `in_xxx`) that follow well-known prefixed patterns. Without a `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a typed ID schema, code-generation tools cannot model the relationship between this endpoint and the resources it filters by. At minimum, `customer` should reference the Customer resource ID, `invoice` the Invoice resource ID, and the cursor parameters should document their expected ID format.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent typed relationship generation in SDKs and client libraries.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID patterns to customer and invoice filter parameters

findings.title: Missing constraint on `limit` parameter (no minimum or maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema definition has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` keywords. This means clients and validators cannot enforce the documented range, and the default value of 10 is invisible to generated clients that rely on schema defaults. A consumer could submit `limit=0` or `limit=9999` and only discover the constraint at runtime via an API error.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints in prose should be encoded in the schema so validators and codegen tools can enforce them.
findings.patchSummary: Encode minimum=1, maximum=100, default=10 on the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Prose-only mutual-exclusion rule between `customer` and `invoice` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `invoice` parameter description states: "If specifying an invoice, no customer identifier is needed." This implies that `customer` and `invoice` are in a partially exclusive or superseding relationship — when `invoice` is provided, `customer` is redundant or ignored. This conditional relationship exists only in prose. It should be expressed as a schema-level `oneOf` or at minimum flagged via a structured `description` with an `x-mutuallyExclusive` extension, so tooling and generated clients can surface the constraint without runtime discovery.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules documented only in prose are a well-known source of integration bugs; they should be encoded structurally.
findings.patchSummary: Mark invoice as mutually exclusive with customer/customer_account via extension

findings.title: GET list endpoint has a requestBody
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though it is empty (no properties). GET requests with a body are non-standard per RFC 7231 and HTTP semantics; many HTTP clients (proxies, frameworks, browsers) silently drop GET request bodies. While this body carries no properties and is not `required`, its presence is misleading and may cause confusion for consumers. The empty requestBody should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a requestBody per HTTP semantics; the presence of an empty one is misleading and may cause tooling issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET list endpoint

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `customer` and `customer_account` documented only in prose
findings.narration: The schema exposes both `customer` and `customer_account` as optional string fields with no constraint tying them together. Based on their descriptions ('The ID of the customer' vs 'The ID of the account representing the customer'), these appear to be alternative ways to specify the target customer — exactly one should be provided. This mutual-exclusion / conditional-required rule is expressed nowhere in the schema and must be inferred by a reader examining both descriptions side-by-side. Codegen tools and validators cannot enforce it.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules kept only in prose (or implied by semantics) should be encoded as JSON Schema `oneOf` / `not` / `if-then-else` so validators and code generators can enforce them.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual-exclusion of `customer` / `customer_account` as schema oneOf constraints

findings.title: `quantity` and `quantity_decimal` are mutually exclusive but only prose hints at it
findings.narration: The description of `quantity` explicitly says 'Use `quantity_decimal` instead to provide decimal precision. This field will be deprecated in favor of `quantity_decimal`', which implies callers should choose one or the other but not both. No schema constraint enforces this. A client submitting both would receive an ambiguous or erroneous server-side interpretation, and no validator would catch the mistake.
findings.rationale: Deprecation notes and 'use X instead of Y' guidance in descriptions should be accompanied by schema-level mutual exclusion so validators reject invalid combinations before the request reaches the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add `not: { required: [quantity, quantity_decimal] }` to enforce mutual exclusion

findings.title: `price_data` and `pricing` are alternative price-specification mechanisms with no schema constraint
findings.narration: The request schema offers both `price_data` (inline price creation) and `pricing` (reference to an existing price via `pricing.price`). These two mechanisms are semantically exclusive — providing both would be contradictory — yet the schema permits any combination. The exclusion rule is not encoded anywhere, leaving it entirely up to server-side validation to catch the conflict. Codegen and validation tools will happily generate request objects with both fields populated.
findings.rationale: Semantically exclusive parameter groups that are only implicitly mutually exclusive should be encoded as `oneOf` to surface the constraint to client tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Encode `price_data` / `pricing` mutual exclusion via schema oneOf or not constraint

findings.title: POST returns HTTP 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This operation creates a new invoice item resource, which by HTTP semantics should return `201 Created`. Returning `200 OK` is technically valid but goes against REST conventions and confuses clients that check the status code to determine whether a new resource was created vs. an existing one was updated. This also means the `Location` header convention for newly created resources is never established.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 recommends 201 for successful resource creation. Using 200 forces clients to rely on other signals (e.g., request method) to know a new resource was created.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 for resource creation semantics

findings.title: prose-only mutual-exclusion rule: `unit_amount_decimal` at top-level vs inside `price_data`
findings.narration: The request body contains both a top-level `unit_amount_decimal` field and a `price_data.unit_amount_decimal` field. Additionally, `price_data` itself is described as 'data used to generate a new Price object inline', implying it is mutually exclusive with direct amount/pricing fields such as top-level `amount`, `pricing`, and `unit_amount_decimal`. Similarly, `price_data.unit_amount` and `price_data.unit_amount_decimal` should be mutually exclusive (exactly one). These exclusivity constraints are documented nowhere in the schema and rely entirely on runtime validation or out-of-band developer knowledge. Codegen tools and validators cannot enforce them.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required and mutually-exclusive field relationships described only in prose (or not at all) are high-severity because they lead to silent runtime errors and cannot be validated client-side.

patchOps.value: The unit amount in cents. Mutually exclusive with `unit_amount_decimal`; provide exactly one.
The unit amount as a decimal string (up to 12 decimal places). Mutually exclusive with `unit_amount`; provide exactly one.

findings.patchSummary: Document mutual exclusion of unit_amount/unit_amount_decimal inside price_data, and price_data vs direct amount fields

findings.title: `quantity` deprecated in description but no `deprecated: true` marker on the field
findings.narration: The description of the `quantity` field states 'This field will be deprecated in favor of `quantity_decimal` in a future version.' However, the field itself is not marked with `deprecated: true` in the schema. OpenAPI 3.x supports `deprecated: true` at the property level to signal this to tooling (code generators, linters, documentation renderers). Relying solely on prose means generated SDKs will not emit deprecation warnings, and documentation portals will not visually flag it.
findings.rationale: Missing `deprecated: true` on a field the description explicitly calls out as deprecated means generated clients won't warn consumers, increasing the risk of continued usage after removal.
findings.patchSummary: Add deprecated:true to the quantity field to match its prose deprecation notice

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain `string` with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields reference Stripe resource IDs — `discounts[].coupon`, `discounts[].discount`, `discounts[].promotion_code`, `pricing.price`, and `price_data.product` — but are all declared as bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Stripe IDs have well-known prefixes (`coupon_`, `di_`, `promo_`, `price_`, `prod_`) and follow a deterministic format. Without a pattern or format hint, code generators cannot build typed relationships, and clients have no machine-readable way to validate they are passing the correct ID type.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent typed SDK generation and offer no validation signal to API consumers about acceptable values.
findings.patchSummary: Add format/pattern hints to resource ID fields (pricing.price, price_data.product, discounts sub-fields)

findings.title: invoiceitem path parameter lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `invoiceitem` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Stripe invoice item IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ii_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, clients and generated SDKs receive no machine-readable signal that this is a typed resource identifier. This makes it impossible for codegen tools to create typed relationships between resources.
findings.rationale: A plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID prevents typed codegen and omits useful validation for API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and tighten maxLength on invoiceitem path parameter

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer`, `customer_account`, and `subscription` query parameters are cross-resource reference IDs (they accept Stripe object IDs like `cus_xxx`, `acct_xxx`, `sub_xxx`) but are declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` is applied to communicate the expected ID shape to consumers or code-generation tools. This means clients have no machine-readable indication of what kind of value is expected, and generated SDKs cannot build typed relationships between these IDs and their corresponding resource types.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format that reflects the expected Stripe ID prefix (e.g. `^cus_`, `^acct_`, `^sub_`) so tooling can enforce and document the relationship.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer, customer_account, and subscription query params

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100', but the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum: 1` or `maximum: 100`. This means validators and code-generation tools have no way to enforce the stated bounds automatically. Consumers passing `limit=0` or `limit=200` will only learn of the violation at runtime from the API error response rather than from schema validation.
findings.rationale: Stated numeric ranges should always be encoded as schema constraints so that validators and SDKs can reject out-of-range values before sending a request.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1 and maximum:100 constraints to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: `due_date` parameter has no description
findings.narration: The `due_date` query parameter is fully defined in terms of its schema (a range-query object or a Unix timestamp integer) but has no `description` field at all. Unlike the other filter parameters (e.g. `created`, `collection_method`, `status`), a consumer reading the spec has no prose explanation of what the field filters on, what timezone semantics apply, or when it is applicable (e.g. only for `send_invoice` collection method invoices). This is a clarity gap that could lead to misuse.
findings.rationale: Every parameter, especially date-range filters with non-obvious applicability conditions, should carry a description explaining its semantics and any conditional constraints.

patchOps.value: Filter invoices by due date. Accepts a Unix timestamp or a range object with `gt`, `gte`, `lt`, `lte` keys. Applicable only to invoices with `collection_method=send_invoice`.

findings.patchSummary: Add a description to the `due_date` query parameter

findings.title: Response should be 201 Created, not 200 OK for invoice creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new draft invoice resource. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 200 misrepresents the nature of the operation to clients and tools that rely on HTTP status codes to distinguish creation from update or read operations.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status for a successful resource creation. Using 200 blurs the distinction between create and update semantics.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response status from 200 to 201 Created

findings.title: Conditional-required fields `days_until_due` and `due_date` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: Both `days_until_due` and `due_date` carry prose descriptions stating they are 'Valid only for invoices where `collection_method=send_invoice`.' This conditional-required relationship exists only in natural language and is not encoded as a JSON Schema `if/then`, `dependencies`, or `oneOf` construct. Code generators and validation tools cannot enforce or communicate this constraint automatically, leading to runtime errors that developers must discover empirically.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements described only in prose cannot be enforced by validators or surfaced by code generation tools. They should be expressed as JSON Schema constraints.
findings.patchSummary: Encode collection_method-dependent constraints for days_until_due and due_date in schema

findings.title: Resource ID fields lack format or pattern constraints for typed relationships
findings.narration: Several fields that clearly represent references to Stripe resource IDs — `customer` (customer ID), `subscription` (subscription ID), `default_payment_method` (payment method ID), `default_source` (source ID), `on_behalf_of` (account ID) — are typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint and no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`. Codegen tools cannot infer the resource relationship, and validators cannot reject malformed IDs. At minimum, a `pattern` such as `^cus_`, `^sub_`, `^pm_` could communicate the expected ID prefix.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and validators from rejecting malformed inputs.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern or x-stripeResourceId format hints to resource ID fields like customer, subscription

findings.title: No request body examples provided for a highly complex schema
findings.narration: The request body schema is very large, with deeply nested objects for `payment_settings`, `shipping_cost`, `shipping_details`, `automatic_tax`, `rendering`, and `transfer_data`. Despite this complexity, no `examples` or `example` are provided at the request body level or on individual complex properties. Developers integrating with this endpoint must infer valid payloads entirely from schema structure. Even a minimal example (e.g., creating a basic draft invoice for a customer) and an advanced example (with shipping, discounts, and payment settings) would materially improve usability.
findings.rationale: Complex nested request bodies without examples create significant integration friction. Examples are especially important for form-encoded bodies where nesting serialization is non-obvious.
findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating minimal and advanced invoice creation payloads

findings.title: Mutually exclusive parameter groups documented in prose only — not encoded as schema constraints
findings.narration: The descriptions of `schedule`/`schedule_details` explicitly state 'Cannot be used with subscription or subscription fields', and `subscription_details` states 'Cannot be used with `schedule` or `schedule_details` fields.' These mutual-exclusion rules are expressed only in natural language. No `not`, `oneOf`, or `dependencies` constraint in the JSON Schema encodes this relationship. As a result, SDK generators, validators, and form builders cannot automatically enforce the constraint, and API consumers can submit invalid combinations that rely on server-side rejection with no spec-level indication of the error.
findings.rationale: Conditional constraints in prose-only are a high-leverage anti-pattern. They should be encoded as JSON Schema to enable tooling to surface them at design/generation time.

value.description: schedule/schedule_details and subscription/subscription_details are mutually exclusive

findings.patchSummary: Add schema-level `not`/`oneOf` to encode schedule vs subscription mutual exclusion

findings.title: Conditional-required `automatic_tax` customer/schedule fields expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `customer` field description reads: 'If `automatic_tax` is enabled then one of `customer`, `customer_details`, `subscription`, or `schedule` must be set.' This conditional-required rule is entirely in prose. Similarly `customer_account` and `customer_details` carry the same conditional requirement. There is no JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependencies` structure that encodes this. SDK generators and client-side validators will not be able to enforce this rule.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships documented only in field descriptions cannot be machine-enforced. They should use JSON Schema `if/then/else` or `dependencies`.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then schema to require customer/subscription/schedule when automatic_tax.enabled=true

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain `string` with no format, pattern, or $ref
findings.narration: Several fields that are clearly Stripe object identifiers — `customer` (cus_… prefix), `schedule` (sub_sched_… prefix), `subscription` (sub_… prefix), `issuer.account`, `on_behalf_of`, and `automatic_tax.liability.account` — are all typed as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a typed resource schema. This means codegen tools produce plain `string` parameters with no indication of the expected ID prefix or format, losing the ability to build typed cross-resource relationships and depriving client libraries of useful hints.
findings.rationale: Per the review guidelines, resource ID fields named after known resources that are plain strings without format or pattern are a notable finding for codegen and clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Add x-format hints or pattern constraints to Stripe resource ID fields for codegen clarity

findings.title: No 4xx error response definitions beyond the generic `default`
findings.narration: The responses object defines only a `200` success and a `default` error response. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `402`, `404`, or `422` response definitions. Given that this endpoint has complex conditional validation rules (mutual exclusions, conditional required fields), a `400` (or `422`) response with a structured error schema would significantly improve developer experience and allow tooling to surface expected error shapes. The `default` catch-all alone is insufficient for typed client generation.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses for an endpoint with rich validation logic means clients cannot distinguish error classes and tools produce untyped error handling.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters, missing required fields, or mutually exclusive fields set simultaneously.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 response for invalid/conflicting parameter combinations

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and no tool or client library will send it. Its presence is misleading and may cause some HTTP clients or intermediaries to reject the request or behave unexpectedly.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 discourages message bodies on GET requests. The body adds noise with no functional value here since all inputs are query parameters.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints encoded. This means validators and client code generators cannot enforce the valid range, and a caller passing `limit=0` or `limit=999` would only discover the error at runtime from an API error response rather than at the schema-validation layer.

findings.title: Response body `url` field lacks format or pattern constraint

No `format: uri` or pattern is applied, so generated clients and validators cannot distinguish a well-formed URL from arbitrary text. For a field semantically required to be a URL, adding `format: uri` improves generated documentation, client validation, and mock generation.
findings.rationale: A field named `url` with known URL semantics should carry `format: uri` to enable tooling to enforce and communicate its type correctly.

findings.title: Path parameter 'invoice' typed as unconstrained string with no ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `invoice` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe invoice IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `in_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Invoice resource, and clients cannot validate IDs before sending requests. A pattern like `^in_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would communicate the expected format and allow client-side pre-validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and reduce API clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to invoice path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: discounts.coupon, .discount, .promotion_code are plain strings with no format or pattern constraints
findings.narration: Within the `discounts` array items, the `coupon`, `discount`, and `promotion_code` fields are typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. They represent cross-resource IDs (coupon IDs, discount IDs, promotion code IDs) but carry no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to indicate that relationship. Codegen tools cannot build typed references from these fields; clients are left to guess what kind of identifier is expected. At minimum a description clarifying the resource type and a consistent naming convention (e.g. `x-stripeResource`) would help, but ideally these should reference typed schemas.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format/pattern prevent codegen tools from inferring typed relationships and make client integration error-prone.

findings.title: DELETE returns 200 instead of 204 for a deletion with no meaningful body
findings.narration: The operation is a permanent delete (the description explicitly says 'Permanently deletes') yet it declares a `200` response with a JSON body. Per REST conventions, a successful deletion that returns no meaningful resource state should use `204 No Content`. If Stripe returns a small deleted-confirmation object (e.g., `{id, object, deleted: true}`), 200 is acceptable, but the response schema is a cyclic ref making it impossible to verify. Even so, a `204` with an empty body, or a well-described `200` with a typed deleted-object schema, would be cleaner. The current shape (200 + cyclic ref) gives consumers no useful type information.
findings.rationale: DELETE operations that confirm deletion often use 204. Using 200 with an unresolvable cyclic schema provides no type safety or documentation for the response body.
findings.patchSummary: Consider using 204 or providing a typed deleted-confirmation schema for the 200 response.

findings.title: Conditional field relationships in line items expressed only in prose
findings.narration: Within each line item, several fields are mutually exclusive or conditionally required based on context, but no schema constraints encode these relationships. For example, `price_data` contains both `product` and `product_data` fields — Stripe's API only allows one of these at a time. Similarly, `unit_amount` and `unit_amount_decimal` are mutually exclusive alternatives (submitting both would be an error), and `quantity` and `quantity_decimal` follow the same pattern. These rules exist only in external documentation, not in the schema itself, so codegen tools and validators cannot enforce them.
findings.rationale: Conditional exclusivity rules that live only in prose cannot be enforced by validators or code generators. Using `oneOf` / `not` / `dependencies` in the schema would catch client errors at validation time.

Stripe IDs follow known prefixes (e.g. `ii_`, `co_`, `dc_`, `promo_`, `price_`, `prod_`) and have consistent patterns. Without a `format` or `pattern`, codegen tools cannot build typed cross-resource relationships, and client-side validation cannot distinguish these IDs from arbitrary strings.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and prevent validators from catching obviously wrong values.

GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). Many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will strip or reject a body on GET requests. Stripe uses this pattern across many list endpoints, but it remains a semantic mismatch that can cause issues with strict HTTP implementations.
