Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed resource reference, and client-side validation cannot catch obviously malformed IDs before the request is sent. A pattern such as `^in_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode this constraint explicitly.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings with no format/pattern prevent typed relationship generation in codegen tools and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to invoice path parameter to encode ID format.

findings.title: Status parameter description does not match enum values
findings.narration: The `status` query parameter description says 'One of `pending`, `closed`, or `reversed`', but the schema enum actually contains four values: `closed`, `expired`, `pending`, `reversed`. The value `expired` is present in the enum but missing from the description. This is a copy-paste or documentation drift bug — API consumers reading the description will not know that `expired` is a valid filter value.
findings.rationale: Description mismatch causes client confusion and is classified as a clarity issue. Developers relying on prose documentation rather than the schema will not discover the `expired` filter value.

patchOps.value: Only return authorizations with the given status. One of `pending`, `closed`, `reversed`, or `expired`.

findings.patchSummary: Sync status description to include the missing `expired` enum value.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` fields set. Consumers relying solely on the machine-readable schema (e.g., code generators, validators) will not enforce or communicate these constraints and will generate unconstrained integer inputs.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but not encoded in the schema cannot be validated automatically. This is a high-severity design gap as it allows out-of-range values to reach the API without client-side rejection.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `card` and `cardholder` filter IDs typed as plain strings with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `card` and `cardholder` query parameters reference resource IDs (Stripe card and cardholder objects) but are typed only as `type: string` with a loose `maxLength: 5000`. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` is provided. Stripe card IDs follow the pattern `ic_*` and cardholder IDs follow `ich_*`. Without a pattern or typed reference, code generators cannot build a typed relationship between this operation and the underlying resources, and clients cannot perform basic client-side validation of the ID format before sending a request.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed codegen relationships and basic input validation. This is a design clarity issue.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to `card` (ic_) and `cardholder` (ich_) parameters.

findings.title: Path parameter 'authorization' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `authorization` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Issuing authorization IDs have a well-known Stripe prefix (e.g., `iauth_`). Without a `pattern` (e.g., `^iauth_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at minimum a descriptive `format`, codegen tools and validators cannot distinguish a valid authorization ID from an arbitrary string. This is especially relevant here since the ID directly scopes an access-controlled financial resource.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern reduce type safety and hinder SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'authorization' path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared for this GET operation with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema containing no properties and `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). While Stripe uses form-encoded bodies on some GET endpoints for query parameters in practice, this empty body definition adds noise, may confuse client libraries, and is semantically incorrect. The request body should be removed entirely; query parameters should be represented as `in: query` parameters instead.
findings.rationale: An empty, no-op request body on a GET endpoint is semantically incorrect and may confuse HTTP clients and codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect empty request body from GET operation.

findings.title: Authorization path parameter lacks pattern constraint for Stripe ID format
findings.narration: The `authorization` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but Stripe authorization IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `iauth_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` constraint, clients and code-generation tools cannot validate the ID before sending a request, and the API surface is documented more loosely than necessary. A simple regex such as `^iauth_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would narrow the contract and improve SDK type safety.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string without pattern lose codegen type relationships and permit obviously invalid values to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to authorization path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format

findings.title: Authorization path parameter typed as plain string without ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `authorization` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe authorization IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `iauth_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Issuing Authorization resource, and client validation is essentially absent. A pattern like `^iauth_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and a realistic maxLength (e.g. 5000 is excessively large for an ID) would significantly improve correctness.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern are a flagged pattern per review guidelines. The maxLength of 5000 is also impractically large for an authorization ID.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten authorization path param: reduce maxLength and add ID pattern.

findings.title: Conditional field `amount` controlled by prose only — not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `amount` field description states it may only be provided when `pending_request.is_amount_controllable` is `true`. This is a conditional-required rule expressed purely in prose. Since `is_amount_controllable` is a property of the existing authorization resource (not a request field), the constraint cannot be fully encoded in JSON Schema here. However, the description at minimum should make clear whether omitting the field defaults to the full pending amount and should note any bounds (e.g. must be ≤ pending amount). As-is, a consumer who misses the prose note could accidentally submit an `amount` on a non-controllable authorization with no schema-level warning. Adding a minimum constraint (`minimum: 1`) to encode the positivity rule would partially improve this.
findings.rationale: The field description says 'Must be positive' but there is no `minimum: 1` constraint in the schema. Conditional rules in prose that should be partially encodable as JSON Schema constraints are a flagged pattern.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 to amount field to encode the 'must be positive' constraint.

findings.title: Authorization path parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `authorization` path parameter is a resource ID (likely prefixed `iauth_...`) but is declared only as `type: string` with a `maxLength` of 5000. No `format`, `pattern`, or `example` communicates to consumers and codegen tools the expected shape of this identifier. This allows callers to pass arbitrary strings up to 5000 characters where a short, structured Stripe object ID is expected, and prevents tooling from building typed cross-resource relationships.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no pattern or format prevent codegen from expressing typed relationships and allow invalid inputs to pass schema validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and example to `authorization` path param to communicate expected Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Deprecated operation lacks a `x-sunset` date or migration deadline hint
findings.narration: The operation is marked `deprecated: true` and the description instructs callers to respond directly to webhook requests instead. However, there is no `x-sunset` extension or any machine-readable date indicating when this endpoint will be removed or cease to function. Consumers integrating the spec into their tooling or client libraries cannot automatically surface the urgency of migration without a sunset date, reducing the actionability of the deprecation notice.
findings.rationale: A deprecated endpoint without a sunset hint gives no signal to automated tools or developers about migration urgency or timeline.
findings.patchSummary: Add `x-sunset` date to deprecated operation to communicate migration deadline to consumers.

findings.title: Sensitive PII (phone_number, email) passed as query parameters
findings.narration: The `email` and `phone_number` filter parameters are passed as URL query strings. Although HTTPS encrypts traffic in transit, query parameters are routinely logged in server access logs, proxy logs, CDN logs, browser history, and Referer headers. For PII such as email addresses and phone numbers, this represents a meaningful data-exposure risk. The Stripe API is consumed by many intermediaries and logging pipelines; these values appearing in URLs increases the blast radius of any log leak.
findings.rationale: PII in URL query strings violates common data-handling best practices and privacy regulations (GDPR, CCPA). Even over TLS, query params are frequently logged.
findings.patchSummary: Mark email and phone_number query params as privacy-sensitive via extension.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. Clients and generated SDKs have no machine-readable way to validate or enforce these bounds, leading to runtime errors for out-of-range values that could have been caught at the schema layer. The default of 10 is also absent from the schema, meaning generated client code cannot apply it automatically.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints (min=1, max=100, default=10) should be encoded in the schema so validators, SDKs, and docs generators can enforce and display them correctly.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests with request bodies are non-standard; RFC 7231 does not forbid it but notes that semantics are undefined, and many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks drop or reject bodies on GET requests. Including this empty body definition adds noise, may confuse generated clients, and could cause interoperability issues. All filter parameters are already expressed as query parameters, so the request body serves no purpose.
findings.rationale: GET + request body is non-standard and problematic in practice. The empty body should be removed entirely.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Cardholder `name` field missing `maxLength` constraint documented in description
findings.narration: The description for `name` states 'The maximum length of this field is 24 characters', but the schema property has no `maxLength` constraint. This means client-side validators and codegen tools will not enforce the 24-character limit, and clients will only discover the constraint at runtime when the server rejects their request. The constraint is documented in prose but not encoded in the schema.
findings.rationale: Machine-readable constraints belong in the schema, not just description text. Missing maxLength forces server-side-only validation discovery.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength: 24 to the name field to match its description constraint

findings.title: Conditional-required fields `company` and `individual` not encoded as schema constraints
findings.narration: The cardholder `type` field accepts either `individual` or `company`, and the API documentation (referenced in the description) distinguishes between these two types with separate sub-objects (`individual` and `company`). The rule 'use `company` when type is company, use `individual` when type is individual' is implied by naming convention and external docs, but is not expressed as a JSON Schema `if/then` or `oneOf` construct. Consumers cannot determine from the schema alone which sub-object is relevant or required for a given `type` value.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements expressed only through naming convention or external docs are not machine-readable. This prevents accurate client-side validation and correct codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Encode if/then rules: if type=company then company object is relevant; if type=individual then individual object is relevant

findings.title: Response always returns HTTP 200 for resource creation; should return 201
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new Issuing Cardholder resource, but the only success response defined is HTTP 200. REST convention and HTTP semantics specify that resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, ideally with a Location header pointing to the newly created resource. Using 200 for creation conflates creation with retrieval, making it harder for clients and intermediaries to distinguish between the two operations.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the semantically correct status for successful resource creation per RFC 9110. Using 200 violates REST conventions and reduces API clarity.

value.description: Cardholder created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response alongside or replacing 200 for resource creation semantics

findings.title: `preferred_locales` enum list is inconsistent with its description
findings.narration: The description for `preferred_locales` states supported locales are `da`, `de`, `en`, `es`, `fr`, `it`, `pl`, or `sv`, but the schema enum only contains `["de", "en", "es", "fr", "it"]` — missing `da`, `pl`, and `sv`. This inconsistency means clients following the description may submit `da`, `pl`, or `sv` and receive unexpected validation errors, while clients following the schema will not know those values are supposedly supported.
findings.rationale: Description and enum values are contradictory; clients and codegen tools will derive different allowed values depending on which they consult.
findings.patchSummary: Align preferred_locales enum values with the description: add da, pl, sv

findings.title: Empty request body on GET operation
findings.narration: This GET operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false`, no properties). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 notes that a body on GET has no defined semantics and many intermediaries will strip it). The empty body definition adds noise to client SDKs and codegen tooling and may cause some HTTP clients to reject or mishandle the request.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body; this is an HTTP semantic violation and a codegen/SDK hazard.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/issuing/cardholders/{cardholder}

findings.title: Path parameter `cardholder` lacks pattern/format for typed resource ID
findings.narration: The `cardholder` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe cardholder IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ich_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a shorter `maxLength` reflecting actual ID lengths, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Cardholder resource, and client-side validation is trivially bypassable. A `maxLength` of 5000 is also far too permissive for what is in practice a short identifier.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string without pattern or format prevent typed SDK generation and allow obviously invalid values to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and tighten maxLength on `cardholder` path parameter

findings.title: company vs. individual fields are mutually exclusive but constraint is prose-only
findings.narration: The request body exposes both `company` (for company cardholders) and `individual` (for individual cardholders) as top-level optional fields with no schema-level constraint preventing both from being submitted simultaneously. The Stripe documentation implies that a cardholder is either a `company` or an `individual`, making these two fields mutually exclusive. This conditional relationship exists only implicitly (through the field descriptions naming cardholder types) and is not encoded as a JSON Schema `oneOf`, `not`, or `if/then/else` construct. Codegen tools and validators will happily accept a payload with both `company` and `individual` populated, which is semantically invalid.
findings.rationale: Conditional field exclusivity expressed in prose but not in schema is a high-leverage finding; it causes incorrect client code generation and allows client-side validators to pass invalid payloads.

value.description: A cardholder cannot be both a company and an individual; `company` and `individual` are mutually exclusive.

findings.patchSummary: Add `not: { required: [company, individual] }` to schema to encode mutual exclusivity

findings.title: `preferred_locales` enum omits `da`, `pl`, and `sv` documented in the field description
findings.narration: The `preferred_locales` field description explicitly states: "Locales can be `da`, `de`, `en`, `es`, `fr`, `it`, `pl`, or `sv`." However, the items `enum` only contains `["de", "en", "es", "fr", "it"]` — `da` (Danish), `pl` (Polish), and `sv` (Swedish) are missing. This discrepancy means validators will reject those three locale values even though the documentation promises they are valid. The `x-stripeBypassValidation: true` extension on the item schema is a signal Stripe itself knows the enum is incomplete, but the description mismatch still creates confusion for developers.
findings.rationale: A mismatch between the documented accepted values and the schema enum causes client-side validation rejections for values that the API actually accepts, directly harming developer experience.
findings.patchSummary: Add missing locales `da`, `pl`, `sv` to the `preferred_locales` items enum to match description

findings.title: `company.tax_id` should be marked `writeOnly` as it is sensitive PII/financial data
findings.narration: The `company.tax_id` field accepts a tax identification number (EIN/TIN), which is sensitive financial/PII data. It is not marked `writeOnly: true` in the schema. Without this flag, documentation generators will display the field as readable in responses, and codegen tools will generate response models that include it — even though Stripe never returns raw tax IDs in API responses. Marking it `writeOnly` correctly signals that the value is accepted on write but never echoed back, preventing inadvertent logging or exposure of the value in client-side response handling.
findings.rationale: Tax IDs are sensitive PII/financial identifiers. The `writeOnly` keyword exists precisely to signal credential/sensitive fields that flow in only one direction.
findings.patchSummary: Mark `company.tax_id` as `writeOnly: true` to flag it as a sensitive write-only field

findings.title: Missing request/response examples on a complex, nested request body
findings.narration: The request body is deeply nested with multiple complex objects (`billing`, `individual`, `spending_controls`, etc.), yet no examples are provided at either the media-type level or on any individual property. For a financial API where correct construction of nested spending controls and billing addresses is critical to avoid rejected requests, the absence of examples significantly increases integration friction. An illustrative example showing a minimal update (e.g., changing status and updating spending limits) would allow developers to understand the structure without reading deeply nested schema definitions.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas without examples reduce developer experience and increase integration errors, especially for compliance-sensitive fields like individual verification and spending controls.
findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the request body showing a typical cardholder update

findings.title: Missing description on `personalization_design` query parameter
findings.narration: The `personalization_design` query parameter has no `description` field at all. Every other filter parameter on this endpoint has a clear description explaining its purpose and the type of value expected. Consumers and documentation generators will see a blank entry for this parameter, making it impossible to understand without consulting external documentation. At minimum it should say something like 'Only return cards with the given personalization design ID.'
findings.rationale: Missing descriptions on parameters reduce API usability and documentation quality, especially for less obvious fields.

patchOps.value: Only return cards with the given personalization design ID.

findings.patchSummary: Add missing description to personalization_design query parameter

findings.title: `limit` parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100', but the schema does not encode `minimum: 1` and `maximum: 100`. Clients relying on schema validation (e.g. generated SDKs) will not catch out-of-range values at the client side. The description correctly states the rule in prose, but schema constraints would allow validators and code generators to enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose should be encoded as schema constraints so they can be validated programmatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1 and maximum:100 constraints to limit parameter schema

findings.title: `last4` parameter should be constrained to exactly 4 digits
findings.narration: The `last4` query parameter is described as 'only return cards that have the given last four digits', but its schema is a plain `string` with only `maxLength: 5000`. There is no `minLength`, `maxLength: 4`, or `pattern` constraining it to exactly 4 numeric characters. This means the schema permits values like empty string, letters, or extremely long strings that the API would reject at runtime. A `pattern: '^[0-9]{4}$'` constraint would prevent invalid requests from being constructed by generated clients.
findings.rationale: A field semantically constrained to exactly 4 digits should carry a pattern or length constraints so clients can validate before sending.
findings.patchSummary: Constrain last4 to exactly 4 numeric digits via pattern and length bounds

findings.title: `cardholder` filter typed as plain string with no ID format hint
findings.narration: The `cardholder` parameter accepts a Cardholder resource ID but is declared as a plain `type: string` with only `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe Cardholder IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `ich_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a `format` annotation, code-generation tools cannot build a typed cross-resource reference, and validators cannot distinguish a cardholder ID from arbitrary text. Adding a `pattern` such as `^ich_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow generated clients to validate this relationship statically.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as unstructured strings prevent typed cross-resource relationships in codegen and schema validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID pattern hint to cardholder parameter to signal cross-resource reference

findings.title: replacement_reason conditionally required when replacement_for is set — rule only in prose
findings.narration: The field `replacement_for` names the card being replaced, and the API semantically requires `replacement_reason` whenever `replacement_for` is provided. This conditional dependency is implicit: there is no schema-level `if/then` or `dependentRequired` constraint encoding it. Codegen tools and validators will not enforce it, leaving clients to discover the requirement only at runtime via a 400 error.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields documented only in prose are a high-leverage finding; JSON Schema `dependentRequired` can encode this precisely and improve both client tooling and documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Add dependentRequired so replacement_reason is required when replacement_for is present

findings.title: shipping required when card type is 'physical' — conditional dependency not encoded
findings.narration: Physical cards require a shipping address (`shipping` field), while virtual cards do not. The spec marks `shipping` as optional at the schema level with no conditional constraint. This means validators will happily accept a `type: physical` request without `shipping`, and the server must reject it with a runtime error. An `if/then` or `oneOf` discriminating on the `type` field would encode this requirement properly.
findings.rationale: A conditional field requirement expressed only through documentation (or only enforced server-side) is a high-severity design gap; schema-level encoding enables client-side validation and cleaner SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add if/then to require shipping when card type is physical

findings.title: cardholder, financial_account, replacement_for, and personalization_design typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The fields `cardholder` (an Issuing Cardholder ID, prefix `ich_`), `financial_account` (prefix `fa_`), `replacement_for` (an Issuing Card ID, prefix `ic_`), and `personalization_design` (prefix `ipd_`) are all resource-ID references typed as bare `string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref` to a typed schema. Code-generation tools cannot infer the cross-resource relationship, and there is no client-side hint that an `ich_` vs a random string is expected.
findings.rationale: Resource-ID fields named after related objects that are typed as unadorned strings prevent typed SDK generation and remove useful documentation about expected value shape.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to cardholder, replacement_for, and personalization_design fields

findings.title: pin.encrypted_number lacks writeOnly: true
findings.narration: The `pin` object contains `encrypted_number`, which carries an encrypted PIN value. Even though it is encrypted, it is a sensitive credential-equivalent field that should be marked `writeOnly: true` so that documentation and SDK generators know it should never appear in response bodies or logs. Without this annotation, tooling may inadvertently surface it in generated response types.
findings.rationale: Sensitive write-only credential fields should be annotated with writeOnly: true to prevent inclusion in response type codegen and to signal their sensitive nature in documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Mark pin.encrypted_number as writeOnly: true

findings.title: card path parameter lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `card` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe issuing card IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `ic_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tooling cannot distinguish this from a free-form string, cannot validate the ID shape client-side, and cannot build a typed relationship back to the Issuing Card resource. The maxLength of 5000 is also far too permissive for what is effectively a short resource identifier.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern or format lose the typed relationship that enables codegen and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint and tighten maxLength on card path parameter.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A GET endpoint should not carry a `requestBody` at all per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 discourages it; many HTTP clients and intermediaries will reject or strip it). The declared body here is completely empty (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`) and `required: false`, so it carries no information value while creating confusion for consumers and tooling. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a request body violate HTTP conventions and confuse client libraries, proxies, and API gateways that correctly reject or strip body content from GET requests.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, unnecessary requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: cancellation_reason only valid when status is 'canceled' — conditional rule in prose only
findings.narration: The `cancellation_reason` field description states it represents 'Reason why the `status` of this card is `canceled`', and the `status` field description says 'If this card is being canceled because it was lost or stolen, this information should be provided as `cancellation_reason`'. This implies `cancellation_reason` is only meaningful (and arguably required) when `status` is set to `canceled`. This conditional relationship exists only as prose and is not encoded in the JSON Schema. Tooling, validators, and SDK generators cannot enforce it automatically. It should be expressed using a JSON Schema `if/then` construct.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields described only in prose are a well-known high-leverage pattern; schema-level encoding enables automatic validation and better SDK generation.

value.description: cancellation_reason should be provided when status is 'canceled'

findings.patchSummary: Encode cancellation_reason/status conditional relationship as if/then in JSON Schema

findings.title: pin.encrypted_number lacks writeOnly marker — credential field visible in tooling
findings.narration: The `pin` object contains `encrypted_number`, which holds an encrypted PIN value for the card. Credential-like fields that are write-only (never returned in responses) should carry `writeOnly: true` to signal to SDK generators, documentation tools, and OpenAPI validators that this value should never be echoed back. Without this marker, generated clients may inadvertently log or display the field, and documentation tools will not flag it as sensitive.
findings.rationale: writeOnly should be set on credential fields per security best practices; its absence is a risk finding.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to pin.encrypted_number to mark it as a credential field

findings.title: personalization_design field lacks description and cross-reference
findings.narration: The `personalization_design` field is a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint and no description, no `format`, no `pattern`, and no indication that it represents a Stripe Personalization Design resource ID (e.g., `pd_xxx`). Consumers cannot infer the relationship from the schema alone; codegen tools cannot produce a typed resource reference. A description explaining it is an ID referencing the `PersonalizationDesign` resource, plus a format hint or pattern such as `^pd_`, would substantially improve clarity and enable typed SDKs.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no description, format, or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships.

patchOps.value: The ID of the desired personalization design for this card. References a PersonalizationDesign object (e.g., `pd_xxx`).

findings.patchSummary: Add description and resource reference hint to personalization_design field

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values encoded. This means clients and validation tooling cannot enforce the documented range, and codegen tools will not apply the default automatically. The constraint exists only as prose.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but not encoded in schema cannot be enforced by validators or used by code generators, leading to runtime errors for consumers who rely on the spec.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: transaction filter typed as plain string with no ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `transaction` query parameter is used to filter disputes by a related transaction object ID, but its schema is simply `type: string, maxLength: 5000` with no `pattern` or format hint indicating it is a Stripe object ID (typically prefixed with `ipi_` or similar). Codegen tools have no way to establish a typed relationship between this parameter and the Transaction resource. A pattern such as `^ipi_` or a note like `format: issuing-transaction-id` would enable downstream tooling to resolve the cross-resource reference.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and make the schema harder to validate client-side.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID pattern constraint to the transaction filter parameter

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation
findings.narration: This GET endpoint includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are non-standard per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 discourages it) and many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will silently drop the body. While this appears to be a Stripe-wide pattern for passing the `expand` array via form body, the more idiomatic approach for a GET list endpoint is to use query parameters exclusively, which is already done here for `expand`. The empty body adds noise and may confuse consumers.
findings.rationale: An empty request body on a GET endpoint is non-standard and may cause issues with clients or proxies that drop GET bodies; it adds unnecessary noise to the spec.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty request body from this GET operation

findings.title: Conditional field relationship between `transaction` and `treasury.received_debit` encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description of `transaction` says 'For transaction on Treasury FinancialAccounts, use `treasury.received_debit`', implying these two fields are mutually exclusive — you supply either `transaction` or `treasury.received_debit`, not both. This conditional constraint lives only in natural-language prose; there is no `oneOf`, `not`, or `dependencies` construct in the schema to enforce or signal it to codegen tools and validators.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules stated only in prose are invisible to validators and code generators. This should be expressed as a JSON Schema `oneOf` with two branches: one requiring `transaction` and forbidding `treasury`, the other requiring `treasury` and forbidding `transaction`.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutually-exclusive transaction/treasury constraint as oneOf instead of prose only

findings.title: `evidence.reason` field should imply which evidence sub-object is active — constraint not encoded
findings.narration: The `evidence` object contains a `reason` enum (e.g. `canceled`, `duplicate`, `fraudulent`, …) alongside eight sibling sub-objects with matching names. The implied semantics are that when `reason` is set to a particular value, the corresponding sub-object is the relevant evidence container and the others should be ignored. This one-of-the-sub-objects-per-reason constraint is entirely absent from the schema; all sub-objects remain independently optional regardless of `reason`, which means validators cannot enforce coherence and SDK code generators cannot model the discriminator relationship.
findings.rationale: A discriminator-like relationship between `reason` and the evidence sub-objects is semantically important and should be expressed via `if/then` or `oneOf` with a discriminator, not left implicit.

patchOps.value: When `reason` equals one of the enum values, only the correspondingly-named sub-object (e.g. reason=canceled → canceled sub-object) is relevant. This constraint should be enforced via JSON Schema if/then or a discriminator.

findings.title: `transaction` and `treasury.received_debit` are plain strings with no format or pattern identifying them as resource IDs
findings.narration: Both `transaction` (an issuing transaction ID, e.g. `ipi_…`) and `treasury.received_debit` (a received debit ID, e.g. `rd_…`) are typed as bare `type: string` with only `maxLength`. No `format`, `pattern`, or `x-stripeResource` hint is attached. Codegen tools and API linters cannot determine that these fields are foreign-key references to other Stripe resources, which breaks typed relationship generation in SDKs.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields that reference other objects should carry a pattern (e.g. `^(ipi_)[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or a vendor extension (`x-stripeResource`) so tooling can build typed relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern or format hints to transaction and received_debit ID fields

findings.title: Successful response should be 201 Created, not 200 OK
findings.narration: This is a POST endpoint that creates a new Issuing Dispute resource. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource-creation response should use HTTP 201 Created rather than 200 OK. Using 200 obscures the creation semantics and is inconsistent with REST conventions, potentially confusing clients that inspect status codes to determine whether a resource was newly created versus returned unchanged.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for successful resource creation. Returning 200 understates the effect of the operation.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 Created for resource creation

findings.title: evidence.reason field should enforce that only the matching evidence sub-object is populated
findings.narration: The `evidence` object contains a `reason` enum field alongside eight named sub-objects (`canceled`, `duplicate`, `fraudulent`, etc.). The relationship is purely semantic: only the sub-object matching the selected `reason` should be populated. This constraint is expressed nowhere in the schema — it exists only in Stripe's documentation prose. As a result, a caller can submit `reason: 'fraudulent'` while also providing a fully-populated `canceled` sub-object, and the schema will not reject it. This should be encoded as a JSON Schema `if/then` or `oneOf` construct so that tooling and client-side validators can enforce the constraint automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional field relationships expressed only in prose cannot be validated by generated clients, form validators, or linters. Schema encoding via `if/then` or `oneOf` would make the constraint machine-verifiable.
findings.patchSummary: Encode reason↔evidence sub-object mutual exclusivity as if/then or oneOf in evidence schema

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields inside evidence sub-objects reference Stripe resource IDs by name but are typed as bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Specifically: `evidence.duplicate.original_transaction` (an Issuing Transaction ID), and all `additional_documentation` fields (which reference file upload IDs, e.g. `file_...`). Without a pattern like `^(isxt|file)_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or a semantic format hint, code-generation tools have no way to establish a typed relationship to the referenced resource. This makes it impossible for SDKs to produce typed accessors or for validators to check ID format at input.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string prevent codegen from building typed relationships and deprive validators of format information needed to reject malformed IDs early.
findings.patchSummary: Add format or pattern hints to resource ID fields like original_transaction and additional_documentation

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions for client errors
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error catch-all. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `402`, `403`, or `404` response definitions. For a write endpoint that updates a financial dispute object — a sensitive resource that can be locked (e.g., already submitted to the card network) — callers need to distinguish between 'invalid input' (400), 'not found' (404), 'permission denied' (403), and 'state machine violation' (422). Using only a `default` bucket for all errors forces consumers to parse the Stripe error object at runtime rather than handling HTTP status semantics declaratively.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx responses allow client generators, API gateways, and mock servers to handle distinct error cases. A catch-all `default` loses HTTP-semantic richness important for dispute state management.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters.
Dispute not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default error catch-all

findings.title: No request body example for a complex nested evidence object
findings.narration: The request body schema is deeply nested, with eight possible evidence sub-objects each containing multiple `anyOf` fields that use the empty-string trick to represent 'unset'. There are no `examples` or `example` annotations anywhere on the request body or the `evidence` property. Developers integrating with this endpoint must mentally parse a multi-hundred-line schema to understand how to, say, submit evidence for a 'canceled' dispute or clear an existing evidence field. Even a single annotated example per evidence reason would dramatically reduce integration friction.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas with non-obvious unset conventions (empty string) need examples to communicate intended usage clearly. The absence of any example increases integration time and risk of misuse.
findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating evidence sub-object usage and the empty-string unset convention

findings.title: Dispute path parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `dispute` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe dispute IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `idp_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Issuing Dispute resource, and clients receive no early validation signal for obviously malformed IDs.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from establishing typed relationships and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to dispute path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response codes defined
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a catch-all `default` error response. For an action endpoint that submits a dispute to a card network — a sensitive operation that can fail with well-known business errors such as 400 (invalid dispute state or missing evidence), 404 (dispute not found), or 422 (validation failure) — the absence of explicit error codes makes it impossible for client developers to write precise error-handling logic without reading external documentation. The `default` catch-all is insufficient for documenting the distinct failure modes that Stripe itself documents.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx response definitions leave clients without machine-readable contracts for recoverable error cases, reducing API usability and forcing reliance on out-of-band documentation.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` keywords. This means validators, SDK generators, and documentation tools have no machine-readable constraint to enforce. A caller passing `limit=0` or `limit=999` will only discover the error at runtime from a 400 response, rather than being caught by client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints that should be encoded in schema are a high-leverage correctness issue. The description explicitly names bounds (1–100) and a default (10).
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `content: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and an empty properties object. GET requests with a body are semantically incorrect per RFC 9110 (servers and intermediaries may reject or ignore them), and Stripe's own convention for GET list endpoints passes all filters as query parameters — which this operation already does correctly. The empty body adds noise to generated SDKs and documentation without any functional benefit.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody is a known anti-pattern; all filterable fields are already expressed as query parameters, making the body entirely unnecessary.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET list endpoint

findings.title: POST creates a resource but returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new personalization design object. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource creation should respond with 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 200 conflates creation with retrieval/update, making it harder for clients and tooling to distinguish the operation type from the response alone.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for successful resource creation (POST that results in a new resource). Using 200 is a common but semantically incorrect practice.
findings.patchSummary: Rename 200 response to 201 Created for POST resource creation semantics.

findings.title: physical_bundle is a plain string ID with no format or pattern constraint

It is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. There is no `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^ics_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`), and no `$ref` to a typed schema. Codegen tools cannot infer the cross-resource relationship, and consumers have no hint about expected value shape.

findings.title: card_logo is a plain string file ID with no format or pattern

Without schema-level encoding, validators and SDK generators cannot enforce the rule automatically, leaving API consumers to discover the constraint at runtime.

While Stripe uses this pattern across many endpoints (likely to satisfy their SDK generation pipeline), the body here is entirely empty — it carries no information and may confuse code generators, client libraries, or intermediaries that reject GET requests with bodies. At minimum, it should not be listed as a recognized content type if there is nothing to encode.
findings.rationale: GET requests with empty request bodies are semantically incorrect and can cause interoperability issues with proxies and HTTP clients that strip or reject bodies on GET requests.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: session path parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `session` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe Financial Connections session IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `fcsess_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code generators produce untyped string fields with no validation, and API consumers have no machine-readable way to recognise the resource type. Adding a regex pattern (e.g., `^fcsess_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) or at least a meaningful `description` would improve type safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string without pattern or format lose typed relationship information useful to codegen tools and client-side validators.

findings.title: account_holder fields are plain strings with no format or pattern for resource IDs
findings.narration: The `account_holder[account]` and `account_holder[customer]` fields are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Both represent Stripe resource identifiers (`acct_...` and `cus_...` respectively) that follow well-known prefix patterns. Without a `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a typed schema, codegen tools cannot infer the relationship to those resources, and API consumers cannot validate inputs client-side before sending. The same applies to `account_holder[customer_account]`.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings lose typed relationships in codegen; adding patterns like `^acct_` and `^cus_` enables client-side validation and richer SDK types.
findings.patchSummary: Add prefix patterns to account_holder[account] and account_holder[customer] string fields.

findings.title: Mutually-exclusive account_holder fields encoded only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: The parameter description states: '`account_holder[customer]` and `account_holder[account]` are mutually exclusive.' This constraint is expressed only as natural language in the `description` field and is invisible to validators, code generators, and linters. JSON Schema provides `oneOf` / `not` / `dependentSchemas` constructs that can encode this relationship formally, making it machine-enforceable. As written, a client can supply both fields and only discover the conflict at runtime via an API error.
findings.rationale: Prose-only mutual-exclusion rules are a classic high-severity API clarity gap; encoding them in schema prevents ambiguous client implementations.
findings.patchSummary: Encode account/customer mutual exclusion with a 'not required' constraint in the schema.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100', but the schema specifies only `type: integer` with no `minimum: 1` or `maximum: 100`. This means validators and SDK generators will not enforce the documented range. A client can send `limit=0` or `limit=9999` and only learn the constraint from a runtime API error, not from the spec itself.
findings.rationale: Documented numeric ranges should always be encoded as schema constraints so validators and generated clients can catch invalid values before the request is sent.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, and default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty form-encoded request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content that contains an empty schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1); many HTTP intermediaries, proxies, and client libraries strip or ignore GET bodies. The presence of this request body definition could confuse consumers and tooling into thinking form parameters should be sent in the body rather than the query string.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies conflict with HTTP semantics and should be removed; all inputs for this operation are already correctly defined as query parameters.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty GET request body; all parameters are query-string based.

findings.title: Path parameter 'account' typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Financial Connections account IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `fca_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDKs and codegen tools cannot distinguish this resource ID from a free-form string, and no early validation can reject clearly malformed IDs before the round-trip to the server occurs. Adding a regex pattern such as `^fca_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would improve both client-side validation and generated SDK type safety.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings without pattern or format lose the ability for codegen tools to build typed relationships and prevent obvious misuse.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'account' path parameter to reflect FC account ID format

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared on this GET operation, containing an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema with `additionalProperties: false` and no properties. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP/1.1 semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients and intermediaries will silently drop it. Including an empty request body in the spec is misleading to consumers, may confuse code generators, and adds unnecessary noise. The `requestBody` block should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET operations with request bodies violate HTTP semantics and confuse SDK generators. An empty body schema compounds the issue.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation — GET requests must not carry a body

findings.title: Path parameter 'account' lacks format or pattern constraint for resource ID validation
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Financial Connections account IDs in Stripe follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `fca_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client-side validation and SDK codegen cannot distinguish this ID from arbitrary strings, increasing the chance of misuse or confusing error messages when an invalid ID is supplied.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern are a codegen and validation gap; a simple pattern like `^fca_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode the constraint properly.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error responses documented beyond the catch-all 'default'
findings.narration: The operation only documents a `200` success and a `default` error response. In practice, this endpoint can produce well-known HTTP error codes: `400` (invalid request parameters), `404` (account not found), and `403` (permission denied / account already disconnected). Collapsing all errors into `default` prevents clients and documentation generators from providing actionable error handling. Stripe's own error object structure is meaningful per status code, so distinguishing at least `400` and `404` would significantly improve the contract.
findings.rationale: Missing specific 4xx response definitions is a design and clarity gap that prevents typed error handling in generated SDKs and makes API documentation less useful.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and an empty schema on a GET request. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that a body on a GET has no defined semantics), and tooling (browsers, proxies, some HTTP clients) may strip or reject it. findings.title: `ownership` query parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The required `ownership` query parameter is described as 'The ID of the ownership object to fetch owners from.' It is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. As a cross-resource reference (an ownership object ID), it should carry a `pattern` (e.g. `^fcaowns_`) or at minimum a note in `format` so codegen tools can establish a typed relationship between this parameter and the ownership resource. Without this, the relationship is invisible to generated clients and validators.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed only as plain strings prevent codegen tools from building typed cross-resource relationships and make validation weaker.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema defines only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default`. This means a client passing `limit=0` or `limit=99999` would only fail at the server level with no prior schema validation feedback. The described constraints should be encoded directly in the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but absent from the schema cannot be enforced by client-side validators or codegen tooling, leading to avoidable server-side errors.

findings.title: Path parameter `account` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `account` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Financial Connections account IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g. `fca_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client-side validation tools and SDK code generators cannot enforce the correct ID format, potentially allowing arbitrary strings to reach the API where the server must reject them. Adding a pattern such as `^fca_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength` (Stripe IDs are nowhere near 5000 chars) would improve both safety and developer ergonomics.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference typed as plain string without format or pattern — a high-leverage finding for codegen and client validation.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response definitions (only `default` catch-all)
findings.narration: The responses object defines only `200` and `default`. For an operation that requires a specific resource ID in the path and a required `features` body field, there are well-known, actionable error conditions: `400 Bad Request` (invalid or missing `features`), `404 Not Found` (account not found), and `429 Too Many Requests` (rate limit). Collapsing all of these into a single `default` response hides the error contract from consumers, making it harder for clients to handle expected failure modes programmatically. At a minimum, `400` and `404` should be explicitly defined.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses reduces the API contract's precision; clients cannot distinguish expected failures from unexpected ones without explicit status code definitions.

findings.title: Path parameter 'mandate' lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `mandate` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or description. Stripe mandate IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g. `mandate_...`). Without a pattern or description, clients and codegen tools have no way to validate the ID format before making the request, increasing the chance of malformed requests and poor SDK ergonomics.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters typed as bare strings without pattern or description prevent codegen tools from building typed references and prevent client-side validation.

value.description: The ID of the Mandate to retrieve.

findings.title: Empty request body should be omitted on GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual per HTTP/1.1 and OpenAPI best practice; this empty body provides no value and may confuse HTTP clients, proxies, or code generators that encounter a GET with a body declaration. The request body should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET endpoints should not declare a requestBody. An empty, closed-schema body adds noise and can trigger incorrect behaviour in some HTTP client libraries.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Missing `ending_before` pagination cursor parameter
findings.narration: The operation provides `starting_after` for forward pagination but omits `ending_before`, which is the standard Stripe cursor-based pagination pattern for bidirectional traversal. Every other Stripe list endpoint that exposes `starting_after` also exposes `ending_before`, allowing callers to page backwards through a result set. Without it, clients cannot navigate to previous pages unless they cache all prior results themselves.
findings.rationale: Incomplete pagination support forces clients into forward-only traversal and deviates from the established Stripe list API convention, reducing usability.

value.description: A cursor for use in pagination. `ending_before` is an object ID that defines your place in the list. For instance, if you make a list request and receive 100 objects, starting with `obj_bar`, your subsequent call can include `ending_before=obj_bar` in order to fetch the previous page of the list.

findings.patchSummary: Add standard `ending_before` cursor parameter to enable backward pagination.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100', but the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means any API client, code generator, or validation layer using the schema alone will not enforce the documented bounds. A caller could submit `limit=0` or `limit=99999` and receive an opaque server error rather than a clear schema validation failure.

findings.title: `payment_record` filter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The required `payment_record` query parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. This is a cross-resource reference to a Payment Record ID (presumably prefixed, e.g. `prcd_...`). Without a `pattern`, `format`, or `$ref` to a typed ID schema, code generators cannot infer the relationship, and validation layers cannot detect obviously malformed IDs (e.g. a blank string or a charge ID passed by mistake) before the request hits the server.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields used as foreign-key filters benefit from a pattern or format annotation so that generated clients and validators can surface type mismatches early.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern and resource annotation to the `payment_record` ID parameter.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with an empty properties object and `required: false`. GET requests with a body are discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 notes many intermediaries will drop or reject GET bodies). All filtering parameters are already expressed as query parameters, making the request body redundant and potentially confusing to consumers and proxy infrastructure alike.
findings.rationale: Including a request body on a GET operation violates conventional HTTP semantics and may cause interoperability issues with proxies, CDNs, or HTTP clients that strip GET bodies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty request body from the GET operation.

findings.title: GET request body is semantically incorrect
findings.narration: This GET operation defines a `requestBody` containing an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. Per HTTP semantics and the OpenAPI 3.x specification, GET requests should not carry a request body. While some HTTP implementations tolerate it, most clients, proxies, and frameworks will ignore or reject it. The body here is also empty (no properties), making it completely useless. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 and OpenAPI 3.x both discourage/disallow request bodies on GET. This is a design violation that confuses consumers and code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/payment_attempt_records/{id}

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000, which provides no useful validation. Stripe resource IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `par_...` for Payment Attempt Records). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a meaningful `minLength`, consumers and code generators have no ability to validate the identifier or infer its type. Adding a pattern such as `^par_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at least a `minLength: 1` would close this gap.
findings.rationale: Untyped resource ID strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow trivially invalid inputs (empty string) past schema validation.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema is simply `{ "type": "integer" }` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints encoded. This means client validation tools and code generators cannot enforce the documented range, and API clients may accidentally send out-of-range values without compile-time or lint-time feedback. The documented default of 10 should also be set as `default: 10` so generated SDKs and documentation tools surface it accurately.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints that belong in the schema prevent automated validation and reduce SDK quality. The minimum/maximum/default can and should be encoded in JSON Schema.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 constraints to `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `customer` and `customer_account` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Both `customer` and `customer_account` are resource ID references (to Stripe Customer objects and account objects respectively) but are declared as bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. Stripe resource IDs have well-known prefixes (e.g. `cus_` for customers, `acct_` for accounts). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a `format` annotation, code generators and client validators have no way to distinguish these from arbitrary free-text strings. This hampers type-safe SDK generation and makes it harder to detect obviously malformed IDs early.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent typed relationship modeling in generated clients and miss cheap client-side validation opportunities.
findings.patchSummary: Add Stripe prefix patterns to `customer` and `customer_account` ID params.

findings.title: Superfluous empty `requestBody` on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`) and `required: false`. HTTP GET requests should not carry a request body per RFC 9110 §9.3.1 semantics; many HTTP clients and intermediaries strip or reject bodies on GET. Including it here — even as `required: false` — signals to client generators that a body is expected, potentially producing broken clients. The body carries no information anyway (all filters are query parameters) and should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies violate HTTP semantics and confuse code generators; an empty, non-required body on a read endpoint is dead weight that can cause real client issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically incorrect requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Conditional-required fields expressed only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: Several parameters are described as only usable with `confirm=true` but this constraint is expressed purely in prose descriptions rather than being encoded as schema-level dependencies. Affected fields include: `error_on_requires_action`, `mandate`, `mandate_data`, `off_session`, `return_url`, `payment_method` (partial guidance), and `use_stripe_sdk`. For example, `error_on_requires_action` states 'This parameter can only be used with `confirm=true`', but there is no JSON Schema `if/then`, `dependencies`, or `oneOf` construct enforcing this. Code generators, validators, and SDK authors cannot automatically enforce these relationships, leading to silent misuse where a caller sends these fields without `confirm=true` and only discovers the error at runtime via a server-side error response.
findings.rationale: Conditional field constraints expressed only in prose are a high-leverage schema gap; they cannot be enforced at the client or SDK-generation layer without schema encoding.

patchOps.value: Set to `true` to fail the payment attempt if the PaymentIntent transitions into `requires_action`. This parameter can only be used with `confirm=true`. NOTE: enforce via schema dependency on confirm=true.

findings.patchSummary: Add schema-level if/then or dependentRequired to enforce confirm=true dependency for conditional params

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that reference other Stripe resource IDs are typed as `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref` to a typed schema. Specifically: `customer` (Customer ID, e.g. `cus_...`), `customer_account` (Account ID, e.g. `acct_...`), `on_behalf_of` (Account ID), `payment_method` (PaymentMethod ID, e.g. `pm_...`), `payment_method_configuration` (PaymentMethodConfiguration ID), `confirmation_token` (ConfirmationToken ID), `mandate` (Mandate ID), and `transfer_data.destination` (Account ID). Without a `format` or `pattern` (e.g. `pattern: '^cus_'`), code generators produce no typed cross-resource relationships, and client-side validators cannot catch values like an arbitrary free-form string passed where a Customer ID is expected.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare string with no format or pattern prevent codegen from building typed relationships and prevent client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add format: stripe-id (or pattern) to resource ID fields: customer, on_behalf_of, payment_method, mandate, etc.

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions; only 200 and a generic 'default'
findings.narration: The responses object defines only `200` (success) and `default` (error). There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `402`, `403`, or `422` response codes defined. For an operation as complex as creating a PaymentIntent — which can fail due to invalid parameters, authentication errors, card declines, currency mismatches, and more — the absence of explicit 4xx entries means API clients and documentation consumers cannot programmatically discover what error shapes to expect for which HTTP status code. The generic `default` entry does not substitute for explicit per-status-code error documentation, especially for payment-critical workflows where distinguishing a 400 validation error from a 402 card decline is essential.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx response codes reduce discoverability and correctness for payment-critical error handling by clients and SDK generators.

value.description: Bad request. Invalid parameter or missing required field.
Payment required. Card decline or insufficient funds.
Unauthorized. Invalid or missing API key.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400, 401, 402 response definitions alongside the generic default error response

findings.title: payment_method_data.type discriminator not linked to sub-object presence
findings.narration: The `payment_method_data` object requires a `type` field (discriminator) but does not use a JSON Schema `discriminator` object or `oneOf`/`if-then` constructs to enforce that the matching sub-object (e.g., `type: 'sepa_debit'` requires `sepa_debit.iban`) must be present. This relationship is implicit: the `sepa_debit` sub-schema has `required: ['iban']`, but nothing enforces that when `type=sepa_debit`, the `sepa_debit` key must be present. The same applies to `fpx` (requires `bank`), `boleto` (requires `tax_id`), and `sofort` (requires `country`). Callers can set `type=sepa_debit` and omit the `sepa_debit` object entirely without any schema-level error, only failing at server runtime.
findings.rationale: Type discriminator without schema-level enforcement of corresponding sub-object presence is a high-leverage design gap for payment method data.

patchOps.value: When type=sepa_debit, sepa_debit is required; when type=fpx, fpx.bank is required; when type=sofort, sofort.country is required; when type=boleto, boleto.tax_id is required. These constraints should be encoded as oneOf or if/then branches.

findings.patchSummary: Encode type-discriminator constraints in payment_method_data as oneOf/if-then rather than implicit co-presence

findings.narration: This GET operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP/1.1 semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients and proxies will silently drop or reject a GET body. All meaningful inputs here are already expressed as query parameters, so the request body declaration is both unnecessary and potentially confusing for SDK/codegen consumers.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 discourages a body on GET requests; an empty body schema adds noise and may cause codegen tools to emit body-serialization code for a GET call.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description says it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema contains no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` keywords. This means a client passing `limit=0` or `limit=9999` would not be flagged by schema validation, and codegen tools cannot surface the valid range or the default to end users. The constraint exists only in prose, which is lower-fidelity than a machine-readable schema.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are not enforced by validators or surfaced by SDKs; encoding them in the schema prevents out-of-range values reaching the server.

findings.title: Missing example on the `query` parameter
findings.narration: The `query` parameter is the core input to this endpoint and accepts a domain-specific search query language. Without an example, developers must navigate to external documentation to understand what a valid query looks like. Adding at least one example (e.g., `status:'succeeded' AND amount>5000`) directly in the spec would significantly improve usability for both human readers and tools that render interactive docs.

findings.title: client_secret transmitted as a URL query parameter
findings.narration: The `client_secret` parameter is defined as an optional query parameter (`in: query`). Even though it is described as occasionally required when using a publishable key, transmitting it in the query string means the secret can appear in server access logs, browser history, proxy logs, CDN/WAF request logs, and HTTP referrer headers. The `client_secret` is a sensitive credential that grants the bearer ability to confirm and complete a PaymentIntent. Stripe's own documentation warns about this; at minimum the spec should mark it as sensitive and the description should carry a security warning. Ideally, server-side retrieval should use a header, though that would be a bigger API change.
findings.rationale: Sensitive secrets in URL query strings are exposed to logging infrastructure, browser history, and referrers, constituting a critical security risk per OWASP API Security Top 10 (API8).

patchOps.value: The client secret of the PaymentIntent. Required when using a publishable key. WARNING: This value is transmitted in the URL query string and may appear in server logs or browser history. Use server-side retrieval with a secret key wherever possible.

findings.patchSummary: Add security warning to client_secret description and mark it as sensitive.

findings.title: Conditional-required field (client_secret) expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The description states that `client_secret` is required when using a publishable key to retrieve the PaymentIntent, yet it is marked `required: false` with no schema-level conditional encoding. This prose-only rule cannot be validated by client libraries, code generators, or schema validators. The relationship 'required when authenticated with a publishable key' cannot be expressed purely in OpenAPI 3.x query parameters, but at minimum a note using `x-conditionally-required` or a dedicated description callout should accompany this, and the pattern/format of the secret should be constrained so tooling can identify its role.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required constraints expressed only in prose are missed by automated validation, code generation, and API linting tools. High severity per spec review guidelines.

findings.patchSummary: Mark client_secret as conditionally required and add a pattern constraint to enable tooling validation.

Without a `pattern` or `format`, code generators cannot produce typed resource references, client-side validation cannot reject obviously malformed IDs early, and documentation tooling cannot link this parameter to the PaymentIntent resource.
