findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual and discouraged by RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), as intermediaries (proxies, CDNs, load balancers) may strip or ignore the body. This empty body serves no purpose and may confuse SDK generators into emitting unnecessary body-handling code for a read-only endpoint.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a body violate HTTP semantics expectations and may be dropped by intermediaries; an empty body definition adds noise for code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields in the request body represent references to other Stripe resources but are declared as bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Specifically: `customer` (Customer ID), `customer_account` (Account ID), `payment_method` (PaymentMethod/Card/Source ID), and `payment_method_configuration` (PaymentMethodConfiguration ID). Without a format hint (e.g., `format: stripe-id`) or a pattern (e.g., `^(cus_|acct_|pm_|card_)[A-Za-z0-9]+$`), codegen tools cannot build typed cross-resource relationships, and clients cannot perform lightweight client-side validation on the ID shape before making the API call.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and deprive API consumers of any structural hint about what kind of value is expected.
findings.patchSummary: Add format: stripe-id to customer, customer_account, payment_method, payment_method_configuration fields

findings.title: transfer_group conditional-required rule encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `transfer_group` field description states: "You can only provide `transfer_group` if it hasn't been set." This is a conditional write constraint that cannot be expressed as a JSON Schema rule in OpenAPI 3.x, but no attempt has been made to even call it out clearly as a constraint. More importantly, a related conditional rule exists implicitly: `application_fee_amount` and `transfer_data` only apply when the PaymentIntent is created on a connected account. These relationships are documented elsewhere in Stripe's docs but are absent from the field descriptions here, meaning an API consumer reading only this spec has no way to know when these fields are applicable. The `transfer_group` one-time-set constraint in particular should be highlighted with a dedicated `x-` extension or at minimum a more explicit description note.
findings.rationale: Conditional constraints expressed only in prose are easy to miss and cannot be enforced by validators or surfaced by codegen. The transfer_group rule is a subtle one-way door that can cause permanent state issues if ignored.

patchOps.value: A string that identifies the resulting payment as part of a group. You can only provide `transfer_group` if it has not already been set on the PaymentIntent; once set it cannot be changed. Learn more about the [use case for connected accounts](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/connected-accounts). Note: this field can only be set once; subsequent updates that include this field when it is already set will be rejected.

findings.patchSummary: Strengthen transfer_group description to make the one-time-set constraint unambiguous

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions (only 'default' error documented)
findings.narration: The operation documents only a `200` success response and a `default` error response. There are no explicit `400`, `402`, `403`, `404`, or `422` response definitions. For an update endpoint that can fail in well-known ways — e.g., 404 if the PaymentIntent does not exist, 400 for invalid parameter combinations, 402 for payment-specific errors — having only a catch-all `default` error definition means consumers cannot write precise error-handling logic or generate strongly-typed error handlers. Stripe's API is known to return structured error objects with distinct HTTP status codes, and these should be enumerated.
findings.rationale: Without explicit 4xx response codes, API consumers and code generators cannot distinguish between client errors (invalid input, not found) and server errors, making it harder to write correct error handling.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.
PaymentIntent not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default error catch-all

findings.title: Empty request body on GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` media type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). While Stripe uses this pattern across its API to pass query parameters, the presence of a body definition on a GET endpoint is semantically incorrect and will confuse HTTP clients, proxies, and OpenAPI tooling. The body serves no purpose here since all parameters are already declared via `parameters`.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP semantics. The empty body schema adds noise and may cause issues with strict HTTP clients or code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET endpoint

findings.title: Missing minimum/maximum constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. This means API consumers and validators cannot enforce the documented range, and code generators will not produce idiomatic typed parameters with sensible defaults. The constraints exist in prose but should be encoded in the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but not encoded in the schema are a high-leverage finding: validators cannot enforce them, and code generators cannot surface them to consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: `intent` path parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `intent` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. PaymentIntent IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `pi_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format`, code generation tools cannot build typed references between this endpoint and the PaymentIntent resource, and client-side validation cannot catch obviously malformed IDs before making a network call. At minimum, a `pattern` such as `^pi_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would improve safety.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no format or pattern prevent code generators from building typed cross-resource relationships and allow malformed IDs to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `intent` path parameter schema

findings.title: No format or pattern constraint on 'intent' path parameter
findings.narration: The `intent` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. PaymentIntent IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `pi_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code generators and API clients cannot validate that the supplied value is actually a PaymentIntent ID rather than an arbitrary string. A `pattern` like `^pi_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode this constraint formally and improve developer experience and static analysis.
findings.rationale: Resource ID typed as plain string with no pattern or format; codegen cannot build a typed relationship.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'intent' path parameter to enforce PaymentIntent ID format

findings.title: Conditional relationship between 'amount' and 'currency' encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `amount` field description notes that when an amount is supplied, it applies from the customer's cash balance. The `currency` field is a sibling property with no documented relationship to `amount`. In practice, applying a partial balance amount likely requires currency to be specified consistently with the PaymentIntent currency. Even if not strictly conditional, the interplay between these two fields is expressed purely in prose. If `currency` is relevant only when `amount` is set, that constraint should be encoded as a JSON Schema `dependentRequired` or `if/then` clause rather than left implicit. This makes the relationship invisible to validators and code generators.
findings.rationale: Field relationship (currency relevant alongside amount) is prose-only; should be JSON Schema encoded.
findings.patchSummary: Encode currency-depends-on-amount relationship via dependentRequired in request schema

findings.title: No example provided for the request body
findings.narration: The request body schema for this action endpoint has meaningful optional fields (`amount`, `currency`) whose interplay is non-trivial, especially given the Invoice override behaviour documented in the `amount` description. No `example` or `examples` block is present on the request body schema or its encoding. Adding at least one example (e.g., applying a partial amount of 500 in USD) would significantly aid developer understanding and allow tools to auto-populate test requests.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on a non-trivial request body with conditional field semantics reduces clarity for consumers.

partial_apply.summary: Apply a partial customer balance amount

findings.patchSummary: Add a request body example demonstrating partial balance application with amount and currency

findings.title: Path parameter 'intent' typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `intent` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. PaymentIntent IDs follow a well-known Stripe prefix pattern (`pi_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, generated client code and documentation cannot distinguish this from an arbitrary freeform string, making it harder to validate inputs early or produce typed cross-resource references in SDKs.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields named after a known resource type that lack pattern or format constraints prevent typed relationship building in codegen and reduce early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'intent' path param to reflect PaymentIntent ID format.

findings.title: Missing explicit 4xx error response definitions (e.g. 400, 402, 404, 422)
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` catch-all error response. Cancelling a PaymentIntent has well-known failure modes: calling it when the status is not cancellable results in a 402 or 400 error; an invalid `intent` ID returns a 404. Callers relying on generated clients get no typed information about when to expect which status codes. The `default` bucket collapses all error cases into one opaque shape, removing the ability for tools and developers to branch on HTTP status.
findings.rationale: Distinct 4xx response codes are well-known for this operation type and their absence forces developers to read prose docs rather than relying on the machine-readable spec.

value.description: Bad request — e.g. invalid cancellation_reason value.
PaymentIntent not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add 400 and 404 response definitions to document known error cases explicitly.

findings.title: Conditional prose rule for `statement_descriptor` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `statement_descriptor` field description states 'Setting this value for a card charge returns an error. For card charges, set the `statement_descriptor_suffix` instead.' This mutual-exclusion rule between `statement_descriptor` and card charges is documented only in prose. Additionally, the relationship between `statement_descriptor` and `statement_descriptor_suffix` (effectively 'not both at once for card charges') cannot be enforced by API clients or SDK generators because it lives only in free text. Ideally this should be encoded as a JSON Schema `not` / `oneOf` constraint, or at minimum the description should clarify the exact condition under which the field is disallowed.
findings.rationale: Conditional field rules left only in prose are invisible to validators and code generators, increasing the risk of client-side misuse and hard-to-debug API errors.

patchOps.value:
Text that appears on the customer's statement as the statement descriptor for a non-card charge. This value overrides the account's default statement descriptor. For information about requirements, including the 22-character limit, see [the Statement Descriptor docs](https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/account/statement-descriptors).

Must not be used for card charges; use `statement_descriptor_suffix` instead. Passing this field for a card charge will return an error. Mutually exclusive with card payment method types.

findings.patchSummary: Strengthen prose to explicitly call out mutual exclusivity; ideally encode as schema constraint.

findings.title: `intent` path parameter typed as unbounded string — no ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `intent` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe PaymentIntent IDs follow the well-known prefix pattern `pi_[alphanumeric]+`. Without a `pattern` or at minimum an example, code generators treat this as an arbitrary free-form string, losing the typed relationship to the PaymentIntent resource. A `pattern` such as `^pi_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or an `example` value would make the relationship explicit and allow client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters typed as plain strings without format, pattern, or example prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow obviously wrong inputs past client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and example to `intent` path param to encode PaymentIntent ID format.

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body contains a deeply nested schema with `amount_details`, `line_items`, `payment_details`, `transfer_data`, and `hooks` — all of which interact in non-obvious ways (e.g., multicapture, connected accounts, industry-specific line items). There are no `examples` or `example` fields on the request body or any of its complex sub-objects. Without examples, developers relying on the spec as documentation must infer correct usage from field descriptions alone, increasing integration errors particularly around amount arithmetic validation and line-item structure.
findings.rationale: Complex, multi-level schemas without examples significantly hamper developer experience and increase misuse of conditionally required nested fields like `amount_details.line_items` and `transfer_data`.

partial_capture_with_transfer.summary: Partial capture with connected account transfer

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples illustrating common capture scenarios.

findings.title: client_secret transmitted in request body without writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The `client_secret` field in the request body is the PaymentIntent's client secret — a sensitive credential that grants the holder the ability to confirm the payment on behalf of the customer. It is transmitted in the POST body (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) but lacks `writeOnly: true`, meaning API documentation generators and SDK code generators will treat it as a readable/printable field. Logging middleware that echoes back parsed request bodies, generated client models that include this field in toString() output, and documentation tools that show sample responses could all inadvertently expose this secret. Adding `writeOnly: true` to this field is the correct mitigation per OpenAPI 3.x §4.8.25.
findings.rationale: Credentials and secrets in request schemas should be marked writeOnly to signal to tooling that they must not be echoed in logs, responses, or generated model output.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to client_secret in the request body schema

findings.title: mandate_data conditional requirements expressed only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: The `mandate_data` field uses a three-branch `anyOf` (secret_key_param, empty string, client_key_param) where the correct branch depends on whether the caller is using a secret key or a publishable/client key. This distinction is described in the Stripe documentation but is not encoded in the schema itself — there is no discriminator, no `if/then/else`, and no prose description on the field explaining the branching rule. Consumers relying solely on the OpenAPI schema cannot determine which branch to use or when each is applicable. At minimum, descriptions should be added to each `anyOf` branch; ideally, a `discriminator` or description on the parent field should explain the mutual exclusivity of the two keyed variants.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements that exist only in prose and not in schema encoding prevent validators and SDK generators from enforcing correct usage, leading to integration errors.

patchOps.value: Mandate details. Use the `secret_key_param` shape when authenticating with a secret key; use the `client_key_param` shape when authenticating with a publishable key (only `online` customer acceptance type is permitted in that case). Pass an empty string to unset.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to mandate_data explaining which anyOf branch applies to secret vs. publishable key callers

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error catch-all. Stripe's API commonly returns 400 (invalid request), 402 (payment failed / card declined), 404 (intent not found), and 422 (unprocessable entity) with structured error objects. Without explicit 4xx definitions, client SDK generators cannot produce typed error-handling code, and developers reading the spec have no schema-level guidance on what error shapes to expect for foreseeable failure modes of a confirm operation. The `default` handler is not a substitute because it collapses all failure modes into one undifferentiated bucket and many tools skip it when generating typed error models.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx responses allow tooling to generate typed error handlers and give API consumers schema-level documentation of expected failure modes.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.
Payment failed (e.g. card declined).
PaymentIntent not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400, 402, and 404 response definitions alongside the default error catch-all

findings.title: confirmation_token and payment_method_data precedence rule encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description of `confirmation_token` states: "If the provided ConfirmationToken contains properties that are also being provided in this request, such as `payment_method`, then the values in this request will take precedence." This is a field-interaction rule that affects how callers should combine these parameters, but it is expressed only in the description string of `confirmation_token`. There is no cross-field constraint in the schema (e.g., a note on `payment_method_data` or a `oneOf`/`not` dependency) indicating that `confirmation_token` and `payment_method_data` interact. Callers reading `payment_method_data` in isolation will not discover this overriding behavior.
findings.rationale: Field interaction rules documented only on one of the two interacting fields are frequently missed; the rule should appear on both fields or be encoded as a schema constraint.

patchOps.value: If provided, this hash will be used to create a PaymentMethod. The new PaymentMethod will appear in the `payment_method` property on the PaymentIntent. If `confirmation_token` is also provided and contains overlapping properties (such as `payment_method`), values supplied directly in this request take precedence over those from the ConfirmationToken.

findings.patchSummary: Add cross-field precedence note to payment_method_data description referencing confirmation_token interaction

findings.title: Cross-resource ID field `hooks.inputs.tax.calculation` typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `hooks.inputs.tax.calculation` field references a Tax Calculation resource ID (Stripe IDs typically follow a prefix pattern like `taxcalc_...`). It is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint and no `format`, `pattern`, or description that clarifies its resource type beyond the property name. Without a pattern constraint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Tax Calculation resource, and API consumers cannot validate the value before submission.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed cross-resource relationships and allow malformed values to reach the API.

value.description: ID of the Tax Calculation object representing the tax applied to this payment.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `hooks.inputs.tax.calculation` to identify it as a Tax Calculation resource ID.

findings.title: Missing request body example for a complex multi-field endpoint
findings.narration: The `increment_authorization` endpoint accepts a rich request body with nested objects (`amount_details`, `hooks`, `payment_details`, `transfer_data`) and several optional monetary and metadata fields. There are no examples provided at either the request body or schema level. Given the business-critical nature of incrementing a payment authorization (irreversible financial operation), the absence of an example makes it substantially harder for integrators to understand correct usage, especially for edge cases like partial field updates or industry-specific `amount_details`.
findings.rationale: Complex financial operation endpoints with nested schemas should include at least one request body example to reduce integration errors.

value.description: Updated authorization for hotel stay

findings.patchSummary: Add a request body example illustrating a minimal incremental authorization call.

findings.title: `amount` field missing minimum constraint — must be greater than current authorized amount but no minimum is enforced
findings.narration: The `amount` field is declared as `type: integer` and marked `required`, but has no `minimum` constraint. The description states the value 'must be greater than the currently authorized amount', which is a server-side constraint that cannot be fully encoded statically. However, a `minimum: 1` (or at least `minimum: 0`, excluding zero and negative values) would prevent obviously invalid payloads from being submitted and enable client-side validation to catch clearly wrong inputs before a round-trip to the API.
findings.rationale: Required numeric fields representing monetary amounts should carry at minimum a `minimum: 1` constraint to reject non-positive values at the schema validation layer.
findings.patchSummary: Add `minimum: 1` to the `amount` field to prevent non-positive integer values.

findings.title: descriptor_code field lacks pattern constraint for SM-prefixed six-character code
findings.narration: The description for `descriptor_code` states it is 'a six-character code starting with SM present in the microdeposit sent to the bank account.' This means the field has an implicit format: exactly 6 characters, beginning with 'SM'. However, the schema only declares `maxLength: 5000` and `type: string`, which is far too permissive. A client sending a 10-character arbitrary string would pass schema validation but fail at the API level. The constraint should be encoded as a `pattern` (e.g. `^SM[A-Z0-9]{4}$`) and the `maxLength` should be tightened to 6. Without this, code generators produce no validation hint and clients get confusing runtime errors instead of client-side validation failures.
findings.rationale: Field-level constraints expressed only in prose are a classic high-leverage finding — they should be machine-readable so clients validate before sending.
findings.patchSummary: Constrain descriptor_code to exactly 6 chars matching ^SM[A-Z0-9]{4}$

findings.title: amounts array missing minItems/maxItems constraints despite documented semantics
findings.narration: The description for `amounts` says 'two positive integers, in cents, equal to the values of the microdeposits sent to the bank account.' This clearly specifies exactly two items, but the schema has no `minItems` or `maxItems` constraints. A consumer could submit an empty array or an array of 10 values, which would pass schema validation but fail at the API. Additionally, the items should carry a `minimum: 1` constraint since the description states they must be positive integers. These omissions mean validation tools and generated SDK clients cannot catch malformed requests before they hit the wire.
findings.rationale: Documented cardinality and value constraints (exactly two, positive) should be machine-encoded to enable client-side validation and accurate SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Constrain amounts to exactly 2 positive integers (minItems:2, maxItems:2, minimum:1)

findings.title: Conditional-required relationship between amounts and descriptor_code encoded only in prose
findings.narration: Microdeposit verification for ACH supports two distinct flows: an amounts-based verification and a descriptor_code-based verification. Only one of `amounts` or `descriptor_code` should be provided depending on the microdeposit type configured — providing both or neither is likely an error. This mutual-exclusivity or exactly-one-of requirement is not encoded in the schema at all; it exists implicitly in the Stripe documentation. As a result, a client that sends both fields, or neither, will only discover the error at runtime. Using `oneOf` with two sub-schemas (one requiring `amounts`, the other requiring `descriptor_code`) would make this constraint machine-checkable.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually exclusive field relationships documented only in prose should be encoded as JSON Schema oneOf/not to enable validation tooling and accurate SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Encode amounts/descriptor_code mutual exclusivity as oneOf in the request schema

findings.title: client_secret transmitted in POST body without writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The `client_secret` field is a sensitive credential that authenticates client-side calls to the PaymentIntent. Including it in the request body is acceptable for a form-encoded endpoint, but the field should be marked `writeOnly: true` to signal to documentation generators and SDK tools that this value must never be echoed back in a response or logged. Without this marker, generated clients and API explorers may inadvertently expose the secret in response display panels, log aggregators, or test harnesses. This is a low-friction addition that significantly reduces the risk of credential leakage through tooling.
findings.rationale: Credential fields included in request bodies should carry writeOnly:true to prevent accidental exposure in logs, generated docs, and API explorers.
findings.patchSummary: Mark client_secret as writeOnly:true to prevent accidental exposure in tooling

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter's description explicitly states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema definition for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. Consumers relying on machine-readable schema (e.g., form generators, SDK validators) cannot enforce these bounds without reading prose. A request with `limit=0` or `limit=999` would appear valid according to the schema.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints belong in the schema, not only in prose. Missing `minimum`, `maximum`, and `default` means client-side and codegen tooling cannot enforce or reflect the valid range.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema object. GET requests with a body are discouraged by RFC 7231 and many HTTP clients and intermediaries drop or reject GET request bodies. All relevant inputs for this list endpoint are already covered by query parameters. Defining a body here creates confusion and may cause interoperability issues.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 states GET request bodies have no defined semantics. An empty, no-op request body adds noise and may confuse tooling or clients into thinking a body is expected.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/payment_links

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `application_fee_amount` and `application_fee_percent` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The descriptions for `application_fee_amount` and `application_fee_percent` each describe a constraint that makes them mutually exclusive by use-case: `application_fee_amount` applies only when there are no recurring prices, while `application_fee_percent` requires at least one recurring price. This conditional relationship exists only in prose. JSON Schema `oneOf` or a `not` / `dependencies` construct should encode this so validators and codegen tools can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules expressed only in prose are a high-leverage finding; the schema should encode exclusivity to prevent misuse at the API boundary.

value.description: application_fee_amount and application_fee_percent are mutually exclusive

findings.patchSummary: Add `not` constraint to prevent both application_fee_amount and application_fee_percent being set together

findings.title: Conditional field `after_completion.redirect` required only when `type` is `redirect` — not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `after_completion` object has a `type` enum of `hosted_confirmation` or `redirect`, but the `redirect` sub-object (which has `url` as required) is only required when `type` equals `redirect`. This conditional requirement is implicit from structure but is not encoded via `if/then/else` or `oneOf`. Consumers cannot statically determine when `redirect` is mandatory, leading to potential runtime errors.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields expressed via structure rather than schema keywords prevent static validation and reduce client-side safety.

value.description: Behavior after the purchase is complete.
value.title: after_completion_params

findings.patchSummary: Encode after_completion type-conditional requirement for `redirect` via oneOf

findings.title: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields reference other Stripe resources by ID but are declared only as `type: string` without any `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`: `on_behalf_of` (account ID), `transfer_data.destination` (account ID), `automatic_tax.liability.account` (account ID), `invoice_creation.invoice_data.issuer.account` (account ID), `subscription_data.invoice_settings.issuer.account` (account ID), `line_items[].price` (price ID), and `line_items[].price_data.product` (product ID). Codegen tools cannot build typed relationships from these, and API consumers have no machine-readable hint about expected ID format (e.g., `acct_`, `price_`, `prod_`).
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields without format or pattern prevent typed SDK generation and give consumers no validation hint about the expected identifier prefix or shape.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-format patterns to cross-resource reference string fields (account, price, product IDs)

findings.title: No examples provided for the complex request body
findings.narration: The request body schema is very large with many nested objects and conditional fields (line_items, after_completion, automatic_tax, invoice_creation, subscription_data, etc.). Despite this complexity, no `examples` or `example` block is provided at the request body level or on any individual property. This significantly hinders developer understanding and makes documentation tooling (e.g., Swagger UI, Redoc) show blank example panels. At minimum, one representative example showing a basic one-time payment link and one showing a subscription link would be valuable.
findings.rationale: Complex schemas with no examples increase integration time and error rates for API consumers; examples are especially important for multi-mode objects like this one.
findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples for basic one-time and subscription payment link creation

findings.title: Conditional field rule for `after_completion.redirect` only expressed in prose
findings.narration: The `after_completion` object has a `type` field (enum: `hosted_confirmation` | `redirect`) and two sub-objects `hosted_confirmation` and `redirect`. The semantic rule — that `redirect` sub-object is required when `type` is `redirect`, and that `hosted_confirmation` sub-object is only meaningful when `type` is `hosted_confirmation` — is not encoded in the schema. It exists only by the presence of `required: ["url"]` inside `redirect` itself (which would always be validated, even when `type` is `hosted_confirmation`). This should be expressed as a `oneOf` / `if-then-else` discriminated by `type`, so that validators and codegen tools can model the relationship correctly.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields in prose (or implicitly via always-required sub-properties) not encoded as schema is a high-leverage pattern that causes misleading validation errors and poor codegen output.

value.description: Behavior after the purchase is complete.
value.title: after_completion_params

findings.patchSummary: Encode after_completion type-discriminated shape as oneOf instead of implicit always-required sub-object

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain `string` with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that clearly reference Stripe resource IDs — `automatic_tax.liability.account`, `invoice_creation.invoice_data.issuer.account`, `subscription_data.invoice_settings.issuer.account`, and `line_items[].id` — are typed as plain `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Stripe resource IDs have a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `acct_`, `li_`). Without at least a `pattern` or a dedicated format annotation, codegen tools cannot model these as typed foreign-key references, and documentation consumers cannot distinguish them from free-form strings.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and hide the expected value shape from API consumers.

patchOps.value: The connected account ID (e.g. acct_...) used as the tax liability account. Required when type is `account`.

findings.patchSummary: Annotate account-ID string fields with resource type hints and descriptions

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` catch-all error response. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `402`, `403`, or `404` response definitions. For a write operation that accepts a resource ID in the path and a rich request body, clients benefit from documented distinct error status codes — particularly `404` (payment link not found), `400` (validation error), and `401`/`403` (auth failures). The `default` alone is insufficient for clients that need to handle specific HTTP status codes programmatically.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses forces clients to rely on the catch-all `default`, making it harder to distinguish between authentication errors, not-found, and validation errors at the code level.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.
Payment link not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default catch-all

findings.title: Empty request body on GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). While technically not forbidden, many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will strip or reject a body on GET requests. This body definition serves no purpose and misleads consumers into thinking a body is expected or supported.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a meaningful request body. Including one in the spec — even an empty one — is incorrect HTTP semantics and can cause client/proxy interoperability issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100, with a default of 10. However, the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. Consumers and codegen tools cannot enforce or communicate the valid range automatically, and clients relying on the schema alone will not know the default value.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints (min=1, max=100, default=10) should be encoded in the schema so validators and SDK generators can enforce them without parsing prose.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum, maximum, and default constraints to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Response `url` field lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `url` property on the 200 response schema is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000, but it represents a URL. Without `format: uri` (or at minimum a pattern), client code generators and validators cannot distinguish it from a generic string, reducing type safety and client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Fields that represent URLs should use `format: uri` so that tooling can validate and type them correctly.
findings.patchSummary: Add format: uri to the response url property

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. This means clients and validators cannot enforce the documented contract, and code generators will produce unconstrained integer fields. A value of 0 or -5 would pass schema validation even though the API would reject it.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints should reflect documented rules; prose-only constraints are not machine-enforceable and reduce the value of the spec for validation and codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum, maximum, and default to `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Request body on a GET endpoint is semantically incorrect
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is defined on this GET operation with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content and an empty schema. GET requests must not carry a message body per RFC 9110 §9.3.1, and several HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will ignore or reject it. All parameters for this operation are already expressed as query parameters, making the body superfluous and potentially confusing to API consumers and code generators.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a body violate HTTP semantics and can cause interoperability problems with clients and intermediaries that discard or reject bodies on GET requests.
findings.patchSummary: Remove requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Malformed markdown link in `payco` description (missing closing bracket)
findings.narration: The `payco` field description reads: `"PAYCO is a [single-use](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-methods#usage local wallet available in South Korea."` — the closing parenthesis of the markdown link is missing, making the URL bleed into the prose. The same defect is present in the `samsung_pay` description: `"Samsung Pay is a [single-use](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-methods#usage local wallet available in South Korea."`. Both are broken markdown links that will render as garbled text in any documentation renderer.
findings.rationale: Broken markdown links degrade documentation quality and may confuse automated doc generators and API consumers.

findings.title: `parent` field typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `parent` field is described as "Configuration's parent configuration. Specify to create a child configuration." and is typed as `type: string, maxLength: 100`. This is a cross-resource reference to another `payment_method_configuration` object, but it is not annotated with any format (e.g., `format: "stripe-id"`) or pattern (e.g., `^pmc_`) that would allow codegen tools to understand the relationship. Without this, generated SDKs treat it as an opaque string rather than a typed reference.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and make it harder for API consumers to understand what value is expected.

findings.title: No example provided for the large, complex request body
findings.narration: This endpoint accepts a highly complex request body with over 60 optional payment-method configuration fields, yet no `example` or `examples` object is provided on the request body schema. Without an example, API consumers and documentation tools have no quick reference for how to construct a valid request. Given the breadth of payment methods supported, even a minimal example showing one or two methods with `display_preference` set would significantly improve usability.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies without examples create onboarding friction and increase support burden; examples are especially important when a body has many optional but semantically meaningful nested fields.
findings.patchSummary: Add a minimal example to the request body to aid API consumers

findings.title: GET request includes an empty requestBody
findings.narration: This GET operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema containing no properties. HTTP semantics (RFC 7231) strongly discourage a body on GET requests, and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will silently discard it. The presence of this empty body adds noise and may mislead consumers into thinking a body is meaningful or permitted. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty body definition on a GET operation is at best misleading and at worst breaks clients that reject bodies on GET.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Path parameter `configuration` is an untyped resource ID string
findings.narration: The `configuration` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Based on Stripe's conventions, this value is a payment method configuration object ID (e.g. `pmc_...`). Without a `pattern` constraint documenting the expected prefix/format, code generators and validators cannot enforce the correct shape, increasing the likelihood of subtle bugs where an ID of the wrong resource type is passed undetected.
findings.rationale: Stripe resource IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern. Encoding that as a `pattern` improves validation, code generation, and documentation clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `configuration` path parameter for Stripe PMC ID format

findings.title: Malformed markdown link in `payco` description
findings.narration: The `payco` field description contains a broken markdown hyperlink: `[single-use](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-methods#usage local wallet available in South Korea.` — the closing parenthesis for the URL is missing, so the URL and surrounding text are merged into one malformed token. The same defect appears in the `samsung_pay` description: `[single-use](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-methods#usage local wallet available in South Korea.`
findings.rationale: Broken markdown links render incorrectly in generated documentation and API reference portals, degrading developer experience.

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions (400, 404)
findings.narration: The operation only declares a `200` success response and a `default` error catch-all. For an update endpoint identified by a path parameter (`{configuration}`), callers should expect at minimum a `404` when the configuration ID does not exist and a `400` when the request body is invalid. Without explicit 4xx definitions, SDK generators and client code cannot distinguish a not-found condition from a validation error, forcing all error handling through the generic `default` schema.
findings.rationale: Explicit 400 and 404 response codes are standard for resource-update endpoints and aid SDK generation, documentation, and client error handling.

Payment method configuration not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions to the update operation

findings.title: Minor typo in `nz_bank_account` description: "Zeland" should be "Zealand"
findings.narration: The description for `nz_bank_account` reads "customers with a New Zeland bank account" — "Zeland" is a typo for "Zealand". While cosmetic, it appears in the public-facing API reference documentation.
findings.rationale: Typos in public-facing documentation reduce perceived API quality.

patchOps.value: Stripe users in New Zealand can accept Bulk Electronic Clearing System (BECS) direct debit payments from customers with a New Zealand bank account. Check this [page](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/nz-bank-account) for more details.

findings.patchSummary: Fix typo: 'New Zeland' → 'New Zealand' in nz_bank_account description

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it 'can range between 1 and 100', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means API clients and generated SDKs have no machine-readable enforcement of this range, allowing values like 0 or 200 to be sent without schema-level validation warnings.
findings.rationale: Schema-level constraints should match documented business rules. Prose-only range documentation is not enforced by validators or code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: POST creates a resource but returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new payment method domain resource, which by REST conventions and HTTP semantics should return a 201 Created status code. The current spec defines only a 200 response. While Stripe historically uses 200 for all successful responses (including creates), this represents a semantic deviation from RFC 9110 which reserves 201 for successful resource creation. Clients and generated SDKs that follow HTTP semantics strictly may not handle this correctly, and the spec itself signals incorrect intent to developers reading it.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 defines 201 Created specifically for requests that result in a new resource being created. A POST that creates should return 201, not 200.

value.description: Payment method domain created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response alongside existing 200 for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: domain_name field lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `domain_name` field is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000, but it represents an internet domain name. There is no `format`, `pattern`, or minimum length constraint applied. A `maxLength` of 5000 is also extremely permissive for a domain name (ICANN limits domain names to 253 characters). Without a pattern such as a domain name regex or at least a reasonable `maxLength`, clients can submit clearly invalid values (e.g., empty strings, arbitrary text) and only learn about the error from the API at runtime. Adding a `pattern` matching a domain name and reducing `maxLength` to 253 would improve validation at the schema level.
findings.rationale: Domain names have well-defined structure and character limits (253 chars per ICANN). A pattern constraint encodes this in the schema so clients and codegen tools can validate before sending.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten domain_name to maxLength:253 and add a domain-name pattern constraint.

findings.title: No example provided for the request body
findings.narration: The request body schema for this operation has no `example` or `examples` field. For an endpoint accepting a domain name and an optional `enabled` boolean, a concrete example would help consumers quickly understand the shape of a valid request without having to read prose documentation. This is especially useful for generated API clients and documentation portals.
findings.rationale: Examples on request bodies improve developer experience in documentation portals and generated clients. The request shape is simple enough that a minimal example is trivial to add.
findings.patchSummary: Add a concrete example to the request body for clarity.

findings.title: customer and customer_account ID parameters typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` and `customer_account` query parameters are used as resource-identifier references (to Customer and Account objects respectively) but are declared as bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_`, `^acct_`) or `format` is provided. Codegen tools cannot infer the typed relationship to those resources, and clients receive no machine-readable hint about the expected ID shape, making it harder to validate inputs or generate typed SDKs.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields with no format or pattern prevent codegen from building typed relationships and prevent client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add patterns to customer and customer_account query params to indicate expected ID format.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter clearly states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema declaration only specifies `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` value encoded. Clients and validators cannot enforce these rules without reading the prose description. An API consumer could send `limit=0` or `limit=999` and only discover the constraint at runtime.
findings.rationale: Documented numeric constraints stated in prose should be encoded in the schema so validators and codegen tools can enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Encode limit minimum (1), maximum (100), and default (10) in schema instead of prose only.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive customer vs customer_account constraint only in prose
findings.narration: The presence of both `customer` and `customer_account` parameters implies a choice between listing payment methods for a regular customer or for a connected account. Their descriptions do not explicitly say they are mutually exclusive, but semantically they represent two distinct filtering modes. If the API rejects requests where both are provided, or requires at least one when `type` is not set, that constraint lives nowhere in the schema. Even if they are independently optional, the interaction between them should be documented more explicitly — ideally encoded as a `oneOf` or at minimum described precisely in the operation description.
findings.rationale: Conditional relationships between parameters that are only implied by domain knowledge should be encoded in schema constraints or at minimum documented precisely to avoid ambiguous client implementations.

patchOps.value: Returns a list of all PaymentMethods. Provide either customer or customer_account to filter by owner — these parameters are mutually exclusive. If neither is supplied, all PaymentMethods accessible to the authenticated account are returned.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify mutual exclusivity of customer and customer_account in operation description.

findings.title: Empty requestBody on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is defined on this GET endpoint with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema containing no properties (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual per HTTP/1.1 (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and many HTTP clients and proxies strip or ignore bodies on GET requests. This empty body object adds spec weight, may confuse codegen tools into generating a body parameter on a read-only method, and signals nothing useful to consumers.
findings.rationale: GET operations should not declare a requestBody. An empty, locked-down body schema on a GET is misleading and may cause codegen or client issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Summary says 'Shares a PaymentMethod' but operation creates one
findings.narration: The operation's `summary` field reads 'Shares a PaymentMethod', which describes a different action — cloning or sharing an existing PaymentMethod to a connected account. The operation's own description, operationId (`PostPaymentMethods`), and request body all clearly describe creating a new PaymentMethod from scratch (card details, bank account numbers, etc.). This is a copy-paste error that will confuse API consumers and auto-generated SDK documentation.
findings.rationale: A misleading summary directly contradicts the operation's actual behavior, causing developer confusion and incorrect documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Replace incorrect 'Shares a PaymentMethod' summary with 'Create a PaymentMethod'

findings.title: Conditional field relationships encoded only in prose, not as schema constraints
findings.narration: The `type` field determines which payment-method-specific hash (e.g. `card`, `sepa_debit`, `fpx`) is relevant and in many cases required. For example, if `type` is `sepa_debit`, the `sepa_debit` hash with `iban` is required; if `type` is `fpx`, the `fpx` hash with `bank` is required. These mutual dependencies are expressed nowhere in the schema — neither as `if/then`, `oneOf`, nor `discriminator`. Consumers and validators cannot mechanically enforce which sub-hash is required for a given `type` value, nor which sub-hashes are mutually exclusive. Additionally, the `payment_method` and `customer` fields (used for cloning) are silently optional but effectively required together when cloning, with no prose or schema encoding that relationship.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields documented only implicitly lead to runtime errors and prevent client-side or tooling validation.

patchOps.value: The type of the PaymentMethod. The corresponding hash for the selected type must be provided. For example, if `type` is `card`, the `card` hash is required; if `type` is `sepa_debit`, the `sepa_debit` hash with `iban` is required. To clone an existing PaymentMethod, omit `type` and provide both `payment_method` and `customer` instead.

findings.patchSummary: Document type-to-subhash conditional requirements in the type field description

findings.title: Sensitive card number and account numbers lack writeOnly marker
findings.narration: Several fields in the request body contain sensitive financial data that should never be returned in any response: `card.number`, `card.cvc`, `acss_debit.account_number`, `au_becs_debit.account_number`, `bacs_debit.account_number`, `sepa_debit.iban`, `us_bank_account.account_number`, `nz_bank_account.account_number`, and similar. None of these fields carry `writeOnly: true`. Without this marker, code generators and documentation tools may treat these as readable response fields, potentially leading to implementations that log or expose sensitive PII/PCI data.
findings.rationale: Missing writeOnly on credential/PCI-sensitive fields is a risk finding; codegen tools may expose these in read paths.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly:true to card number, CVC, IBAN, and bank account number fields

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions
findings.narration: The responses object only defines `200` (success) and `default` (generic error). There are no explicit `400`, `402`, or `404` response definitions. For a POST endpoint that creates a resource, a `400` (invalid request / validation failure) and a `404` (customer not found when cloning) are common, actionable errors that clients should be able to discriminate from unexpected 5xx errors. The `default` catch-all conflates all error types, reducing the contract value of the spec for client error handling.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses reduce the spec's usefulness for client error handling and SDK generation.

value.description: Bad request. The request body is invalid or missing required fields for the specified payment method type.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 response definition for invalid request errors

findings.title: customer and payment_method fields typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` field (description: 'The Customer to whom the original PaymentMethod is attached') and `payment_method` field (description: 'The PaymentMethod to share') are both typed as plain `string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to indicate they are Stripe resource IDs. Stripe customer IDs have a well-known prefix (`cus_`) and payment method IDs (`pm_`). Without a pattern or format hint, SDK generators cannot build typed resource relationships, and API consumers have no schema-level cue that these are references to other objects rather than arbitrary strings.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as plain string without pattern/format prevent codegen from building typed relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer and payment_method reference fields

findings.title: Path parameter `payment_method` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `payment_method` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe payment method IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `pm_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `format`, codegen tools and client validators cannot enforce or communicate the expected ID format. This also weakens the cross-resource typed relationship that downstream consumers rely on when building integrations.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with a known prefix pattern should carry a `pattern` constraint so clients can validate inputs before making the request and codegen can produce typed references.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to payment_method path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: This GET operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not have a body per HTTP semantics — while technically not forbidden by HTTP/1.1, many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks strip or reject bodies on GET requests. Declaring it here is misleading to consumers and could cause integration issues. The body carries no data and should be removed.
findings.rationale: GET endpoints must not declare request bodies; the declaration is semantically incorrect and may confuse client generators and intermediary proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation — GET requests should not have a body.

findings.title: Prose-only constraint: PaymentMethod must be attached to a customer to be updated
findings.narration: The operation description states 'A PaymentMethod must be attached to a customer to be updated.' This is a business rule that could cause a 400/422 error at runtime, but it is expressed only in prose. There is no schema-level or response-level encoding of this constraint. Callers who attempt to update an unattached PaymentMethod will receive a runtime error with no static indication from the spec that this scenario is invalid. At minimum, a 400 response definition should be present, and ideally the constraint should be surfaced via a description on the `payment_method` path parameter.
findings.rationale: Conditional constraints expressed only in prose prevent static analysis, codegen, and client-side validation from catching invalid usage before a request is made.

value.description: Bad request. For example, the PaymentMethod is not attached to a customer.

findings.patchSummary: Add 400 response and document the customer-attachment constraint explicitly.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx response definitions beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The responses object contains only `200` and a `default` error response. For an update operation that has documented preconditions (must be attached to a customer), and which accepts a path parameter (`payment_method`) that could reference a non-existent resource, at least a 400 (bad request / constraint violation) and 404 (resource not found) response should be enumerated explicitly. Relying solely on `default` provides no useful guidance to consumers about expected error shapes or status codes, and prevents tools from generating typed error handlers.
findings.rationale: Explicit error response codes enable client code generators and API documentation tools to produce typed error handling code. A catch-all `default` is insufficient for operations with known failure modes.

value.description: The requested PaymentMethod was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add 404 response definition for unknown payment_method resource.

findings.title: payto sub-fields lack mutual exclusivity constraint encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `payto` hash exposes three fields: `account_number`, `bsb_number`, and `pay_id`. In the PayTo payment method context, these typically represent mutually exclusive account identification strategies (BSB+account number vs PayID). The schema allows all three to be set simultaneously with no validation constraint. If the API rejects combinations of these fields at runtime, the constraint should be encoded with a `oneOf` or `not` schema rule rather than left purely implicit. Even if all combinations are accepted, adding descriptions clarifying the relationship between these fields would reduce integration errors.
findings.rationale: Unencoded field-relationship rules force integrators to discover constraints through trial and error or external documentation, increasing integration risk.

patchOps.value: The PayID identifier for this PayTo payment method. Mutually exclusive with bsb_number and account_number.
The BSB number for this PayTo payment method. Must be provided together with account_number. Mutually exclusive with pay_id.

findings.patchSummary: Document mutual exclusivity between pay_id and bsb_number+account_number in payto hash.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive 'customer' vs 'customer_account' fields not encoded as schema constraint
findings.narration: The request body contains two fields, `customer` and `customer_account`, that represent two distinct ways to identify the target customer (a regular Customer ID vs an Account ID). Based on Stripe's broader API patterns and the field descriptions, exactly one of these should be provided. However, the schema currently allows both to be submitted simultaneously or neither to be submitted — neither scenario is valid. This conditional-required / mutual-exclusion relationship exists only implicitly through the field names and descriptions, not through any JSON Schema constraint (`oneOf`, `not`, `dependencies`, etc.). Code generators and validation tools will not be able to surface this constraint to API consumers.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required and mutually-exclusive field relationships expressed only in prose (or implied by naming) should be encoded in the schema to enable automated validation and accurate SDK generation.

customer.description: The ID of the customer to which to attach the PaymentMethod.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

customer_account.description: The ID of the Account representing the customer to which to attach the PaymentMethod.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

findings.patchSummary: Encode customer/customer_account mutual exclusion as oneOf with required constraints

findings.title: 'customer' and 'customer_account' ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Both `customer` and `customer_account` are resource ID fields (referencing a Customer and an Account respectively) but are typed as bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Stripe resource IDs have well-known prefixes (`cus_` for customers, `acct_` for accounts). Without a pattern or format hint, code generation tools cannot build typed relationships between these fields and the resources they reference. Adding a `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and `^acct_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) would allow client-side validation and richer SDK types.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without patterns or formats prevent codegen tools from building typed cross-resource relationships and allow obviously invalid values to pass schema validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID prefix patterns to customer and customer_account fields

findings.title: No request body example for the attach operation
findings.narration: The request body schema has no `examples` or `example` field. Given the non-obvious choice between `customer` and `customer_account` and the Stripe-specific ID formats, a concrete example would significantly improve developer experience and reduce integration errors. An example showing a `cus_` prefixed customer attachment would make the most common use case immediately clear.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on operations with resource-ID fields and non-obvious mutual exclusion increase the risk of integration errors.
findings.patchSummary: Add example request body showing customer attachment

findings.title: payment_method path parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `payment_method` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. In the Stripe API, payment method IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `pm_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, SDK code generators and validation tools cannot distinguish this resource ID from an arbitrary string, which weakens client-side validation and makes auto-generated documentation less useful. Adding a pattern such as `^pm_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode the ID structure explicitly.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent typed relationship building in codegen tools and weaken validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to payment_method path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `failed` and `guaranteed` not encoded as schema constraint
findings.narration: The request body contains both a `failed` object (with `failed_at`) and a `guaranteed` object (with `guaranteed_at`), alongside an `outcome` enum with values `failed` and `guaranteed`. These three fields are clearly coupled: `outcome` must match whichever of `failed`/`guaranteed` is provided, and only one of `failed` or `guaranteed` should be present at a time. This conditional relationship is expressed nowhere in the schema — it exists only as implicit intent from the field names and the `outcome` enum values. Codegen tools and validators will happily accept a payload with both `failed` and `guaranteed` present simultaneously, which is almost certainly invalid. The schema should use `oneOf` or `if/then/else` to enforce that exactly one terminal-state object is provided when `outcome` is set, and that `outcome` aligns with the object provided.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually exclusive relationships expressed only by field naming are a high-leverage schema defect; validators pass invalid payloads silently.

findings.title: `customer_details.customer` typed as plain string but represents a Stripe Customer ID
findings.narration: The `customer_details.customer` field is clearly a reference to a Stripe Customer resource (the field name and context make this explicit), but it is typed as a bare `type: string` with only `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe customer IDs follow a well-known `cus_...` pattern. Without a `pattern` constraint or a semantic format hint, codegen tools will generate a generic string property with no indication that it is a resource reference. At minimum, a `pattern` such as `^cus_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` should be added, and the `maxLength` should be tightened to a realistic ID length rather than 5000.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no pattern or format prevent typed codegen relationships and allow obviously wrong values to pass validation.

findings.narration: The `payment_method_details.payment_method` field is a reference to a Stripe PaymentMethod resource (`pm_...` prefix), but is typed as `type: string` with `maxLength: 5000` and no further constraints. Similar to the `customer` field above, this prevents codegen tools from understanding the typed relationship and allows nonsensical values through validation. A `pattern` matching the `pm_` prefix should be added.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with no pattern or format hint lose their semantic meaning in generated clients and allow incorrect values through schema validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to payment_method_details.payment_method to mark it as a Stripe PaymentMethod ID

findings.title: No 4xx error responses defined beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error response. There are no explicit `400`, `402`, or `422` response definitions. For a reporting endpoint that accepts a complex, conditionally-structured body, clients need to know what happens when validation fails (e.g., both `failed` and `guaranteed` are provided, or required fields are missing). A `default` catch-all is technically sufficient per OpenAPI spec but provides no actionable guidance to consumers — tooling cannot surface expected error shapes for specific status codes. At a minimum, a `400` for malformed/invalid input should be explicitly called out.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses reduce API discoverability and prevent tooling from generating typed error-handling code for known failure modes.

value.description: Bad request — invalid or missing required fields.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 response for invalid/missing input fields

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will silently drop or reject it. Even Stripe's own pattern of accepting form-encoded bodies applies only to POST/PATCH operations. The presence of this body declaration will confuse generated SDK clients and documentation consumers who will wonder what fields to send.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies violate HTTP semantics and mislead consumers. The body carries no properties, making it purely noise that should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/payment_records/{id} operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks a format or pattern hint for the Payment Record ID
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe resource IDs typically follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `pyr_...` for payment records). Without a `pattern` or `format`, codegen tools and validators cannot distinguish a Payment Record ID from an arbitrary string, nor can they generate meaningful client-side validation. Adding a regex pattern (e.g., `^pyr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) would improve type safety and developer experience without being a breaking change.
findings.rationale: Untyped string IDs for cross-resource references reduce SDK type safety and documentation clarity. A pattern encodes the implicit contract explicitly.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `id` path parameter schema.

findings.title: Conditional field relationship between `outcome`, `failed`, and `guaranteed` encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The schema includes an `outcome` enum (`failed` | `guaranteed`) and two sibling objects `failed` and `guaranteed`. The semantics clearly require that when `outcome` is `failed`, the `failed` object should be provided, and when `outcome` is `guaranteed`, the `guaranteed` object should be provided. This conditional-required relationship exists only implicitly and is not encoded as a JSON Schema `if/then`, `oneOf`, or `dependentRequired` construct. Clients and code-generation tools cannot infer this constraint programmatically, leading to potential misuse (e.g., sending `outcome: 'failed'` with a `guaranteed` object and no `failed` object).
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules that exist only in prose are a high-leverage correctness issue; they should be encoded as machine-readable schema constraints.
findings.patchSummary: Encode outcome↔failed/guaranteed conditional-required relationship as if/then JSON Schema instead of leaving it implicit

findings.title: `payment_method_details.payment_method` is a plain untyped string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The field `payment_method_details.payment_method` is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Given that Stripe payment method IDs have a well-known prefix convention (e.g., `pm_...`) and are cross-resource references, this field should at minimum carry a `pattern` constraint (e.g., `^pm_`) or a description making the ID format explicit. As-is, codegen tools cannot build a typed reference, and clients cannot validate the value format before submission.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and clients from validating values.

findings.title: No 4xx error responses defined beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The responses object contains only a `200` success and a `default` error response. There are no explicit 4xx responses defined, such as `400` (invalid request, e.g., malformed `initiated_at`), `404` (Payment Record not found), or `422` (business-logic conflict, e.g., a non-canceled/non-failed attempt already exists). The operation description itself mentions a specific conflict condition ('A new payment attempt can only be specified if all other payment attempts are canceled or failed'), which should map to a documented `409` or `422` response. Relying solely on `default` gives clients no structured way to distinguish recoverable from unrecoverable errors.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx responses improve discoverability and allow clients to handle known error conditions; the operation's own description implies a conflict case that warrants a distinct response code.

findings.title: Missing example on `canceled_at` — unix-time format not self-evident to consumers
findings.narration: The `canceled_at` field uses a custom `format: unix-time` which is not a standard OpenAPI format. Without an example, API consumers and codegen tools may not know this expects a Unix epoch integer (e.g. 1715000000). Adding an `example` value directly on the property makes the expected value crystal-clear and prevents integration errors.
findings.rationale: Custom formats without examples leave consumers guessing; a concrete integer example costs nothing and prevents misuse.

findings.title: failed_at field lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `failed_at` field is typed as `integer` with `format: unix-time`, but has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. A caller could supply a timestamp of 0 (Unix epoch 1970) or a far-future value, both of which would be semantically nonsensical for a failure timestamp. Adding a `minimum` (e.g., a reasonable floor like a plausible platform launch date in epoch seconds) and optionally a `maximum` (e.g., 'not more than X seconds in the future') would catch client errors at the validation layer rather than requiring server-side rejection with an opaque error.
findings.rationale: Missing numeric bounds on a timestamp field can lead to silent acceptance of garbage data, making debugging difficult and corrupting reporting history.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum constraint to failed_at unix-time integer to prevent obviously invalid timestamps.

findings.title: No 4xx error response definitions beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success and a `default` catch-all error response. Specific 4xx codes (e.g., `400` for invalid `failed_at` values, `404` for a non-existent Payment Record `id`, `422` for a business-rule violation such as reporting a failure on a record with no pending attempt) are not enumerated. Without explicit 4xx definitions, SDK generators and API consumers cannot implement precise error-handling logic. The generic `default` entry provides no actionable information about what specific errors this endpoint can produce.

findings.title: processor_details.type enum has only one value; conditional 'custom' sub-object rule is prose-only
findings.narration: The `processor_details` object has a `type` field with only one enum value (`"custom"`), and a `custom` nested object that is presumably required only when `type` is `"custom"`. However, the schema does not encode this conditional requirement — the `custom` property is optional with no `if/then` or `dependencies` rule enforcing that it must be present when `type` is `"custom"`. Future enum expansion (e.g. new processor types) would also leave the schema unable to express which sub-object applies for each type. This discriminated-union relationship should be encoded formally.
