This means callers must always send `outcome: "refunded"` with no other valid choice. This adds friction to API consumers without providing meaningful expressiveness — if the field is always `"refunded"`, it either should be a fixed/default value (not required from the caller) or the enum should be extended to include other meaningful outcomes. A single-value required enum also prevents tooling from generating useful client code. If additional outcomes (e.g., `"partially_refunded"`, `"pending"`) are anticipated, they should be included now; otherwise the field should be made implicit.

findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new payout object, which is a resource-creation operation. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 201 signals to clients and intermediaries that a new resource was created, and conventionally includes a Location header pointing to the new resource. Using 200 here is semantically incorrect and may confuse HTTP-aware clients, API gateways, and code-generation tools that differentiate between 200 and 201.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 reserves 201 Created for responses that result in a new resource being created. This operation creates a payout resource, so 201 is the correct status code.

findings.title: POST /v1/plans returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new Plan resource (a POST to a collection URL) and returns HTTP 200. REST semantics and the HTTP specification (RFC 9110) indicate that a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, optionally with a `Location` header pointing to the new resource. Returning 200 is not incorrect per se, but it obscures the creation semantics and may confuse clients expecting standard REST conventions. This is a consistent Stripe-wide pattern, but worth noting for this operation.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 reserves 201 for successful resource creation. Using 200 loses the semantic signal that a new resource was created.
findings.patchSummary: Consider returning 201 Created for new Plan resource creation

findings.title: Path parameter `plan` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `plan` path parameter is typed as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe plan IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `plan_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDKs and codegen tools cannot validate the ID format, and tooling cannot build a typed relationship between this field and the Plan resource. A regex pattern such as `^plan_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` (or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`) would improve both safety and generated-client quality.
findings.rationale: A cross-resource ID typed as plain string with no format or pattern prevents codegen tools from building typed relationships and misses an opportunity for early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `plan` path parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A GET request should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). The presence of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` request body with an empty schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`) on this GET endpoint is misleading and may confuse HTTP clients, proxies, or code-generation tools that treat a `requestBody` presence as a signal the method accepts a body. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body according to HTTP semantics. An empty form-encoded body definition adds confusion and may break strict HTTP clients or codegen pipelines.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation.

findings.title: product field typed as plain string — cross-resource reference not encoded
findings.narration: The `product` field in the request body represents a Product resource ID but is declared simply as `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. The description confirms this is a foreign-key reference ('The product the plan belongs to'). Codegen tools cannot infer a typed relationship to the Product resource from this schema, making typed SDK generation and documentation linking harder than necessary.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields should carry a pattern (e.g. `pattern: '^prod_'`), a format hint (`format: stripe-product-id`), or reference a shared schema so tooling can establish the relationship.

value.description: The product the plan belongs to. This cannot be changed once it has been used in a subscription or subscription schedule.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and x-stripeResource annotation to product field to express cross-resource reference.

findings.title: Conditional-immutability constraint for product expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `product` field description states 'This cannot be changed once it has been used in a subscription or subscription schedule.' This is a meaningful business constraint — effectively making the field conditionally read-only after first use — but it is expressed only as prose. While this particular constraint is a runtime/state-based restriction that cannot be fully encoded in a static JSON Schema, it warrants at minimum a `readOnly`-style annotation or an `x-stripe-immutable` extension so client-facing tooling and linters can flag unexpected updates. In its current form clients have no machine-readable signal about this limitation.
findings.rationale: Constraints stated in description text only are invisible to validators and SDK generators; they should be surfaced via extensions or schema keywords wherever possible.
findings.patchSummary: Add x-stripe-immutable-after-use extension to product field to signal the constraint to tooling.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no min/max)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema has neither `minimum`, `maximum`, nor `default` defined. Clients and validators have no machine-readable way to enforce this range, and code generators will not produce useful validation or documentation from the prose alone.
findings.rationale: Constraints described only in prose cannot be enforced by validators or code-gen tools; they should be encoded as schema keywords.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `product` filter typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `product` query parameter is described as filtering prices for a given product, making it a reference to a Stripe product resource (IDs typically look like `prod_...`). It is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a maxLength. Without a `pattern` or recognized format, code generators cannot model the cross-resource relationship, and API consumers get no hint that this must be a valid product ID rather than an arbitrary string.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format so that code-gen tools can build typed relationships and validators can reject obviously wrong values.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint (^prod_) to the `product` parameter schema to signal it is a resource ID.

findings.title: Empty `requestBody` on a GET operation is unusual and may confuse clients
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`) is declared on this GET endpoint. GET requests conventionally carry no body; many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers silently drop GET bodies. Including a body here may cause SDK generators to emit client code that sends a body on a GET, which is unreliable. The body carries no fields anyway, so it provides zero value and should be removed.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a body violate common HTTP conventions and may be silently dropped by intermediaries; an empty body schema adds no value.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/prices operation.

findings.title: `lookup_keys` description says up to 10 keys, but no maxItems constraint is encoded
findings.narration: The `lookup_keys` parameter description reads 'You can specify up to 10 lookup_keys', yet the array schema has no `maxItems: 10` constraint. This leaves the limit purely in prose, making it invisible to validators and code generators. A client passing 50 keys will not receive a client-side validation error; they will only learn of the limit via an API error at runtime.
findings.rationale: Array-length constraints stated in prose should be encoded as maxItems so validators and generators can enforce them without runtime round-trips.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxItems:10 to the `lookup_keys` array schema to match the prose constraint.

findings.title: Conditional-required fields encoded only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: Several fields have mutual-exclusivity or conditional-required relationships documented only in description text, not encoded as JSON Schema constraints. Specifically: (1) `unit_amount`, `unit_amount_decimal`, or `custom_unit_amount` is required unless `billing_scheme=tiered` — this 'one of' rule is prose only; (2) `tiers` requires `billing_scheme=tiered` — prose only; (3) `tiers_mode` is presumably required when `billing_scheme=tiered` — undocumented; (4) `product` and `product_data` are mutually exclusive ways to associate a product — not encoded; (5) `transform_quantity` cannot be combined with `tiers` — prose only. These constraints cannot be validated automatically by tooling, increasing the risk of malformed requests that pass schema validation but are rejected at runtime.
findings.rationale: Prose-only conditional requirements are a high-leverage gap: codegen tools, validators, and client SDK authors all miss the rules. Per severity calibration this is high.

patchOps.value: A positive integer in cents (or local equivalent) (or 0 for a free price) representing how much to charge. Exactly one of `unit_amount`, `unit_amount_decimal`, or `custom_unit_amount` is required, unless `billing_scheme=tiered`. Cannot be set together with `unit_amount_decimal`.

findings.patchSummary: Document mutual-exclusivity of unit_amount/unit_amount_decimal/custom_unit_amount and tiers constraints as schema oneOf/not where possible

findings.title: `product` field typed as plain string without format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `product` field references a Stripe Product resource ID (e.g. `prod_xxx`) but is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^prod_`), or `$ref` to a typed ID schema is present. Similarly `product_data.tax_code` and `recurring.meter` reference other resource IDs as plain strings. Code generation tools cannot infer a typed relationship between a Price and its parent Product from this schema alone, making it harder to build strongly-typed SDKs.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain strings prevent tooling from building typed relationships. Flagged as medium per severity calibration.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `product` field to identify it as a typed Product resource ID

findings.title: Missing examples on a complex request body with many conditional fields
findings.narration: The request body schema for creating a price is highly complex, with support for tiered pricing, custom unit amounts, recurring intervals, currency options, and more. No `examples` or `example` values are provided on the request body or on any of the nested schemas. Without examples, developers integrating the API must mentally parse a large schema to understand even basic use cases like creating a one-time price versus a recurring tiered price. Adding at minimum two examples (one-time per-unit price and recurring tiered price) would significantly improve usability.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on complex schemas with many conditional relationships is a medium-severity clarity issue per calibration.
findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples for a one-time price and a recurring price to aid developer integration

findings.title: Empty request body on GET search operation
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false`, no properties). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 discourages it, and many proxies/clients strip it). All search parameters are already encoded as query parameters, making the request body both semantically incorrect and functionally useless. Removing it eliminates ambiguity for client generators.
findings.rationale: GET + request body is non-standard and confusing to codegen tools and HTTP intermediaries. It adds noise with no benefit since all params are query-based.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty GET request body from /v1/prices/search

findings.title: limit parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints encoded. Without these, validators and codegen tools cannot enforce the stated range, allowing clients to pass values like 0 or 9999 without a schema-level error. The constraint exists only as prose documentation.
findings.rationale: Constraints stated in prose but absent from the schema cannot be enforced at validation time, leading to potential runtime errors that could be caught earlier.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1 and maximum:100 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Response schema missing additionalProperties constraint
findings.narration: The 200 response schema for the SearchResult object does not set `additionalProperties: false`. While the required fields are listed, the schema is open by default, meaning any extra fields are silently accepted by validators. For a well-known, stable response envelope like this, closing it helps clients detect unexpected fields and aids in code generation of strictly typed models.
findings.rationale: An open response schema means codegen tools generate loose types and validators cannot warn when the API returns unexpected fields, reducing type safety.
findings.patchSummary: Close 200 response SearchResult schema with additionalProperties:false

findings.title: Path parameter `price` typed as unconstrained string with no ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `price` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe price IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `price_*`). Without a `pattern` constraint or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools and client validators cannot distinguish a price ID from arbitrary string input. This weakens type safety for consumers generating typed SDKs and provides no hint to users about the expected format.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern are a named anti-pattern in the review guidelines. A pattern like `^price_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode the Stripe ID convention.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and tighter maxLength to the `price` path parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: A `requestBody` block is included on this GET operation with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). RFC 7231 and OpenAPI best practices strongly discourage request bodies on GET requests — they are semantically undefined and many HTTP intermediaries, proxies, and client libraries will strip or reject them. The presence of this empty body adds noise to generated SDKs and documentation without providing any value.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty, disallowed-properties body definition serves no purpose and can confuse generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: tax_behavior field: irreversible constraint documented only in prose
findings.narration: The `tax_behavior` description states: 'Once specified as either `inclusive` or `exclusive`, it cannot be changed.' This is a critical business constraint — once the field is set to a non-`unspecified` value, POSTing a different value (other than the current one) is an error. This conditional rule is expressed only in prose and is not encoded in the schema. Clients and code-generation tools have no machine-readable way to detect or enforce this constraint. Ideally, this would be documented with a schema-level annotation or at minimum a `readOnly` hint once set, though OpenAPI 3.x has no perfect construct for 'write-once' semantics. At minimum, a `x-stripe-once-set` extension or a `deprecated`/`x-immutable` marker on the field would signal the constraint to tooling.
findings.rationale: Constraints like 'cannot be changed after set' are high-risk business rules. Prose-only documentation means clients can silently send invalid state transitions, causing server-side errors that are not predictable from the schema alone.
findings.patchSummary: Add x-immutable-once-set extension to tax_behavior to signal write-once semantics to tooling

findings.title: transfer_lookup_key description references lookup_key field relationship in prose only
findings.narration: `transfer_lookup_key` is described as: 'If set to true, will atomically remove the lookup key from the existing price, and assign it to this price.' This implies `transfer_lookup_key: true` is only meaningful when `lookup_key` is also provided in the same request. This field-relationship constraint (transfer_lookup_key requires lookup_key) is documented only in prose. Without encoding this dependency in the schema (e.g. via `if/then` or `dependentRequired`), validation tools and SDK generators cannot enforce it.
findings.rationale: Field interdependencies expressed only in prose create silent API misuse. The rule 'transfer_lookup_key requires lookup_key' is a hard dependency that should be machine-readable.
findings.patchSummary: Encode transfer_lookup_key dependency on lookup_key using if/then/required in schema

findings.title: Missing examples on complex currency_options request body field
findings.narration: The `currency_options` field accepts a nested structure with per-currency tiers, custom unit amounts, and tax behavior — one of the more complex inputs in this operation. No example is provided for this field or for the request body as a whole. Without examples, developers must reverse-engineer the schema to understand valid payloads, particularly for multi-tier or custom-unit-amount configurations. Adding at least one example to the `currency_options` property or a full request body example in the encoding section would substantially improve DX.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas without examples increase integration time and misuse risk. currency_options has multiple sub-schemas and anyOf branches that are non-obvious.
findings.patchSummary: Add examples to currency_options to illustrate multi-currency and tiered pricing configurations

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema defines only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. Clients and validation tools cannot enforce or communicate these bounds automatically. A server sending limit=0 or limit=500 would not be caught at the schema layer.
findings.rationale: Prose-described constraints (min, max, default) should be encoded in the schema for automated validation and accurate codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: ids parameter mutually exclusive with starting_after/ending_before — prose only
findings.narration: The `ids` parameter description says 'Cannot be used with starting_after or ending_before', but this mutual-exclusion rule is expressed only as prose. There is no schema-level or parameter-level encoding that prevents a caller from supplying both. Codegen tools, validators, and client SDKs have no way to enforce this constraint automatically, increasing the chance of confusing runtime errors.
findings.rationale: Conditional-incompatibility rules described in prose should be surfaced at the schema level; at minimum they should be flagged so API tooling authors are aware.

patchOps.value: Only return products with the given IDs. **Mutually exclusive with `starting_after` and `ending_before`** — cannot be used with either cursor parameter.

findings.patchSummary: Emphasise mutual-exclusion rule in description; ideally encode via schema not/dependencies

findings.title: GET list endpoint carries an empty application/x-www-form-urlencoded requestBody
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with content type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` and an empty object schema, with `required: false`. A GET request should not carry a request body; RFC 7231 notes that a GET body has no defined semantics and most HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks will ignore or reject it. Its presence here is likely a spec generation artefact and misleads consumers into thinking a form body is a valid input channel.
findings.rationale: GET operations must not have a requestBody per HTTP semantics and OpenAPI best practice; it should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/products

findings.title: Response uses 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new product resource, which by HTTP semantics should return HTTP 201 Created. Using 200 OK conflates creation with retrieval and violates RFC 9110 §15.3.2 guidance that 201 should be used when a new resource has been created as a result of the request. Stripe uses 200 broadly across its API, but it is still a semantic misrepresentation for client tooling and API consumers who rely on status codes to distinguish creation from update.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 specifies 201 for successful resource creation. Using 200 for a POST that creates a resource is a well-known HTTP semantic violation.
findings.patchSummary: Change 200 response to 201 Created for new product creation

findings.title: tax_code field typed as plain string without format or pattern for resource ID
findings.narration: The `tax_code` field is described as 'A tax code ID' but is typed as a bare `string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref` to a typed schema. Stripe tax code IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `txcd_*`). Without a format or pattern constraint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the TaxCode resource, and clients have no validation hint. This is a cross-resource reference typed as a plain string.
findings.rationale: Fields named as resource IDs should carry a pattern or format hint so codegen tools can build typed relationships and clients can validate inputs.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to tax_code to reflect Stripe tax code ID format

findings.title: images array items lack URL format annotation
findings.narration: The `images` field is described as 'a list of up to 8 URLs of images for this product' but the array items are typed as `string` with no `format: uri` and no `maxItems: 8` constraint. Both the URL format and the documented maximum count are missing from the schema, leaving validation entirely to the server. Clients and validators cannot enforce the documented 8-item limit or validate URL syntax.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints (max 8 items, must be URLs) should be encoded in the schema for client-side validation and accurate documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxItems:8 and format:uri to images array per documented constraints

findings.title: marketing_features array lacks maxItems constraint matching documentation
findings.narration: The description for `marketing_features` states 'A list of up to 15 marketing features', but the schema has no `maxItems` constraint. This means no schema-level validation enforces the documented limit of 15, placing the enforcement burden entirely on runtime server logic and leaving API consumers without a machine-readable constraint they can rely on for client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Documented numeric limits should be encoded as schema constraints (maxItems) so they are enforceable client-side and visible to tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxItems:15 to marketing_features array per documented constraint

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests must not include a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and clients, proxies, or frameworks may silently discard it. Even for Stripe's convention of accepting form-encoded parameters, a truly empty body schema adds no value and misleads consumers into thinking a body is valid or expected here.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody violates HTTP semantics and produces confusing SDK/codegen output; no parameters are passed via body here.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/products/search

findings.title: Missing minimum/maximum constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The description of the `limit` parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100', but the schema for the parameter (`type: integer`) has no `minimum: 1` or `maximum: 100` constraints. Without these constraints, schema validation tools and generated SDKs will accept out-of-range values (e.g., 0 or 500), leaving enforcement to the server at runtime rather than at the client or gateway level. This wastes a round-trip and degrades the developer experience.
findings.rationale: Prose-described constraints must be encoded in the schema so validators and codegen tools can enforce them without runtime API calls.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Response schema missing `additionalProperties: false` — loose object shape
findings.narration: The 200 response `SearchResult` object schema does not set `additionalProperties: false`. For what is documented as a well-defined result envelope with a fixed set of fields (`data`, `has_more`, `next_page`, `object`, `total_count`, `url`), leaving `additionalProperties` open signals to consumers and codegen tools that arbitrary extra fields may appear. This creates looser typed clients and obscures the contract. Stripe's search result envelope should be a closed schema given the defined field set.
findings.rationale: A closed schema improves codegen fidelity and makes the contract explicit; the fields are fully enumerated already.
findings.patchSummary: Close the SearchResult response schema with additionalProperties: false

findings.title: statement_descriptor conditional constraint ('type=service') documented only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `statement_descriptor` states 'May only be set if `type=service`', and similarly `unit_label` states 'May only be set if `type=service`'. However, the request body schema has no `type` field at all in this update operation, and the conditional restriction is expressed only in free-text prose. Codegen tools, validators, and SDK consumers cannot derive this rule from the schema alone. At minimum, the description of this constraint should note that setting these fields on a non-service product will be rejected by the API at runtime, and ideally a JSON Schema `if/then` or `not` construction should encode the restriction.
findings.rationale: Conditional field constraints expressed only in prose are invisible to automated validators and SDK generators, increasing integration errors.

patchOps.value: May only be set if product type=service. Enforced server-side; schema-level constraint cannot be expressed without a `type` field in the update schema.
May only be set if product type=service. Enforced server-side; schema-level constraint cannot be expressed without a `type` field in the update schema.

findings.patchSummary: Annotate service-type-only fields with x-conditional extension to surface the runtime constraint.

findings.title: `default_price` and `tax_code` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `default_price` field is described as 'The ID of the Price object' and `tax_code` is described as 'A tax code ID', yet both are simply `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^price_...` / `^txcd_...`), and no `$ref` to a typed identifier schema. Code-generation tools cannot infer the relationship to the Price or TaxCode resources from the schema alone, and client libraries cannot validate ID format before sending the request. A `pattern` or at least an `x-stripeResource` extension would allow generators to produce typed cross-resource references.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and deprive clients of early format validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to default_price and tax_code for typed cross-resource linking.

findings.title: images array lacks maximum item count constraint documented in description
findings.narration: The `images` field description states 'A list of up to 8 URLs of images for this product', but the schema for the array variant within the `anyOf` does not encode `maxItems: 8`. Similarly, `marketing_features` says 'up to 15' but has no `maxItems: 15`. These limits are enforced server-side but are invisible to schema validators and client-side tooling. Adding `maxItems` allows form libraries, validators, and API testing tools to catch over-limit submissions before a round-trip.
findings.rationale: Prose-only cardinality limits are not enforced by schema validators; encoding them as maxItems enables client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxItems:8 to images array and maxItems:15 to marketing_features array to match documented limits.

findings.title: GET list endpoint sends a request body (application/x-www-form-urlencoded)
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type, even though the schema is an empty object with `additionalProperties: false`. Sending a body on a GET request violates HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 explicitly notes that a body on GET has no defined semantics) and will be rejected or silently ignored by many intermediaries, proxies, and HTTP client libraries. The correct approach is to remove the requestBody entirely; all query parameters are already declared as path/query parameters.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 §4.3.1 says GET requests SHOULD NOT include a body. An empty, closed schema requestBody adds no value and introduces interoperability risk.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET list operation.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The description of the `limit` query parameter states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema does not encode `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10`. Without these constraints, client SDK generators and validators cannot enforce the stated rules, potentially allowing callers to pass 0 or 1000 without any schema-level warning. The schema should be tightened to match the prose description.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are not machine-readable; tooling cannot enforce them for validation or code generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: `url` field in list response has no format or pattern to indicate it is a URL
findings.narration: The `url` property in the `EntitlementsResourceProductFeatureList` response schema is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Adding `format: uri` (or at minimum a `pattern`) would allow SDK generators and validators to treat this field as a URI, enabling typed link handling and better documentation. Without it, the field is indistinguishable from an arbitrary string.
findings.rationale: format:uri is standard for URL string fields and enables typed codegen and validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add format:uri to the url property in the list response schema.

findings.title: Response should be 201 Created, not 200 OK, for resource creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new `product_feature` resource (attaching a feature to a product). The HTTP specification and REST best practices dictate that a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Using 200 incorrectly signals to clients that an existing resource was updated rather than a new one created. This matters especially for client code generators and API consumers that inspect status codes to determine whether to follow a `Location` header or handle idempotency.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 specifies 201 for successful resource creation. Returning 200 misrepresents the semantics of the operation.
findings.patchSummary: Change 200 response to 201 Created for resource creation semantics

findings.title: entitlement_feature is typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `entitlement_feature` field carries a reference to an Entitlements Feature resource ID (e.g., `feat_xxx`). It is typed as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` hints its identity as a foreign-key reference to the Feature resource. Codegen tools and documentation generators cannot infer the typed relationship, making it impossible to auto-link this field to the Feature object or validate that the value is a Stripe-prefixed ID. Adding a `pattern` such as `^feat_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or noting the format would significantly improve API consumer experience.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and hinder input validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern to entitlement_feature to encode it as a typed Feature resource ID

findings.title: product path parameter lacks format or pattern to distinguish it as a resource ID
findings.narration: The `product` path parameter accepts any string up to 5000 characters with no format or pattern. Stripe product IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `prod_xxx`). Without a pattern constraint, clients cannot validate IDs client-side, and documentation generators cannot distinguish this as a Stripe product ID reference rather than a free-form string. Adding a pattern (e.g., `^prod_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) aligns with the resource-ID typing concern and helps API consumers and SDK generators.
findings.rationale: Path parameters referencing resource IDs should carry format or pattern constraints so codegen and validation tools can treat them as typed references.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern to product path parameter to encode it as a typed Product resource ID

findings.title: Path parameter 'product' typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `product` path parameter represents a Stripe product resource ID (e.g., `prod_xxxxx`) but is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `pattern` (e.g., `^prod_`) or `format` hint is provided. Codegen tools cannot infer the relationship to the Product resource, reducing type safety and discoverability.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and make validation weaker.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'product' path param to reflect Stripe product ID format.

findings.title: Path parameter 'id' (product_feature ID) typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter represents a Stripe product_feature resource ID but is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `pattern` or `format` hint identifies this as a structured resource identifier. This weakens client-side validation and prevents codegen tools from building typed relationships to the ProductFeature resource.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern reduce type safety and prevent codegen tools from inferring resource relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'id' path param to reflect Stripe product_feature ID format.

findings.title: Empty requestBody included on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests MUST NOT include a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and including one is semantically incorrect. Many HTTP clients and proxies will reject or ignore a body on a GET request, and its presence here could confuse consumers and codegen tools alike.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not carry a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty, locked-down body schema adds noise without value and violates the spec contract.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: Path parameters typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraints
findings.narration: Both `id` and `product` path parameters are typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. In Stripe's API, these are resource IDs with known prefixes (e.g., `prod_` for product IDs, `feat_` for feature IDs). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, codegen tools cannot build typed resource references, and clients receive no guidance on the expected shape of these identifiers. Adding a pattern such as `^feat_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` for `id` and `^prod_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` for `product` would make the relationship explicit and enable client-side validation before the request is sent.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and miss an opportunity for early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to id and product path parameters to encode resource ID shapes.

findings.title: Resource ID parameters typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `coupon`, `customer`, and `customer_account` query parameters accept resource IDs but are typed as bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. This provides no hint to codegen tools or API consumers that these fields are references to specific Stripe resource types. For `coupon` (a coupon ID), `customer` (a customer ID), and `customer_account` (an account ID), the schema should at minimum include a pattern (e.g., `^cus_`, `^acct_`, `^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$`) or a description-referenced $ref to signal the relationship. Without this, client generators produce anonymous string fields with no type-safe link to the referenced resource.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and reduce API discoverability.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID patterns to coupon, customer, and customer_account parameters to signal resource references.

findings.title: The `limit` parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. This means the rule is documented only in prose, not machine-enforced. Client generators will produce an unconstrained integer field, and validation middleware cannot automatically reject out-of-range values. The constraints should be encoded directly in the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented only in prose cannot be machine-enforced; they should be encoded as JSON Schema minimum/maximum/default.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` and `customer_account` fields are cross-resource ID references (to Customer and Account objects respectively) but are declared only as `type: string` with a `maxLength`. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` hints exist to let codegen tools understand these are typed identifiers (e.g., `cus_*` and `acct_*` prefixes). Similarly, `promotion.coupon` is a coupon ID reference typed as plain string. This prevents SDK generators from building typed relationships between resources.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as plain strings impede codegen and client validation. Patterns like `^cus_` or a `format: stripe-customer-id` would encode the relationship.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraints to customer and customer_account ID fields

findings.title: Conditional field relationship between `customer` and `customer_account` expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The descriptions for `customer` and `customer_account` are nearly identical ('The customer/account representing the customer who can use this promotion code'). It is not clear whether these fields are mutually exclusive, whether one takes precedence over the other, or whether both can be set simultaneously. If only one should be provided at a time, this constraint should be encoded as a `oneOf` or `not`/`dependencies` rule in the JSON Schema rather than left to prose interpretation. Callers may inadvertently provide both, leading to undefined or error behavior.
findings.rationale: Conditional exclusion rules expressed only in prose are high-leverage findings because they can silently produce invalid requests that only fail at runtime.

patchOps.value: The account representing the customer who can use this promotion code. If not set, all customers can use the promotion code. Mutually exclusive with `customer`; only one of `customer` or `customer_account` may be set.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify mutual exclusion of customer vs customer_account; encode as oneOf if applicable

findings.title: Successful resource creation returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new promotion code resource, yet the only success response is defined as HTTP 200. Per HTTP semantics, resource creation should respond with 201 Created (with a Location header pointing to the new resource). Returning 200 obscures the creation semantics from clients and intermediaries, and makes it harder for clients to distinguish between a 'created' and an 'updated' result. This is a consistent pattern in the Stripe API, but it is still an HTTP semantics deviation worth noting.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 specifies 201 for successful resource creation. Using 200 prevents clients from reliably distinguishing creation from update.

value.description: Promotion code created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response for successful promotion code creation

findings.title: Missing `max_redemptions` minimum constraint allows zero or negative values
findings.narration: The `max_redemptions` field is described as 'a positive integer' in its description, but the schema specifies only `type: integer` with no `minimum` constraint. This means a client can submit 0 or a negative integer and pass schema validation, with the constraint enforced only server-side. Adding `minimum: 1` to the schema encodes the documented invariant and allows client-side validators and SDK generators to catch invalid values before the request is sent.
findings.rationale: Prose constraints ('positive integer') should be encoded in JSON Schema minimum/maximum to enable client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 to max_redemptions to enforce positive-integer constraint in schema

findings.title: Missing example on `restrictions.currency_options` additionalProperties schema
findings.narration: The `restrictions.currency_options` field uses an `additionalProperties` pattern where keys are currency codes and values contain a `minimum_amount` integer. This is a non-obvious structure for API consumers, but no example is provided anywhere in the encoding or schema to illustrate the expected format (e.g., `{"usd": {"minimum_amount": 500}}`). Without an example, developers are likely to misformat the form-encoded payload for this nested object.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas with dynamic keys are prime candidates for inline examples; their absence increases integration friction.
findings.patchSummary: Add example to restrictions.currency_options to clarify dynamic-key currency structure

findings.title: `promotion_code` path parameter lacks a format/pattern hint for ID validation
findings.narration: The `promotion_code` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe promotion code IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `promo_...`). The lack of a `pattern` or at least a descriptive `format` means client-side validation and code-generation tools cannot distinguish a valid Stripe promotion code ID from an arbitrary 5000-character string. This makes it harder to detect accidental misuse (e.g., passing a coupon ID instead of a promotion code ID).
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and reduce client-side validation quality.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to promotion_code path param to reflect Stripe ID format

findings.title: customer and customer_account parameters typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` and `customer_account` query parameters are typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. These are foreign-key references to Stripe Customer and Account objects respectively. Without a `format` hint (e.g. `format: "stripe-id"`) or at minimum a `pattern` that captures Stripe ID prefixes (`cus_...`, `acct_...`), codegen tooling cannot build typed cross-resource relationships, and client-side validation cannot catch obviously wrong values early.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format so tooling can infer relationships and emit typed references rather than raw strings.
findings.patchSummary: Add Stripe ID patterns to customer and customer_account query parameters.

findings.title: Conditional relationship between test_clock and customer/customer_account encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `test_clock` parameter description states: "The response will not include quotes with test clocks if this and the customer parameter is not set." This conditional dependency — that `test_clock` only has effect when `customer` or `customer_account` is also present — is expressed purely in prose. OpenAPI 3.x allows encoding such mutual constraints via `dependentRequired` (JSON Schema draft 2019-09) or at minimum a `description` note in the parent schema, but the current spec places it only in the parameter-level description, making it invisible to validators and codegen tools.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships expressed only in prose cannot be enforced by validators or leveraged by SDK generators; they should be expressed in schema constraints.
findings.patchSummary: Encode test_clock/customer conditional dependency in schema constraints, not just prose.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states "Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10", but the schema contains only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values. This means validators and SDK generators cannot enforce the stated range, and callers who pass `limit=0` or `limit=200` will only receive an error at runtime rather than at the client side.
findings.rationale: Numeric constraints documented in prose should be encoded as schema constraints so tooling can validate before the call is sent.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema.

findings.title: GET list endpoint carries an empty application/x-www-form-urlencoded request body
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content and an empty properties object. GET requests should not carry a request body; HTTP semantics do not prohibit it, but many intermediaries (proxies, CDNs, caching layers) will strip or reject a body on GET requests. All filter parameters are already correctly modelled as query parameters, making this body definition entirely redundant and potentially confusing to consumers and codegen tools that may emit unexpected body-encoding code.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body; the presence of an empty form-encoded body on a GET is a semantic anti-pattern that can confuse intermediaries and SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET list operation.

findings.title: from_quote parameter has undocumented mutual-exclusivity constraint in prose only
findings.narration: The description for `from_quote` states: 'When using this parameter, you cannot specify any other parameters except for `expires_at`.' This is a significant conditional constraint that restricts which other fields may be used, but it is expressed only in prose and not encoded in the JSON Schema. There is no `oneOf`, `if/then/else`, or `not` + `dependencies` construct that enforces this at the schema level. Clients and codegen tools have no machine-readable way to know about this restriction, increasing the chance of invalid API calls.
findings.rationale: Conditional field exclusions documented only in prose are a high-leverage finding: they cannot be validated automatically and often cause runtime errors for API consumers.

patchOps.value: Clone an existing quote. The new quote will be created in `status=draft`. When using this parameter, you cannot specify any other parameters except for `expires_at`. Mutually exclusive with all other fields besides `expires_at` — encode this constraint via an `if/then` or `oneOf` schema rule.

findings.patchSummary: Document mutual-exclusivity of from_quote with all other fields except expires_at in schema, not just prose.

findings.title: application_fee_amount and application_fee_percent are mutually exclusive but constraint is prose-only
findings.narration: The description for `application_fee_amount` says 'There cannot be any line items with recurring prices when using this field', and `application_fee_percent` says 'There must be at least 1 line item with a recurring price to use this field.' These are effectively mutually exclusive with different line item configurations — and more broadly, they represent an either/or choice for application fees (amount vs. percent). Neither constraint is encoded in the schema as a `not`, `oneOf`, or `if/then` rule. Clients consuming this spec cannot discover at schema-validation time that using both would be invalid.
findings.rationale: Conditional requirements between fields that are only documented in prose cannot be auto-validated and represent a schema design gap.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusivity of application_fee_amount and application_fee_percent in schema (oneOf/not).

findings.title: customer and customer_account are alternative identifiers with conditional-required rule undocumented in schema
findings.narration: The `customer` field description says 'A customer is required before finalizing the quote' and `customer_account` says 'A customer or account is required before finalizing the quote.' This implies that at least one of `customer` or `customer_account` must be provided before finalization, and they are likely mutually exclusive alternatives. However, neither field has a `pattern` nor a typed `$ref` to indicate the resource ID format (e.g. `cus_...` vs `acct_...`), and the either/or constraint is not encoded as `oneOf` or `not` in the schema. This makes it impossible for clients to determine which to use or that they are alternatives.
findings.rationale: Cross-field conditional-required rules that are only in prose descriptions are a high-severity design gap that cannot be auto-validated by clients.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusivity and conditional requirement of customer vs customer_account in schema.

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body contains several deeply nested objects (`automatic_tax`, `invoice_settings`, `subscription_data`, `transfer_data`, `line_items`, `from_quote`) but no top-level or field-level `examples`/`example` are provided on the request body schema. For a resource as complex as a quote — with multiple nullable/clearable fields, conditional constraints, and nested objects — at least one annotated example request body would significantly aid developer integration.
findings.rationale: Complex request schemas without examples are a medium-severity clarity issue that reduces usability for consumers and documentation tooling.

basic_quote.summary: Create a basic quote for a customer

findings.patchSummary: Add at least one annotated example to the request body for this complex quote creation endpoint.

findings.title: Path parameter `quote` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `quote` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe quote IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `qt_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship or validate the ID shape at the client layer. A regex pattern like `^qt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` (or similar) would make the constraint machine-readable and improve SDK generation quality.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed relationship inference in codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `quote` path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET operation
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared on this GET operation with `required: false` and an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1); many HTTP clients, proxies, and load balancers will drop or reject it. The empty body serves no purpose and is misleading to consumers of this spec. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET operations must not define a requestBody per HTTP semantics; this entry is semantically incorrect and will confuse tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect empty requestBody from GET operation.

findings.title: Conditional mutual-exclusion between `customer` and `customer_account` encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `customer` field description says 'A customer is required before finalizing the quote. Once specified, it cannot be changed.' and `customer_account` says 'A customer or account is required before finalizing the quote.' This implies exactly one of `customer` / `customer_account` should be set, but there is no `oneOf`, `not`, or `dependencies` constraint encoding this mutual-exclusion or the 'required before finalizing' rule. Consumers and codegen tools will treat both as independent optional strings with no relationship.
findings.rationale: Conditional field relationships described only in prose cannot be validated automatically or expressed in generated SDKs. This is a high-leverage pattern to encode as JSON Schema.

value.description: Cannot specify both customer and customer_account

findings.patchSummary: Add `not: { required: [customer, customer_account] }` to encode mutual-exclusion in schema

findings.title: Conditional-required rule for `application_fee_amount` vs recurring prices only in prose
findings.narration: The `application_fee_amount` description states 'There cannot be any line items with recurring prices when using this field', and `application_fee_percent` states 'There must be at least 1 line item with a recurring price to use this field.' Both fields appear to be mutually exclusive with each other and each has specific line-item cardinality requirements. None of these constraints are encoded in the schema — they exist only as prose, so validation and code generation cannot enforce them.
findings.rationale: Business rules coupling fields (`application_fee_amount` vs `application_fee_percent`) must be expressible in schema to be enforceable by validators and SDKs. Prose-only rules are invisible to tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual-exclusion of application_fee_amount and application_fee_percent via schema constraint

findings.title: Resource ID fields (`customer`, `customer_account`, `on_behalf_of`, IDs in nested objects) typed as plain `string` with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields represent references to Stripe resource IDs: `customer` (Customer ID, e.g. 'cus_...'), `customer_account` (Account ID, e.g. 'acct_...'), `on_behalf_of` (Account ID), `transfer_data.destination` (Account ID), `discounts[].coupon`, `discounts[].discount`, `discounts[].promotion_code`, `line_items[].price`, `line_items[].id`. All are typed as plain `string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `x-stripeResourceID` hint. Codegen tools cannot build typed relationships between these IDs and their referenced resource schemas, reducing the utility of generated SDKs.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as bare strings prevent SDK generators from creating strongly-typed accessors or relationships. Adding `format` (e.g. `format: stripe-id`) or `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_`) communicates the intent.
findings.patchSummary: Annotate resource ID string fields with x-stripeResource or pattern to enable typed codegen relationships

findings.title: Operation description is generic and does not describe update semantics or constraints
findings.narration:
The operation description reads '

A quote models prices and services for a customer.

' — this is a generic definition of what a quote is, not a description of what this update endpoint does. It does not mention which fields can be updated, what states a quote must be in to be updated (e.g. only `draft` or `open` quotes can be updated), or what happens on success. The `summary` ('Update a quote') provides more information than the description.
findings.rationale: The description field should document the update operation's behavior, pre-conditions, and key constraints, not just re-state what a quote object is.

patchOps.value: Updates the specified quote by setting the values of the parameters passed. Any parameters not provided are left unchanged. You may only update a quote in draft status. Once a quote is open or accepted, certain fields become immutable (e.g. customer, customer_account).

findings.patchSummary: Replace generic quote-definition description with an update-specific description covering status preconditions

findings.title: Missing explicit 4xx error response definitions
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a generic `default` error response. Missing explicit definitions for `400` (bad request, e.g. quote already accepted/cancelled), `401` (unauthenticated), `404` (quote not found), and `422` (unprocessable entity) means API clients and codegen tools cannot differentiate between error types at the schema level. For a state-transition endpoint like accepting a quote, specific error codes are particularly important — a client needs to know whether a 404 (quote not found) or 409/422 (quote in wrong state) occurred.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx response codes allow client codegen tools to generate typed error handlers and help API consumers understand the failure modes without consulting external documentation.

value.description: Bad request — e.g. the quote is in a state that cannot be accepted.
Quote not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions to complement the generic default error.

findings.title: Quote path parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `quote` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe quote IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `qt_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, codegen tools treat this as a free-form string, and no client-side validation of the ID format is possible. The `maxLength` of 5000 is also extremely permissive for what is a compact identifier.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed relationship generation in codegen tools and allow obviously invalid values to pass client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint and tighten maxLength on the quote path parameter.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 discourages it, and many HTTP clients/proxies strip or reject GET bodies). The `requestBody` block serves no purpose here and may cause interoperability issues with certain clients or reverse proxies that reject GET requests with a body.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a body violate common HTTP client and proxy behavior and add no value when the schema has no properties.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, unused requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. Without machine-readable constraints, client SDKs and validation middleware cannot enforce the documented range, and a caller could send `limit=0` or `limit=999` without receiving a schema-level validation error. Adding `minimum: 1, maximum: 100, default: 10` aligns the schema with the prose description.
findings.rationale: Prose-only range constraints are not enforceable by schema validators or code generators; they should be encoded in the schema.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: Response `url` field lacks a format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `url` property in the 200 response schema is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Its description states it is 'The URL where this list can be accessed', which semantically implies it should always be a valid URL. Adding `format: uri` would allow validators and code generators to treat it as a URL type, improving correctness checks and client SDK typing.
findings.rationale: A field documented as a URL should carry format: uri for tooling correctness.
findings.patchSummary: Add format: uri to the url field in the 200 response schema.

findings.title: Missing explicit 4xx response definitions
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` error response. The `default` bucket is a catch-all, but for consumer tooling, SDK generation, and documentation quality, key client-error cases — notably `400 Bad Request` (invalid expires_at value), `404 Not Found` (quote not found), `422 Unprocessable Entity` (quote in wrong state, e.g. already finalized), and `401/403` for auth failures — should each be explicitly enumerated. Without them, clients cannot distinguish between a transient server error and a permanent client error programmatically.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx response codes allow SDK generators and API consumers to write correct, granular error-handling logic. The `default` fallback is insufficient for documentation and client generation.

findings.title: No format or pattern constraint on `quote` path parameter
findings.narration: The `quote` path parameter is typed as `string` with only `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe resource IDs have a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `qt_` for quotes). Without a `pattern` constraint such as `^qt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`, the schema communicates nothing about expected format, which means client-side validation tools and SDK generators cannot catch obviously invalid IDs before making a network call. The extremely loose `maxLength: 5000` is also misleading — Stripe IDs are far shorter in practice.
findings.rationale: Typed resource ID patterns enable codegen tools to build meaningful relationships and allow client-side validation to reject malformed IDs early.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `quote` path parameter reflecting the Stripe quote ID prefix.

findings.title: GET request includes an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests must not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will reject or ignore bodies on GET requests. Even though the body is marked `required: false`, its presence as a declared construct is misleading and potentially harmful. The body should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies violate HTTP semantics and can cause interoperability issues with intermediaries that drop or reject bodies on GET.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` query parameter states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema definition (`type: integer`) has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` annotations. This means client code generators and validators cannot enforce the documented range. A client sending `limit=0` or `limit=999` would not be caught at the SDK/validation layer. The schema should encode `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, and `default: 10`.
findings.rationale: Numeric constraints documented in prose but absent from the schema cannot be enforced by generated clients or validators.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum, maximum, and default constraints to `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Response `url` field lacks a format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `url` property in the 200 response schema is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Since this field is explicitly described as 'The URL where this list can be accessed', it should carry `format: uri` or a regex `pattern` so that generated clients and validators can confirm the value is a well-formed URL rather than an arbitrary string. Without this, mis-typed or empty strings would pass validation silently.
findings.rationale: A string field explicitly described as a URL should carry `format: uri` to enable client-side validation and improve code generation output.
findings.patchSummary: Add `format: uri` to response `url` field

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type, but the schema contains no properties and is entirely empty. GET requests with a body are semantically unusual (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes GET requests SHOULD NOT have a body) and many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers silently strip GET bodies. This empty body definition is likely a copy-paste artifact and should be removed. Keeping it may confuse client generators into emitting code that sends a body with the request, which can cause failures at the network level.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a body violate common HTTP conventions and can cause interoperability issues with clients and proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty GET requestBody entirely

findings.title: quote path parameter lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `quote` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe quote IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `qt_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client generators and validators cannot enforce the expected ID shape, making it easy for callers to pass arbitrary strings and get opaque 404/invalid-id errors rather than clear client-side validation failures. Adding a pattern such as `^qt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at minimum a short `minLength` would improve safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters should carry enough constraints to enable client-side validation and typed codegen relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern/minLength constraints to the quote path parameter schema

findings.title: Missing 4xx error responses (404, 401, 403)
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` and a catch-all `default` error response. While `default` technically covers all error codes, best practice is to enumerate at least the most common client error codes explicitly — specifically `401` (unauthenticated), `403` (forbidden/insufficient permissions), and `404` (quote not found or not in a finalized state that allows PDF download). Without explicit status codes, OpenAPI tooling cannot generate accurate client-side error-handling branches, and documentation portals show only vague 'Error response' copy. Given this is a file-download endpoint with a specialized server (`files.stripe.com`), a `404` for non-finalized or missing quotes is especially likely.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx response codes improve documentation clarity and enable typed error handling in generated clients.
