findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter's description states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema for the parameter (`type: integer`) has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints encoded. This means API clients and SDK generators cannot enforce the stated bounds at the schema level, and callers may inadvertently pass values outside the valid range without static validation catching it.
findings.rationale: Described constraints ('between 1 and 100') must be encoded in the schema so validators and codegen tools enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1, maximum: 100, and default: 10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `charge` filter parameter lacks maxLength and ID format constraints
findings.narration: The `charge` query parameter accepts a Stripe charge ID (typically prefixed `ch_`) but its schema is a bare `type: string` with no `maxLength`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^ch_`), and no format hint. By contrast, the sibling `payment_intent` parameter at least constrains `maxLength: 5000`. Omitting these constraints means no static check prevents callers from passing arbitrary strings, and codegen tools cannot infer the relationship to the Charge resource.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without any format, pattern, or maxLength prevent typed cross-resource relationships and allow invalid inputs to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength: 5000 to the `charge` parameter schema, consistent with sibling ID params.

findings.title: GET list operation includes an empty `requestBody`
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, but the schema's `properties` object is entirely empty and `additionalProperties` is `false`. GET requests with a body are semantically problematic per HTTP/1.1 (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 discourages it) and many HTTP clients and proxies drop or reject GET request bodies. The body here carries no data and should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: An empty, non-functional request body on a GET operation is a design anti-pattern that can confuse clients and violates common HTTP semantics.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically-invalid requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `early_fraud_warning` lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The path parameter `early_fraud_warning` is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe early fraud warning IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `issfr_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build a typed resource reference, and clients cannot perform basic client-side validation before sending the request. A `pattern` like `^issfr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would make the contract explicit and allow SDK generators to distinguish this ID type from generic strings.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed SDK generation and weaken the API contract.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to early_fraud_warning path parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content whose schema has no properties and `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests with a body are semantically incorrect per HTTP/1.1 (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients and intermediaries will strip or reject a body on GET requests. This empty body declaration is noise that could confuse SDK generators into emitting a body argument for a read-only endpoint. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies violate HTTP semantics and mislead consumers; the body here is empty and serves no purpose.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation.

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that are clearly foreign-key references to Stripe objects are typed as plain `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Specifically: `customer_details.customer` (references a Customer object), `customer_details.customer_account` (references a connected account), and `payment_details.payment_method_details.payment_method` (references a PaymentMethod object). Without any structural hint, code-generation tooling cannot infer that these are resource IDs, cannot validate ID prefix formats (e.g. `cus_`, `acct_`, `pm_`), and cannot generate typed relationship models. Adding a `pattern` constraint matching the Stripe ID prefix convention (or at minimum a `format: 'stripe-id'` annotation) would dramatically improve client SDK quality and API contract clarity.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as bare strings without format or pattern are a documented anti-pattern that prevents codegen tools from building typed relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer, customer_account, and payment_method reference fields

findings.title: Conditional relationship between money_movement_type and card sub-object only in implicit structure, not validated
findings.narration: The `money_movement_details` object has a `money_movement_type` enum with only the value `"card"`, and a sibling `card` sub-object. The structure strongly implies that `card` is required when (and only when) `money_movement_type` is `"card"`. Currently this relationship is entirely unencoded — `card` is optional and there is no `if/then` or `oneOf` discriminator. If Stripe ever adds more `money_movement_type` values (e.g. `bank_transfer`), the schema will have no way to express which sub-object is required for which type, and clients submitting a card type without the card details will receive a runtime error rather than a validation-time error. This conditional-required relationship should be encoded via JSON Schema `if/then/required`.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules implied by schema structure but not encoded as schema constraints are a high-leverage issue; servers reject invalid payloads at runtime that could be caught at design time.
findings.patchSummary: Encode card-required-when-money_movement_type=card rule as if/then schema constraint

findings.title: Missing example on the complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body is a deeply nested object with multiple required sub-objects (`customer_details`, `payment_details`, `payment_method_details`) and several optional sub-trees (`shipping_details`, `money_movement_details`, `client_device_metadata_details`). There are no examples at any level — neither on the top-level schema, nor on individual properties. For a fraud pre-evaluation API that developers will need to integrate carefully before going live, the absence of a concrete example makes it very difficult to understand the minimal required payload versus the full payload, or to understand how `money_movement_type` and its sibling `card` object interact. A single end-to-end example would substantially reduce integration friction.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on complex request bodies are a medium-severity clarity issue; they increase integration time and support burden.

full.summary: Full payload with card money movement details

findings.patchSummary: Add minimal and full request body examples for the payment evaluation endpoint

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties. Clients and code-generators cannot enforce or communicate the valid range, and no default is surfaced in the schema itself.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints stated in prose but absent from the schema definition are a high-severity finding because they cannot be machine-validated, leading to potential runtime errors when out-of-range values are supplied.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: `value_list` ID parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern hint
findings.narration: The required `value_list` query parameter is a reference to a parent ValueList resource (expected to be a Stripe ID like `rsl_...`), but it is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. No `format`, `pattern`, or example is provided to convey the expected shape of the identifier. Code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to the ValueList resource, and client-side validation cannot reject obviously malformed IDs early.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as bare strings without format or pattern are a documented high-severity pattern because they prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and eliminate early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern ^rsl_ and an example to the `value_list` parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A GET endpoint should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). The spec includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`required: false`, no properties). While harmless in practice for Stripe's HTTP stack, it contradicts the HTTP method semantics, may confuse generated clients that do not expect a body on GET requests, and adds unnecessary schema surface area.
findings.rationale: GET requests with a request body violate common HTTP semantics and can confuse code generators or proxies that strip bodies from GET requests. The body carries no data here and should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation

findings.title: POST creates a resource but returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new `ValueListItem` resource, which is a side-effectful creation operation. The HTTP specification and RESTful conventions dictate that successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Returning 200 conflates creation with a generic success response, making it harder for clients to distinguish between a resource being created versus an existing resource being returned or updated. While Stripe uses 200 broadly across its API, this is a notable deviation from REST semantics worth flagging at the per-operation level.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 specifies 201 for resource creation. Clients and generated SDKs use the status code to differentiate creation from other operations.

value.description: ValueListItem created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response to indicate successful resource creation

findings.title: `value_list` field typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `value_list` field is described as 'The identifier of the value list which the created item will be added to.' This is a cross-resource reference to a `RadarValueList` object (identifiers typically follow the pattern `rsl_...`). It is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint but no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a dedicated type. Codegen tools cannot establish a typed relationship between this field and the parent resource, making it impossible to automatically validate or hint the expected identifier format to consumers.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with no format or pattern prevent typed cross-resource relationships in generated SDKs and client validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to value_list field to reflect Radar value list ID format

findings.title: GET operation defines an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). While Stripe uses this pattern broadly as a spec convention, it is still semantically incorrect and may confuse HTTP clients, proxies, or code-generation tools that enforce GET body prohibition.
findings.rationale: GET with a request body is semantically undefined in HTTP and can cause interoperability issues with proxies and generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty GET requestBody to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: Path parameter `item` has no format or pattern constraint to identify it as a resource ID
findings.narration: The `item` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe value list item IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `rsli_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to this resource, and clients receive no hint that an arbitrary string is not a valid identifier. Adding a regex pattern such as `^rsli_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would make the contract explicit.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as bare strings without pattern or format prevent codegen from building typed relationships and give no validation hint to clients.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `item` path parameter to identify it as a Stripe value list item ID.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. Clients and code-generation tools have no machine-readable way to enforce or advertise these boundaries, which means nothing stops a consumer from sending limit=0 or limit=999 and relying on the server to reject it.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are a high-leverage finding: the minimum/maximum values and the default are actionable schema attributes that tools can use for validation, documentation, and SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A GET endpoint should not carry a request body at all per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). Including a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema — even with `required: false` — is misleading to consumers and code generators, many of which will generate a body parameter or emit warnings for this pattern. All filterable inputs are already covered by the query parameters.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody is semantically incorrect and creates confusion for client libraries and reverse proxies that may strip or reject bodies on GET requests.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation

findings.title: Response schema title 'RadarListListList' is cryptic and confusing
findings.narration: The 200 response schema is titled `RadarListListList`. This triple-repeated suffix is almost certainly a code-generation artifact (a list of a list of Radar value lists), but it will surface verbatim in generated SDKs, documentation, and type definitions, causing confusion for integrators who see class or type names like `RadarListListList`. A name like `RadarValueListCollection` or `ValueListList` would be far more self-explanatory.
findings.rationale: Schema titles flow directly into SDK type names. A confusing title reduces clarity and increases support burden.
findings.patchSummary: Rename response schema title from RadarListListList to RadarValueListCollection

findings.title: POST resource creation returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new ValueList resource but declares a 200 response code. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), successful resource creation should return 201 Created, optionally with a Location header pointing to the newly created resource. Returning 200 conflates creation with a generic success, making it harder for clients to distinguish between a creation and an update operation, and preventing HTTP-aware intermediaries from treating the response correctly.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for a successful POST that results in resource creation. Using 200 is semantically incorrect and reduces interoperability.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: Missing example on request body for a complex enum field
findings.narration: The `item_type` field has 12 possible enum values with meaningful behavioral differences (e.g., `card_fingerprint` vs `ip_address` vs `customer_id`), yet the request body schema has no examples. Without an example, integrators must infer the most common or appropriate item type from the description alone. Adding an example showing a typical use case (e.g., `item_type: 'email'`, `alias: 'blocked_emails'`, `name: 'Blocked Emails'`) would significantly improve developer experience and reduce integration errors.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies with enum fields benefit from examples to guide integrators and reduce misconfiguration. Medium severity as it is a clarity issue, not a correctness issue.

blocked_emails.summary: Create a value list for blocked email addresses

findings.patchSummary: Add a representative request body example for the value list creation operation.

findings.title: Filter parameter `charge` lacks maxLength constraint and cross-resource type annotation
findings.narration: The `charge` query parameter is used to filter refunds by a Charge ID, but its schema is `{type: string}` with no `maxLength`, no `pattern`, and no indication that this is a Stripe Charge ID (e.g. `ch_...`). The sibling `payment_intent` parameter correctly applies `maxLength: 5000`. Without any constraint or format hint, codegen tools and validators cannot tell that this is a resource identifier rather than an arbitrary string, and clients have no guidance on what values are valid.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain unadorned strings miss the opportunity to communicate the expected format or length, reducing discoverability and making generated clients less type-safe.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength: 5000 to the `charge` filter parameter schema, consistent with `payment_intent`.

findings.title: GET list endpoint sends an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false`, no properties). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual and discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). Proxies, caches, and some HTTP clients may strip or reject GET request bodies. Since this body carries no information (the schema is intentionally empty), the `requestBody` block should be removed entirely to avoid client-library confusion and proxy incompatibility.
findings.rationale: An empty, disallowed-additional-properties request body on a GET is noise that can cause misbehaviour in strict HTTP clients and is contrary to standard HTTP semantics.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `charge`, `payment_intent`, and `customer`/`origin` not encoded as schema constraints
findings.narration: The description states that a Charge or a PaymentIntent object must be specified to create a refund. The `origin: 'customer_balance'` enum value and the `customer` field together form a third path. These mutual-exclusivity and co-requirement rules exist only in the human-readable description; they are not encoded as `oneOf` or `if/then/else` schema constraints. API consumers and code generators cannot derive these rules automatically, which increases the chance of sending invalid requests that only fail at runtime.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields documented only in prose should be encoded in the JSON Schema. This is a high-severity pattern per the review rubric.

findings.narration: The operation `summary` is 'Create customer balance refund', which implies the endpoint is exclusively for customer balance refunds. However, the description and the request schema clearly show the endpoint handles three distinct refund paths: refunding a Charge, refunding a PaymentIntent, and refunding a customer balance via `origin: customer_balance`. The misleading summary will confuse API consumers browsing generated documentation who may look elsewhere for how to refund a charge or PaymentIntent.
findings.rationale: A summary that only describes one of three supported use-cases is a clarity issue. It can mislead developers and fragment discoverability.

findings.title: Path parameter `refund` typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `refund` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `maxLength`. Stripe refund IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `re_...`). Without a pattern or maxLength, clients and generated SDKs have no way to validate input before sending the request, and documentation tooling cannot surface the expected shape. At minimum a `maxLength` and ideally a `pattern` such as `^re_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` should be added to tighten the contract.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and prevent client-side validation.

findings.title: Empty request body defined on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation declares an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` request body with an empty schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`) marked as `required: false`. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1); many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will silently drop or reject it. The presence of a request body on a GET is semantically wrong and may confuse generated clients. The requestBody block should be removed entirely from this operation.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate HTTP semantics. RFC 9110 §9.3.1 states that a server MUST NOT apply any meaning to a request body on a GET. Tooling that generates clients will produce incorrect code.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty request body from GET /v1/refunds/{refund}

findings.title: Refund path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern

Adding a `pattern` such as `^re_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow client-side pre-validation and improve generated SDK type fidelity.

findings.title: Refund path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint

Codegen tools and validators cannot enforce the documented rules without the schema constraints.

This requestBody definition adds noise, could confuse codegen tools into emitting a body argument for a GET method, and does not serve any functional purpose.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 notes that GET request payloads have no defined semantics; an explicitly empty, closed body schema on a GET is misleading and potentially harmful to clients.

findings.title: report_type field typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or constraint
findings.narration: The `report_type` field is described as an ID referencing a report type resource (e.g. `"balance.summary.1"`), but its schema is a bare `type: string` with no `maxLength`, no `pattern`, and no `format`. The description even shows an example value inline in prose rather than in a proper `example` or `examples` annotation. Codegen tools cannot build a typed reference to the ReportType resource, and there is no validation hint to help clients catch invalid values before submitting the request.

findings.title: parameters.connected_account and parameters.payout typed as unqualified strings

Returning `200` is semantically misleading and inconsistent with RESTful conventions, making it harder for clients and middleware to distinguish creation from updates or reads.

Fields like `interval_start`, `interval_end`, `currency`, `timezone`, `reporting_category`, `payout`, `columns`, and `connected_account` may be required or forbidden depending on the chosen `report_type` value, yet no `oneOf`, `if/then/else`, or `dependencies` construct encodes these rules in the schema. Clients consuming the spec programmatically have no machine-readable way to discover which parameter combinations are valid for a given report type.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements expressed only in prose are a high-leverage finding: the rules should be machine-readable to enable proper validation and codegen.

findings.title: Path parameter `report_run` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `report_run` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe report run IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `frr_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK generators cannot build a typed reference, and validators cannot reject obviously malformed IDs early — for example, an accidental UUID or an unrelated resource ID would pass schema validation silently.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without pattern/format are a documented high-severity finding pattern. A pattern like `^frr_` would enable early client-side validation.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests conventionally have no request body, and RFC 9110 discourages it. Including an explicit empty body schema can confuse HTTP clients and proxies, and may cause issues with intermediaries that strip GET bodies. Since `required: false`, it is unused in practice, but its presence adds noise and signals a copy-paste artifact from a POST/PATCH template.
findings.rationale: A requestBody on a GET operation violates HTTP semantics and is a design issue. The body carries no properties and can simply be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation; GET requests should not carry a body.

findings.title: List endpoint response includes has_more/url but no pagination parameters
findings.narration: The response schema includes `has_more` (indicating there may be additional pages) and a `url` field typical of Stripe's paginated list responses, yet the operation defines no pagination parameters such as `starting_after`, `ending_before`, or `limit`. Without these parameters, clients have no way to paginate through additional results even though `has_more` signals they exist. Stripe's standard list convention exposes cursor-based pagination via `starting_after`/`ending_before` and a `limit` parameter; their absence here is inconsistent with the response contract.
findings.rationale: A `has_more` field in the response promises paginability but without pagination parameters the promise cannot be fulfilled. This is a high-severity design gap.

findings.patchSummary: Add limit, starting_after, and ending_before pagination parameters to match has_more response field

findings.title: Empty requestBody on a GET endpoint is unnecessary and semantically incorrect
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 discourages it; many clients and proxies drop or reject it). This body carries no information and is either a copy-paste artifact or tooling default. Its presence may confuse client generators into emitting a body-encoding call for what is a parameter-only request.
findings.rationale: GET + request body is semantically wrong and misleads client code generators. The body adds no value here.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/reporting/report_types

findings.title: report_type path parameter lacks maxLength and pattern constraints
findings.narration: The `report_type` path parameter is typed as a bare `type: string` with no `maxLength`, no `pattern`, and no `format`. Stripe report type identifiers follow a recognizable pattern (e.g., `balance.summary.1`, `connected_account_balance.summary.1`). Without constraints, codegen tools cannot validate input, and clients have no guidance on what values are valid. A `maxLength` (e.g., 5000, consistent with other string params in this spec) and ideally a `pattern` (e.g., `^[a-z_]+\.[a-z_.]+$`) would materially improve safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Missing string constraints on a path parameter that identifies a named resource type means no client-side or spec-driven validation is possible.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength constraint to report_type path parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty requestBody on a GET operation is semantically incorrect
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is defined on this GET operation with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests with a body are explicitly discouraged by RFC 7231 and many HTTP intermediaries (proxies, gateways, CDNs) may strip or reject the body. Since the schema has no properties and no body parameters are needed, the `requestBody` block should be removed entirely. Its presence is likely a copy-paste artifact from a POST/PATCH operation template.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 §4.3.1 states GET requests SHOULD NOT include a body. An empty requestBody adds noise and may cause compatibility issues with HTTP infrastructure.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation; GET requests should not have a body.

findings.title: Missing min/max constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema does not encode `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10`. Clients and generated SDKs cannot enforce this range without the constraints being present in the schema itself.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are not machine-readable. Adding minimum, maximum, and default lets validators and codegen tools enforce the documented contract automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual and actively discouraged by HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 semantics; many proxies, gateways, and client libraries will strip or reject such a body. All parameters this endpoint needs are already expressed as query parameters. The empty request body definition adds confusion without benefit.
findings.rationale: GET + request body is a well-known HTTP anti-pattern. The empty schema provides no value and may cause interoperability issues with conformant HTTP clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect empty request body from GET /v1/reviews

findings.title: Path parameter `review` lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `review` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe review IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `prv_`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `format`, client code generators and validators cannot enforce the expected ID shape, increasing the risk of malformed requests reaching the API.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent typed client generation and offer no early-validation signal to consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint and tighten maxLength on the `review` path parameter.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema and `required: false` is attached to this GET operation. GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks discard or reject GET bodies. Including an empty requestBody here is misleading to consumers and code generators.
findings.rationale: GET operations should not declare a requestBody. Its presence implies clients should send a body, which violates HTTP semantics and may cause interoperability issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: review path parameter lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `review` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe review IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `prv_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools and client validators cannot distinguish this ID from an arbitrary string, and callers have no machine-readable contract about what constitutes a valid value. A simple regex pattern such as `^prv_[0-9a-zA-Z]+$` (or a Stripe-standard ID pattern) would make the relationship explicit and enable earlier client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format lose typed relationship information in generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to review path parameter to document expected ID format.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default declared)
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema encodes none of these constraints — no `minimum`, no `maximum`, and no `default`. This means client-side validation libraries and SDK generators cannot enforce the stated contract, and callers could send `limit=0` or `limit=999` without the schema rejecting it. The prose-only constraint is a well-known anti-pattern in OpenAPI that should instead be machine-readable.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented only in prose cannot be enforced by validators or communicated by code-generators; encoding minimum/maximum/default is a basic schema hygiene requirement.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: `setup_intent` ID parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The required `setup_intent` query parameter is the primary filter for this endpoint — it is a SetupIntent resource ID. It is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000, but no `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^seti_`), and no cross-reference to the SetupIntent schema. Without a format hint or pattern, code-generation tools cannot establish a typed relationship between this list endpoint and the SetupIntent resource, and client-side validation cannot detect misrouted IDs (e.g. a PaymentIntent ID passed here by mistake). Stripe IDs have a well-known prefix pattern that should be encoded.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with no format or pattern prevent codegen from building typed relationships and allow structurally invalid IDs to pass schema validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern `^seti_` to the `setup_intent` query parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body present on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` of type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with an empty property set (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically undefined in HTTP/1.1 (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and actively rejected by many HTTP clients and proxies. Stripe's pattern of attaching an empty form body to GET endpoints is a known SDK artifact, but it remains a spec-level misrepresentation that could confuse implementors. The `requestBody` block should be omitted entirely from GET operations.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 defines GET as having no payload semantics; including a requestBody on GET is non-standard and rejected by some HTTP intermediaries and client libraries.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: customer_account description copy-paste error: says 'customer ID' instead of 'account ID'
findings.narration: The `customer_account` parameter description reads: "Only return SetupIntents for the account specified by this customer ID." The phrase 'customer ID' is incorrect — this parameter filters by account, so it should say 'account ID'. This appears to be a copy-paste error from the adjacent `customer` parameter, and will mislead API consumers about what value to supply.
findings.rationale: Misleading parameter documentation causes integration errors. Consumers may pass a customer ID where an account ID is expected.

patchOps.value: Only return SetupIntents for the account specified by this account ID.

findings.patchSummary: Fix copy-paste error in customer_account description: replace 'customer ID' with 'account ID'.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema only specifies `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties. This means client-side validation and code generation tools cannot enforce the documented constraints, and the default of 10 is undiscoverable programmatically.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints should mirror documented behaviour so validators and codegen tools can enforce them without reading prose.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: customer and payment_method filter parameters typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer`, `customer_account`, and `payment_method` query parameters accept resource IDs (Stripe customer IDs like `cus_xxx`, account IDs like `acct_xxx`, and payment method IDs like `pm_xxx`) but are typed as bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. No `pattern` or `format` hint is provided to indicate the ID prefix conventions. This prevents codegen tools from building typed relationships to the referenced resources and makes it harder for consumers to validate their inputs.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with known prefix patterns should at minimum document a pattern so consumers and tooling can validate them without reading external documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer and payment_method query parameter schemas.

findings.title: mandate_data only valid when confirm=true — conditional constraint in prose only
findings.narration: The `mandate_data` field description states: 'This parameter can only be used with `confirm=true`'. Similarly, `return_url` description states: 'This parameter can only be used with `confirm=true`'. These conditional-required / conditional-forbidden relationships are expressed only in prose. Codegen tools and validators cannot enforce the rule that `mandate_data` and `return_url` are only valid when `confirm` is `true`. This should be encoded as a JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependentSchemas` construct to allow automated validation.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules expressed only in prose cannot be enforced by tooling. Both `mandate_data` and `return_url` have documented dependencies on `confirm=true` that are not schema-encoded.

value.description: mandate_data and return_url are only valid when confirm=true

findings.patchSummary: Encode confirm=true dependency for mandate_data and return_url as if/then schema

findings.title: Resource ID fields (customer, on_behalf_of, payment_method, etc.) typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Multiple fields that represent cross-resource references are typed as `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Specifically: `customer` (Customer ID), `customer_account` (Account ID), `on_behalf_of` (Stripe Account ID), `payment_method` (PaymentMethod/Card/Source ID), `payment_method_configuration` (PaymentMethodConfiguration ID), and `confirmation_token` (ConfirmationToken ID). Without a format like `format: stripe-id` or a pattern such as `^cus_`, codegen tools cannot build typed relationships between resources, and client SDKs cannot validate IDs before transmission.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships. This is a recurring pattern affecting 6 fields in this operation.
findings.patchSummary: Add stripe-id format to customer, on_behalf_of, payment_method, confirmation_token fields

findings.title: Missing examples on complex payment_method_data and payment_method_options request body
findings.narration: The `payment_method_data` and `payment_method_options` objects are extremely large and complex, containing dozens of nested sub-objects for different payment method types. There are no `example` or `examples` annotations at the request body level or on these individual properties. API consumers and documentation generators are left without concrete guidance on how to construct a valid request for common flows like setting up a card or a SEPA debit. Adding at least one end-to-end example (e.g., creating a SetupIntent with a card payment method) would significantly improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: Complex nested request schemas without examples are harder to consume correctly. This is especially important for an operation with 50+ nested payment method type sub-schemas.

card_setup.summary: Create a SetupIntent for a card payment method

sepa_debit_setup.summary: Create a SetupIntent with inline SEPA debit payment method data

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples for common SetupIntent creation flows

findings.title: client_secret sent as query parameter exposes sensitive credential in URL
findings.narration: The `client_secret` parameter is transmitted as a plain query string parameter (`in: query`). Query parameters are routinely logged by web servers, reverse proxies, CDNs, load balancers, and browser history. A client secret is a sensitive credential that grants access to the SetupIntent on the client side; exposing it in the URL materially increases the risk of credential leakage. Stripe's own documentation acknowledges this pattern for publishable-key flows, but from an API design perspective this should at minimum be flagged. The mitigation options are: (a) move client_secret to a header (e.g., `X-Stripe-Client-Secret`), (b) use `writeOnly: true` plus a note about logging risks, or (c) document the risk explicitly with a security advisory note in the parameter description. As currently documented there is no warning to integrators about URL logging risks.
findings.rationale: Sensitive credentials in URL query strings are logged by infrastructure at every layer. This is a well-known OWASP risk (OAT-011, CWE-598). Severity is critical per the rubric.

patchOps.value: The client secret of the SetupIntent. Required when using a publishable key to retrieve the SetupIntent. WARNING: Transmitting this value as a query parameter causes it to appear in server logs, browser history, and proxy access logs. Treat this value as a credential and avoid logging or caching URLs that include it.

findings.patchSummary: Add security warning to client_secret query param description about URL logging risks.

findings.title: client_secret conditional-required rule documented only in prose, not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The description of `client_secret` states: "We require this string if you use a publishable key to retrieve the SetupIntent." This is a conditional-required relationship between the authentication context (publishable key) and the presence of `client_secret`. While this particular condition depends on the caller's auth key type — which is hard to fully encode in OpenAPI schema — at minimum the parameter description should cross-reference this dependency clearly, and a note in the operation description should enumerate the two distinct usage patterns (secret key: no client_secret needed; publishable key: client_secret required) as structured documentation. More importantly, tooling and codegen consumers have no machine-readable signal of this dependency.
findings.rationale: Per review guidelines, conditional-required fields documented only in prose should be flagged as high severity. Codegen and validation tooling cannot enforce this constraint.

patchOps.value: The client secret of the SetupIntent. Conditionally required: MUST be provided when authenticating with a publishable key; MUST NOT be provided when authenticating with a secret key. When provided, only a subset of SetupIntent properties is returned.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify conditional-required rule for client_secret in parameter description.

findings.title: Sensitive bank account numbers in payment_method_data lack writeOnly annotation
findings.narration: Several fields within `payment_method_data` carry real financial credentials — notably `acss_debit.account_number`, `au_becs_debit.account_number`, `bacs_debit.account_number`, `sepa_debit.iban`, `us_bank_account.account_number`, `us_bank_account.routing_number`, and `nz_bank_account.account_number`. None of these fields are marked `writeOnly: true`. Without this annotation, code-generation tools and documentation renderers may treat these fields as readable response values, potentially including them in serialized logs or client models. OpenAPI 3.x `writeOnly: true` signals that a field is accepted on write but never returned on read, which is the correct semantic for raw account/routing numbers on Stripe's API.
findings.rationale: Credential/PII fields that are accepted on write but never echoed back in responses should be marked writeOnly to prevent tooling from surfacing them in response models.
findings.patchSummary: Mark bank account numbers, IBANs, and routing numbers as writeOnly in payment_method_data

findings.title: customer and customer_account are plain strings with no format or pattern — resource ID relationship not encoded
findings.narration: The `customer` field is described as 'ID of the Customer this SetupIntent belongs to' and `customer_account` as 'ID of the Account this SetupIntent belongs to', yet both are typed as bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint and no `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`), or `$ref` to a Customer/Account schema. Code-generation tools have no way to understand the cross-resource relationship, and client libraries cannot build a typed reference. Adding at least a `pattern` matching the known Stripe ID prefix convention, or a format like `stripe-id`, would allow tooling to associate these with the Customer and Account resources.
findings.rationale: Fields named as resource IDs should carry a pattern or format so that codegen tools can model the typed cross-resource relationship rather than treating them as arbitrary strings.
findings.patchSummary: Add stripe-id format to customer, customer_account, payment_method, payment_method_configuration fields

findings.title: attach_to_self and customer mutual exclusion expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The description of `attach_to_self` states 'it cannot be set to true when setting up a PaymentMethod for a Customer' — meaning `attach_to_self: true` and a non-null `customer` value are mutually exclusive. This business rule is expressed only in free-text prose and is not encoded as a JSON Schema constraint (e.g. `if/then/else`, `not`, or `oneOf` at the object level). As a result, validators, code-generators, and API gateway policies cannot automatically enforce it. Adding an inline schema constraint would allow tooling to surface the conflict before the request hits the server.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required or mutually exclusive field rules in prose descriptions should be encoded as schema-level constraints for automated validation.

value.description: attach_to_self:true is not allowed when customer is set

findings.patchSummary: Encode attach_to_self / customer mutual exclusion as an if/then schema constraint

findings.title: No 4xx error response definitions beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The responses object defines only a `200` success and a `default` catch-all error. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `402`, `404`, or `422` response definitions. For an update endpoint this complex — accepting dozens of payment method types, each with their own validation rules — specific 4xx responses (particularly 400 Bad Request and 404 Not Found for the `intent` path parameter) carry important documentation value. Consumers cannot distinguish between a schema-validation failure, a missing resource, and an upstream Stripe API business error by looking at the spec alone. Even if the schema behind `default` handles all errors at runtime, the absence of explicit 4xx entries reduces clarity for SDK generators and API portals.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses reduce clarity and prevent SDK generators from handling well-known error classes distinctly.

value.description: Bad request — invalid or missing parameters.
SetupIntent not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the existing default catch-all

findings.title: Path parameter `intent` lacks format/pattern constraint for SetupIntent ID
findings.narration: The `intent` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. SetupIntent IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix format (e.g., `seti_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDKs and codegen tools cannot validate the value or establish a typed relationship to the SetupIntent resource. A simple pattern such as `^seti_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would catch obvious caller mistakes at the SDK layer rather than at runtime.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow obviously invalid IDs to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `intent` path parameter to enforce SetupIntent ID format

findings.title: payment_method field typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `payment_method` field accepts a PaymentMethod, Card, or saved Source object ID, but is modelled as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Resource IDs in Stripe follow predictable prefix patterns (e.g. `pm_`, `card_`, `src_`). Without a `pattern` or custom `format`, codegen tools cannot infer the relationship to a typed resource, and nothing in the schema prevents arbitrary strings from being supplied. This is a known pain point for typed SDK generation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern lose typed relationship information that SDK generators could exploit.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to payment_method to reflect valid resource ID prefixes

findings.title: confirmation_token field typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `confirmation_token` field references a ConfirmationToken resource by ID but is modelled as a plain `type: string`. Stripe ConfirmationToken IDs carry a consistent prefix (`ctoken_`). Without a `pattern` or `format`, SDK generators and validators cannot enforce or document the relationship. This mirrors the same issue as `payment_method`.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields without format/pattern lose typed relationship information for codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern to confirmation_token to identify it as a typed resource ID

findings.title: Conditional mutual-exclusivity of payment_method and payment_method_data expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `confirmation_token` states that if it contains properties also provided in the request (such as `payment_method`), the request-level values take precedence. Separately, having both `payment_method` and `payment_method_data` simultaneously is semantically contradictory — `payment_method_data` creates a new PaymentMethod while `payment_method` attaches an existing one. This relationship is documented only implicitly through field descriptions and Stripe's broader documentation, not encoded in the schema. A `oneOf` or `not` constraint would allow validators to catch misuse at request-validation time rather than at the Stripe API layer.
findings.rationale: Conditional field exclusivity rules expressed only in prose are not machine-enforceable and lead to runtime errors that could be caught earlier.

patchOps.value: Provide either `payment_method` (existing PaymentMethod ID) or `payment_method_data` (inline PaymentMethod creation params), but not both simultaneously.

findings.patchSummary: Document mutual exclusivity of payment_method vs payment_method_data at schema level

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` error catch-all. Stripe's API commonly returns `400 Bad Request` (e.g. invalid parameters), `402 Payment Required` (e.g. card error), `404 Not Found` (intent not found), and `422 Unprocessable Entity` for semantic validation failures. Without explicit 4xx response definitions, client SDK generators cannot generate typed error-handling branches, and API consumers have no machine-readable contract for expected failure modes. The `default` bucket merges all errors into an untyped blob.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses prevent typed error handling in generated clients and obscure the API's failure contract.

value.description: Bad request — invalid or missing parameters.
Payment required — e.g. card was declined.
SetupIntent not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400, 402, and 404 response definitions alongside the existing default catch-all

findings.title: Conditional-required fields (amounts vs descriptor_code) expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The schema for the request body includes two mutually exclusive verification mechanisms: `amounts` (two integer microdeposit values) and `descriptor_code` (a six-character SM-prefixed code). The choice between them depends on the microdeposit verification method configured on the bank account, yet no schema-level constraint encodes this relationship. A consumer reading only the schema (not the prose descriptions) cannot tell that exactly one of these two fields must be provided, nor that they are mutually exclusive. This is a classic conditional-required-in-prose anti-pattern. The correct encoding is a `oneOf` or `if/then/else` at the schema level, ensuring validators and codegen tools can enforce the constraint automatically.
findings.rationale: Mutual exclusivity and conditional requirements buried in `description` strings are invisible to validators, linters, and SDK generators. JSON Schema `oneOf` is the correct mechanism here.

amounts.description: Two positive integers, in *cents*, equal to the values of the microdeposits sent to the bank account. Required when verifying via the amounts method; mutually exclusive with `descriptor_code`.

client_secret.description: The client secret of the SetupIntent.

descriptor_code.description: A six-character code starting with SM present in the microdeposit sent to the bank account. Required when verifying via the descriptor code method; mutually exclusive with `amounts`.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

findings.patchSummary: Encode amounts/descriptor_code mutual exclusivity as oneOf; add pattern and array length constraints.

findings.title: descriptor_code lacks pattern constraint encoding the SM-prefix rule
findings.narration: The `descriptor_code` field description states it is "a six-character code starting with SM", but the schema only enforces `maxLength: 5000` — which is far too permissive and does not enforce the six-character length, the SM prefix, or the expected character set. Any string up to 5000 characters would pass schema validation, meaning validation tools and SDKs will accept clearly invalid values. A `pattern` such as `^SM[A-Z0-9]{4}$` and `minLength: 6` / `maxLength: 6` should be added.
findings.rationale: Format constraints stated in prose but absent from the schema allow invalid inputs through all schema-level validation layers, increasing error surface at the API boundary.

value.description: A six-character code starting with SM present in the microdeposit sent to the bank account.

findings.patchSummary: Restrict descriptor_code to exactly 6 chars with SM prefix via pattern and length constraints.

findings.title: amounts array lacks minItems/maxItems constraint
findings.narration: The description for `amounts` explicitly states 'Two positive integers', yet the schema specifies only `type: array` with `items: { type: integer }` and no `minItems`, `maxItems`, or `minimum` constraint on the integers. A client could send an empty array, a single value, or three values and pass schema validation. Adding `minItems: 2`, `maxItems: 2`, and `minimum: 1` on items would align the schema with the documented contract.
findings.rationale: Array length and value constraints stated in prose must be mirrored in the schema to be enforceable by validators and SDKs.

value.description: Two positive integers, in *cents*, equal to the values of the microdeposits sent to the bank account.

findings.patchSummary: Add minItems:2, maxItems:2, and minimum:1 on items to the amounts array schema.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (min/max not encoded in schema)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. Clients and code-generation tools have no machine-readable way to enforce these bounds, and the default value is documented only in prose. A client passing `limit=0` or `limit=999` would discover the constraint only at runtime.
findings.rationale: Constraints expressed only in prose create validation gaps; minimum/maximum/default should be encoded in the schema.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum, maximum, and default to `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary and misleading
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `required: false` and an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks will drop or reject it. This body conveys no information and may confuse integrators or cause silent failures. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET request bodies are semantically undefined; an empty, closed schema adds no value and violates HTTP semantics.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty request body from GET /v1/shipping_rates.

findings.title: Conditional-required field 'fixed_amount' only enforced in prose
findings.narration: The description for 'fixed_amount' states 'Must be present if type is `fixed_amount`', but this constraint is only expressed in prose. Since 'type' currently has only one enum value ('fixed_amount'), in practice fixed_amount is always required when type is provided, yet neither the schema 'required' array nor a JSON Schema 'if/then' or 'dependentRequired' block encodes this rule. Tooling, validators, and SDK generators cannot enforce or surface this relationship automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships documented only in prose are invisible to validators and code generators. This should be encoded as a JSON Schema constraint.
findings.patchSummary: Add dependentRequired so fixed_amount is required when type is set

findings.title: 'tax_code' field typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The 'tax_code' field references a tax code ID (e.g. 'txcd_92010001') but is declared only as 'type: string' with no format, pattern, or structural hint. This means client libraries and validators cannot distinguish a tax code ID from any arbitrary string. The description even names the canonical Stripe prefix ('txcd_') and a specific example value, making a pattern trivially expressible.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with a known prefix pattern should carry a pattern constraint so validators and codegen tools can build typed references.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to tax_code matching Stripe tax code ID format

findings.title: Success response returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new shipping rate resource. Per HTTP semantics, a successful resource creation should respond with 201 Created, not 200 OK. Using 200 is technically functional but violates REST conventions and makes it harder for consumers to detect whether a resource was newly created versus an idempotent update. Most Stripe creation endpoints share this pattern, but at the per-operation level this is worth flagging.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for resource creation; 200 implies a read or update operation. Correct semantics aid client-side logic and documentation clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Consider returning 201 Created instead of 200 OK for new resource creation

findings.title: No example provided for the complex request body
findings.narration: The request body schema is moderately complex, with nested objects (delivery_estimate, fixed_amount with currency_options), multiple enum fields, and metadata. No request body example is provided at the operation or schema level. Adding at least one example showing a minimal valid payload (display_name + fixed_amount + type) would significantly aid integrators and tooling that auto-generates API explorers or test scaffolding.
findings.rationale: Complex request schemas without examples reduce developer experience and make it harder to verify correct usage at a glance.
findings.patchSummary: Add a minimal example to the request body for the new shipping rate

findings.title: shipping_rate_token path parameter lacks format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `shipping_rate_token` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe shipping rate IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `shr_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, clients cannot validate the token locally before sending a request, and code-generation tools cannot build a typed reference to the shipping rate resource. The `maxLength` of 5000 is also far too permissive for what is in practice a compact identifier.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as bare strings without pattern or format prevent codegen from building typed relationships and allow obviously malformed values to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint and tighten maxLength on shipping_rate_token path param

findings.title: fixed_amount description references a condition that should be schema-encoded
findings.narration: The `fixed_amount` field's description states 'Must be present if type is `fixed_amount`'. This is a conditional-required relationship: when the shipping rate's type equals `fixed_amount`, the `fixed_amount` object is required. Expressing this rule only in prose means validators, code-generators, and SDK authors must parse English to understand the constraint. It should be encoded with a JSON Schema `if/then` or equivalent structural assertion so tooling can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Prose-only conditional requirements are a well-known high-severity pattern: the rule is invisible to validators and codegen tools, silently allowing invalid payloads to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Encode fixed_amount conditional-required rule in schema (if/then or oneOf) rather than prose only

findings.title: No 4xx error responses defined beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The responses object defines only `200` and `default`. In practice, this endpoint can return `400 Bad Request` (invalid parameters), `404 Not Found` (unknown shipping rate token), and `422 Unprocessable Entity` (invalid state transitions). Relying solely on a generic `default` entry means API consumers and code-generation tools have no typed signal for common client-error conditions, making error-handling code harder to write correctly.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx status codes with structured schemas allow clients and SDKs to handle predictable error conditions without guessing, and are a standard OpenAPI best practice.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.
Shipping rate not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the generic default

findings.title: Redundant and slightly awkward operation description
findings.narration: The operation description reads "Update an existing Sigma query that previously exists" — the phrase "that previously exists" is redundant since 'existing' already conveys that. The summary already says "Update an existing Sigma Query", making the description nearly a copy-paste duplicate with minor wording differences. The description should add meaningful detail such as which fields are updatable or what happens if neither `name` nor `sql` is provided.
findings.rationale: Redundant prose reduces documentation quality and provides no additional value over the summary field.

patchOps.value: Update an existing saved Sigma query. You may update the query's name, its sql statement, or both. At least one updatable field should be provided.

findings.patchSummary: Remove redundant wording and add meaningful guidance to the description.

findings.title: No constraint enforcing at least one updatable field in request body
findings.narration: The request body is marked `required: false` and neither `name` nor `sql` is listed under `required`. This means a client can submit a POST with an empty body (or only `expand`), which is semantically a no-op update. The description's prose does not explicitly state this is disallowed either. A `minProperties` constraint or `anyOf`/`oneOf` rule should encode that at least one of `name` or `sql` must be present when calling this update endpoint.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required field relationships expressed only implicitly risk silent no-op calls; encoding them in schema enables validation at the client and gateway layers.
findings.patchSummary: Add anyOf requiring at least one of name or sql to prevent no-op updates.

findings.title: Missing explicit 4xx error response definitions
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` and a catch-all `default` error response. Standard error cases for this endpoint — such as `400` (bad request / invalid SQL), `401` (unauthorized), `404` (query not found by the given id), and `422` (unprocessable entity) — are not individually documented. Relying solely on `default` prevents client developers and code generators from handling specific error cases with typed branching logic.
findings.rationale: Distinct 4xx response codes carry semantic meaning that improves client error handling; a single `default` is insufficient for production API documentation.

value.description: Bad request. The supplied parameters are invalid (e.g., malformed SQL).
No saved query found with the given id.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions for better client error handling.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter schema is typed as `integer` but has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` annotation. The description says the range is 1–100 and the default is 10, but these constraints live only in prose. Code generators and validators cannot enforce them without schema-level constraints, meaning a client could send `limit=0` or `limit=999` without a spec-level validation error. The information should be encoded where tooling can act on it.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints cannot be enforced by validators or used by code generators. This is a high-leverage fix that aligns the schema with the described behaviour.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` integer schema.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type whose schema has no properties (`additionalProperties: false, properties: {}`). GET requests with a body are semantically unusual (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 explicitly notes GET bodies have no defined semantics) and many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks silently drop GET bodies. Declaring an empty, forbidden-additional-properties form body on a read-only list operation is misleading and may confuse generated SDK code into attempting to send a body. The `requestBody` field should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET with a body is non-standard and the schema admits no fields anyway. Its presence is likely a spec-generator artefact and should be removed to avoid confusing clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, no-op requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: GET operation includes an unnecessary empty request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`additionalProperties: false`, no properties). GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and including one is misleading to client generators and consumers. While Stripe commonly does this for form-encoded parameters, for a GET request with no body properties, this is both semantically incorrect and noisy.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 states that a GET request has no defined semantics for a request body. An empty body definition adds noise without value and may cause issues with strict HTTP clients or code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Path parameter `scheduled_query_run` has no format, pattern, or description
findings.narration: The path parameter `scheduled_query_run` is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint but lacks a `format`, `pattern`, or `description`. Stripe resource IDs for scheduled query runs follow a predictable prefix pattern (e.g. `sqr_`). Without a pattern or description, client code generators and API consumers have no hint about expected ID structure, making validation and typed SDK generation harder.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or description are a low-signal finding but do impact codegen quality and client-side validation capability.

patchOps.value: The ID of the scheduled query run to retrieve. Has the prefix `sqr_`.

findings.patchSummary: Add description and pattern to the scheduled_query_run path parameter

findings.title: Description uses incorrect article: 'an scheduled' should be 'a scheduled'
findings.narration: The operation description reads "Retrieves the details of an scheduled query run." The article 'an' is used before a consonant sound ('s'), which is grammatically incorrect and should be 'a scheduled query run'.
findings.rationale: Minor grammar error in the description reduces perceived quality of the API documentation.

patchOps.value: Retrieves the details of a scheduled query run.

findings.patchSummary: Fix grammar: 'an scheduled' → 'a scheduled' in description

findings.title: Summary contradicts operation purpose: 'Shares a source' vs 'Creates a new source object'
findings.narration: The operation's `summary` field reads 'Shares a source', which describes source-cloning/sharing behavior (attaching an existing source to another customer). However, the `description` reads 'Creates a new source object', and the endpoint clearly handles both new source creation and source cloning. The summary is misleading and appears to be a copy-paste error or incomplete edit — it should reflect the primary purpose of creating a new source.
findings.rationale: A mismatched summary misleads both developers reading documentation and tooling that surfaces only summaries. This is a clarity issue that could cause integration mistakes.
findings.patchSummary: Replace misleading 'Shares a source' summary with 'Create a source'

findings.title: Conditional-required fields expressed only in prose, not schema constraints
findings.narration: Multiple fields have conditional-required rules documented in prose but not encoded as schema constraints: (1) `amount` is described as 'Required for `single_use` sources'; (2) `type` is described as 'Required unless `customer` and `original_source` are specified'; (3) `redirect` object is described as 'Required if the source is authenticated by a redirect (`flow` is `redirect`)'; (4) `customer` field says 'Must be set when the original source is not a `Source`'. None of these interdependencies are encoded as `oneOf`, `if/then/else`, or `dependencies` constraints in the JSON Schema. Tooling, validators, and SDK generators cannot enforce these rules and clients will only discover them at runtime via API errors.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships in prose only means validation tools and generated SDKs cannot enforce invariants. This leads to runtime errors that could be caught earlier.

patchOps.value: To create a new source, `type` is required unless both `customer` and `original_source` are provided. For `single_use` usage, `amount` is required. If `flow` is `redirect`, the `redirect` object is required.

findings.patchSummary: Add top-level schema description noting conditional-required field rules (full if/then encoding recommended)

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string without pattern or format
findings.narration: The `customer` field (referencing a Stripe Customer object) and `original_source` field (referencing an existing Source object) are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe resource IDs follow well-known prefix patterns (e.g., `cus_`, `src_`). Without a `pattern` or a custom `format`, codegen tools cannot establish a typed relationship to the referenced resource, and clients cannot validate they are passing the right ID type.
findings.rationale: Untyped resource ID references prevent typed SDK generation and allow silent misuse (e.g., passing a PaymentIntent ID where a Customer ID is expected).
findings.patchSummary: Add ID prefix patterns to customer and original_source fields to enable typed resource references

findings.title: Response uses 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This is a POST endpoint that creates a new source resource, yet the success response is documented as `200 OK` rather than `201 Created`. Per HTTP semantics, resource creation should return `201 Created` with a `Location` header pointing to the new resource. While Stripe consistently uses 200 across their API for this pattern, it deviates from REST convention and may confuse developers expecting standard HTTP status codes for creation operations.
findings.rationale: Using 200 instead of 201 for resource creation contradicts HTTP RFC 9110 semantics. While a Stripe-wide pattern, it is worth flagging per operation.
findings.patchSummary: No patch recommended as this is a consistent Stripe-wide API convention

findings.title: client_secret sent as query parameter exposes secret in server logs and browser history
findings.narration: The `client_secret` parameter is passed in the URL query string (`in: query`). Query parameters appear in server access logs, browser history, referrer headers, and CDN logs. Even though this is a GET request and the secret is not strictly a server-side API key, it is still a credential that authorizes access to a source object without the normal authentication requirements. Transmitting it in the URL is a well-known anti-pattern for sensitive values and violates the principle of least exposure. The conventional alternative is to move it to a request header (e.g., `in: header`) so it is not persisted in standard log infrastructure.
findings.rationale: Secrets in URL query strings are persistently exposed in logs, referrer headers, and browser history, increasing the attack surface significantly compared to header-based transmission.
findings.patchSummary: Move client_secret from query string to request header to avoid credential exposure in logs

findings.title: Conditional-required rule for client_secret documented in prose only, not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The description for `client_secret` states: "Required if a publishable key is used to retrieve the source." This conditional-required relationship is expressed only in prose. OpenAPI 3.x supports encoding such logic via `if/then` or via `oneOf`/`dependencies` constructs at the request-body or parameter level. Because it is prose-only, automated validators, SDK generators, and documentation tools cannot enforce or surface this constraint — consumers will only discover the rule by reading the description carefully. This is a high-leverage pattern to encode in schema.
findings.rationale: Conditional requirements documented only in prose are invisible to validators and SDK generators; they should be encoded as schema constraints to be machine-enforceable.

patchOps.value: The client secret of the source. Required if a publishable key is used to retrieve the source. Must not be supplied when using a secret key.

findings.patchSummary: Encode conditional-required client_secret rule in schema (if/then) rather than prose only

findings.title: Unnecessary empty requestBody on a GET operation
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically undefined per RFC 9110 and many HTTP clients (proxies, caches, and CDNs) will strip or reject the body. The presence of the requestBody in the spec is misleading, may confuse code generators into attempting to send a body, and adds noise with no benefit. It should be removed.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 does not define semantics for GET request bodies; many intermediaries discard them. An empty requestBody on GET is misleading to SDK generators and API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/sources/{source} — GET bodies are semantically undefined

findings.title: mandate.acceptance.type field has conditional-required rules expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `mandate.acceptance` object includes both an `offline` sub-object and an `online` sub-object, and a `type` field with enum values `["offline", "online"]`.
