The Stripe documentation implies (and API behavior enforces) that when `type` is `"offline"`, the `offline` sub-object is required, and when `type` is `"online"`, the `online` sub-object is required. This mutual-exclusion and conditional-requirement relationship is not encoded in the schema at all — it exists only in external documentation prose. Code-generation tools and validators reading this schema alone cannot infer these constraints, leading to incorrect client libraries and missed validation errors.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements that live only in prose (not in schema) are a high-severity design issue per review guidelines. The schema should use `if/then` or `oneOf` to express these constraints.
findings.patchSummary: Encode offline/online conditional-required rules as if/then schema instead of prose-only

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions provided
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error catch-all. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `402`, `404`, or `422` response definitions. For a resource-update endpoint like this, clients commonly encounter `400` (bad request / invalid parameters), `401` (authentication failure), `404` (source not found), and `422` (unprocessable entity) responses. Without explicit response schemas for these status codes, API consumers and code-generation tools cannot produce strongly-typed error handlers, and documentation tooling cannot surface useful error semantics.
findings.rationale: Missing 4xx responses on a write endpoint reduce clarity for API consumers and tooling. The `default` catch-all is insufficient for distinguishing error types.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.
Source not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default catch-all

findings.title: source_order.items[].parent is a plain string with no resource ID typing
findings.narration: The `source_order.items[].parent` field is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. From the Stripe API context, this field references a SKU or order item ID (a cross-resource reference). Without a `pattern` constraint (e.g., matching `^(sku_|oi_)...`), `format`, or at minimum a description clarifying the expected resource type and ID format, code-generation tools and validators cannot build a typed relationship or validate the input. This is a common pattern in the Stripe spec worth flagging here.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings with no pattern or format prevent code-gen tools from building typed relationships and reduce validation quality.

value.description: The ID of the associated SKU or order item this line item references.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to source_order.items[].parent clarifying the referenced resource type

findings.title: Description says 'Retrieves a new' instead of 'Retrieves a'
findings.narration:
The operation description reads '

Retrieves a new Source MandateNotification.

', but this is a GET endpoint that retrieves an existing resource — not a newly-created one. The word 'new' is almost certainly a copy-paste artefact from a creation endpoint's description template. It misleads API consumers into thinking the operation creates or returns a freshly-generated mandate notification rather than fetching an existing one.
findings.rationale: Inaccurate description erodes developer trust and can cause confusion about whether the operation has side effects.
findings.patchSummary: Fix description: replace 'a new' with 'an existing'

findings.title: Path ID parameters lack format or pattern constraints
findings.narration: Both `source` and `mandate_notification` path parameters are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe resource IDs follow a predictable prefix pattern (e.g. `src_...`, `mnot_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, tooling cannot distinguish these IDs from arbitrary strings, codegen cannot build typed resource relationships, and client-side validation is essentially absent. maxLength of 5000 is also unrealistically large for what are compact opaque identifiers.
findings.rationale: Typed resource ID parameters improve codegen fidelity, enable client-side validation, and signal the expected format to API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern + tighten maxLength on source and mandate_notification path params

findings.title: Request body present on GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though the body schema has no properties and the method is GET. GET requests with a body are semantically incorrect per RFC 7231 and are not supported by many HTTP clients, proxies, and frameworks. The empty body definition adds noise and may confuse client generators into emitting unnecessary body-handling code.
findings.rationale: GET semantics prohibit meaningful request bodies; an empty form-encoded body should not be declared.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Missing description and pattern on `source` path parameter
findings.narration: The `source` path parameter has no `description` field and no `pattern` or `format` constraint. Stripe source IDs follow a well-known prefix format (e.g. `src_...`). Without a description or pattern, consumers and code generators have no indication of what kind of identifier is expected, making it harder to validate inputs and generate typed SDK methods.
findings.rationale: Resource ID path parameters should carry a description and a pattern or format to enable validation and typed codegen.

patchOps.value: The identifier of the source whose transactions should be listed. Must be a source ID of the form `src_...`.

findings.patchSummary: Add description and pattern constraint to `source` path parameter

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states the allowed range is 1–100 with a default of 10, but the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values. This means API clients cannot enforce the documented range at the schema level, and code generators will not emit the documented default.
findings.rationale: Documented numeric constraints must be encoded in the schema to be enforceable and usable by validators and SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum (1), maximum (100), and default (10) to `limit` schema

findings.title: Path parameters typed as unconstrained strings with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `source` and `source_transaction` path parameters are typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe source IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `src_...` and `srctxn_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a meaningful `maxLength` that reflects the actual max ID length, client SDKs and validators cannot differentiate a valid ID from arbitrary free-form text. The `maxLength: 5000` is clearly a copy-paste default — Stripe IDs are far shorter than 5000 characters — and provides no useful constraint in practice.
findings.rationale: Typed resource ID fields without a discriminating pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow trivially malformed inputs to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten path param maxLength and add ID-prefix pattern for source and source_transaction

findings.title: Empty requestBody on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests conventionally do not carry a request body, and RFC 7231 explicitly notes that a GET body has no defined semantics. The empty body definition adds confusion for SDK consumers and code generators who may attempt to serialize an empty object as form data. It should be removed.
findings.rationale: An empty request body on a GET endpoint contradicts HTTP semantics and creates unnecessary noise in generated client code.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Missing format/pattern on `source` path parameter
findings.narration: The `source` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a maxLength constraint. Stripe source IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `src_`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a description hinting at the expected format, codegen tools cannot validate or type the reference, and clients may accidentally pass arbitrary strings. Adding a pattern like `^src_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at least a format description would improve both safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow invalid IDs to be submitted.

patchOps.value: The unique identifier of the source object to verify. Must be a valid Stripe source ID (e.g. `src_...`).

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to `source` path parameter

findings.title: Missing constraints on `values` array items
findings.narration: The `values` field is required and represents the verification codes (e.g. micro-deposit amounts) the user must supply to prove ownership of a source. The schema only constrains each item to `maxLength: 5000`, which is far too permissive. In practice, these values are small numeric strings (e.g. two 1–99 cent deposit amounts). The lack of a `minItems`/`maxItems`, `minLength`, or `pattern` constraint means invalid or excessively long payloads pass schema validation silently and only fail server-side. Adding at minimum a `minItems: 1` and `maxItems` would improve client-side safety.
findings.rationale: Absent array size constraints on a required field mean invalid payloads are only caught server-side, weakening client-side validation and documentation quality.
findings.patchSummary: Add minItems/maxItems constraints to the `values` array

findings.title: No example provided for the required `values` field
findings.narration: The `values` array is required to complete source verification but lacks any example. For developers unfamiliar with the Stripe micro-deposit verification flow, it is unclear what kind of values to supply (e.g. two integer cent amounts like `["32", "45"]`). Adding an `example` or `examples` on the request body schema would significantly reduce integration friction.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on a required, domain-specific field forces developers to consult external docs and increases error rate during integration.
findings.patchSummary: Add example micro-deposit values to the `values` field

findings.title: GET list endpoint includes an empty request body definition
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` containing an empty schema. GET requests must not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and including one in the spec is misleading for SDK generators and documentation tools, which may incorrectly treat this as a form-submission endpoint. The body carries no properties, so it is entirely superfluous and should be removed.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 states that a GET request has no defined body semantics. An empty request body on a GET endpoint is a design defect that can confuse code generators and clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from GET /v1/subscription_items

findings.title: The `subscription` query parameter is typed as plain string without ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `subscription` parameter is the primary foreign-key reference to a Subscription resource (IDs typically match `sub_[A-Za-z0-9]+`). It is typed as `type: string` with only `maxLength: 5000`, providing no format, pattern, or semantic link to the Subscription resource. Codegen tools cannot infer a typed relationship, and validators cannot reject obviously malformed IDs like empty strings or arbitrary text. Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^sub_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) would improve both validation and documentation fidelity.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed cross-resource references and allow malformed values to reach the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID pattern to the subscription query parameter schema

findings.title: The `limit` parameter lacks minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum`. This means client-side validators and documentation renderers cannot enforce or surface the constraint; a caller could pass 0 or 10000 and only learn about the restriction from the API error at runtime. The prose-only constraint should be encoded in the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but absent from the schema cannot be validated by client-side tools or surfaced accurately in generated documentation and SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Missing 201 Created response — POST creating a resource should return 201, not 200
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new subscription item (a new resource) via HTTP POST. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a successful resource creation should return 201 Created, not 200 OK. The 200 response implies an update or read operation, which is semantically misleading for clients and code-generation tooling that infers resource creation from the status code.
findings.rationale: HTTP POST creating a new resource should return 201 Created per RFC 9110. Returning 200 conflates creation with update/read semantics and misleads clients.

value.description: Subscription item created successfully.

findings.patchSummary: Add 201 Created response alongside 200 to correctly signal resource creation

findings.title: Cross-field constraint 'price or price_data' expressed only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: The operation accepts both `price` (an existing Price ID) and `price_data` (inline price creation). In practice, these are mutually exclusive — a caller should provide one or the other, not both. This constraint is implied by the API's design but is not encoded in the request body schema as a `oneOf`, `not`, or `if/then/else` construct. Developers relying on schema validation alone cannot detect the invalid combination, and code-generation tools cannot surface it as a typed constraint.
findings.rationale: Prose-only mutual exclusion rules should be encoded in JSON Schema to enable automated validation and accurate SDK generation.

patchOps.value: The ID of the price object. Mutually exclusive with `price_data`; provide one or the other, not both.

value.description: price and price_data are mutually exclusive

findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusion of price and price_data using JSON Schema 'not/required'

findings.title: discount item fields (coupon, discount, promotion_code) are untyped IDs with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Within the `discounts` array items, the fields `coupon`, `discount`, and `promotion_code` are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. These are all references to Stripe resource IDs (coupon IDs, discount IDs, promotion code IDs) and should carry a `pattern` (e.g. `^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$`) or at minimum a documented `format` hint so that code-generation tools can build typed relationships. Without this, clients cannot distinguish them from arbitrary free-form strings.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed references and reduce client-side validation quality.

patchOps.value: The ID of a coupon object.
The ID of a discount object.
The ID of a promotion code object.

findings.patchSummary: Add ID-type descriptions to coupon, discount, and promotion_code fields in discounts items

findings.title: Conditional mutual exclusivity of 'price' and 'price_data' encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description on the `price` field states 'One of `price` or `price_data` is required' and the `price_data` description echoes the same constraint. This mutual-exclusivity rule (exactly one of the two must be supplied) is documented purely in prose, but the JSON Schema does not encode it. Clients and code-generation tools have no machine-readable way to validate this constraint. It should be expressed using a JSON Schema `oneOf` (or `if/then/else` / `not`) construct at the object level so that validators can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields expressed only in prose cannot be validated by schema validators or code generators, leading to runtime errors that could have been caught earlier.
findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf at schema level to enforce mutual exclusivity of 'price' and 'price_data'

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that reference Stripe resource IDs — `price` (Price ID), `discounts[].coupon` (Coupon ID), `discounts[].discount` (Discount ID), `discounts[].promotion_code` (PromotionCode ID), `price_data.product` (Product ID), and `tax_rates[]` items (TaxRate IDs) — are typed as plain `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no `$ref`. Stripe IDs have well-known prefixes and could at minimum carry a `pattern` hint (e.g. `^price_...`, `^prod_...`) or a `format: stripe-id` annotation. Without this, code-generation tools cannot build typed cross-resource relationships, and clients cannot perform client-side ID format validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference fields typed as bare strings lose relationship semantics for codegen and validation tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add format annotations to resource ID string fields for codegen relationship typing

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body fields
findings.narration: The request body includes several complex nested objects (`billing_thresholds`, `discounts`, `price_data`) and union types (anyOf with empty-string sentinel to clear values). There are no `example` or `examples` annotations on these fields or on the schema as a whole. Without examples, developer portal tooling, mock servers, and SDK generators cannot surface representative usage, increasing integration friction especially for the less obvious 'pass empty string to clear' pattern.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas and non-obvious sentinel patterns (empty string to unset) greatly benefit from inline examples for developer experience.
findings.patchSummary: Add inline examples to price_data and discounts to aid developer tooling and docs

findings.title: 'quantity' description references creation context rather than update context
findings.narration: The `quantity` field description reads: 'The quantity you'd like to apply to the subscription item you're creating.' This is an update endpoint (`POST /v1/subscription_items/{item}`), not a create endpoint. The description copy-pastes creation context language, which may confuse developers about whether this field is setting an initial quantity or updating an existing one. It should read something like 'The quantity you'd like to apply to the existing subscription item.'
findings.rationale: A description that references creation when the endpoint is an update operation constitutes a clarity/copy-paste bug that can mislead API consumers.

patchOps.value: The quantity you'd like to apply to the subscription item you're updating.

findings.patchSummary: Fix quantity description from 'creating' to 'updating' to match endpoint semantics

findings.title: conditional-required field 'clear_usage' expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `clear_usage` field description states it is 'Allowed only when the current plan's `usage_type` is `metered`'. This conditional constraint is expressed only in prose, not as a machine-readable schema rule. Client SDK generators, validators, and documentation tools cannot enforce this constraint automatically. The relationship should be encoded in the schema (e.g., as an `if/then` or noted as a `dependencies` rule) so that tooling can surface the restriction at the schema level rather than relying on developers reading prose descriptions.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required or conditional-allowed fields expressed only in prose are a high-leverage pattern — they should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints to enable automated validation.

clear_usage.description: Delete all usage for the given subscription item. Allowed only when the current plan's `usage_type` is `metered`.

payment_behavior.description:
Use `allow_incomplete` to transition the subscription to `status=past_due` if a payment is required but cannot be paid. This allows you to manage scenarios where additional user actions are needed to pay a subscription's invoice. For example, SCA regulation may require 3DS authentication to complete payment. See the [SCA Migration Guide](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/migration/strong-customer-authentication) for Billing to learn more. This is the default behavior.

Use `default_incomplete` to transition the subscription to `status=past_due` when payment is required and await explicit confirmation of the invoice's payment intent. This allows simpler management of scenarios where additional user actions are needed to pay a subscription's invoice. Such as failed payments, [SCA regulation](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/migration/strong-customer-authentication), or collecting a mandate for a bank debit payment method.

Use `pending_if_incomplete` to update the subscription using [pending updates](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/pending-updates). When you use `pending_if_incomplete` you can only pass the parameters [supported by pending updates](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/pending-updates-reference#supported-attributes).

Use `error_if_incomplete` if you want Stripe to return an HTTP 402 status code if a subscription's invoice cannot be paid. For example, if a payment method requires 3DS authentication due to SCA regulation and further user action is needed, this parameter does not update the subscription and returns an error instead. This was the default behavior for API versions prior to 2019-03-14. See the [changelog](https://docs.stripe.com/changelog/2019-03-14) to learn more.

proration_behavior.description: Determines how to handle [prorations](https://docs.stripe.com/billing/subscriptions/prorations) when the billing cycle changes (e.g., when switching plans, resetting `billing_cycle_anchor=now`, or starting a trial), or if an item's `quantity` changes. The default value is `create_prorations`.

proration_date.description: If set, the proration will be calculated as though the subscription was updated at the given time. This can be used to apply the same proration that was previewed with the [upcoming invoice](/api/invoices/create_preview) endpoint.

else.description: clear_usage is only permitted when the plan usage_type is metered; encoding this constraint here as a schema-level reminder.

findings.patchSummary: Annotate clear_usage constraint as schema-level rule, not prose-only

findings.title: DELETE returns 200 instead of semantically appropriate 204 or deleted-object 200
findings.narration: The operation returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body on successful deletion. In Stripe's API convention, a delete endpoint typically returns a deletion confirmation object (e.g. `{id: ..., object: 'subscription_item', deleted: true}`). While 200 with a body is acceptable per Stripe's own convention, the response schema is a cyclic ref and there is no documentation of the shape of the success response or what properties it contains. Consumers cannot distinguish a successful deletion response from any other 200 without inspecting runtime payloads. Adding at minimum an inline description of the expected deletion response shape (or a concrete schema reference) would improve clarity significantly.
findings.rationale: Undocumented 200 response body shape on a DELETE endpoint makes client integration fragile; consumers cannot know what to expect from the response.

patchOps.value: Successful response. Returns a deletion confirmation object with `id`, `object`, and `deleted: true` fields.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify 200 response description to document deletion confirmation shape

findings.title: Typo in `canceled_at` parameter description
findings.narration: The description for the `canceled_at` query parameter reads "Only return subscription schedules that were created canceled the given date interval." The word 'created' is spurious — it should read "that were canceled during the given date interval." This is a copy-paste error from the `created` parameter's description that slipped through.
findings.rationale: Inaccurate documentation misleads API consumers about what the parameter filters on.

patchOps.value: Only return subscription schedules that were canceled during the given date interval.

findings.patchSummary: Fix typo in canceled_at description: remove spurious 'created'

findings.title: `limit` parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states "Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10", but the schema is simply `{ "type": "integer" }` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` fields. Clients relying on schema validation (e.g. generated SDKs) will not enforce the stated bounds, and the default of 10 is undocumented in the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented only in prose are not machine-enforceable. Missing minimum/maximum means client validators will not reject out-of-range values, and the missing default means generated clients cannot populate it automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: `customer` field typed as plain string without ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` query parameter is a Stripe customer ID (e.g. `cus_xxx`) typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_`) and no format hint are present. Code-generation tools cannot infer the typed relationship to the Customer resource, and nothing prevents callers from passing an arbitrary string.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as unformatted strings prevent SDK generators from building typed cross-resource references and offer no validation hint to API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern ^cus_ to customer parameter schema to hint resource ID type

findings.title: Empty request body should be omitted on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a request body are semantically problematic — many HTTP proxies, CDNs, and client libraries strip or reject bodies on GET requests. Since the body has no properties and is not required, it should simply be removed.
findings.rationale: An empty, non-required request body on a GET endpoint is non-standard per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1) and may confuse generated clients and intermediaries.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty, no-op requestBody from GET endpoint

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `customer`, `customer_account`, and `from_subscription` not encoded as schema constraints
findings.narration: The request body has three fields — `customer`, `customer_account`, and `from_subscription` — that are semantically exclusive alternatives: you provide either a customer/customer_account to build a new schedule, or `from_subscription` to migrate an existing subscription. The `from_subscription` description explicitly states 'other parameters (such as phase values) cannot be set' when it is used, implying it is mutually exclusive with `customer`, `phases`, etc. These constraints exist only in prose. JSON Schema `oneOf` or `not` / `dependencies` constructs should encode these rules so validators and code generators can enforce them automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required and mutually-exclusive field relationships expressed only in description text are a high-leverage finding: tooling cannot validate them, and clients can send invalid combinations that only fail at runtime.

value.description: Create from an existing subscription
Create from a customer (or customer_account)

findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf to encode mutual exclusivity between from_subscription and customer/phases

findings.title: `customer` and `customer_account` fields are plain strings without ID format/pattern
findings.narration: Both `customer` (a Stripe Customer ID, e.g. `cus_xxx`) and `customer_account` (a Stripe Account ID, e.g. `acct_xxx`) are typed as bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength`. No `pattern` or `format` hint is present to communicate the expected ID format. Similarly `from_subscription` (a subscription ID `sub_xxx`) follows the same pattern. This makes code generation unable to build typed cross-resource references, and client-side validation cannot pre-screen obviously wrong values.
findings.rationale: Fields named after resource IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer, customer_account, and from_subscription fields

findings.title: `end_behavior` description lists only `release` and `cancel` but schema enum includes `none` and `renew`
findings.narration: The `end_behavior` field description states 'Possible values are `release` or `cancel` with the default being `release`' and describes only those two values. However, the schema `enum` includes four values: `cancel`, `none`, `release`, and `renew`. The undocumented `none` and `renew` values are invisible to consumers reading the description, leading to confusion about what the field actually accepts.
findings.rationale: Description inconsistent with schema enum causes consumer confusion; `none` and `renew` are silently valid but never explained.

patchOps.value: Behavior of the subscription schedule and underlying subscription when it ends. Possible values are `release`, `cancel`, `none`, or `renew`. `release` (default) ends the schedule and keeps the underlying subscription running. `cancel` ends the schedule and cancels the underlying subscription. `none` ends the schedule without any action. `renew` automatically renews the schedule.

findings.patchSummary: Update end_behavior description to document all four enum values: cancel, none, release, renew

findings.title: No request body examples provided for a complex, multi-phase schema
findings.narration: The request body schema is highly complex, featuring nested objects for `phases`, `default_settings`, `billing_mode`, `add_invoice_items`, and many conditional sub-fields. Despite this complexity, no `examples` or `example` are provided on the request body or its schema. Developers integrating this endpoint must reverse-engineer valid payloads from the deeply nested schema alone. At minimum, two examples would be valuable: one showing the simple `from_subscription` migration path, and one showing a multi-phase schedule creation with `customer` and `phases`.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas without examples significantly raise integration effort and error rate; missing examples on request bodies is a medium-severity clarity issue per calibration guidelines.

migrate_from_subscription.summary: Migrate existing subscription to a schedule

new_schedule_two_phases.summary: Create a two-phase schedule for a customer

findings.patchSummary: Add two representative request body examples for migration and new multi-phase schedule creation

findings.title: end_behavior enum includes undocumented values not mentioned in description
findings.narration: The `end_behavior` field description states "Possible values are `release` or `cancel`" but the enum in the schema also includes `none` and `renew`. This is a documentation/schema mismatch — consumers reading only the description will be unaware that `none` and `renew` are valid values. This constitutes a copy-paste or stale-description bug that will confuse API integrators.
findings.rationale: Description says only `release` and `cancel` are possible values, but schema enum has four values: `cancel`, `none`, `release`, `renew`.

patchOps.value: Behavior of the subscription schedule and underlying subscription when it ends. Possible values are `release`, `cancel`, `none`, or `renew`. `release` will end the subscription schedule and keep the underlying subscription running. `cancel` will end the subscription schedule and cancel the underlying subscription.

findings.patchSummary: Fix end_behavior description to list all four valid enum values

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions on a write endpoint
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` and a `default` (error) response. There are no explicit 4xx response codes (e.g. 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 422 Unprocessable Entity). While the `default` catch-all technically covers errors, the absence of explicit 4xx definitions means tooling, generated clients, and SDK documentation cannot distinguish between client-side errors (bad input, not found) and server-side errors (5xx). For a mutating endpoint that accepts complex nested schemas, at minimum 400 and 404 should be documented explicitly.
findings.rationale: Write endpoints should document expected client error responses explicitly so generated clients and documentation clearly communicate failure modes.

value.description: Bad request. Invalid parameters were supplied.
The subscription schedule with the specified ID was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default error response

findings.title: Conditional rule 'account required when type=account' encoded only in prose
findings.narration: In multiple places throughout the schema (e.g. `default_settings.automatic_tax.liability`, `default_settings.invoice_settings.issuer`, `phases[].automatic_tax.liability`, `phases[].invoice_settings.issuer`), there is an `account` field alongside a `type` field with enum `["account", "self"]`. The implicit rule is that `account` is required when `type` is `"account"` and must be absent (or is irrelevant) when `type` is `"self"`. This conditional-required relationship is not encoded in JSON Schema (e.g. via `if/then` or `dependencies`) — it only exists as implicit domain knowledge. Codegen tools and validators cannot enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Field relationships that are conditionally required based on another field's value should be encoded as JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependentRequired`, not left as implicit knowledge.
findings.patchSummary: Encode account-required-when-type=account rule as JSON Schema if/then on liability objects

findings.title: price and price_data fields in phase items have no mutually-exclusive constraint
findings.narration: Both `phases[].items[].price` and `phases[].items[].price_data` are optional fields with no schema-level constraint preventing both from being set simultaneously. In Stripe's API, these are mutually exclusive — you supply either a reference to an existing price (`price`) or inline price data (`price_data`), never both. The same pattern applies to `phases[].add_invoice_items[].price` vs `price_data`. Without a `oneOf` or `not` constraint, schema validators will accept both fields being present, leading to confusing runtime errors from the API.
findings.rationale: Mutually exclusive field groups should be expressed via JSON Schema oneOf/not so validators and codegen tools can enforce the constraint rather than relying on runtime API errors.

value.description: price and price_data are mutually exclusive

findings.patchSummary: Add not constraint to prevent simultaneous use of price and price_data on phase items

findings.title: invoice_now and prorate only applicable when subscription schedule is active — conditional rule in prose only
findings.narration: Both `invoice_now` and `prorate` fields carry descriptions that say 'If the subscription schedule is `active`...' — meaning these fields are effectively no-ops (and potentially misleading) when the schedule is in `not_started` status. This conditional applicability rule is documented only in prose and not encoded in the schema. A consumer generating a cancellation request for a `not_started` schedule might send these fields unknowingly. The rule should ideally be expressed as a JSON Schema `if/then` or documented clearly with an `x-` extension, though in practice the best immediate improvement is to call out in the field description that these values are ignored for `not_started` schedules and ensure the API documents what happens in those cases.
findings.rationale: Conditional field semantics buried in prose descriptions lead to client confusion and cannot be leveraged by code generators or validators.

patchOps.value: If the subscription schedule is `active`, indicates if a final invoice will be generated that contains any un-invoiced metered usage and new/pending proration invoice items. Defaults to `true`. Ignored when the schedule status is `not_started`.
If the subscription schedule is `active`, indicates if the cancellation should be prorated. Defaults to `true`. Ignored when the schedule status is `not_started`.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify that invoice_now and prorate are ignored for not_started schedules.

findings.title: Empty request body on GET list endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` of `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics, and many HTTP clients and intermediaries will strip or reject bodies on GET requests. All filtering parameters are already correctly defined as query parameters. The request body definition adds confusion and should be removed.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 §4.3.1 states that GET request bodies have no defined semantics; including one contradicts HTTP conventions and may cause client or proxy issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove meaningless empty GET request body

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no min/max)
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` annotations. Without schema-level constraints, client validation libraries cannot enforce the range automatically, and tooling cannot surface the default value. This is a common but impactful omission in Stripe's list endpoints.
findings.rationale: Schema constraints should match documented behaviour; missing min/max/default means codegen and validators cannot enforce the documented range of 1–100.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Resource ID parameters typed as plain strings without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer`, `customer_account`, `price`, `test_clock`, `ending_before`, and `starting_after` parameters are all typed as plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Each of these represents a Stripe object ID (with well-known prefixes like `cus_`, `acct_`, `price_`, `clock_`, `sub_`). Without a `pattern` or `format`, code-generation tools and validation layers cannot distinguish these IDs from arbitrary strings, and callers have no machine-readable hint of what ID type is expected.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed only as strings prevent typed relationship modelling in codegen tools and provide no validation hint beyond maxLength.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer, price, and test_clock parameters

findings.title: Misleading description for `current_period_start` filter
findings.narration: The description for `current_period_start` reads "Only return subscriptions whose **maximum** item current_period_start falls within the given date interval." The parallel parameter `current_period_end` uses "minimum". It is unusual and likely a copy-paste artifact that `current_period_end` filters on the minimum and `current_period_start` filters on the maximum — the natural reading would be the reverse or both would use the same aggregation. This inconsistency should be clarified or corrected to avoid misuse by API consumers.
findings.rationale: Inconsistent and potentially incorrect filter semantics (minimum vs maximum) between sibling parameters can lead callers to misunderstand which subscriptions will be returned.

patchOps.value: Only return subscriptions whose current_period_start falls within the given date interval.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify current_period_start description to remove confusing 'maximum item' qualifier

findings.title: billing_cycle_anchor and billing_cycle_anchor_config mutual-exclusion rule encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `billing_cycle_anchor_config` states it is 'Mutually exclusive with billing_cycle_anchor', but this constraint is expressed only in prose. There is no JSON Schema `not` / `oneOf` / `dependencies` construct preventing a caller from supplying both fields simultaneously. Code-generation tools and validators will happily accept a request body containing both, leading to a runtime error that could have been caught at schema validation time.
findings.rationale: Conditional-exclusion rules stated in prose but not encoded as schema constraints are a high-leverage design issue; they should be expressed as JSON Schema to enable automated validation.

value.description: billing_cycle_anchor and billing_cycle_anchor_config are mutually exclusive

findings.patchSummary: Add schema-level mutual-exclusion constraint between billing_cycle_anchor and billing_cycle_anchor_config

findings.title: trial_from_plan and trial_end mutual-exclusion rule encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `trial_from_plan` states 'Setting this flag to `true` together with `trial_end` is not allowed', but this constraint exists only in free-text. No JSON Schema validation prevents a consumer from sending both fields. The rule should be expressed as a schema-level `not` / `if-then-else` or `dependencies` construct so validators and code-generators can enforce it.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / conditional-forbidden field relationships stated in prose only are a high-severity design issue per the review guidelines.

value.description: trial_end must not be set when trial_from_plan is true

findings.patchSummary: Encode trial_from_plan + trial_end mutual-exclusion as if/then schema constraint

findings.title: days_until_due conditional-required on collection_method=send_invoice not schema-encoded
findings.narration: The description for `days_until_due` states it is 'Valid only for subscriptions where `collection_method` is set to `send_invoice`', implying it is conditionally required (or at minimum conditionally meaningful) based on `collection_method`. Similarly, when `collection_method=send_invoice`, `days_until_due` is effectively required to produce a valid invoice. Neither the conditional requirement nor the inapplicability when `collection_method=charge_automatically` is expressed in the schema using `if/then` or `dependencies`.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required field relationships stated only in prose should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints to enable automated validation and correct client-side form generation.

then.description: days_until_due is required when collection_method is send_invoice

findings.patchSummary: Encode days_until_due conditional requirement when collection_method=send_invoice as schema if/then

findings.title: payment_behavior includes pending_if_incomplete which is documented as invalid for creates
findings.narration: The `payment_behavior` enum includes `pending_if_incomplete`, yet the field description explicitly states '`pending_if_incomplete` is only used with updates and cannot be passed when creating a Subscription.' Including this value in the create-endpoint schema means clients will not receive a schema-validation error if they pass it; the error comes only from the server at runtime. Removing the invalid enum value (or encoding it via `not`) would allow consumers and validators to catch this mistake before the HTTP round-trip.
findings.rationale: Enumerating a value in a creation endpoint's schema that is explicitly forbidden at creation time is misleading and prevents early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Remove pending_if_incomplete from payment_behavior enum on create endpoint

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` keywords encoded. This means API clients and generated SDKs cannot enforce or discover the valid range programmatically; they rely entirely on reading prose documentation. A value of 0 or 500 would pass schema validation even though it is invalid at the API level.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but not encoded in the schema reduce the value of the spec for validation and code generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Unnecessary requestBody on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. Per HTTP semantics and OpenAPI guidance, GET requests should not carry a body; the presence of this empty body is misleading and may cause issues with certain HTTP clients or proxies that reject or strip GET bodies. It adds noise without providing any information.
findings.rationale: GET requests with request bodies violate REST conventions and can break HTTP infrastructure. An empty body schema is also meaningless.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Response schema missing additionalProperties constraint
findings.narration: The 200 response schema defines specific properties (`data`, `has_more`, `next_page`, `object`, `total_count`, `url`) but does not set `additionalProperties: false`. While Stripe may intentionally allow forward-compatible additions, the absence of this constraint means the schema is open-ended and generated client code cannot know the full response shape. For a search result envelope that is unlikely to gain arbitrary new top-level fields, this is worth documenting explicitly either way.
findings.rationale: Loose response schemas reduce the usefulness of the spec for client generation and make API contracts ambiguous.
findings.patchSummary: Set additionalProperties:false on the SearchResult response schema

findings.title: Path parameter name 'subscription_exposed_id' is cryptic and leaks internal implementation detail
findings.narration: The path parameter is named `subscription_exposed_id`, which is an unusual, implementation-specific name that leaks internal Stripe terminology ('exposed') into the public API surface. Consumers would expect a simple `subscription_id` or `id` parameter name. The word 'exposed' implies there is also a non-exposed or internal identifier, which is an internal concern that should not be surfaced in the public API contract. This creates confusion in generated client SDKs and documentation.
findings.rationale: Parameter names in a public API should be self-explanatory and free of internal implementation hints. 'exposed' is an internal qualifier that has no meaning to API consumers.

patchOps.value: The identifier of the subscription to retrieve.

findings.patchSummary: Rename path parameter from 'subscription_exposed_id' to 'subscription_id' for clarity.

findings.title: Path parameter lacks description
findings.narration: The `subscription_exposed_id` path parameter has no `description` field. While the parameter's purpose is somewhat inferrable from context, omitting a description means generated documentation and SDK tooling cannot surface helpful guidance (e.g., the format of the ID, such as 'sub_...'). Adding a short description like 'The ID of the subscription to retrieve (e.g., sub_1234).' would significantly improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: All required path parameters should carry a description to aid consumers and documentation generators, especially for resource identifiers whose format may not be obvious.

patchOps.value: The ID of the subscription to retrieve.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to the subscription_exposed_id path parameter.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1); many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers silently drop GET bodies. Declaring one — even if empty and not required — is misleading and may confuse SDK generators into emitting unnecessary body-serialization code for a retrieval operation.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per HTTP semantics. Declaring an empty optional body on a GET endpoint is a design anti-pattern that could confuse clients and code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty request body declaration from GET endpoint.

findings.title: Conditional-required field `days_until_due` only valid when `collection_method=send_invoice` — prose only
findings.narration: The description for `days_until_due` states 'Valid only for subscriptions where `collection_method` is set to `send_invoice`', but there is no schema-level encoding of this relationship. The dependency between `collection_method` being `send_invoice` and `days_until_due` being meaningful (or required) exists only as prose. Code generators and validators cannot enforce this rule, and clients can silently pass `days_until_due` with `charge_automatically` without receiving a schema-level error.
findings.rationale: Conditional field constraints expressed only in description text cannot be validated by OpenAPI tooling. This should be encoded using JSON Schema `dependentSchemas` or `if/then` constructs.
findings.patchSummary: Encode days_until_due dependency on collection_method=send_invoice in schema

findings.title: Mutually exclusive `trial_end` and `trial_from_plan` constraint encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `trial_from_plan` states 'Setting this flag to `true` together with `trial_end` is not allowed', but no schema-level `not` or `if/then` constraint prevents both from being submitted simultaneously. Any OpenAPI-aware validator or SDK generator will accept a request body containing both `trial_from_plan: true` and a `trial_end` value without complaint, pushing the enforcement entirely to runtime server-side logic.
findings.rationale: Mutually exclusive field constraints expressed only in descriptions are invisible to tooling. This is a classic `oneOf`/`not`/`dependentSchemas` case.
findings.patchSummary: Encode trial_end and trial_from_plan mutual exclusion as a schema constraint

findings.title: Resource ID fields typed as plain `string` with no format or pattern
findings.narration: Several fields that are clearly Stripe resource IDs — `default_payment_method` (PaymentMethod ID), `on_behalf_of` (Account ID), `transfer_data.destination` (Account ID), `automatic_tax.liability.account` (Account ID), `add_invoice_items[].price` (Price ID), `items[].price` (Price ID), `items[].id` (SubscriptionItem ID), `items[].price_data.product` (Product ID) — are typed as bare `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`. This prevents code-generation tools from building typed relationship references and removes any hint to API consumers about expected ID prefixes (e.g., `pm_`, `acct_`, `price_`, `si_`).
findings.rationale: Typed resource ID fields improve codegen, IDE autocomplete, and client-side validation. At minimum a pattern like `^(pm|acct|price|si)_` would communicate intent.
findings.patchSummary: Add format or pattern hints to resource ID string fields throughout the request body

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The responses object defines only `200` (success) and `default` (error). There are no explicit 4xx response codes such as `400` (bad request), `401` (authentication failure), `402` (payment required — mentioned in the `payment_behavior` description as a real HTTP status this API returns), `404` (subscription not found), or `422` (unprocessable entity). The `payment_behavior` description explicitly mentions 'Stripe to return an HTTP 402 status code', yet that status is not documented as a response. Consumers relying on OpenAPI for client generation or documentation lose the ability to handle known error scenarios explicitly.
findings.rationale: Explicitly documenting expected 4xx codes, especially 402 which is mentioned in the operation description, improves API usability and client generation quality.

value.description: Bad request. Invalid parameters supplied.
Payment required. Returned when payment_behavior=error_if_incomplete and invoice cannot be paid.
Subscription not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400, 402, and 404 response definitions alongside the existing default error response

findings.title: DELETE returns 200 instead of semantically appropriate status for cancellation
findings.narration: This DELETE endpoint returns HTTP 200 on success, which is acceptable per REST conventions when returning a body. However, Stripe's cancellation semantics are nuanced: the subscription is not deleted but moved to a 'canceled' state and returned in the response body. Using DELETE with a 200 response carrying a full subscription object is a common Stripe pattern, but it is worth noting that the HTTP verb signals 'resource removal' while the actual behavior is a state transition. A POST to a sub-resource (e.g., /v1/subscriptions/{id}/cancel) would better communicate intent and allow idempotent reads of the canceled resource afterward. This is a design-level observation; not a critical blocking issue, but it can confuse API consumers expecting either 204 or true resource deletion.
findings.rationale: DELETE semantically implies resource removal, but this operation transitions the resource to a 'canceled' state and returns it. This is a design smell that affects client developer experience and code generation clarity.
findings.patchSummary: No automated patch; consider adding a POST /cancel sub-resource in a future API version.

findings.title: Conditional relationship between invoice_now and prorate not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The operation description states: 'pending prorations are removed if invoice_now and prorate are both set to true'. This conditional behavior — where prorate only has the proration-removal effect when invoice_now is also true — is documented only in prose and is not encoded in the JSON Schema. Consumers relying solely on the schema (e.g., SDK generators, form builders) have no machine-readable signal about this interaction. Encoding this as a schema-level constraint (e.g., via an `if/then` or prose annotation in the property description) would improve clarity and safety.
findings.rationale: Field relationships described only in prose are invisible to code generators and validators. The invoice_now + prorate interaction is a meaningful behavioral constraint that should be surfaced in the schema.

patchOps.value: Will generate a proration invoice item that credits remaining unused time until the subscription period end. Defaults to `false`. Note: pending prorations are only removed when both `prorate` and `invoice_now` are set to `true`.

Will generate a final invoice that invoices for any un-invoiced metered usage and new/pending proration invoice items. Defaults to `false`. When combined with `prorate: true`, any pending prorations are also removed at cancellation.

findings.patchSummary: Enrich prorate and invoice_now descriptions to capture their conditional interaction.

findings.title: Path parameter name 'subscription_exposed_id' is cryptic and leaks internal naming
findings.narration: The path parameter is named `subscription_exposed_id`, which exposes an internal implementation detail ('exposed') that has no semantic meaning to API consumers. Standard Stripe subscription IDs use the prefix 'sub_', and calling it simply `subscription_id` or `id` would be clearer. The current name may confuse developers about whether this is a different identifier type from the standard subscription ID returned in list/create/retrieve operations.
findings.rationale: Parameter names surface in SDKs, documentation, and client code. 'subscription_exposed_id' leaks an internal naming convention and provides no clarity benefit over 'subscription_id'.
findings.patchSummary: No automated patch; renaming the path parameter requires coordinating across all operations sharing this path.

findings.title: Path parameter name `subscription_exposed_id` is cryptic and leaks internal implementation detail
findings.narration: The path parameter is named `subscription_exposed_id`, which exposes an internal naming convention (the notion of 'exposed' vs. non-exposed IDs is an implementation concern). External API consumers expect a straightforward name like `subscription_id`. This creates confusion in generated SDKs and documentation, where the parameter name becomes part of the public surface.
findings.rationale: Parameter names are part of the public API contract and appear verbatim in generated client code and docs. Internal qualifiers like 'exposed' should not leak into the public interface.
findings.patchSummary: Rename path parameter from `subscription_exposed_id` to `subscription_id`

findings.title: DELETE operation returns 200 instead of 204 for a resource deletion
findings.narration: This DELETE endpoint returns HTTP 200 with a body (the deleted discount object). While Stripe commonly uses this pattern for consistency, strictly following HTTP semantics a successful deletion with no meaningful entity to return should use 204 No Content. However, if Stripe intentionally returns the deleted object (a deleted discount resource), 200 is acceptable but a 204 alternative or explicit documentation of what is returned would improve clarity. The 200 response schema is a cyclic reference and provides no information about what is actually returned, which compounds the ambiguity.
findings.rationale: HTTP DELETE returning 200 is valid when the response body contains the deleted resource, but the lack of any schema detail (only a cyclic ref) means consumers cannot know what to expect.

patchOps.value: Successful response. Returns the deleted discount object.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify 200 response description to state the deleted discount object is returned

findings.title: billing_mode.type enum locked to 'flexible' only — no upgrade path documented
findings.narration: The `billing_mode.type` field is an enum with a single allowed value: `"flexible"`. While this may reflect the current supported state, an enum with one value provides no extensibility signal and prevents clients from understanding what future values might look like. More importantly, the field description says "Controls how prorations and invoices for subscriptions are calculated and orchestrated" — it gives no guidance on what other billing modes might be targetable in the future, or whether this endpoint supports any billing mode type other than `flexible`. At minimum, the description should explain the constraint and intent.
findings.rationale: A single-value enum is either a placeholder or an intentional constraint; either way it deserves a clarifying description so consumers understand the design intent.

patchOps.value: The billing mode type to migrate to. Currently only 'flexible' is supported. Additional types may be added in future API versions.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to billing_mode.type clarifying the single-value enum intent

findings.title: billing_mode.flexible.proration_discounts has no description
findings.narration: The `billing_mode.flexible.proration_discounts` enum field (`"included"` | `"itemized"`) has no `description` property at all. This field controls meaningful billing behaviour — whether proration discounts are bundled into the proration line item or broken out as separate line items — but API consumers have no way to know this from the schema alone. The two enum values are not self-evident to someone unfamiliar with Stripe's billing internals.
findings.rationale: Missing descriptions on enum fields with non-obvious semantics impair integration quality and force developers to consult external docs for every value.

patchOps.value: Determines how discounts are applied to proration line items. 'included' bundles discount amounts into the proration line item; 'itemized' emits a separate discount line item for each proration.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to proration_discounts enum field explaining each value's behaviour

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error response. For a migration endpoint that accepts a required body, common client-side failures — 400 (invalid billing_mode type or malformed request), 404 (subscription not found), 409 (subscription already on requested billing mode or in a conflicting state) — are entirely undocumented at the schema level. The `default` catch-all will capture these at runtime, but tooling (mock servers, validators, SDKs) cannot distinguish expected error shapes from unexpected ones without explicit status-code entries.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx entries allow SDK generators, test harnesses, and API gateways to handle predictable error cases properly; relying solely on 'default' reduces tooling fidelity.

value.description: Bad request — invalid or missing billing_mode parameters.
Subscription not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions to improve tooling fidelity

findings.title: Conditional field relationship between proration_behavior and billing_cycle_anchor encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `proration_behavior` states 'When the `billing_cycle_anchor` is set to `now` (default value), no prorations are generated' and implies `proration_behavior` is only meaningful when `billing_cycle_anchor` is `unchanged`. This conditional relationship (proration_behavior is effectively irrelevant when billing_cycle_anchor=now) is documented only in prose and is not machine-readable. Similarly, `proration_date` is only relevant when prorations are being created. These constraints should be encoded as JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependencies` so that validators and SDK generators can enforce them.
findings.rationale: Prose-only conditional constraints cannot be validated by tooling. Clients may set proration_behavior when billing_cycle_anchor=now and receive confusing or unexpected behavior with no schema-level guidance.

value.description: proration_behavior and proration_date are only applicable when billing_cycle_anchor is unchanged

findings.patchSummary: Encode proration_behavior/proration_date dependency on billing_cycle_anchor=unchanged in schema

findings.title: subscription path parameter lacks format or pattern to indicate it is a resource ID
findings.narration: The `subscription` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe subscription IDs follow a well-known pattern (e.g., `sub_[alphanumeric]`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, SDK generators and validators cannot distinguish this from an arbitrary string and cannot build typed resource references. Adding a pattern like `^sub_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow tooling to enforce correct ID format and generate typed relationships.
findings.rationale: Resource IDs typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent SDK codegen from building typed resource relationships and allow invalid IDs to pass client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern for subscription ID path param to enable typed resource references

findings.title: No example provided for request body fields
findings.narration: The request body schema has no `example` or `examples` defined for any of its fields or at the schema level. While the operation is relatively simple, the interaction between `billing_cycle_anchor`, `proration_behavior`, and `proration_date` creates non-obvious usage patterns (e.g., when prorations are generated vs. not). At least one worked example showing a typical resume-with-proration payload would significantly aid API consumers and documentation generators.
findings.rationale: Absence of examples on schemas with conditional field interactions makes it harder for developers to understand correct usage without reading extensive prose documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Add example to request body schema illustrating proration parameters in use

findings.title: payment_intent query parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `payment_intent` parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint, but it carries a well-known Stripe resource ID format (prefix `pi_` followed by alphanumeric characters). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code generators and validators cannot distinguish this from an arbitrary string, and clients have no machine-readable indication of the expected ID shape. Adding a pattern such as `^pi_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow client-side validation before the round-trip and enable typed SDK generation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent code generators from building typed relationships and allow obviously malformed values to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to payment_intent parameter to encode Stripe PaymentIntent ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). RFC 7231 discourages request bodies on GET requests, and the body here is strictly empty and marked `required: false`, meaning it conveys no information. Its presence confuses HTTP clients, proxies, and code generators that infer method semantics from the body. It should be removed entirely; all relevant parameters are already declared as query parameters.
findings.rationale: A GET request body with no properties serves no purpose and may cause compatibility issues with HTTP clients and proxies that reject or ignore GET bodies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation; all inputs are query parameters.

findings.title: Mutual exclusivity of `customer` and `customer_details` not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `customer` field description states 'the customer's address and tax IDs are copied to `customer_details`', implying these two fields are alternatives. In practice, providing both is redundant or potentially conflicting. This conditional relationship exists only in prose and is not expressed in the schema using `oneOf`, `not`, or similar JSON-Schema constraint. Codegen tools and validators cannot enforce the rule automatically, leaving clients prone to ambiguous or erroneous requests.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship rules in prose that should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints are a high-leverage finding; callers cannot rely on tooling to catch misuse.

value.description: Cannot supply both `customer` and `customer_details` simultaneously.

findings.patchSummary: Add `not` constraint to disallow supplying both `customer` and `customer_details` at once.

findings.title: Response returns 200 for resource creation — should be 201
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new Tax Calculation resource. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), successful resource creation should respond with HTTP 201 Created, not 200 OK. Using 200 conflates creation with a read/update response, making it harder for clients and intermediate layers to distinguish operation types. Stripe historically uses 200 for some create endpoints, but this is a known deviation from REST best practices worth flagging.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status for a POST that creates a new persistent resource; 200 obscures the creation semantic.
findings.patchSummary: Consider returning 201 Created instead of 200 OK for resource creation.

findings.title: `customer_details.ip_address` lacks format hint
findings.narration: The `ip_address` field inside `customer_details` is typed as a plain `string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no description explaining its purpose or expected form. OpenAPI defines `format: ipv4` and `format: ipv6` for IP addresses. Without at least a format hint, client generators cannot validate or distinguish this field from any other free-form string. Additionally, IP addresses can be considered sensitive PII (they are used for geolocation-based tax determination) — this warrants a description note.
findings.rationale: Typed string fields for well-known formats (IP addresses) should declare the appropriate `format` so validation and codegen tools can enforce structure.

patchOps.value: The customer's IP address (IPv4 or IPv6). Used to automatically determine the customer's location for tax purposes when no address is provided.

findings.patchSummary: Add `format: ip` and a description to `customer_details.ip_address`.

findings.title: `line_items[].tax_code` and `shipping_cost.tax_code` are untyped plain strings
findings.narration: Both `line_items[].tax_code` and `shipping_cost.tax_code` are typed as `type: string` with no `maxLength`, no `format`, no `pattern`, and no description. Tax codes are well-known Stripe product tax category identifiers (e.g. `txcd_99999999`). Without a format or description, codegen tools cannot build a meaningful typed reference, and API consumers have no guidance on valid values. A `maxLength` constraint and at minimum a description pointing to Stripe's tax code list would substantially improve usability.
findings.rationale: Fields that reference typed domain identifiers should document format constraints; plain undecorated strings provide no contract for validation or codegen.

patchOps.value: A tax code ID (e.g. `txcd_99999999`). See https://stripe.com/docs/tax/tax-categories for supported tax codes.
A tax code ID for the shipping cost. See https://stripe.com/docs/tax/tax-categories for supported tax codes.

findings.patchSummary: Add descriptions and maxLength to `tax_code` fields in line_items and shipping_cost.

findings.title: Path parameter 'calculation' lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `calculation` path parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe calculation IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `taxcalc_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools and client SDKs cannot infer the resource ID format, validate inputs early, or build typed cross-resource references. Adding a `pattern` such as `^taxcalc_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would both improve documentation fidelity and enable client-side pre-validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings with no format or pattern prevent typed relationship building in codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to 'calculation' path parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a request body are semantically unusual and discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1); some HTTP clients and intermediaries silently drop them. The body carries no fields and serves no functional purpose here. It should be removed to avoid confusing consumers and to conform with standard HTTP GET semantics.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not carry a request body; this conflicts with HTTP semantics and can cause issues with some clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically inappropriate empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema does not encode the `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10` constraints. These are documented only in prose, meaning clients and validators cannot rely on schema-level enforcement. Codegen tools will generate an unconstrained integer field, allowing callers to pass 0 or 1000 without client-side validation feedback.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are a high-severity pattern: the rule exists but cannot be machine-enforced. minimum, maximum, and default should be on the schema itself.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: This GET endpoint includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests semantically must not have a request body per RFC 9110. Including an empty, locked-down request body in the spec is misleading — it signals to client generators that a body should be sent, which many HTTP libraries will discard or reject. It also adds confusion for API consumers reviewing the spec.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody violates HTTP semantics. Even if Stripe's server tolerates it, the spec should not document it. The empty additionalProperties:false body serves no purpose.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET endpoint

findings.title: GET list endpoint includes an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, but the schema is an empty object (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests MUST NOT carry a body per RFC 9110 §9.3.1; many HTTP clients and proxies will silently drop or reject a body on a GET request. The presence of this empty requestBody is misleading and may cause interoperability issues with strict HTTP intermediaries or code-generation tools that flag GET+body combinations as invalid.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.1 advises against sending a body with GET. An empty body schema adds no value and may confuse consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET list operation

findings.title: `limit` parameter lacks minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter's description states it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` encoded. Clients and validators cannot enforce the stated contract programmatically; a client submitting `limit=0` or `limit=9999` would pass schema validation. The constraint and default should be encoded directly in the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints described only in prose are invisible to code generators and validators; encoding them in schema enforces the documented contract.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1, maximum: 100, and default: 10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: country_options sub-object key must match `country` field — conditional constraint in prose only
findings.narration: The `country` field and the `country_options` object are independent flat fields in the schema. The API almost certainly expects the key inside `country_options` (e.g. `us`, `de`, `gb`) to match the value of `country`. This rule is expressed nowhere in the schema — there is no `if/then`, no `dependencies`, no cross-field constraint, and no description text explaining this relationship. As a result, tooling will accept a body with `country: "us"` and `country_options: { de: { type: "standard" } }` as valid, when in reality the server would likely reject or mishandle it. This is a high-leverage schema-expressiveness gap.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required field relationships documented only implicitly (by convention) rather than in schema logic are a known source of integration errors and should be encoded via JSON Schema `if/then` or `dependencies`.

patchOps.value: Two-letter country code ([ISO 3166-1 alpha-2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_3166-1_alpha-2)). The key provided under `country_options` must match this value.

findings.patchSummary: Add prose constraint clarifying that country_options key must match country value

findings.title: Missing 4xx error response definitions
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` error response. There are no explicit `400`, `401`, `402`, `403`, or `422` response entries. For a write operation that accepts complex, deeply nested, country-specific input with many required sub-fields and conditional relationships, the absence of documented error codes leaves API consumers unable to determine how to distinguish validation errors from authentication failures from business-logic rejections. At minimum a `400` (invalid request) and `401` (unauthenticated) should be documented explicitly.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx response documentation makes it impossible for SDK generators and human consumers to write correct error-handling logic for a complex resource creation endpoint.

value.description: Bad request — invalid or missing parameters.
Unauthorized — authentication credentials are missing or invalid.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 401 response definitions

findings.title: country_options `standard` sub-object: conditional requirement on `place_of_supply_scheme` not machine-readable
findings.narration: Several European country option schemas (e.g. `at`, `be`, `de`, `fr`) include a `standard` object where `place_of_supply_scheme` is marked `required`. However, the `standard` object itself is never listed in the parent object's `required` array. Additionally, many non-European country schemas (e.g. `ae`, `au`, `gb`) have a `standard` sub-object where `place_of_supply_scheme` is NOT required, but there is no prose or schema rule explaining when `standard` must be provided vs. is optional. The relationship 'standard sub-object is required when type == "standard"' is implicit and unencoded. Developers cannot determine from the schema alone when `standard` must be populated.
