findings.rationale: 'Required when X is set' field relationships expressed only implicitly should be encoded as JSON Schema conditional constraints; their absence causes incorrect client implementations.

patchOps.value: Germany tax registration options. When `type` is `standard`, the `standard` sub-object is required and `place_of_supply_scheme` within it is required.

findings.patchSummary: Add description clarifying standard sub-object is required when type=standard

findings.title: Path ID parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter for the Tax Registration resource is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe Tax Registration IDs follow a predictable prefix-based format (e.g., `taxreg_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a documented format hint, client-side validation and code generation tools cannot enforce the correct shape, increasing the risk of malformed requests reaching the API.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format lose typed relationships that codegen tools could otherwise leverage.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter to reflect Stripe's ID naming convention.

findings.title: GET request body is superfluous and misleading
findings.narration: This GET operation includes a `requestBody` block containing an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema with `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests should not carry a body; including one contradicts HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes GET has no defined semantics for a body), confuses generated clients that may attempt to serialize it, and some intermediaries may strip it entirely. The block should be removed.
findings.rationale: A GET endpoint with an empty request body object violates HTTP semantics and can cause issues with generated SDKs and HTTP proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty request body from this GET operation to conform to HTTP semantics.

findings.title: active_from and expires_at use deepObject encoding but accept scalar anyOf values
findings.narration: The `active_from` and `expires_at` fields are declared with `style: deepObject` encoding in the `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, but their schemas are scalar `anyOf` types (either a string enum like `"now"` or a Unix-time integer). `deepObject` encoding is intended for nested object structures (e.g., `field[key]=value`), not for scalars. For scalar fields, `style: form` (the default for form-encoded bodies) is correct. Using `deepObject` here may confuse clients and SDK generators, potentially causing incorrect serialization such as `active_from[0]=now` instead of `active_from=now`.
findings.rationale: deepObject encoding applied to scalar/anyOf-of-primitives is semantically incorrect and can break client serialization.
findings.patchSummary: Remove deepObject encoding from scalar fields active_from and expires_at

findings.title: No 4xx error responses explicitly defined beyond 'default'
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a catch-all `default` error response. Stripe commonly returns well-known HTTP error codes such as `400` (invalid parameters), `401` (unauthenticated), `402` (request failed), and `404` (resource not found). Without explicit 4xx entries, API consumers, SDK generators, and documentation tools cannot distinguish between authentication failures, validation errors, and not-found scenarios. The `default` bucket swallows all error cases into one opaque shape, reducing the operation's value as a contract.
findings.rationale: Explicit error response codes improve client error handling, documentation clarity, and generated SDK ergonomics.

value.description: Bad request — invalid parameters supplied.
Registration not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default error response

findings.title: GET request includes an unnecessary empty request body
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`). Per HTTP semantics, GET requests should not carry a request body. While some frameworks tolerate it, many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways will silently drop or reject bodies on GET requests. Including an empty request body on a GET operation adds noise, can confuse code generators, and is contrary to RFC 9110 guidance that GET requests have no defined semantics for a body.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty body schema serves no purpose and can mislead clients and tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET /v1/tax/settings operation.

findings.title: defaults.tax_code lacks format/pattern — cross-resource ID typed as plain string
findings.narration: The `defaults.tax_code` field is typed as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or description indicating what values are valid. Based on Stripe's domain model, this is a reference to a TaxCode resource ID (e.g., `txcd_99999999`). Codegen tools and client SDKs cannot infer the relationship or validate the value format. Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^txcd_`) and a short description improves discoverability and reduces integration errors.
findings.rationale: Fields named like resource IDs that use bare `type: string` without pattern/format prevent typed relationships in generated clients.

patchOps.value: The Stripe tax code ID representing the tax category for the default product type (e.g., `txcd_99999999`).

findings.patchSummary: Add description and pattern to defaults.tax_code to encode the TaxCode ID format.

findings.title: head_office.address has no required fields — country is implicitly mandatory for tax calculations
findings.narration: The `head_office.address` object defines six optional fields with no `required` array. In Stripe's tax calculation model, `country` is functionally mandatory to determine the jurisdiction for tax purposes. The prose description for the endpoint notes settings affect tax calculations, but the schema imposes no constraint. A caller could submit an address with only `city` set, which would likely result in a server-side 400 error. This conditional requirement should be encoded in the schema rather than discovered at runtime.
findings.rationale: Mandatory fields for correct operation should be marked required in the schema to enable client-side validation and accurate documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Mark address.country as required within head_office.address.

findings.title: Missing examples on complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body schema contains nested objects (`defaults`, `head_office.address`) with multiple interrelated fields, but no `examples` or `example` values are provided. Without examples, API consumers cannot quickly understand what a typical request looks like — for instance, how to set a `head_office` in Germany with inclusive tax behavior. Adding at least one example under `requestBody.content['application/x-www-form-urlencoded']` would significantly improve developer experience and reduce integration guesswork.
findings.rationale: Complex nested schemas without examples increase integration time and risk of malformed requests.
findings.patchSummary: Add an illustrative example to the request body schema.

findings.title: calculation field typed as plain string without format or pattern for resource ID
findings.narration: The `calculation` field in the request body is described as a 'Tax Calculation ID' but is typed as a bare `type: string` with only a maxLength constraint. Resource ID fields like this typically carry a well-known prefix (e.g., `taxcalc_...`) and should have at minimum a `pattern` constraint (e.g., `^taxcalc_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or a `format` annotation so that codegen tools can build a typed cross-resource reference rather than treating it as an opaque freeform string.
findings.rationale: Untyped resource ID references prevent codegen tools from producing typed clients and make validation weaker.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to calculation to indicate it is a Tax Calculation resource ID

findings.title: reference field prose rule (uniqueness constraint) not machine-encoded
findings.narration: The description of the `reference` field states it 'Must be unique across all transactions, including reversals.' This is a meaningful business rule that currently lives only in prose. While uniqueness across records cannot be expressed purely in JSON Schema, the description implies a format or naming pattern ('such as myOrder_123') that could be reinforced with a `pattern` constraint. More importantly, the constraint language should ideally be surfaced in a way that tooling or documentation generators can flag it as a uniqueness requirement rather than leaving it as a free-text note discoverable only by reading the description carefully.
findings.rationale: Uniqueness rules embedded only in prose are easily missed by integrators and cannot be validated by client-side tooling.

patchOps.value: Must be unique across all tax transactions including reversals

findings.patchSummary: Surface the uniqueness constraint via an extension property so tooling can recognise it

findings.title: No example provided for the request body
findings.narration: The request body schema has two required fields (`calculation` and `reference`) plus optional ones, but no `example` or `examples` block is provided on either the schema or the media-type object. A concrete example (showing a real-looking `calculation` ID, a `reference` string, and an optional `posted_at` timestamp) would significantly reduce integration friction for developers who encounter this endpoint for the first time and helps documentation generators produce usable sample code.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on non-trivial request bodies reduce discoverability and increase time-to-integrate.
findings.patchSummary: Add a concrete example to the request body media-type object

findings.title: Conditional-required fields encoded only in prose, not in schema
findings.narration: The `mode` field accepts `full` or `partial`, and the description of `flat_amount`, `line_items`, and `shipping_cost` implies that they are only relevant (or required) in `partial` mode. Specifically, when `mode` is `full`, providing line-item-level details is nonsensical, and when `mode` is `partial`, at least one of `flat_amount`, `line_items`, or `shipping_cost` must presumably be provided. These conditional-required relationships exist only in prose today. They should be encoded as JSON Schema `if`/`then`/`else` or `oneOf` constructs so that validators and code generators can enforce them.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements expressed only in descriptions are invisible to automated validators and SDK generators, creating a class of runtime errors that could be caught at schema validation time.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

line_items.description: The line item amounts to reverse. Only used when mode is `partial`.

original_transaction.description: The ID of the Transaction to partially or fully reverse.

reference.description: A custom identifier for this reversal.

shipping_cost.description: The shipping cost to reverse. Only used when mode is `partial`.
shipping_cost.title: transaction_shipping_cost_reversal

findings.patchSummary: Encode partial-mode conditional requirements using if/then/anyOf instead of prose only

findings.title: original_transaction typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The field `original_transaction` is described as 'The ID of the Transaction to partially or fully reverse' and is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` is provided to signal that this is a reference to a Stripe Tax Transaction resource (typically prefixed with `tax_` in Stripe's ID scheme). Code generators and client SDKs cannot build a typed cross-resource relationship from this definition, and validators cannot reject obviously wrong values.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow invalid IDs to pass schema validation silently.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to original_transaction to signal it is a Tax Transaction ID

findings.title: Response returns HTTP 200 for a resource-creation operation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new reversal Transaction resource (a side-effect-producing POST that produces a new entity). The canonical HTTP semantics for resource creation is 201 Created. Returning 200 OK is technically valid but misleads consumers who rely on status codes to distinguish between updated and newly created resources, and is inconsistent with the broader REST convention. Many Stripe endpoints use 200 for mutation results, but for an explicitly creation-oriented endpoint (the path and operationId both contain 'create'), 201 would be more appropriate.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 signals new resource creation; using 200 for a create endpoint is semantically imprecise and may confuse clients relying on status codes.
findings.patchSummary: Consider returning 201 Created instead of 200 for this resource-creation endpoint

findings.title: No examples provided for complex request body
findings.narration: The request body schema has multiple interacting fields (`mode`, `flat_amount`, `line_items`, `shipping_cost`) whose valid combinations are non-trivial. No `example` or `examples` values are provided either at the media-type level or within the schema properties. Without examples, developers must infer valid payloads from description text alone, increasing integration effort and the likelihood of errors on first use.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies with mode-dependent field requirements benefit significantly from concrete examples to reduce developer integration errors.
findings.patchSummary: Add examples for full and partial reversal request bodies

findings.title: Path parameter `transaction` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID validation
findings.narration: The `transaction` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe tax transaction IDs follow a recognizable prefix pattern (e.g., `tax_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK generators and validators cannot enforce the correct ID shape, leading to confusing downstream errors (e.g., a 404 from the API) rather than early client-side validation failures. Adding a pattern such as `^tax_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at minimum a meaningful `format` value would improve type safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: A cross-resource ID typed as plain string with no pattern/format is a known risk for codegen tools and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `transaction` path parameter to enforce Stripe resource ID format.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients and proxies will silently drop or reject bodies on GET requests. While Stripe uses this pattern broadly for form-encoded mutations, a read-only retrieval endpoint has no properties to submit, making this body definition misleading. It should be removed to avoid confusing consumers and code generators that may emit unnecessary body serialization code.
findings.rationale: GET requests semantically must not have a meaningful request body. An empty, disallowed-properties body adds noise and can mislead SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation; GET requests should not carry a body.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. This means schema validation cannot enforce the documented bounds, and code generators will not apply a default value.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints (min, max, default) should be encoded in the schema so validators and code generators can enforce them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum, maximum, and default to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body should not be declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: This GET operation declares a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`). GET requests conventionally carry no body; many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will ignore or reject a body on GET requests. Including an empty request body is misleading to consumers and code generators, which may emit unnecessary body-serialization code.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not have a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). The body here is empty and serves no purpose, so it should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: transaction path parameter missing description
findings.narration: The `transaction` path parameter has no `description` field. Without a description, API consumers and code generators have no guidance on what format or value this identifier should take (e.g., whether it is a `tax_transaction_*` prefixed ID or a user-defined reference).
findings.rationale: Path parameters should include descriptions to clarify the expected format and semantics of the identifier, especially when the resource type is not obvious from context.

patchOps.value: The ID of the tax transaction whose line items should be retrieved.

findings.patchSummary: Add description to the transaction path parameter

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum defined)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter's description states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means clients and validators will not enforce the documented range, allowing values like 0 or 200 to pass schema validation silently. Codegen tools will also not surface these bounds to SDK consumers.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints that are not encoded in the schema are unenforceable by validators and invisible to generated SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: Request body on a GET endpoint is an anti-pattern
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though the schema inside is an empty object with `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests with a body are discouraged by HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and many HTTP/2 clients and proxies will silently drop them. All parameters for this read-only operation are already expressed as query parameters, making the request body both semantically incorrect and functionally empty.
findings.rationale: A GET operation should not carry a request body; doing so violates HTTP semantics and causes interoperability issues with proxies and some HTTP clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: Missing `pattern` or `format` on cursor parameters `ending_before` and `starting_after`
findings.narration: The cursor parameters `ending_before` and `starting_after` are typed as plain `string` with no `pattern`, `format`, or example. These are object IDs with a known prefix structure (e.g. `txcd_...`). Without any constraint, schema validators and codegen tools cannot distinguish them from arbitrary strings, reducing the usefulness of generated client code and error messages. Adding a pattern or at minimum an example would substantially improve client-side validation and documentation quality.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings without pattern or example reduce schema utility for validation and codegen.
findings.patchSummary: Add examples to `ending_before` and `starting_after` cursor parameter schemas

findings.title: owner.account and owner.customer are untyped resource ID strings
findings.narration: The `owner` query parameter contains `account` and `customer` sub-fields that are typed as plain `string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref`. These fields clearly reference Stripe Account and Customer resource IDs (prefixed `acct_` and `cus_` respectively). Without a pattern or format hint, code-generation tools cannot build a typed relationship to those resources, and callers receive no schema-level guidance about acceptable ID formats.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain string with no format/pattern/ref prevent codegen tools from building typed cross-resource relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-format patterns to owner.account and owner.customer fields

findings.title: Conditional field requirements in owner object expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `owner` schema accepts `account`, `customer`, and `customer_account` fields alongside a required `type` discriminator. The intended usage is that only one of these sub-fields is relevant depending on the value of `type` (e.g., `type=customer` implies `customer` should be set; `type=account` implies `account` should be set). These conditional constraints are not encoded in the schema — there is no `if/then/else`, `oneOf`, or `dependencies` construct. Callers who supply mismatched field combinations will only discover the error at runtime from the API, rather than from schema validation.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required/exclusive field rules expressed only through field naming and developer intuition should be encoded as JSON Schema discriminator constructs to enable static validation.
findings.patchSummary: Encode owner type-conditional field requirements using JSON Schema if/then/else

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for the parameter only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default`. This means schema validators will accept any integer (including 0 or negative values), and client code generators will not surface the valid range or default value to consumers.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints on numeric parameters should be encoded as schema minimum/maximum/default to enable validation and improve client generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: GET request body is present but empty and semantically inappropriate
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` of type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` with an empty schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). A GET request should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes that GET has no defined semantics for a message body). The body here is vacuously empty and serves no purpose; its presence may confuse HTTP clients, proxies, and SDK generators.
findings.rationale: GET operations should not include a requestBody. An empty, locked-down form body adds noise and may cause interoperability issues with strict HTTP implementations.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, semantically inappropriate requestBody from this GET operation

findings.title: POST creates a resource but returns HTTP 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new tax_id object (a resource creation action), yet the success response is documented as HTTP 200. REST convention and RFC 9110 §9.3.4 indicate that a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, optionally with a Location header pointing to the new resource. Returning 200 for a creation can confuse clients, caching proxies, and code-generation tools that use the status code to infer idempotency and resource lifecycle semantics.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for successful POST-based resource creation per RFC 9110.
findings.patchSummary: Rename 200 response to 201 Created for resource creation semantics

findings.title: owner.account field lacks maxLength and ID format constraints
findings.narration: The `owner.account` property is typed as a plain `string` with no `maxLength`, no `pattern`, and no format annotation, whereas the sibling fields `owner.customer` and `owner.customer_account` both carry `maxLength: 5000`. More importantly, `account` is clearly a Stripe account ID (e.g., `acct_...`) and should at least carry a `pattern` or description indicating the expected format so that SDK generators and validators can build a typed relationship to the Account resource.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as unconstrained strings lose type-safety in generated SDKs and break field-relationship tracing.

patchOps.value: The Stripe account ID (e.g., `acct_...`) the tax ID belongs to. Required when `owner[type]=account`.

findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength and description to owner.account to align with sibling fields and clarify expected ID format

findings.title: Conditional-required owner sub-fields expressed only in prose (not in schema)
findings.narration: The `owner` object exposes three mutually exclusive sub-fields — `account`, `customer`, and `customer_account` — whose requirement is governed by the value of `owner.type`. For example, when `type` is `account`, only `account` should be provided; when `type` is `customer`, only `customer` should be provided. This conditional requirement exists only implicitly (the enum values mirror the field names) and is not encoded in the schema via `if/then`, `oneOf`, or `dependencies`. Code-generation tools, validators, and API consumers cannot automatically enforce these constraints, leading to silent misuse.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields described only through naming convention instead of schema keywords prevent automated validation and SDK type generation.

patchOps.value: The account or customer the tax ID belongs to. Defaults to `owner[type]=self`. When `type=account`, provide `account`. When `type=customer`, provide `customer`. When `type=application` (customer account context), provide `customer_account`. The fields `account`, `customer`, and `customer_account` are mutually exclusive.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify mutual-exclusivity and conditional-required rules for owner sub-fields in description (schema oneOf recommended)

findings.title: Missing request body example for a complex, high-enum-count operation
findings.narration: The request body schema contains a `type` field with over 100 enum values representing different tax ID types across dozens of jurisdictions, plus a conditionally structured `owner` object. Without at least one concrete example (e.g., creating a US EIN for a customer), developers reading the spec or using generated SDKs have no quick reference for how to assemble a valid request. Adding an `example` or `examples` map on the request body schema would substantially reduce integration friction.
findings.rationale: Complex schemas with large enums and conditional sub-objects benefit greatly from concrete examples to guide integrators.

create_customer_us_ein.summary: Create a US EIN tax ID for a customer

findings.patchSummary: Add a request body example illustrating a typical tax ID creation

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation
findings.narration: This GET endpoint declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. GET requests should never carry a request body; HTTP semantics treat bodies on GET as undefined (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and many proxies, caches, and HTTP clients will strip or reject them. The body object here contains no properties and has `additionalProperties: false`, meaning it can never carry any useful data. It should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody is semantically incorrect. Presence of even an empty body definition confuses SDK generators and violates HTTP semantics.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe tax ID identifiers follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `txi_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client-side validation and SDK code generators cannot enforce the correct shape, making it easy to accidentally pass the wrong ID type (e.g., a customer ID) and receive a confusing 404 or error. Adding a pattern such as `^txi_[A-Za-z0-9]+$` (or at minimum a description noting the expected format) would improve safety.
findings.rationale: Untyped string IDs for cross-resource references miss an opportunity for compile-time type safety in generated SDKs.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the `id` path parameter to match Stripe's tax ID format.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means client-side and server-side validation cannot be driven from the spec alone, and code generators cannot enforce the documented range. Any value outside [1, 100] would pass schema validation.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints should be encoded in the schema, not only in the description, so validators and codegen tools can enforce them.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, and default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary and semantically incorrect
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `required: false` containing an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. GET requests should not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 notes it has no defined semantics), and many HTTP clients and intermediaries will strip it. Including it in the spec misleads consumers and may cause issues with strict clients or proxies. The empty requestBody should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per HTTP semantics; its presence is misleading and potentially harmful.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: POST creates a resource but returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: The operation creates a new tax rate (a resource-creation POST), yet the success response is documented as HTTP 200 rather than HTTP 201 Created. Per RFC 9110 §9.3.5 and REST conventions, a successful resource creation should respond with 201 Created, optionally accompanied by a Location header pointing to the new resource. Using 200 here sends the wrong semantic signal to API consumers and code-generation tools that distinguish between 'action completed' and 'resource created'.
findings.rationale: REST semantics and RFC 9110 require 201 for successful resource creation. This is a design-level semantic error.
findings.patchSummary: Rename 200 response to 201 Created for resource-creation semantics

findings.title: percentage field lacks range/precision constraints
findings.narration: The `percentage` field is typed as `number` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `multipleOf` constraints. A tax rate percentage is a well-bounded domain value (0–100, typically with limited decimal places). Without a minimum of 0 and maximum of 100, a caller could submit negative percentages or values above 100 without any client-side validation failure. Adding `minimum: 0`, `maximum: 100`, and optionally `multipleOf: 0.0001` (to cap precision) would let client validators and code-gen tools enforce the domain contract without a round-trip to the server.
findings.rationale: Missing numeric constraints on a bounded domain value weakens client-side validation and degrades DX for code-gen consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:0 and maximum:100 constraints to the percentage field

findings.title: country field lacks ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `country` field is described as a two-letter ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code, but the schema only enforces `maxLength: 5000` — a wildly permissive upper bound that is completely at odds with the description. A proper constraint would be `minLength: 2`, `maxLength: 2`, and `pattern: ^[A-Z]{2}$`. As written, any 5000-character string passes schema validation, which defeats the intent of the documented field format and offers no help to code-gen consumers.
findings.rationale: The documented format (2-letter country code) is not enforced by the schema constraints, creating a misleading contract.
findings.patchSummary: Constrain country to exactly 2 uppercase letters matching ISO 3166-1 alpha-2

findings.title: Missing request/response body examples
findings.narration: The operation has no `example` or `examples` on either the request body schema or the 200 response body. For a tax-rate creation endpoint with fields like `percentage`, `inclusive`, `tax_type`, `jurisdiction`, and `country`, the absence of an example means developers must infer the shape from field-by-field descriptions. Adding at minimum one representative example (e.g., creating a 7% exclusive US sales tax) would substantially reduce onboarding friction and is especially important given the number of optional-but-interrelated fields.
findings.rationale: Complex request schemas with multiple optional fields benefit significantly from concrete examples for documentation and SDK generation.

value.description: New York state sales tax

findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the request body schema

findings.title: tax_rate path parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `tax_rate` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe tax rate IDs follow a known prefix pattern (e.g., `txr_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, clients and code-generation tools cannot validate the ID before making a request, increasing the risk of malformed requests reaching the API.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters should carry a pattern or format to enable client-side validation and improve SDK codegen fidelity.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to tax_rate path parameter to match Stripe ID format.

findings.title: GET operation includes an empty request body definition
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is defined on this GET endpoint with `required: false` and an empty schema (`properties: {}`). HTTP GET requests should not carry a body — many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers drop or reject GET bodies. The presence of this empty form-encoded body definition is misleading to consumers and code-generation tools, which may attempt to serialize an empty body or set `Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded` unnecessarily.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a requestBody per REST conventions and RFC 7231. The empty body definition should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody definition from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `tax_rate` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `tax_rate` path parameter identifies a Tax Rate resource (IDs typically follow the pattern `txr_...`) but is declared as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDKs and code generators cannot build a typed reference to the Tax Rate resource, and validation tooling cannot catch obviously malformed IDs at the boundary. Adding a pattern such as `^txr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode the known ID format and improve both safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent typed relationships in codegen and allow invalid inputs to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to tax_rate path parameter to encode Stripe resource ID format.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response definitions beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The operation only documents a `200` success response and a catch-all `default` error response. Common client-side error cases for an update operation — such as `400 Bad Request` (invalid field values), `404 Not Found` (unknown tax_rate ID), or `422 Unprocessable Entity` — are not individually enumerated. Relying solely on `default` means consumers have no machine-readable indication of which error codes to expect and handle, reducing the usefulness of the spec for client generation and documentation. At minimum, `400` and `404` should be explicitly declared with appropriate descriptions.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses reduce the spec's value for client generation and consumer error-handling logic.

value.description: Bad request. Invalid parameter values supplied.
Tax rate not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the catch-all default.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema definition has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints encoded. This means clients and validators cannot enforce the stated range programmatically, and code-generated SDKs will accept values like 0 or 9999 without complaint.
findings.rationale: Machine-readable constraints should match the prose description. Without `minimum: 1, maximum: 100`, the documented contract cannot be enforced by validators or SDK generators.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1 and maximum:100 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary and misleading
findings.narration: A `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema is declared on this GET operation. HTTP GET requests should not carry a request body; including one violates HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1) and may confuse clients, proxies, or code-generation tooling that interprets the presence of `requestBody` as meaningful.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a body per HTTP spec. An empty requestBody block on GET is at best a no-op and at worst breaks clients or generators that treat its presence as significant.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: WiFi password fields should be marked writeOnly
findings.narration: The `wifi.enterprise_eap_peap.password`, `wifi.personal_psk.password`, and `wifi.enterprise_eap_tls.private_key_file_password` fields are credential/secret values but are not marked `writeOnly: true`. Without this flag, code generators and documentation tools may include these fields in serialized response objects, and security scanners will not flag them as sensitive. The OpenAPI `writeOnly` keyword exists precisely for credentials submitted in request bodies that should never appear in responses.
findings.rationale: Credential fields lacking `writeOnly: true` risk being leaked in response serialization and are invisible to security tooling that relies on the keyword to identify sensitive data.
findings.patchSummary: Mark WiFi password and private key password fields as writeOnly to flag them as sensitive credentials.

findings.title: WiFi type discriminator not enforced as conditional-required schema rule
findings.narration: The `wifi` object has a `type` field whose enum values (`enterprise_eap_peap`, `enterprise_eap_tls`, `personal_psk`) correspond directly to sub-objects with the same names. The description implies that `type` selects which sub-configuration is applicable, but no `oneOf`/`if-then-else` or `dependencies` rule enforces that exactly one matching sub-object is present when a given `type` is set, nor that the correct sub-object is present for the chosen `type`. This conditional-required relationship is implied structurally but not schema-enforced, so validators will accept requests with `type: personal_psk` and an `enterprise_eap_tls` sub-object simultaneously.
findings.rationale: Structural discriminator relationships expressed only through naming conventions and not through schema composition rules cannot be validated automatically and mislead API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Encode wifi type discriminator relationship using if/then/else so the matching sub-object is required per type.

findings.title: Missing request body examples for a complex, multi-device configuration payload
findings.narration: The request body schema is large and complex, covering settings for six different reader hardware models, tipping configurations for 21 currencies, offline mode, cellular, reboot windows, and WiFi with three authentication schemes. There are no `examples` or `example` fields anywhere in the request body. Developers integrating this endpoint must reverse-engineer the shape purely from the schema, which increases the chance of malformed requests. Even one illustrative example covering a realistic subset of fields (e.g., configuring a BBPOS WisePad3 with tipping and a reboot window) would substantially reduce friction.
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies without examples increase integration errors and require developers to read the full schema tree to understand typical usage.

findings.title: Description says 'Updates a new Configuration' — copy-paste error

The operation description reads '

Updates a new Configuration object.

'. The word 'new' is semantically wrong for an update operation; 'new' belongs in a create (POST to a collection) description. findings.title: WiFi credential fields (password, private_key_file_password) lack writeOnly marker
findings.narration: The `wifi` request body schema contains sensitive credential fields: `personal_psk.password`, `enterprise_eap_peap.password`, and `enterprise_eap_tls.private_key_file_password`. None of these fields are marked `writeOnly: true`. Without this marker, generated clients and documentation tools may attempt to display or log these values in responses, even if the API never returns them. OpenAPI 3.x provides `writeOnly` precisely for credentials sent in requests that must not appear in responses.
findings.rationale: Credential fields not marked writeOnly can be inadvertently surfaced in generated documentation, client SDKs, or debug logs, creating a security risk.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to wifi password and private_key_file_password fields

findings.title: WiFi type discriminator not enforced: sub-config fields conditionally required by type in prose only
findings.narration: The `wifi` object has a required `type` field with enum values `enterprise_eap_peap`, `enterprise_eap_tls`, and `personal_psk`, and three corresponding sub-objects. However, the schema does not encode any conditional requirement: when `type` is `personal_psk`, only `personal_psk` should be populated; when `type` is `enterprise_eap_peap`, only `enterprise_eap_peap` should be required, etc. This is a classic conditional-required relationship that should be expressed via JSON Schema `if/then` or `oneOf` with a discriminator, not left implicit. Clients have no machine-readable way to validate that they are sending the correct sub-object for the chosen type.
findings.rationale: Conditional field requirements expressed only implicitly (via naming convention) rather than as schema constraints lead to client-side errors that cannot be caught by validators or code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Encode wifi type-to-subobject conditional requirements using if/then/else

findings.title: location field typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or resource reference
findings.narration: The `location` field in the request body represents a Terminal Location resource ID (e.g. `tml_xxxxx`), but it is declared simply as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Codegen tools and SDK generators cannot build a typed relationship to the Location resource from this definition. Adding a `pattern` (e.g. `^tml_`) or a descriptive `format` (e.g. `terminal_location_id`) would let tooling understand this is a foreign-key reference rather than arbitrary text.
findings.rationale: Fields named like resource IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from establishing typed cross-resource relationships.
findings.patchSummary: Add format and pattern to location field to signal it is a Terminal Location resource ID.

findings.title: No 4xx error response codes defined beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The operation only declares a `200` success response and a `default` error response. In practice, clients sending an invalid or inaccessible `location` ID will receive a structured 400 or 404 error from Stripe. Relying solely on `default` for all error cases means API consumers and SDK generators cannot distinguish between, say, a 400 validation error and a 401 authentication failure at the schema level, reducing the usefulness of generated client code and documentation. At minimum, a `400` response should be explicitly described.
findings.rationale: Explicit 4xx responses improve client-side error handling and generated SDK quality; a single `default` catch-all obscures expected error conditions.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 response to document invalid-request errors distinct from the catch-all default.

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100, but the schema itself has no `minimum` or `maximum` constraints. This means API clients and generated SDKs cannot validate the value before sending a request, and static analysis tools will not flag out-of-range values. The discrepancy between the prose description and the schema is a reliability risk for client implementors.
findings.rationale: Constraints described in prose but not encoded in the schema cannot be enforced by tooling. High-leverage fix: adding `minimum: 1, maximum: 100` closes the gap.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1 and maximum:100 constraints to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body declared on a GET endpoint
findings.narration: A `requestBody` is declared for this GET operation, but it contains no properties and its schema is an empty object with `additionalProperties: false`. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and intermediaries will strip or reject bodies on GET requests. This empty body adds noise and could confuse generated clients into sending an unnecessary body.
findings.rationale: GET operations with request bodies violate HTTP semantics and break compatibility with many HTTP infrastructure components. The body should be removed entirely.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Missing examples on the 200 response schema
findings.narration: The 200 response schema for this list endpoint has no `example` or `examples` block. Consumers of the spec (documentation generators, mock servers, SDK authors) have no representative payload to validate against or use for integration tests. A minimal example showing a non-empty `data` array, `has_more`, `object`, and `url` would substantially improve usability.
findings.rationale: Examples on list-response schemas are important for tooling such as mock servers and documentation renderers. Without them, developers must reverse-engineer the shape from the schema alone.
findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the 200 response content.

findings.title: POST body not marked required despite mandatory fields (display_name, address)
findings.narration: The requestBody has `required: false`, but the operation logically requires at minimum `display_name` and `address` (with `address.country` already marked required within the address object). A caller who submits no body at all will receive an API-level error rather than a schema validation error. Marking the body `required: true` and adding `display_name` and `address` to the schema-level `required` array allows clients and gateways to validate requests before transmission, improving developer experience and enabling earlier error surfacing.
findings.rationale: A resource-creation POST that mandates certain fields should declare the requestBody required and encode mandatory top-level fields in the schema's required array.
findings.patchSummary: Mark requestBody required and add display_name + address to schema required array

findings.title: configuration_overrides typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The `configuration_overrides` field is described as 'The ID of a configuration that will be used to customize all readers in this location', making it a cross-resource foreign key. It is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. No `pattern` (e.g. `^tmrc_`) and no `format` hint are present. Code-generation tools cannot infer a typed relationship to the Terminal Configuration resource from this schema, and client libraries cannot validate the ID prefix. Adding a `pattern` matching the known Terminal Configuration ID prefix and a description reference to the resource type would materially improve type safety.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields that reference other objects should carry a pattern or format so that codegen and validation tools can model the relationship.

findings.title: Japan-only fields (address_kana, address_kanji, display_name_kana, display_name_kanji) have conditional-required relationship expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The descriptions for `address_kana`, `address_kanji`, `display_name_kana`, and `display_name_kanji` all state '(Japan only)', implying these fields are only valid or meaningful when the address country is Japan. This conditional relationship is expressed solely in natural-language descriptions and is not encoded in the schema (e.g. via `if/then/else` or `dependentSchemas`). As a result, tooling and validators cannot enforce or communicate this constraint, and a caller creating a US location could submit `address_kana` without any schema-level warning. At minimum, a description clarification on these fields should note the constraint clearly; ideally it is encoded structurally.
findings.rationale: Conditional field applicability rules stated only in prose should be encoded as JSON Schema constraints for machine-readable validation.

A minimal example showing at least the required fields (`display_name`, `address.country`, `address.line1`) would significantly improve DX for SDK consumers, API explorers, and documentation generators. findings.title: Path parameter `location` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `location` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but it represents a Terminal Location resource ID (typically prefixed `tml_`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code generation tools cannot build a typed cross-resource reference, and client-side validation cannot reject obviously wrong values (e.g., arbitrary strings, IDs of the wrong resource type).
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern/format prevent typed codegen relationships and weaken validation. A pattern such as `^tml_[\w]+$` would make the constraint explicit.

findings.title: Empty request body definition on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests conventionally carry no body, and including a request body here is misleading. Many HTTP clients and intermediaries will ignore or reject bodies on GET requests. The body definition should be removed entirely to accurately describe the operation's contract.

findings.title: configuration_overrides described as config ID but typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `configuration_overrides` field description says 'The ID of a configuration that will be used to customize all readers in this location.' Resource IDs in Stripe follow a consistent prefix pattern (e.g., `tmc_...`). However, the field is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 1000` constraint and no `format`, `pattern`, or `$ref` to a typed ID schema. Codegen tools cannot infer the relationship between this string and the referenced configuration resource, and API consumers receive no validation hint that the value must be a valid configuration object identifier.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent typed relationship inference by SDK generators and provide no format validation to catch malformed IDs early.

findings.title: Encoding style 'deepObject' incorrectly applied to scalar string fields
findings.narration: The `encoding` block for the `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body sets `style: deepObject` on several scalar (non-object, non-array) fields: `configuration_overrides`, `display_name`, `display_name_kana`, `display_name_kanji`, and `phone`. Per OpenAPI 3.x, `deepObject` is intended for object-type parameters and is meaningless for scalars. This can confuse HTTP client libraries that attempt to apply deepObject serialization to these string values, potentially generating malformed request bodies like `display_name[]=value` instead of `display_name=value`.
findings.rationale: deepObject encoding on scalar fields is semantically incorrect and may cause client libraries to generate malformed form data.

findings.title: country field in address is described as immutable but is still exposed as writable
findings.narration: The `address` description explicitly states 'You can't change the location's `country`.' However, the `country` field inside the `address` object schema is fully writable with no `readOnly` marker, no validation constraint, and no inline schema rule encoding the immutability. An API consumer posting a new `country` value may receive a runtime error with no in-spec indication that this will fail. This prose-only constraint should either be encoded via schema (`readOnly: true`) or the field should be omitted from the update schema entirely.
findings.rationale: Immutability rules described only in prose leave consumers with no machine-readable signal; the `readOnly` keyword or omission from the update schema should encode this constraint.

findings.title: Conditional field relationship between `link_type` and `link_options` not encoded in schema

The implied rule is that the sub-object under `link_options` must match the chosen `link_type`. As the API evolves and more link types are added, clients will need to know exactly which `link_options` sub-object is required/allowed for each `link_type`. This structural constraint is currently expressed only implicitly by the shared naming convention, not by any JSON Schema `oneOf`/`if-then-else` or `dependencies` construct. Codegen tools cannot enforce or surface this relationship.
findings.rationale: Conditional required fields tied to discriminator values should be encoded in schema (oneOf/if-then-else) rather than left as implicit naming conventions, especially since more link types are expected to be added.

This is a recurring pattern in the Stripe spec but is particularly notable on this field since it directly determines which connected account is being onboarded.

findings.title: Response status should be 201 Created for resource creation, not 200 OK
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new Reader resource, yet the success response is documented as HTTP 200. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a response that results in the creation of a new resource should return HTTP 201 Created, typically accompanied by a Location header pointing to the newly created resource. Returning 200 conflates creation with update/retrieval operations and misleads API consumers relying on status codes for conditional logic.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for successful resource creation in REST APIs; 200 implies the operation retrieved or updated an existing resource.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response from 200 OK to 201 Created for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: location field typed as plain string with no resource ID format or pattern

Consumers and code-generation tools have no machine-readable way to know that exactly one of these must be provided, leading to ambiguous client implementations and potential silent failures or server-side errors.

The rule 'cart is required when type is cart' should be expressed via `if`/`then` or `required` at the appropriate schema level.

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields 'charge' and 'payment_intent' not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The request body accepts both `charge` and `payment_intent` as optional fields, but the semantics of refund creation require exactly one of them to be provided — you refund either a charge or a payment intent, not both and not neither. This constraint is expressed nowhere in the schema; it exists only implicitly in the API's runtime behavior. Codegen tools, validators, and API consumers have no way to discover this rule from the spec alone. The schema should use `oneOf` or a `required`/`dependencies` construct (or at minimum a prose `description` warning) to make the mutual exclusivity and collective requirement explicit.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually-exclusive field relationships that live only in runtime logic and not in the schema are a high-leverage finding: they cause silent bad requests and mislead code generators.

A JSON Schema `oneOf` or `not`/`dependencies` construct should encode the constraint so that validators and codegen tools can surface the conflict automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually-exclusive field relationships expressed only in prose (or not at all) are a high-leverage gap; code generators and validators cannot enforce them without schema-level encoding.

findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without pattern or format are a high-leverage codegen and validation gap.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `card` path param to encode Issuing Card ID format

Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client-side validation cannot catch obviously malformed IDs before sending a request, and codegen tools cannot build a typed reference to the Issuing Card resource.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without pattern or format constraints prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow obviously invalid values to reach the server.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `card` path param to reflect Issuing Card ID format

A regex pattern such as `^ic_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode the expected shape in a machine-readable way.

findings.title: Path parameter `personalization_design` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `personalization_design` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe resource IDs for personalization designs follow a predictable prefix pattern (e.g. `pd_`).
