findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings without pattern or format make it impossible for codegen tools to enforce or document ID shapes, and a maxLength of 5000 is misleadingly permissive.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to personalization_design path param to encode its ID format.

findings.title: Path parameter `personalization_design` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The path parameter `personalization_design` is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. In Stripe's API, personalization design IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `ipcd_...`). Without a `pattern` (e.g. `^ipcd_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at minimum a descriptive `format`, codegen tools and client validators cannot distinguish a valid resource ID from arbitrary string input. This also makes it harder for developers reading the spec to understand what value is expected here.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without format or pattern reduce type safety and make spec-driven codegen less useful.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the personalization_design path parameter to reflect the expected ID format.

findings.title: rejection_reasons object has no minProperties / at-least-one constraint encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `rejection_reasons` object accepts `card_logo` and `carrier_text` as optional sub-arrays, but neither property is marked `required` inside the object, meaning a caller can submit an empty `rejection_reasons: {}` and pass schema validation. In practice, at least one of the two sub-arrays must contain at least one value for a rejection to make semantic sense. This field-relationship rule is enforced nowhere in the schema — it exists only implicitly. Adding `minProperties: 1` to the `rejection_reasons` object schema would prevent empty-object submissions and make the constraint machine-readable.
findings.rationale: A required request body field whose own properties are all optional and unconstrained can silently produce server-side validation errors that clients cannot anticipate from the schema alone.
findings.patchSummary: Add minProperties: 1 to rejection_reasons to prevent empty object submissions

findings.title: Path parameter personalization_design lacks format or pattern to identify it as a typed resource ID
findings.narration: The `personalization_design` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`. Stripe personalization design IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `ipcd_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a descriptive `format`, code-generation tooling treats this as a free-form string with no relationship to the personalization design resource. Adding a regex pattern (e.g. `^ipcd_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or a semantic `format` value documents the expected shape and enables client-side pre-validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent typed relationship inference in generated SDKs and reduce early client-side validation opportunities.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern to personalization_design path param to encode expected ID format

findings.title: POST endpoint creating a resource should return 201, not 200
findings.narration: This operation creates a new Issuing settlement resource. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §6.3.2), a successful resource-creation response should use status code 201 Created rather than 200 OK. Using 200 here misrepresents the operation's effect to clients and tooling that rely on HTTP status semantics to distinguish retrieval from creation.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 reserves 201 for successful resource creation. Returning 200 on a POST that creates a resource violates HTTP conventions and confuses clients, proxies, and code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Change 200 response to 201 Created for resource-creation semantics

findings.title: Missing `network` field in `required` array despite being a core identifier
findings.narration: The `network` field identifies the card network for the settlement (one of "visa" or "maestro") and is a fundamental attribute of a settlement record. However, it is not listed in the `required` array alongside `bin`, `clearing_date`, `currency`, and `net_total_amount`. Without it, a caller could submit a settlement creation request without specifying the network, which would likely either fail at runtime or require server-side defaulting logic that is undocumented in the spec. If the field is genuinely optional, the description should clarify the default or omission behavior.
findings.rationale: A settlement's card network is a primary classification attribute. Omitting it from `required` while providing no default or description of what happens if omitted is a design gap.
findings.patchSummary: Add `network` to the required fields of the request body schema

findings.title: `clearing_date` integer type lacks format hint for Unix timestamp
findings.narration: The `clearing_date` field is described as 'the date that the transactions are cleared and posted to user's accounts' and is typed as `integer`. In the Stripe API, date-as-integer fields universally represent Unix timestamps (seconds since epoch). Without a `format: unix-time` or similar hint, and without a description that explicitly states it is a Unix timestamp, clients may pass a calendar day integer (e.g., 20240101) instead of a Unix epoch value, leading to silent data errors. The description should at minimum call this out; ideally a format annotation should be added.
findings.rationale: Ambiguous integer date representations cause silent data errors. Stripe conventionally uses Unix timestamps, but this must be explicit in the schema to be unambiguous.

patchOps.value: The date that the transactions are cleared and posted to user's accounts, as a Unix timestamp (seconds since epoch).

findings.patchSummary: Clarify clearing_date as Unix timestamp and add format annotation

findings.title: No example provided on the complex request body schema
findings.narration: The request body schema has ten properties including multiple integer monetary amounts and an enum. Without an inline example or examples block, developers cannot quickly verify the expected shape of the payload, particularly the monetary integer fields (which in Stripe are in the smallest currency unit, e.g., cents). An example would also disambiguate `clearing_date` encoding and demonstrate a minimal valid request.
findings.rationale: Complex multi-field POST bodies without examples create friction for integrators and increase the chance of miscoded requests, especially for monetary integer fields.
findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the request body schema

findings.title: card field typed as plain string with no format or pattern — cross-resource reference untyped
findings.narration: The `card` field in the request body is described as 'Card associated with this transaction' and carries a `maxLength: 5000`, but it is typed as a bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^ic_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`), and no `$ref` to a card schema. This field is clearly a resource ID referencing a Stripe Issuing Card object. Without a pattern or format hint, code-generation tools cannot infer the relationship, clients cannot validate the value shape before sending, and documentation readers have no indication of what a valid card ID looks like.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed relationship inference in codegen and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to card field to reflect Stripe Issuing Card ID format

findings.title: No 4xx response definitions — only 200 and default error responses defined
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a `default` error response. For a test-helper POST that requires two mandatory fields (`amount` and `card`) and interacts with a real card resource, explicit `400` (invalid input / validation failure) and `404` (card not found) response codes should be declared. Consumers generating client code or performing contract testing cannot distinguish expected validation errors from unexpected server errors when all errors collapse into the `default` bucket. The Stripe API documentation commonly surfaces 400 and 404 for this class of operation.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses collapse all error cases into a single default, reducing consumer ability to handle errors gracefully and making contract testing less precise.

value.description: Bad request — invalid or missing parameters.
Card not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions for missing-field and not-found cases

findings.title: Missing example on complex nested request body
findings.narration: The request body contains deeply nested objects (`merchant_data`, `purchase_details` with sub-objects like `fleet`, `flight`, `fuel`, `lodging`) totalling several dozen fields. No `example` or `examples` entry is present on the schema or the media-type object. Without an illustrative example, consumers and documentation readers must manually assemble a valid payload by reading through the deeply nested property tree, increasing the likelihood of integration errors. Adding even one minimal example demonstrating a basic force capture and one more complete example showing fleet/fuel details would substantially improve usability.
findings.rationale: Complex nested request schemas without examples impose high integration friction and increase the risk of malformed requests.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimal and illustrative examples to the request body media-type object

findings.title: Cross-resource field `card` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `card` field in the request body references an Issuing Card resource ID (typically prefixed `ic_`) but is declared as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Codegen tools cannot infer the relationship to the Card resource, and clients receive no hint about the expected ID format. Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^ic_`) or at minimum a descriptive `format` (e.g., `format: "issuing-card-id"`) would enable typed relationship tracking and improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings prevent codegen from building typed references and leave clients without validation hints.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `card` field to signal it is an Issuing Card resource ID

findings.title: Missing `amount` field minimum constraint
findings.narration: The `amount` field is typed as `integer` and marked required, but there is no `minimum` constraint. A refund amount of 0 or a negative number makes no semantic sense for this operation and would likely result in a server-side error. Adding `minimum: 1` encodes this invariant in the schema, allowing clients and validators to catch invalid values before making a network call.
findings.rationale: Without a minimum constraint, clients can submit zero or negative refund amounts, which the server will reject — better caught at the schema layer.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 to `amount` to reject zero and negative refund amounts at schema validation

findings.title: No request body example provided for a complex, deeply nested schema
findings.narration: The request body contains a deeply nested schema with `merchant_data` and `purchase_details` (which further nests `fleet`, `flight`, `fuel`, `lodging`, and `receipt`). No `example` or `examples` field is provided at the media-type or schema level. Without a concrete example, developers integrating this test-helper endpoint must manually piece together what a valid payload looks like from the schema alone, which is especially burdensome given the large MCC enum in `merchant_data.category`.
findings.rationale: Complex nested request schemas without examples significantly increase integration time and the likelihood of malformed requests.
findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the request body media type for this complex nested schema

findings.title: transaction path parameter typed as plain string without ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `transaction` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe transaction IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ipi_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the Transaction resource, and clients receive no validation hint that they must pass a valid transaction ID. A `maxLength` of 5000 is also far too loose for what is effectively a resource identifier.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen from building typed relationships and offer no client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten transaction path parameter with an ID-like pattern constraint.

findings.title: refund_amount has no minimum or maximum constraint
findings.narration: The `refund_amount` field in the request body is typed as `integer` but has no `minimum` value constraint. A negative or zero refund amount is semantically invalid, and clients have no schema-level signal preventing them from submitting such values. At minimum, `minimum: 1` should be applied to encode the smallest-currency-unit requirement stated in the description.
findings.rationale: Missing numeric constraints allow invalid values to pass schema validation, shifting error handling entirely to the server and away from early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 to refund_amount to prevent zero or negative submissions.

findings.title: Refund ID path parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `refund` path parameter is declared as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or description hint indicating it is a Stripe refund ID (typically prefixed `re_`). Code generation tools cannot infer the relationship to the refund resource, and clients receive no validation guidance on the expected ID shape.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as bare strings prevent typed relationship generation and offer no client-side validation signal.

value.description: The ID of the refund to expire. Must be a valid Stripe refund ID (prefix `re_`).

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and description to refund path parameter to document Stripe ID format.

findings.title: Conditional field relationship between `type` and payment-method objects encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The request body has a `type` field (enum: `card`, `card_present`, `interac_present`) and three sibling objects (`card`, `card_present`, `interac_present`). Logically, when `type` is `card` the `card` object is meaningful, when `type` is `card_present` the `card_present` object applies, and so on. This relationship — that exactly the matching sub-object should be supplied for the given `type` — is not expressed in the schema at all. A code generator or validator cannot enforce it. The schema should use `oneOf` (or `if/then`) discriminated on `type` to make these dependencies machine-readable and reject inconsistent combinations at validation time.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships expressed only in human prose are a high-severity design gap; they cannot be enforced by clients, SDKs, or middleware without bespoke code.

expand.description: Specifies which fields in the response should be expanded.

card.description: Simulated data for the card payment method.

card_present.description: Simulated data for the card_present payment method.

interac_present.description: Simulated data for the interac_present payment method.

findings.patchSummary: Replace flat schema with oneOf discriminated on `type` to encode conditional sub-object requirements.

findings.title: Card `number` and `cvc` fields in request body lack `writeOnly` and format hints
findings.narration: The `card.number` and `card.cvc` fields represent payment card data. Even in a test-helper context, these fields should be marked `writeOnly: true` to signal to documentation generators and SDK tooling that they should never be read back or logged. Additionally, `card.number` would benefit from a `pattern` or `format: "card-number"` annotation so that mock generators and validators know the expected shape. Without `writeOnly`, there is a risk that tooling will treat these as normal readable fields and include them in response type definitions or logging middleware.
findings.rationale: Credential and PAN fields without writeOnly risk being exposed in generated SDKs, response schemas, or logging; even in test helpers this is worth enforcing as a consistent policy.
findings.patchSummary: Mark card.number and card.cvc as writeOnly to prevent leakage via generated SDK response types.

findings.title: Reader path parameter lacks format/pattern hint for typed resource reference
findings.narration: The `reader` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint, but it is a Terminal Reader resource ID (typically prefixed `tmr_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` annotation, code-generation tools cannot build a typed resource reference, and clients cannot validate the expected ID format before making a network call.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent code-gen from building typed relationships and prevent early client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to reader path param to communicate expected ID format

findings.title: skip_non_required_inputs enum semantics not sufficiently described
findings.narration: The `skip_non_required_inputs` field has only a brief description ('This parameter defines the skip behavior for input collection') without explaining what `all` vs `none` actually does in the simulation. Callers testing with this helper cannot determine whether `all` skips every non-required input field or just some, and whether `none` means 'skip nothing' (i.e., fill everything) or has some other meaning. This is a clarity issue that could lead to incorrect test setups.
findings.rationale: Enum values without per-value documentation force callers to experiment or consult external docs to understand behaviour, reducing API usability.

patchOps.value: Controls which non-required inputs the simulated reader skips during input collection. `all` — skip all non-required inputs (only required inputs are collected). `none` — do not skip any inputs; all inputs, required and optional, are collected.

findings.patchSummary: Expand skip_non_required_inputs description to clarify the effect of each enum value

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum/maximum)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values encoded. This means clients and codegen tools have no machine-readable way to validate or default the parameter — they must rely on prose alone. A value of 0 or 10000 would pass schema validation but be rejected at the API layer.
findings.rationale: Field-relationship and constraint rules expressed only in prose should be encoded as schema constraints (`minimum`, `maximum`, `default`) per best practice.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET endpoint is unnecessary
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests with a body are semantically incorrect per RFC 7231 and many HTTP clients and proxies strip or reject bodies on GET requests. This requestBody conveys no information and adds noise for SDK generators, which may erroneously generate a body parameter for a list/read operation.
findings.rationale: GET operations should not have request bodies per HTTP semantics and RFC 7231 §4.3.1. An empty, non-required body with no properties should be removed.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: POST creating a resource returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This operation creates a new test clock resource (a POST that results in resource creation), but the success response is documented as HTTP 200 rather than HTTP 201 Created. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), a 201 response is the correct status code when a new resource has been successfully created. Using 200 obscures the creation semantics for API consumers and tooling that relies on status codes to distinguish creation from update.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the canonical status code for successful resource creation; 200 implies a retrieval or non-creating mutation.
findings.patchSummary: Rename 200 response to 201 Created for resource-creation semantics.

findings.title: Missing example on frozen_time field
findings.narration: The `frozen_time` field is the only required parameter in this request and carries a non-obvious format (`unix-time` integer). Without an example value, developers cannot quickly understand what a valid value looks like (e.g., 1675209600 for a specific date). Adding an example would reduce integration friction and improve generated documentation.
findings.rationale: Complex or formatted fields benefit from examples; unix timestamps are not immediately intuitive to all developers.
findings.patchSummary: Add a unix-timestamp example value to the frozen_time property.

findings.title: Path parameter `test_clock` has no format or pattern to indicate resource ID type
findings.narration: The `test_clock` path parameter is declared as a plain `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. In Stripe's API, test clock IDs follow a consistent prefix pattern (e.g., `clock_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive example, SDK generators and validators cannot distinguish a valid test clock ID from arbitrary string input. Adding a regex pattern like `^clock_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at least an `example` value would improve client-side validation and documentation clarity.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain strings without format, pattern, or example are a known low-leverage documentation and codegen issue.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and example to `test_clock` path parameter schema

findings.title: test_clock path parameter lacks ID prefix pattern/format constraint
findings.narration: The `test_clock` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe test clock IDs follow the pattern `clock_[alphanumeric]`. Without a `pattern` or at least a stricter `maxLength`, clients and generated SDKs cannot validate whether a supplied value is actually a test clock ID versus any arbitrary string. A `pattern` such as `^clock_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and a tighter `maxLength` (e.g., 5000 is clearly borrowed from generic text fields, not an ID field) would improve type safety and serve as documentation for integrators.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain `string` with no format or pattern make it impossible for codegen tools to build typed relationships or for clients to perform local validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to test_clock path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format

findings.title: Complex business-rule constraints on frozen_time expressed only in prose
findings.narration: The `frozen_time` field description contains multiple conditional constraints: it must be after the clock's current frozen time, it cannot be more than two intervals in the future from the shortest subscription, and if there are no subscriptions it cannot be more than two years in the future. These are meaningful business rules that currently exist only as free-text documentation. While some of these constraints (e.g., 'after current frozen time') are inherently server-side and dynamic, the 'no more than two years in the future' rule for the no-subscription case could be approximated with a note or a `maximum` hint. More broadly, the multi-condition constraint should at minimum be extracted into a structured `description` with clear enumeration, and ideally tracked as a known schema limitation. Clients relying solely on machine-readable schema will silently violate these constraints.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required or bounded-value constraints expressed only in prose cannot be enforced by client-side validators or communicated by generated SDKs, increasing the risk of rejected requests.

patchOps.value: Server enforces: (1) must be > current frozen_time, (2) must be <= current time + 2 subscription intervals (shortest), (3) if no subscriptions, must be <= now + 2 years.

findings.patchSummary: Surface server-side constraints on frozen_time via x-constraint-note extension

findings.title: No 4xx error response codes defined beyond the catch-all default
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` error response. Specific HTTP error codes such as `400` (invalid frozen_time value, time in the past), `404` (test clock not found), and `422` (clock in non-advanceable state) are not enumerated. Relying solely on `default` means client code generators cannot produce typed error handlers for common failure scenarios. At a minimum, `400` and `404` should be explicitly declared so tooling can differentiate client errors from unexpected errors and surface them appropriately.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses mean SDKs and documentation tools cannot surface expected error shapes, making it harder for integrators to handle errors correctly.

value.description: Bad request — e.g., frozen_time is in the past or exceeds allowed advance window.
Test clock not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the catch-all default

findings.title: Conditional field constraint encoded only in prose: `ach` required when type is `ach`, `us_domestic_wire` required when type is `us_domestic_wire`
findings.narration: The `tracking_details` object has a `type` discriminator field with two allowed values (`ach`, `us_domestic_wire`), and the corresponding sub-objects (`ach`, `us_domestic_wire`) implicitly must be provided to match the declared type. This relationship is documented only implicitly via the schema structure and not enforced via JSON Schema constructs like `if/then/else` or `oneOf`. A client supplying `type: 'ach'` with a `us_domestic_wire` object (or neither) would not be caught by schema validation tooling. The rule 'if type is ach then ach is required; if type is us_domestic_wire then us_domestic_wire is required' should be machine-readable.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships expressed only structurally (not as schema constraints) cannot be validated by standard JSON Schema validators or code generators, leading to runtime errors that could be caught at schema validation time.

value.description: Details about network-specific tracking information.
value.title: tracking_details_params

findings.patchSummary: Replace tracking_details schema with if/then/else to enforce type-conditional required sub-objects

findings.title: No example provided for the complex `tracking_details` request body
findings.narration: The request body contains a moderately complex nested structure (`tracking_details` with discriminated sub-objects for `ach` and `us_domestic_wire` networks), but no examples are provided at the media-type level or on the schema properties. Without examples, API consumers must reverse-engineer the shape from the schema, which is especially cumbersome for the discriminated union pattern used here. Adding at least one example showing an `ach`-type payload and one showing `us_domestic_wire` would significantly improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: Missing examples on complex request bodies reduce clarity for API consumers and documentation generators; this is especially true for discriminated union patterns.
findings.patchSummary: Add examples for ACH and US domestic wire tracking_details payloads

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern constraint for OutboundPayment ID
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. OutboundPayment IDs in Stripe follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `obp_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK generators and validation tooling cannot enforce the expected shape, and users get no guidance on what a valid ID looks like. A regex pattern such as `^obp_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would make the constraint machine-readable and self-documenting.
findings.rationale: A cross-resource identifier typed as plain string with no pattern or format means codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship and clients can pass syntactically invalid IDs without early rejection.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter to document expected OutboundPayment ID format.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response codes defined
findings.narration: The operation only defines a `200` success response and a `default` catch-all error response. For a state-transition endpoint like this one, specific 4xx conditions are very predictable: `404` when the OutboundPayment ID does not exist, `400` when the OutboundPayment is not in the `processing` state (a precondition the description explicitly calls out), and potentially `403` for authorization failures. Relying solely on the `default` schema leaves client developers without any machine-readable signal about which error codes to handle and how. Adding at least `400` and `404` improves developer experience and enables better client-side error handling code generation.
findings.rationale: Known, predictable failure modes (resource not found, wrong state) should be explicitly enumerated as response codes, not left to a generic default catch-all.

value.description: Bad request — e.g. OutboundPayment is not in the `processing` state.
OutboundPayment with the given ID was not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions for predictable failure modes.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format/pattern constraint for OutboundPayment resource ID
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe OutboundPayment IDs have a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `obp_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot validate or document the expected format, and clients may inadvertently pass arbitrary strings. Adding a `pattern` such as `^obp_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` or at minimum tightening the `maxLength` to a realistic value (e.g., 255) would meaningfully improve client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and degrade validation quality.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten id parameter maxLength and add pattern for OutboundPayment IDs

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response definitions beyond the catch-all `default`
findings.narration: The operation only declares a `200` success and a `default` error response. Common, actionable error scenarios — such as `404 Not Found` (when the OutboundPayment ID does not exist), `400 Bad Request` (when the OutboundPayment is not in the `processing` state, which the description explicitly calls out as a precondition), and `422 Unprocessable Entity` — are all collapsed into the `default` bucket. Clients cannot write conditional error-handling logic against specific status codes. At minimum, `400` and `404` should be enumerated with their own response objects so API consumers and SDK generators understand the expected failure modes.
findings.rationale: Missing explicit 4xx responses force clients to treat all errors identically and prevent SDK generators from producing typed error handling.

findings.title: Conditional schema relationship between `tracking_details.type` and sub-objects encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `tracking_details` object has a `type` field that is an enum of `ach` or `us_domestic_wire`. The schema implies that when `type` is `ach`, the `ach` sub-object should be provided (and `us_domestic_wire` should be absent), and vice versa. However, this mutual-exclusivity and conditional-requirement relationship is expressed nowhere in the schema — there is no `oneOf`, `if/then/else`, or `dependencies` construct to encode it. A client submitting `type: "ach"` with no `ach` object, or submitting both `ach` and `us_domestic_wire`, will receive no schema-level feedback. Tooling (validators, code generators, SDK generators) cannot enforce this constraint. The rule should be captured as a `oneOf` at the `tracking_details` level, with one branch requiring `ach` when `type` is `ach` and another requiring `us_domestic_wire` when `type` is `us_domestic_wire`.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required fields expressed only in implicit convention rather than schema constraints are a high-leverage pattern that creates integration bugs and hinders code generation.

findings.title: Path parameter `outbound_transfer` lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The path parameter `outbound_transfer` is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Stripe OutboundTransfer IDs follow a well-known prefix format (e.g., `obt_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a meaningful `maxLength` (5000 is the generic Stripe string cap, not a real constraint on an ID), code generators produce untyped string fields and documentation gives no hint of what a valid ID looks like. Adding a `pattern` such as `^obt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would enable client-side validation and improve SDK ergonomics.
findings.rationale: Resource ID parameters typed as unconstrained strings lose the ability for tooling to build typed cross-resource references and perform basic input validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint and realistic maxLength to outbound_transfer path parameter

findings.title: Path parameter 'outbound_transfer' lacks ID format/pattern constraint

Stripe OutboundTransfer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `obt_...`). A regex pattern such as `^obt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would encode the expected shape and enable static validation.

Without `writeOnly: true`, code-generation tools and client SDKs may inadvertently serialize or log this field when round-tripping request/response objects. While this is a request body field and won't appear in the response schema, the absence of the `writeOnly` marker means documentation tooling and generated models treat it as a bidirectional field.
findings.rationale: Bank account numbers are sensitive PII/financial data. The `writeOnly` annotation prevents SDK generators and documentation tools from treating the field as readable.

The `us_bank_account` sub-object is implicitly required whenever `type` is `us_bank_account`, but this conditional requirement is not encoded in the schema — there is no `if/then`, `oneOf`, or `dependencies` construct enforcing it. Clients relying on schema validation will not receive a machine-readable signal that `us_bank_account` must be provided when `type` is set to `us_bank_account`. This is a common source of runtime 400 errors that could be caught at the client side.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required relationships expressed only through naming convention rather than schema keywords cannot be enforced by validators or surfaced by SDK generators.

If future enum values are added (e.g. `sepa_debit`), the implicit rule will become silently broken and clients will receive runtime errors instead of schema-validation errors.

findings.title: Summary says 'Create a CVC update token' but operation creates multiple token types
findings.narration: The `summary` field reads 'Create a CVC update token', which is just one of seven distinct token types this endpoint can create: bank account tokens, card tokens, account tokens, person tokens, PII tokens, CVC update tokens, and customer clone tokens. A developer scanning the API reference will completely miss the primary use cases (bank account tokenization, card tokenization) because the summary is named after the least common variant. The description body is accurate, but the summary — the most visible field in generated docs and SDK tooling — is badly misleading.
findings.rationale: The summary is the first string shown in docs UIs and OpenAPI tooling. It should reflect the full scope of the endpoint, not a single sub-use-case.

findings.title: Mutually-exclusive top-level token-type fields not enforced in schema
findings.narration: The request body accepts `card`, `bank_account`, `account`, `person`, `pii`, `cvc_update`, and `customer` as sibling properties, but only one meaningful token-type payload should be submitted per request. The API semantics are that these are mutually exclusive — you create exactly one kind of token per call. This constraint is expressed nowhere in the schema; a client could send both `card` and `bank_account` in the same request and receive a runtime error instead of a clear schema-level validation failure. The correct encoding is a `oneOf` (or at minimum a prose note with a machine-readable `not` / `dependencies` block) to express that exactly one of these groups is permitted. This is a significant DX and safety gap: SDK generators and validation middleware will accept requests that the server will reject.
findings.rationale: Conditional-required / mutually-exclusive field rules expressed only implicitly (by omission) should be encoded as JSON Schema `oneOf` or `dependencies` so validators and code-generators can enforce them.

patchOps.value: Exactly one of `card`, `bank_account`, `account`, `person`, `pii`, or `cvc_update` must be provided per request. Providing more than one token-type payload in a single call is not supported. The `customer` field may accompany `card` to reference a saved card belonging to that customer.

findings.patchSummary: Add description clarifying mutual exclusivity of token-type fields

findings.title: `customer` field typed as plain string with no format or pattern — cross-resource reference untyped
findings.narration: The `customer` field is a Stripe customer ID (prefix `cus_`) but is declared as `type: string` with only `maxLength: 5000` and no `format`, `pattern`, or description of the ID format. Code generators cannot build a typed relationship between this field and the Customer resource. Additionally, the description states this field requires either an OAuth access token or a `Stripe-Account` header — a conditional-auth requirement that is expressed only in prose and is not machine-readable.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields should carry a pattern (e.g. `^cus_[A-Za-z0-9]+$`) or a custom format so SDK generators can produce typed references and validators can catch obviously wrong values.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `customer` field to identify it as a typed Customer ID reference

findings.title: Sensitive fields (`id_number`, `ssn_last_4`, `cvc`, card `number`) lack `writeOnly: true`
findings.narration: Multiple fields in this request carry highly sensitive PII and payment data: `pii.id_number` (national ID), `person.id_number`, `person.ssn_last_4`, `account.individual.id_number`, `account.individual.ssn_last_4`, `card[cvc]`, and `card[number]`. None of these fields have `writeOnly: true` set. Without this marker, documentation generators may render these fields in response-body examples, and SDK generators may include them in response models, creating a false impression that the server echoes back raw PAN, CVV, or SSN data. Setting `writeOnly: true` on these fields is a security-documentation best practice.
findings.rationale: Credential and PII fields that are write-only in practice should be marked `writeOnly: true` to prevent docs/SDK generators from suggesting the data is readable from responses.
findings.patchSummary: Mark sensitive PII and payment credential fields as writeOnly: true

findings.title: GET list endpoint carries an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, but the schema is an empty object (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests must not carry a body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1). Many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers will discard or reject a body on a GET request, making this declaration both semantically incorrect and potentially misleading to SDK generators that may serialize an empty form body.
findings.rationale: HTTP GET requests MUST NOT include a body. An empty, locked-down form body on a GET endpoint serves no purpose and violates HTTP semantics.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty request body from the GET /v1/topups operation

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing min/max constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states "Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10", but the schema defines it only as `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` constraints. This means any integer (including 0, negative values, or values exceeding 100) is schema-valid. Validators, SDK generators, and documentation tools will not enforce the documented range, increasing the chance of bad requests reaching the server and misleading API consumers.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but not encoded in the schema cannot be validated client-side and lead to avoidable 400-class errors.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the `limit` parameter schema

findings.title: `amount` parameter description is misleading for a filter
findings.narration: The `amount` parameter is described as "A positive integer representing how much to transfer." This description is copy-pasted from the top-up creation endpoint and documents the creation semantics rather than the filtering semantics applicable here. In the context of GET /v1/topups, `amount` is a filter that narrows results to top-ups matching a given amount or amount range. The description should reflect that this is a filter criterion, not a transfer instruction.
findings.rationale: A description that documents a different operation's semantics (create vs. filter) constitutes a copy-paste bug that misleads API consumers.

findings.title: Response should be 201 Created, not 200 OK, for resource creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new top-up resource, but the success response is documented as HTTP 200 rather than HTTP 201. Per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §15.3.2), 201 Created is the correct status code when a new resource has been created as a result of a request. Using 200 here is a semantic inconsistency — clients and tooling that check response codes to distinguish 'updated' from 'created' will be misled. Stripe's actual API does return 200 here, which is a known deviation from REST conventions, but it should at minimum be called out if the spec is meant to be normative.
findings.rationale: 201 is the semantically correct HTTP response for resource creation; 200 implies the resource already existed or was retrieved.
findings.patchSummary: Rename success response from 200 to 201 to reflect resource creation semantics

findings.title: source field typed as plain string with no format or pattern

No `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^src_` or `^ba_`), or `$ref` is present. Code-generation tools cannot infer the typed relationship between this field and the Source resource. Adding a pattern constraint that matches known Stripe source prefixes (e.g., `^(src|ba)_`) would allow client generators to validate IDs client-side and signal the cross-resource relationship clearly.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and block client-side format validation.

findings.title: amount field has no minimum constraint despite being documented as positive integer
findings.narration: The `amount` field is described as 'A positive integer representing how much to transfer', yet the schema only specifies `type: integer` with no `minimum` constraint. A `minimum: 1` (or platform-specific minimum like 100 for cents) should be encoded in the schema so validation tools and generated clients can enforce the positivity constraint without relying on prose documentation alone. Without it, values of 0 or negative integers pass schema validation and would only be rejected at the API layer.
findings.rationale: Documented constraints ('positive integer') should be machine-readable; omitting minimum forces clients to rely on prose and risks avoidable API round-trips.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 to amount schema to enforce documented 'positive integer' constraint

For financial APIs especially, examples are critical: they communicate currency/amount conventions (e.g., smallest currency unit), valid source ID formats, and statement descriptor constraints. Without examples, integrators may misunderstand the expected units or formats and submit incorrect values. Adding at least one concrete example in the `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` encoding entry would significantly improve developer experience.
findings.rationale: Financial endpoints without examples create ambiguity around unit conventions (minor vs major currency units) and acceptable field formats.

findings.title: POST creates a resource but returns 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new transfer reversal object, which is a resource-creation operation. By HTTP semantics (RFC 9110), a successful resource creation should return HTTP 201 Created, optionally with a Location header pointing to the newly created resource. Returning 200 OK is semantically ambiguous — it suggests the request was processed but does not communicate that a new resource was created. Stripe uses 200 broadly across its API, but this is a deviation from REST best practices that can confuse API consumers and code-generation tooling that maps status codes to behavior.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §9.3.5 specifies 201 Created for successful POST that results in a new resource. Using 200 obscures creation semantics.

findings.title: Conditional constraint for `amount` encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The `amount` field description states: "Partial transfer reversals are only allowed for transfers to Stripe Accounts." This is a conditional business rule — supplying a partial amount is invalid unless the transfer target is a Stripe Account. This constraint exists only in the prose description and is not encoded in the schema (e.g. via `if`/`then`, `oneOf`, or a linked description on the parent). API consumers relying on generated clients or JSON Schema validators will not be alerted to this constraint at the schema level; they will only discover the restriction at runtime when the API returns an error.
findings.rationale: Field-level constraints that depend on context should be encoded in JSON Schema where possible, or at minimum flagged so downstream tooling can surface them. Prose-only rules are a high-leverage missing encoding.

patchOps.value: A positive integer in cents (or local equivalent) representing how much of this transfer to reverse. Can only reverse up to the unreversed amount remaining of the transfer. Partial transfer reversals are only allowed for transfers to Stripe Accounts. Defaults to the entire transfer amount. NOTE: Supplying a value less than the full transfer amount is only valid when the transfer destination is a Stripe Account; submitting a partial amount for other transfer types will result in an error.

findings.patchSummary: Clarify prose constraint on partial reversal; ideally encode as schema rule

findings.title: Transfer ID path parameter lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Stripe transfer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `tr_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, code-generation tools cannot produce typed ID references, and API consumers receive no schema-level validation guidance. A regex pattern such as `^tr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow client SDK generators to differentiate this ID type from generic strings and provide early validation feedback.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent typed relationship generation in SDKs and reduce client-side validation quality.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to transfer `id` path parameter to match Stripe's tr_ prefix

findings.title: GET request body is semantically incorrect
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though it is a GET request. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). While the schema inside the body is an empty object with `additionalProperties: false`, which means no properties can be sent, its very presence is misleading. Clients that strictly conform to HTTP (e.g., some HTTP/2 implementations, proxies, and codegen tools) may reject, strip, or flag this. The body should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per HTTP semantics. Even an empty, unusable body definition misleads client generators and tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the request body from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameters `id` and `transfer` lack format or pattern constraints
findings.narration: Both `id` and `transfer` path parameters are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. In Stripe's API, these are resource identifiers with well-known prefixes (e.g., `trr_` for transfer reversals, `tr_` for transfers). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, codegen tools cannot build typed resource references, and clients cannot perform client-side input validation. Adding a pattern such as `^trr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for `id` and `^tr_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` for `transfer` would substantially improve safety and documentation fidelity.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with known formats should encode that format via pattern or format to enable typed references in codegen and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add known-prefix patterns to `id` and `transfer` path parameters.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema for this parameter declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` properties. Clients and generated SDKs have no machine-readable way to validate or communicate the legal range, and the default value of 10 is not encoded. This means a client could send `limit=0` or `limit=999` without the spec indicating it is invalid.
findings.rationale: Constraints stated only in prose rather than encoded in the schema are invisible to validators and codegen tools, reducing spec utility.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: financial_account typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The required `financial_account` query parameter is described as a FinancialAccount ID but is typed as a bare `type: string` with no `maxLength`, `pattern`, or format hint (e.g., `format: "stripe-id"` or a pattern like `^fa_`). Cross-resource ID fields typed this way give codegen tools no information about the relationship or expected shape of the value. Other resource-ID query parameters in this operation (e.g., `ending_before`, `received_credit`) at least carry `maxLength: 5000`; `financial_account` has no constraints at all.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields without any constraint or format annotation prevent typed relationship modelling in generated client code.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength:5000 to financial_account parameter schema for consistency.

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type whose schema has no properties and `additionalProperties: false`. A GET request with a body is semantically unusual (RFC 7231 §4.3.1 does not prohibit it, but many proxies and HTTP clients ignore or reject GET bodies). Since all parameters are already expressed as query parameters, this empty request body definition adds noise and could confuse generated clients that try to serialize a body for a GET request.
findings.rationale: GET bodies are non-standard; an empty, closed-schema body definition serves no purpose and may cause interoperability issues.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty, no-op requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: received_credit field typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `received_credit` field is a reference to a ReceivedCredit resource ID (e.g. `rc_...`) but is typed as a bare `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Codegen tools and client SDKs cannot infer the cross-resource relationship from this, and no `pattern` (e.g. `^rc_`) is provided to allow format validation. Adding a `pattern` or at minimum a prose `format` hint would make the ID recognizable as a Stripe resource reference.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent typed relationship inference in generated clients.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern ^rc_ to received_credit to signal it is a ReceivedCredit resource ID.

findings.title: POST endpoint returns HTTP 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This operation creates a new CreditReversal object (the description says 'creates a CreditReversal object' and the summary is 'Create a CreditReversal'), yet the only success response is `200 OK`. Per HTTP semantics, a successful resource creation should return `201 Created`, ideally with a `Location` header pointing to the newly created resource. Returning 200 for a create operation is misleading to consumers and deviates from REST conventions, making it harder for generic HTTP clients and caching layers to understand the outcome.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status code for successful resource creation; 200 implies retrieval or update.
findings.patchSummary: Change 200 success response to 201 Created for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: Path parameter `credit_reversal` lacks format/pattern constraint for resource ID
findings.narration: The `credit_reversal` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe CreditReversal IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `credrev_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot produce a typed reference and clients receive no validation hint that an arbitrary 5000-character string is not a valid ID. A pattern such as `^credrev_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and a more realistic `maxLength` (e.g. 64) would improve both documentation fidelity and client-side validation.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as plain strings with no pattern or format prevent typed codegen relationships and remove client-side validation opportunity.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten credit_reversal path param: realistic maxLength and ID pattern

findings.title: financial_account parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The required `financial_account` query parameter represents a FinancialAccount resource ID but is typed as a bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^fa_`), and no `maxLength` constraint. This prevents codegen tools from building a typed relationship between this parameter and the FinancialAccount resource, and allows any arbitrary string to pass schema validation without warning.
findings.rationale: Resource-ID parameters should carry at minimum a `maxLength` and ideally a `pattern` matching the ID prefix so that tooling can surface type errors early.

findings.title: received_debit filter parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern

This is the same cross-resource reference typing gap as `financial_account`; codegen tools cannot derive the relationship to ReceivedDebit objects.
findings.rationale: Resource-ID filters should be constrained with at least a pattern so generated clients reflect the typed relationship.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix pattern to received_debit parameter schema.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema encodes none of these constraints: no `minimum`, no `maximum`, and no `default`. A caller passing `limit=0` or `limit=9999` will not be rejected at the schema-validation layer, and generated client documentation will not surface the valid range.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints are not machine-enforceable; they should be encoded as JSON Schema keywords so validators and codegen tools honour them.
findings.patchSummary: Encode minimum 1, maximum 100, and default 10 on limit parameter schema.

findings.title: GET list endpoint carries an empty application/x-www-form-urlencoded request body
findings.narration: A GET request with a request body is semantically ambiguous and many HTTP intermediaries (proxies, CDNs, caches) will ignore or strip it. The `requestBody` here is an empty object schema with `additionalProperties: false`, so it cannot convey any data. Including it on a GET endpoint is misleading and may break clients that strictly follow HTTP semantics. It should be removed.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a meaningful body per RFC 9110 §9.3.1; even an empty schema signals intent to send one.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET list operation.

findings.title: Response status should be 201 Created, not 200 OK, for resource creation
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new DebitReversal resource, yet it declares a 200 OK response. Per HTTP semantics, endpoints that create new resources should return 201 Created to signal that a new resource was successfully created. Using 200 misleads clients and tooling into treating this as a non-creating operation, and prevents clients from reliably distinguishing creates from updates.
findings.rationale: HTTP RFC 9110 §15.3.2 reserves 201 Created for POST operations that result in a new resource being created. The response should include a Location header pointing to the new resource.
findings.patchSummary: Rename 200 response to 201 Created to match HTTP semantics for resource creation

findings.title: received_debit field is a plain string with no format, pattern, or typed relationship

No `format`, `pattern` (e.g. `^rd_`), or `$ref` is provided. Codegen tools cannot infer the typed relationship, and API clients lose the ability to validate that they are supplying the correct ID type. This is a common Stripe pattern but worth flagging per review rules.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields should carry a pattern or format hint so tooling can build typed relationships and clients can validate inputs early.

findings.title: supported_currencies items lack format or pattern constraints
findings.narration: The `supported_currencies` array items are typed as plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000`, but currency codes are standardized 3-letter ISO 4217 strings. The current schema permits arbitrary strings up to 5000 characters, providing no machine-readable constraint to guide validation or codegen. A `pattern: "^[a-zA-Z]{3}$"` (or `maxLength: 3`) would enforce the expected format without breaking valid input.
findings.rationale: Consumers and code generators cannot infer the expected format; a pattern or tighter maxLength encodes the business rule and enables client-side validation.

findings.title: Response returns HTTP 200 for a resource-creation operation instead of 201
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new FinancialAccount (POST on a collection URL), which by REST convention and HTTP semantics should return `201 Created` to signal that a new resource was created. The spec currently declares only a `200 OK` response. Returning 201 also allows clients and intermediaries to distinguish creation from update operations and enables inclusion of a `Location` header pointing to the new resource.
findings.rationale: HTTP 201 is the correct status for successful resource creation via POST; 200 implies the operation read or updated an existing resource.

findings.title: forwarding_settings conditional-required fields expressed only in prose
