findings.title: statement_descriptor character set constraint documented only in prose
findings.narration: The `statement_descriptor` field description states 'Can only include -#.$&*, spaces, and alphanumeric characters' — this is a character-set constraint that is expressed only in the prose description, not as a machine-readable `pattern` in the JSON Schema. API consumers relying on the schema alone (e.g., generated validation code, form builders) will not enforce this constraint and may submit values with disallowed characters, only to receive a server-side error. The constraint should be encoded as a `pattern` property so it is enforceable by schema validators.
findings.rationale: Validation constraints expressed only as prose are not enforced by schema validators or generated clients, leading to avoidable server-side errors that could be caught client-side.
findings.patchSummary: Encode statement_descriptor character-set constraint as a JSON Schema pattern.

findings.title: amount field has no minimum value constraint
findings.narration: The `amount` field is described as 'Amount (in cents) to be transferred' and typed as `integer`, but has no `minimum` constraint. For a financial transfer, a zero or negative amount is almost certainly invalid and should be rejected. Without a `minimum: 1` (or at least `minimum: 0`) constraint in the schema, clients and auto-generated validators will accept nonsensical values like 0 or -100 without complaint, relying entirely on server-side validation to catch the error. Adding a minimum value makes the contract explicit and enables earlier client-side rejection.
findings.rationale: Financial amount fields should always carry a minimum constraint to prevent zero or negative values from passing schema validation silently.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1 constraint to the amount field to disallow zero/negative values.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks pattern constraint for InboundTransfer ID format
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe InboundTransfer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ibt_...`). Without a `pattern` constraint, clients and code-generation tools cannot validate or type the relationship to the InboundTransfer resource. A regex pattern such as `^ibt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would allow downstream tools to distinguish this ID from other Stripe resource IDs typed identically.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and reduce client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter to scope it to InboundTransfer IDs.

findings.title: Empty request body definition on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: This is a GET endpoint that retrieves a single resource by ID. It includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). While some HTTP clients technically allow it, including a `requestBody` on a GET operation is misleading, generates spurious client stubs in code generators, and violates REST conventions. The body carries no useful data given `additionalProperties: false` and an empty `properties` map.
findings.rationale: GET operations should not define a requestBody; it contradicts HTTP semantics and confuses code generators and API consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: Path parameter `inbound_transfer` lacks format/pattern to identify it as a typed resource ID
findings.narration: The `inbound_transfer` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe InboundTransfer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `ibt_...`). Without a `pattern` or at least a descriptive `format`, codegen tools cannot model this as a typed resource reference, and client-side validation cannot catch obviously wrong inputs (e.g., passing a FinancialAccount ID instead).
findings.rationale: Cross-resource references typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent typed relationship modeling in codegen and weaken validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern to the inbound_transfer path parameter to identify it as a typed resource ID.

findings.title: Request body on GET endpoint is unnecessary and semantically incorrect
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema. HTTP GET requests should not carry a request body; this is contrary to RFC 7231 semantics and is ignored or rejected by many HTTP clients, proxies, and servers. All filtering parameters are already correctly expressed as query parameters. The empty request body definition adds confusion and may cause issues with strict HTTP clients or code generators that flag GET+body combinations.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 §4.3.1 states GET has no defined semantics for a request body. Stripe uses this pattern across many GET endpoints, but it is still a design anti-pattern that may confuse consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect request body from GET list endpoint

findings.title: `financial_account` parameter typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `financial_account` parameter is a required resource ID (referencing a FinancialAccount object) but is typed as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `maxLength` constraint. This makes it indistinguishable from an arbitrary string to code-generation tools and API consumers. Adding at minimum a `maxLength` consistent with other ID fields (e.g. 5000 or a tighter bound like 255) and a `pattern` matching Stripe's `fa_...` ID format would allow clients to validate inputs before sending requests.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as plain strings without format/pattern prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and allow invalid values to pass client-side validation silently.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength and pattern to financial_account ID parameter

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states it can range between 1 and 100 with a default of 10, but the schema has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` fields to enforce this. A consumer relying solely on the schema (e.g. through code generation or automated validation) could send `limit=0` or `limit=10000` and only get a runtime error from the API. The constraints documented in prose should be encoded in the schema.
findings.rationale: Constraints stated in prose but absent from the schema cannot be enforced client-side and represent a clarity/design gap where the schema contradicts the documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Encode minimum=1, maximum=100, default=10 on limit parameter schema

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `destination_payment_method` and `destination_payment_method_data` encoded only in prose
findings.narration: The description for `destination_payment_method` states it is 'Exclusive with `destination_payment_method_data`', and vice versa. This mutual-exclusion constraint is expressed only as free-text prose and is invisible to JSON Schema validators, SDK generators, and API clients. The correct encoding is a `oneOf` or `not`/`dependentSchemas` combination at the schema level so that submitting both fields simultaneously is rejected before reaching the server.
findings.rationale: Prose-only field-relationship rules are a documented anti-pattern; they cannot be enforced by tooling, leading to confusing runtime errors instead of clear validation messages.
findings.patchSummary: Add oneOf constraint encoding mutual exclusivity of destination_payment_method vs destination_payment_method_data

findings.title: `account_number` in `us_bank_account` carries no `writeOnly` annotation
findings.narration: The `us_bank_account.account_number` field inside `destination_payment_method_data` accepts a raw bank account number. Sensitive payment credentials submitted in requests should be marked `writeOnly: true` so that documentation generators, SDK builders, and logging tooling know not to include the field in response representations or debug output. Without this annotation, the field appears as a normal readable string, increasing the risk that integrators log or cache it.
findings.rationale: Raw bank account numbers are high-sensitivity PII/financial data. OpenAPI's `writeOnly` keyword exists precisely for credentials and secrets that must not be echoed back.
findings.patchSummary: Mark us_bank_account.account_number as writeOnly to signal it is a sensitive credential field

findings.title: `customer` field typed as plain `string` with no ID format or pattern
findings.narration: The `customer` field holds a Stripe Customer ID (typically prefixed `cus_`). It is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Without a `pattern` (e.g. `^cus_`) or a named format, code-generation tools cannot build a typed reference to the Customer resource, and validators cannot catch obviously malformed IDs before they reach the API. The same concern applies to `destination_payment_method` (expected prefix `pm_`) and `financial_connections_account` (expected prefix `fca_`).
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare strings prevent SDK generators from building typed relationships and allow obviously wrong values to pass client-side validation silently.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to customer and destination_payment_method string fields

findings.title: Missing request body examples for a complex multi-path payment creation endpoint
findings.narration: This endpoint accepts two quite different request shapes depending on whether the caller supplies `destination_payment_method` (an existing PaymentMethod ID) or `destination_payment_method_data` (inline us_bank_account or financial_account details). There are no `examples` on the request body or individual property schemas. Absent examples, documentation portals render bare schema trees, and SDK generated code offers no guidance on the two primary code paths, increasing integration errors for a sensitive financial operation.
findings.rationale: Complex request schemas with mutually exclusive paths greatly benefit from concrete examples; their absence is a medium-severity clarity issue per the severity calibration guide.

with_existing_payment_method.summary: Pay using an existing PaymentMethod ID

with_us_bank_account_data.summary: Pay using inline US bank account details

findings.patchSummary: Add request body examples covering both destination_payment_method and destination_payment_method_data paths

findings.title: GET endpoint carries an empty request body
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content, even though the schema inside it is an empty object (`properties: {}`). GET requests must not carry a body according to HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1), and many HTTP clients, proxies, and gateways silently drop the body or reject the request outright. Declaring a request body on a GET operation also confuses generated client SDKs, which may attempt to serialize it. The `requestBody` block should be removed entirely.
findings.rationale: GET with a body violates HTTP semantics and causes interoperability issues with clients and intermediaries.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from the GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format or pattern to identify OutboundPayment resource IDs
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Stripe OutboundPayment IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `obp_*`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive example, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship between this endpoint and the OutboundPayment resource, and consumers cannot validate that they are passing the correct resource ID type. Adding a `pattern` such as `^obp_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` and an `example` value would materially improve both safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Untyped ID strings prevent codegen from building resource relationships and make it easier for callers to pass wrong ID types silently.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and example to the `id` path parameter schema.

findings.title: Path parameter `id` lacks format/pattern constraint for OutboundPayment resource ID
findings.narration: The `id` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe OutboundPayment IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `obp_*`). Without a `pattern` constraint, clients and generated SDKs cannot validate the ID format before making the request, increasing the chance of meaningless round-trips and unhelpful error messages.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as bare strings without pattern or format lose codegen type safety and client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to `id` path parameter to match Stripe OutboundPayment ID format.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response definitions beyond `default`
findings.narration: The operation defines only a `200` success response and a catch-all `default` error response. Common, predictable client errors for a cancel operation — such as `400 Bad Request` (e.g., payment already in a terminal state), `404 Not Found` (unknown ID), and `409 Conflict` (payment cannot be cancelled in its current state) — are not individually documented. Using only `default` makes it impossible for client generators or documentation tools to distinguish error types and produce meaningful handling code.
findings.rationale: Missing granular 4xx responses reduce API usability and client code quality; a cancel operation has well-known failure modes that should be documented explicitly.

value.description: Bad request — e.g., the OutboundPayment is already in a terminal state and cannot be cancelled.
OutboundPayment not found.

findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400 and 404 response definitions alongside the default error catch-all.

findings.title: Request body on GET operation is semantically incorrect
findings.narration: This GET endpoint includes a `requestBody` with `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content. GET requests should not carry a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1). While the body schema is empty (`properties: {}`), its presence can confuse HTTP clients, proxies, and code generators that correctly reject or ignore bodies on GET requests. The body should be removed entirely; all parameters are already expressed as query parameters.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 defines GET as a safe method with no defined body semantics. An empty request body on a GET is at best a no-op and at worst causes interoperability issues with strict HTTP clients.
findings.patchSummary: Remove semantically incorrect requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: financial_account parameter typed as plain string without format or pattern
findings.narration: The `financial_account` required query parameter is typed as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `maxLength` constraint. In the Stripe API, FinancialAccount IDs follow a consistent prefix-based format (e.g., `fa_...`). Without a pattern or at minimum a `maxLength`, code generators cannot produce typed relationships and clients cannot validate input before sending. Adding a `maxLength` (consistent with other ID fields in the spec, typically 5000) and ideally a `pattern` matching known ID formats would improve clarity and safety.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as bare `string` prevent code generators from producing typed relationships and allow arbitrarily long input. Other cursor/ID params in this same operation already carry `maxLength: 5000`.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength constraint to financial_account query parameter schema

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter's description states it 'can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema (`type: integer`) encodes none of these constraints — no `minimum`, no `maximum`, and no `default`. This means a client could pass `limit=0` or `limit=99999` and only learn of the error at runtime. The described rules should be encoded directly in the schema so validators and code generators can enforce them without parsing prose.
findings.rationale: Numeric constraints expressed only in prose create a validation gap. Clients and generated SDKs will not enforce the 1–100 range, leading to unnecessary API errors. These are high-leverage schema rules to encode.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema

findings.title: Mutually exclusive fields `destination_payment_method` and `destination_payment_method_data` enforced only in prose
findings.narration: The description of `destination_payment_method_data` states it is 'Exclusive with `destination_payment_method`', but this constraint is not encoded in the schema. Clients and code-generation tools have no way to discover or enforce this mutual exclusivity from the schema alone. The rule should be expressed as a JSON Schema `oneOf` or `not` construct so validators can enforce it automatically.
findings.rationale: Conditional field exclusivity in prose only is a high-leverage schema gap; codegen tools cannot model the relationship, and incorrect payloads will only fail at runtime.
findings.patchSummary: Encode mutual exclusivity of destination_payment_method and destination_payment_method_data in schema

findings.title: `destination_payment_method` typed as plain string with no format or pattern for a resource ID
findings.narration: The field `destination_payment_method` is a PaymentMethod ID (typically prefixed `pm_...`) but is declared as `type: string` with only a `maxLength` constraint. Without a `format` or `pattern`, codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the PaymentMethod resource, and validation cannot reject obviously wrong inputs (e.g. random strings). Adding a regex pattern such as `^pm_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would improve both validation and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with no format or pattern prevent typed codegen and weak input validation, per the cross-resource reference rule.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to destination_payment_method to identify it as a PaymentMethod ID

findings.title: `statement_descriptor` constraints described in prose not encoded in schema
findings.narration: The `statement_descriptor` description says the maximum is 10 characters for ACH or 140 characters for US domestic wire, and restricts the allowed character set to `-#.$&*`, spaces, and alphanumeric characters. The schema only sets `maxLength: 5000`, which is far too permissive and contradicts the description. The network-dependent maximum lengths cannot be encoded with a single `maxLength`, but the allowed character set should at minimum be encoded as a `pattern` constraint, and the `maxLength` should be corrected to 140 (the highest valid bound). The discrepancy between 5000 and the described limits is confusing and could cause hard-to-debug server-side rejections.
findings.rationale: A maxLength of 5000 directly contradicts the documented max of 10 or 140; the allowed character set should be encoded as a pattern.
findings.patchSummary: Correct statement_descriptor maxLength to 140 and add character-set pattern

findings.title: Successful creation response uses 200 instead of 201
findings.narration: This POST endpoint creates a new OutboundTransfer resource, which per HTTP semantics should return HTTP 201 Created rather than 200 OK. Using 200 for a resource-creation operation is technically incorrect and can mislead clients that inspect status codes to determine whether a resource was newly created versus retrieved or updated.
findings.rationale: RFC 9110 §15.3.2 reserves 201 for successful resource creation; returning 200 is a common but incorrect practice that reduces semantic clarity.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 for resource creation semantics

findings.title: Empty request body defined on GET operation
findings.narration: The operation defines a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (no properties, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.1 explicitly discourages it, and many HTTP clients will drop it). Including this body definition misleads client generators into attempting to send a form body with a GET request, which may cause interoperability issues or silent failures.
findings.rationale: GET requests should not carry a request body. An empty, closed schema body on a GET endpoint provides no value and violates HTTP conventions.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Path parameter `outbound_transfer` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `outbound_transfer` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe outbound transfer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `obt_...`). Without a `pattern` or `format` hint, client SDK generators and validators cannot enforce or communicate the expected ID format, increasing the risk of misuse (e.g. passing a payment intent ID where a transfer ID is required). Adding a regex pattern like `^obt_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would improve both safety and developer experience.
findings.rationale: Resource ID path parameters typed as plain strings with no pattern prevent typed relationship modeling and miss input validation opportunities.
findings.patchSummary: Add a pattern constraint to the outbound_transfer path parameter schema.

findings.title: Path parameter `outbound_transfer` lacks ID format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `outbound_transfer` path parameter is typed as a plain `string` with only a `maxLength` of 5000. Stripe OutboundTransfer IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g. `obt_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot establish a typed relationship to the OutboundTransfer resource, and clients receive no validation hint about acceptable ID shapes. This is especially relevant for treasury operations where passing an ID from the wrong resource type could have financial consequences.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields typed as plain strings without pattern or format prevent codegen tools from building typed relationships and reduce client-side validation quality.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID pattern and tighten maxLength on outbound_transfer path parameter

findings.title: financial_account parameter lacks format/pattern — plain string with no ID constraints
findings.narration: The required `financial_account` query parameter is typed as a plain `type: string` with no `maxLength`, no `pattern`, and no format hint (e.g. `format: 'stripe-id'` or a regex like `^fa_`). This means codegen tools cannot derive that the value is a FinancialAccount resource ID, cannot validate the shape at the client, and cannot build a typed relationship between this endpoint and the FinancialAccount resource. Adding at minimum a `maxLength` and a `pattern` (or a Stripe-convention `x-stripeResource` annotation) makes the constraint machine-readable.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource IDs typed as bare strings without pattern or format prevent client SDK generators from producing typed resource references and miss validation opportunities.
findings.patchSummary: Add maxLength and pattern to financial_account query param to encode it as a FinancialAccount ID

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation — should be omitted entirely
findings.narration: The operation includes a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). GET requests MUST NOT have a body per RFC 7231 §4.3.1, and many HTTP clients and intermediaries will strip or reject a body on a GET. Even though `required: false` is set, advertising a request body on a GET operation is misleading, breaks strict clients, and can confuse codegen tools into generating a body parameter. The entire `requestBody` block should be removed from this operation.
findings.rationale: GET operations with request bodies violate HTTP semantics (RFC 7231) and confuse client generators; the body here is empty anyway.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation — GET bodies violate HTTP semantics

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100', but the schema only declares `type: integer` with no `minimum` or `maximum`. Without these constraints, validators and codegen tools cannot enforce the documented range, allowing clients to send out-of-range values (e.g., 0 or 10000) and relying solely on server-side rejection rather than spec-level validation. The schema should be `minimum: 1, maximum: 100, default: 10`.
findings.rationale: Documented numeric constraints in prose must be encoded in the schema to enable client-side validation and accurate SDK generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to limit parameter schema to match its description

findings.title: Response url field missing pattern — cannot be validated as a URL
findings.narration: The `url` field in the 200 response list schema is declared as `type: string, maxLength: 5000` with no `format: uri` and no `pattern`. The description clearly says it is 'The URL where this list can be accessed', so it should at minimum carry `format: uri` to let validators and codegen tools treat it as a proper URI rather than an arbitrary string.
findings.rationale: Fields semantically representing URLs should carry format:uri to enable machine-readable validation and accurate type generation.
findings.patchSummary: Add format:uri to the response list url field

findings.title: financial_account parameter typed as plain string with no format, pattern, or $ref
findings.narration: The `financial_account` query parameter references a FinancialAccount resource ID (likely prefixed `fa_`) but is declared as bare `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern` (e.g. `^fa_`), and no `$ref` to a FinancialAccount schema. Codegen tools and SDK generators cannot build a typed relationship from this parameter to the FinancialAccount resource, making the API contract weaker than it could be.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference IDs typed as plain strings with no format/pattern/ref lose type-relationship information that benefits codegen and documentation consumers.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to financial_account parameter schema to reflect FinancialAccount ID format.

findings.title: limit parameter missing minimum and maximum constraints
findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter explicitly states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but the schema does not encode `minimum: 1`, `maximum: 100`, or `default: 10`. These constraints exist only in prose, meaning validators and codegen tools cannot enforce or surface them automatically. A client sending `limit=0` or `limit=999` will only discover the error at runtime.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented in prose but absent from the schema are high-leverage findings: they should be encoded so validators, SDKs, and documentation generators can use them automatically.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema.

findings.title: Empty request body on GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an empty `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema (`properties: {}, additionalProperties: false`). HTTP GET semantics do not use a request body; most HTTP clients and gateways will ignore or reject a body on GET requests. Including an empty `requestBody` in the spec misleads consumers and SDK generators into thinking a body may be sent, which is incorrect and potentially harmful.
findings.rationale: GET operations should not declare a requestBody per HTTP semantics and OpenAPI best practice; an empty body declaration adds noise and may confuse codegen tools.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody from this GET operation.

findings.title: Missing description on `effective_at` parameter
findings.narration: The `effective_at` query parameter has no `description` field, leaving API consumers with no guidance on what this filter does or what values are acceptable. Every other date/filter parameter in this operation includes a description. Given that `effective_at` differs semantically from `created`, the absence is especially confusing — users cannot tell whether this is the settlement date, posting date, or something else without consulting external documentation.
findings.rationale: Missing parameter descriptions reduce clarity and developer experience. Stripe's own parameters like `created` and `ending_before` all have descriptions; consistency requires `effective_at` to have one too.

patchOps.value: Only return TransactionEntries with an effective_at date within the given date interval (Unix timestamp).

findings.patchSummary: Add missing description to the `effective_at` query parameter.

findings.title: `financial_account` and `transaction` typed as plain string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `financial_account` parameter (a required FinancialAccount resource ID) and the `transaction` parameter (a Transaction resource ID) are both typed as `type: string` with no `format`, no `pattern`, and no indication of their ID prefix conventions (e.g. `fa_...`, `trxn_...`). Codegen tools cannot build typed cross-resource relationships from plain strings, and client-side validation cannot reject clearly malformed IDs before the round-trip. A `pattern` such as `^fa_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$` would at minimum document the expected shape.
findings.rationale: Resource ID fields with no format or pattern prevent typed SDK generation and give no machine-readable clue about the referenced resource. Stripe IDs follow predictable prefix patterns that should be documented.
findings.patchSummary: Add ID-prefix patterns to `financial_account` and `transaction` string parameters.

findings.title: `limit` parameter missing minimum/maximum constraints
findings.narration: The `limit` parameter description states "Limit can range between 1 and 100", but the schema declares only `type: integer` with no `minimum: 1` or `maximum: 100`. This means the machine-readable schema does not enforce the constraint documented in prose. Clients and generated validators will not reject `limit=0` or `limit=999` before making a network call, and codegen tools will not surface the valid range to end users.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints that are not encoded in schema are a high-leverage finding: the rule exists but is invisible to tooling. Adding minimum/maximum closes the gap between documentation and validation.

findings.title: status_transitions filter has conditional-required fields documented only in prose
findings.narration: The description for the `status_transitions` parameter states: "When using this filter, `status=posted` and `order_by=posted_at` must also be specified." This is a conditional requirement that affects the validity of the request but is expressed only in natural language. There is no machine-readable schema enforcement (e.g., `if`/`then`, `dependencies`, or a top-level `oneOf`) that binds these three parameters together. Clients and code-generation tools will not be aware of the constraint, leading to calls that set `status_transitions` without the required companion parameters, which will presumably fail at runtime.
findings.rationale: Conditional required relationships expressed only in prose cannot be enforced by validators or communicated reliably by generated SDK clients.

patchOps.value: A filter for the `status_transitions.posted_at` timestamp. When using this filter, `status=posted` and `order_by=posted_at` must also be specified. NOTE: These co-constraints are not yet machine-encoded; see related parameters.

findings.narration: The `financial_account` parameter is a required resource identifier for a FinancialAccount object (typically a Stripe ID with a prefix like `fa_`). Adding a `pattern` (e.g., `^fa_[a-zA-Z0-9]+$`) or at minimum a descriptive `format` would allow clients to validate the value before sending the request and would make the cross-resource relationship explicit.

findings.patchSummary: Add pattern and maxLength to financial_account to signal resource ID type

findings.narration: The description for the `limit` parameter states: "Limit can range between 1 and 100". However, the schema for `limit` is simply `{"type": "integer"}` with no `minimum` or `maximum` constraint. This means a client could pass 0, -1, or 999 and the spec would consider it valid. The stated constraints should be reflected in the schema so that validators and generated SDKs can enforce them without making a round-trip to the server.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints on numeric parameters cannot be enforced by schema validators or generated client-side guards.
findings.patchSummary: Encode minimum=1 and maximum=100 on limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary and misleading
findings.narration: The operation declares a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` content type containing an empty schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`). GET requests should not carry a body according to HTTP semantics (RFC 7231 §4.3.1); many HTTP clients, proxies, and server frameworks will silently drop or reject bodies on GET requests. Having this declared in the spec can confuse generated clients into serializing a body, and the `additionalProperties: false` with no properties ensures nothing useful can even be placed there. The `requestBody` should be removed.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per HTTP semantics; declaring an empty one misleads clients and code generators.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation

findings.title: Missing constraints on `limit` parameter (no minimum, maximum, or default)
findings.narration: The `limit` query parameter schema is declared as `type: integer` but has no `minimum`, `maximum`, or `default` values. The parameter description states 'Limit can range between 1 and 100, and the default is 10', but this invariant is expressed only in prose. Codegen tools and client validators cannot enforce the 1–100 range or apply the default of 10 without machine-readable constraints. This means clients may send limit=0 or limit=999 and only learn about the constraint via a runtime error.
findings.rationale: Constraints documented only in prose are not machine-enforceable. The schema should encode minimum: 1, maximum: 100, and default: 10 to match the stated invariant.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum:1, maximum:100, default:10 to the limit parameter schema

findings.title: Empty request body on a GET operation is unnecessary noise
findings.narration: A GET endpoint with a `requestBody` of an empty schema (`properties: {}`, `additionalProperties: false`) is semantically incorrect and likely confusing. HTTP GET requests should not carry a body per RFC 9110 semantics, and many HTTP clients and proxies will discard or reject a GET request body. Declaring an empty, locked-down form body on every GET endpoint creates noise in generated SDKs and documentation. The requestBody should be removed entirely from this operation.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not have a request body per HTTP semantics. An empty form body adds no value and can confuse clients, tooling, and proxies.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET /v1/webhook_endpoints

findings.title: Response schema missing `additionalProperties: false` — allows unspecified fields silently
findings.narration: The 200 response schema (`NotificationWebhookEndpointList`) does not set `additionalProperties: false`. While the `required` array ensures mandatory fields are declared, the absence of `additionalProperties: false` means the schema is open by default and validators will accept responses with arbitrary extra fields without warning. For a list envelope type like this—with a small, well-known set of fields—closing the schema would improve correctness guarantees and catch unexpected API drift.
findings.rationale: An open schema on a well-defined list envelope makes it harder to detect API contract changes and allows silent schema drift to go unvalidated.
findings.patchSummary: Close the 200 response envelope schema with additionalProperties: false

findings.title: POST endpoint returns 200 instead of 201 for resource creation
findings.narration: This endpoint creates a new webhook endpoint resource, but the success response is declared as HTTP 200 rather than the semantically correct HTTP 201 Created. Per RFC 9110, a POST that results in the creation of a new resource should return 201 Created with a Location header pointing to the new resource. Using 200 blurs the distinction between creation and update operations and makes it harder for clients and tooling to distinguish these cases.
findings.rationale: HTTP semantics (RFC 9110 §9.3.3) specify that resource creation via POST should respond with 201 Created. Returning 200 is a design inconsistency.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 Created for resource creation semantics.

findings.title: url field missing format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `url` field in the request body is declared as `type: string` with no `format`, `pattern`, or `maxLength` constraint. A webhook URL must be a valid HTTPS URL. Without a `format: uri` and ideally a pattern enforcing the HTTPS scheme, clients receive no machine-readable guidance about what constitutes a valid value. Code generators and validators will not be able to perform any structural validation, and users may not realize HTTPS is required.
findings.rationale: A webhook URL should carry format:uri (and ideally maxLength) so validators and generators can enforce it without relying solely on prose documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Add format:uri and maxLength to the url field for structural validation.

findings.title: Missing example on enabled_events array field
findings.narration: The `enabled_events` field accepts a large closed enum array and is a required field, but no example value is provided. Given the breadth of the enum (200+ values) and the special `['*']` wildcard behavior described in the description, an example would substantially improve the developer experience by showing idiomatic usage (e.g., selecting specific events vs. using the wildcard).
findings.rationale: Required fields with complex enum semantics and special wildcard behavior benefit significantly from inline examples for developer onboarding and codegen tooling.
findings.patchSummary: Add an example value to enabled_events illustrating typical event selection.

findings.title: Path parameter `webhook_endpoint` typed as unconstrained string with no format or pattern
findings.narration: The `webhook_endpoint` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe webhook endpoint IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `we_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a descriptive `format`, codegen tools cannot build a typed cross-resource reference, and client SDKs cannot validate the ID before sending the request. This also means any arbitrary string up to 5000 characters is considered valid by schema validators, which is far too permissive for a resource identifier.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain string without format or pattern prevent typed relationship generation in codegen tools and weaken client-side validation.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern constraint to webhook_endpoint path param to enforce Stripe ID format.

findings.title: GET operation includes an unnecessary empty request body
findings.narration: This GET operation defines a `requestBody` with an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` schema that contains no properties (`properties: {}`) and is marked `required: false`. Per HTTP semantics, GET requests should not carry a body; including one is semantically incorrect and can cause issues with certain HTTP clients, proxies, and caching intermediaries that strip or reject bodies on GET requests. The empty schema provides no value and adds noise to the spec.
findings.rationale: GET requests must not include a request body per HTTP/1.1 semantics. An empty, unrequired body definition is both semantically wrong and potentially harmful with HTTP infrastructure.
findings.patchSummary: Remove empty requestBody from GET operation to comply with HTTP semantics.

findings.title: webhook_endpoint path parameter lacks format/pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `webhook_endpoint` path parameter is typed as `string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe webhook endpoint IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `we_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a tighter `maxLength`, codegen tools cannot build a typed reference to the webhook endpoint resource, and validation is essentially absent. A `maxLength` of 5000 is also far too permissive for what is effectively a short opaque ID.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource ID fields typed as plain strings without format or pattern prevent codegen from building typed relationships and allow clearly invalid values to pass schema validation.
findings.patchSummary: Tighten webhook_endpoint path param: reduce maxLength and add ID pattern constraint.

findings.title: url field lacks format or pattern validation
findings.narration: The `url` field in the request body is typed as a plain `string` with no `format: uri` or `pattern` constraint. This means any arbitrary string value passes schema validation. Since this field will be used to deliver webhook events, accepting non-URL values could cause runtime errors or security issues (e.g., SSRF-adjacent misuse). At minimum `format: uri` should be applied.
findings.rationale: A field described as 'The URL of the webhook endpoint' should have `format: uri` to enable client-side validation and communicate the expected value domain.
findings.patchSummary: Add format: uri and maxLength to the url request body field.

findings.title: No request body example for complex update operation
findings.narration: The request body has no `example` or `examples` defined despite having several distinct field shapes (metadata as object or empty string, description as string or empty string, large enum array for enabled_events). Consumers and documentation generators would benefit from at least one representative example showing a typical partial update (e.g., changing the URL and toggling a subset of events).
findings.rationale: Complex request bodies with union types (anyOf) and large enum arrays benefit from examples to clarify correct usage for API consumers.

value.description: Production webhook for charge events

findings.patchSummary: Add a representative example to the request body for clarity.

findings.title: Path parameter `webhook_endpoint` lacks format or pattern constraint
findings.narration: The `webhook_endpoint` path parameter is typed as `type: string` with only a `maxLength: 5000` constraint. Stripe webhook endpoint IDs follow a well-known prefix pattern (e.g., `we_...`). Without a `pattern` or at minimum a shorter `maxLength`, there is no machine-readable signal that this is a resource identifier rather than arbitrary text. Codegen tools cannot build a typed relationship to the webhook endpoint resource, and client-side validation is weakened.
findings.rationale: Cross-resource reference typed as plain string with no format or pattern; codegen tools lose the typed relationship.
findings.patchSummary: Add a `pattern` constraint to the webhook_endpoint path parameter to reflect Stripe ID format.

findings.title: DELETE returns 200 instead of 204 for a deletion with no meaningful body
findings.narration: The operation returns HTTP 200 with a JSON body on successful deletion. While Stripe's API consistently returns a deletion confirmation object (with `id` and `deleted: true`), the cyclic schema reference means the response schema is opaque in this snippet. If the body is a meaningful deletion confirmation object, 200 is acceptable. However, if the body contains no actionable data beyond a status flag, the conventional REST choice would be 204 No Content. Given Stripe's known pattern of returning `{id, object, deleted: true}`, 200 is defensible but the schema should be explicit rather than a cyclic reference.
findings.rationale: Minor HTTP semantics concern; 200 is acceptable if the body carries a typed deletion confirmation, but the opaque cyclic schema makes this unverifiable.
findings.patchSummary: Consider documenting the deletion confirmation schema explicitly instead of relying on a cyclic reference.

findings.title: Virtually all GET endpoints declare an empty application/x-www-form-urlencoded request body
findings.narration: Across the entire spec, nearly every GET operation includes a requestBody block with an empty, property-less application/x-www-form-urlencoded schema (required: false). This pattern appears on well over 200 GET endpoints spanning every resource domain: /v1/account, /v1/accounts, /v1/balance, /v1/charges, /v1/customers, /v1/invoices, /v1/payment_intents, /v1/subscriptions, /v1/treasury/*, /v1/issuing/*, and so on. HTTP semantics do not define request body semantics for GET; many HTTP clients, proxies, and security gateways will drop or reject bodies on GET requests. OpenAPI tooling typically warns or errors on this pattern, and generated SDKs may transmit spurious empty bodies. The fix is to remove the requestBody declaration from all GET operations.
findings.rationale: GET + requestBody is an HTTP anti-pattern that can break clients and proxies, and it recurs across the vast majority (~200+) of this spec's GET operations.
findings.patchSummary: Remove the empty requestBody block from all GET operations across the spec.

findings.title: All resource-creation POST endpoints return HTTP 200 instead of 201 Created
findings.narration: Every POST endpoint that creates a new resource in this spec returns HTTP 200 OK rather than the semantically correct 201 Created. This pattern is pervasive across all resource domains: /v1/account_links, /v1/accounts, /v1/billing/alerts, /v1/checkout/sessions, /v1/customers, /v1/invoices, /v1/payment_intents, /v1/payment_methods, /v1/subscriptions, /v1/transfers, /v1/treasury/*, /v1/issuing/*, /v1/radar/*, and at least 100 more. RFC 7231 specifies 201 for successful resource creation with a Location header pointing to the new resource. Using 200 makes it impossible for clients to distinguish creation from update responses, prevents HTTP intermediaries from behaving correctly, and misleads API consumers about idempotency and caching semantics. This appears to be a deliberate Stripe-wide API design choice, but it constitutes a meaningful deviation from REST conventions that should be explicitly documented as intentional.
findings.rationale: RFC 7231 designates 201 for resource creation. Returning 200 for all creates across 100+ endpoints is a spec-wide pattern that deviates from REST standards and affects client correctness.
findings.patchSummary: Change success response code from 200 to 201 on all resource-creating POST endpoints.

findings.title: Sensitive fields (PAN, CVC, account numbers, SSN, tax IDs, secrets) lack writeOnly: true across the spec
findings.narration: A significant number of operations across the Stripe spec accept highly sensitive data in request bodies without marking those fields with writeOnly: true. Affected field categories include: raw card numbers (card.number) and CVCs (card.cvc) in /v1/charges, /v1/customers/*/cards, /v1/customers/*/sources, /v1/test_helpers/terminal/readers/*/present_payment_method and /v1/tokens; bank account numbers (account_number, routing_number) in /v1/accounts/*/bank_accounts, /v1/accounts/*/external_accounts, /v1/customers/*/bank_accounts, /v1/treasury/outbound_payments; SSN fragments and government ID numbers (ssn_last_4, id_number) in /v1/accounts/*/people, /v1/accounts/*/persons, /v1/tokens; secret payload strings in /v1/apps/secrets; encrypted PIN numbers in /v1/issuing/cards; client_secret in /v1/payment_intents/*/confirm and /v1/setup_intents/*/confirm. Without writeOnly: true, code generators will include these fields in response models and documentation, SDK serialisers may round-trip them in responses, and logging middleware may inadvertently capture them. This is a security-critical gap affecting dozens of endpoints.
findings.rationale: PCI DSS, PII regulations, and general security best-practice require that credential and sensitive identity fields be marked write-only so they are excluded from response schemas and generated documentation.
findings.patchSummary: Add writeOnly: true to all PAN, CVC, account number, SSN, ID number, PIN, and secret payload fields across the spec.

findings.title: Virtually every resource-ID field across the spec is typed as a plain string with no format, pattern, or $ref
findings.narration: Across the entire 587-operation spec, cross-resource identifier fields — path parameters and request/response body fields that reference Stripe resource IDs — are typed as type: string with only a large maxLength: 5000. No field carries a format hint, a pattern such as /^cus_/, /^pm_/, /^pi_/, /^acct_/ etc., or a $ref to a dedicated ID schema. This affects path parameters (account, customer, payment_method, invoice, charge, subscription, etc.) and body fields (customer, on_behalf_of, price, product, tax_code, financial_account, received_credit, etc.) across virtually every operation in the spec. The consequence is that: (1) SDK generators cannot produce typed resource-ID wrappers or distinguish ID types; (2) client-side validation is impossible; (3) copy-paste errors (passing a customer ID where a payment method ID is expected) will not be caught by schema validation. A spec-wide pattern of x-stripe-resource-id or at minimum per-type pattern constraints should be adopted.
findings.rationale: Typed resource IDs are essential for SDK generation, validation, and discoverability. The complete absence of patterns across 587 operations is a systemic clarity and tooling gap.
findings.patchSummary: Add format or pattern constraints to all Stripe resource ID fields (path params and body fields) across the spec.

findings.title: Hundreds of conditional-required and mutually-exclusive field relationships are encoded only in prose descriptions
findings.narration: Throughout the entire spec, field-relationship rules that should be machine-readable JSON Schema constraints are expressed exclusively in human-readable description text. Examples include: mutual exclusivity between customer and customer_account across at least 30 endpoints; amount_off vs percent_off in /v1/coupons; billing_scheme=tiered requiring tiers in /v1/plans and /v1/prices; confirm=true requiring mandate_data and return_url in /v1/setup_intents; type discriminators not linked to sub-object presence in /v1/billing/alerts, /v1/payment_intents, /v1/setup_intents/*/confirm, /v1/terminal/readers/*/set_reader_display; replacement_reason required with replacement_for in /v1/issuing/cards; destination vs payout_method in /v1/payouts; shipping required for physical cards in /v1/issuing/cards; scope.user conditionally required in /v1/apps/secrets; and hundreds more. These prose-only rules are invisible to validators, SDK generators, and automated testing tools, meaning invalid payloads will pass schema validation and only fail at runtime. This is the single most pervasive design gap in the spec.
findings.rationale: Prose-only constraints cannot be validated by tooling. The pattern recurs in well over 100 operations and represents a fundamental gap between documented and machine-enforceable API contracts.
findings.patchSummary: Encode conditional-required and mutually-exclusive field rules as JSON Schema constraints (oneOf, if/then, required) across the spec.

findings.title: The `limit` pagination parameter lacks minimum, maximum, and default constraints on all list endpoints
findings.narration: Every list (GET) and search endpoint in the spec includes a limit query parameter documented in prose as accepting 1–100 with a default of 10. However, not a single one of these parameters encodes minimum: 1, maximum: 100, or default: 10 in its JSON Schema definition. This affects all ~120 list endpoints across all resource domains. As a result, schema validators will accept limit: 0, limit: -5, and limit: 999 without error. Generated client SDKs will not enforce the bounds, and documentation tooling will not display the valid range. The fix is to add minimum: 1, maximum: 100, and default: 10 to the limit parameter schema on every list operation.
findings.rationale: Missing numeric constraints on a universally-present parameter across all 120+ list endpoints is a systemic validation gap that affects every consumer of the API.
findings.patchSummary: Add minimum: 1, maximum: 100, and default: 10 to the `limit` parameter schema on all list/search endpoints.

findings.title: No explicit 4xx error response definitions on any operation — universal reliance on a single `default` catch-all
findings.narration: Across all 587 operations in this spec, error responses are handled exclusively through a single default response entry. Not a single operation defines explicit 400, 401, 402, 403, 404, 409, 422, or 429 response codes. This is a universal pattern affecting every resource domain. The consequences are significant: API consumers cannot write status-code-specific error handling; documentation tools cannot surface specific failure modes; contract testing cannot assert that a 404 is returned for missing resources or a 422 for validation failures; and the numerous business-rule failure modes documented in operation descriptions (e.g., cannot delete a customer with active subscriptions, cannot finalize a draft invoice in certain states) are invisible to automated tooling. At minimum, 400 (bad request), 404 (not found), and 402 (payment/card errors, which Stripe uses extensively) should be defined on write and retrieve operations.
findings.rationale: The complete absence of explicit 4xx response definitions across all 587 operations prevents correct error handling in generated SDKs and contract tests.
findings.patchSummary: Add explicit 400, 402, 404 (and where applicable 409, 422) response definitions to all write and retrieve operations.

findings.title: client_secret credentials transmitted as URL query parameters on GET endpoints
findings.narration: At least three GET operations transmit a client_secret credential as a plain URL query string parameter: GET /v1/payment_intents/{intent}, GET /v1/setup_intents/{intent}, and GET /v1/sources/{source}. URL query parameters are routinely captured in server access logs, browser history, CDN logs, proxy logs, referrer headers, and analytics tools. A client_secret is a sensitive single-use credential that grants the ability to confirm a payment or setup intent without full API authentication. Transmitting it in a URL exposes it to broad unintended disclosure. The parameters lack any security note, writeOnly marker, or format: password annotation. The correct approach is to transmit these credentials in request headers (Authorization) or, where GET semantics are required, to use a POST with a request body.
findings.rationale: Sensitive credentials in URL query strings are a well-documented security vulnerability (CWE-598) with high likelihood of unintended log capture.

patchOps.value: WARNING: Transmitting client_secret as a query parameter exposes it in server logs, browser history, and CDN caches. Consider using the Authorization header or a POST endpoint instead.

findings.patchSummary: Move client_secret from query parameters to request headers or POST body; add security warning to all three GET operations.

findings.title: Top-level `tags` array is absent from the spec — all operations are untagged
findings.narration: The OpenAPI spec contains no top-level tags array and no operation-level tags assignments across all 587 operations. Tags are the primary mechanism by which documentation generators (Swagger UI, Redoc, Stoplight), SDK generators, and API gateways group and navigate operations. Without tags, every operation appears in an undifferentiated flat list, making the spec unusable for human navigation. The Stripe API naturally groups into logical domains: core payments (charges, payment_intents, refunds), billing (invoices, subscriptions, coupons), connect (accounts, transfers), issuing, terminal, treasury, identity, radar, and so on. Adding tags to both the top-level and to each operation is a low-effort, high-impact improvement.
findings.rationale: Absent tags make the 587-operation spec impossible to navigate in any standard documentation or SDK generation tool.

value.name: core
value.description: Core payment processing operations

value.name: billing
value.description: Subscriptions, invoices, and billing management

value.name: connect
value.description: Stripe Connect platform operations

value.name: issuing
value.description: Stripe Issuing card management

value.name: terminal
value.description: Stripe Terminal point-of-sale operations

value.name: treasury
value.description: Stripe Treasury financial account operations

value.name: identity
value.description: Stripe Identity verification operations

value.name: radar
value.description: Stripe Radar fraud prevention operations

findings.patchSummary: Add a top-level tags array and assign appropriate tags to all 587 operations.

findings.title: info.contact and info.license are absent from the spec metadata
findings.narration: The spec's info block contains only title, version, and description. It is missing contact (name, url, email for API support), license (name, url for usage terms), and termsOfService fields. These fields are important for: (1) API marketplace registrations that require contact information; (2) automated SDK generators that embed license information in generated code; (3) enterprise procurement processes that require ToS references; (4) developer portals that surface support contact details. Stripe's public API documentation at https://stripe.com/docs/api contains all this information but it is not machine-readable in the spec.
findings.rationale: Missing standard info fields reduces the spec's usefulness in automated tooling pipelines and API registries.
findings.patchSummary: Add contact, license, and termsOfService fields to the info block.

findings.title: Server URL has a trailing slash which may cause double-slash path issues in some clients
findings.narration: The single server entry is defined as https://api.stripe.com/ (with a trailing slash). OpenAPI 3.x path items all begin with /v1/... (a leading slash). When clients concatenate the server URL with path items, the result is https://api.stripe.com//v1/... (double slash). While most HTTP clients normalise this, some strict clients, reverse proxies, and generated SDKs may not. Additionally, the spec does not define a separate server for the files.stripe.com host used by POST /v1/files and GET /v1/quotes/{quote}/pdf, nor for the test-helper server distinction, forcing consumers to infer the correct host from operation descriptions rather than the servers array.
findings.rationale: Trailing slash on the server URL combined with leading-slash paths produces double slashes. Missing alternate server entries (files.stripe.com) for multipart uploads and PDF downloads.
findings.patchSummary: Remove trailing slash from server URL and add files.stripe.com as an additional server entry for file upload/download operations.

findings.title: Deprecated operations and fields lack machine-readable `deprecated: true` markers
findings.narration: Several operations and fields are described as deprecated in their prose descriptions but do not carry the OpenAPI deprecated: true boolean. Affected operations include GET /v1/balance/history (which redirects to /v1/balance_transactions), GET /v1/exchange_rates and GET /v1/exchange_rates/{rate_id}, POST /v1/issuing/authorizations/{authorization}/approve, POST /v1/issuing/authorizations/{authorization}/decline, GET /v1/customers/{customer}/bank_accounts and its sub-operations (tagged as deprecated in summaries), POST /v1/plans (superseded by Prices API), and POST /v1/charges (superseded by Payment Intents). Without deprecated: true, SDK generators will not mark these methods as deprecated in generated code, documentation tools will not visually distinguish them, and linting tools cannot flag their use. None of the deprecated operations include a machine-readable x-sunset date either.
findings.rationale: Prose-only deprecation notices are invisible to SDK generators and linting tools, causing deprecated endpoints to be used in new integrations.
findings.patchSummary: Add deprecated: true to all operations marked as deprecated only in prose, and add x-sunset extension with timeline.

findings.title: Numerous operations have empty or missing descriptions, summaries, or misleading summaries
findings.narration: A pattern of missing, empty, or copy-paste-incorrect documentation appears across many operations. Notable examples: POST /v1/application_fees/{id}/refund has an entirely empty description; POST /v1/charges/{charge}/dispute has an empty description; POST /v1/charges/{charge}/dispute/close has an empty description; POST /v1/customers/{customer}/discount has an empty description; GET /v1/customers/{customer}/subscriptions/{subscription_exposed_id}/discount has an empty description; POST /v1/payment_methods has a summary that says 'Shares a PaymentMethod' when it creates one; POST /v1/sources has a summary that says 'Shares a source' when it creates one; POST /v1/tokens has a summary that says 'Create a CVC update token' when it creates multiple token types; DELETE /v1/customers/{customer}/subscriptions/{subscription_exposed_id}/discount describes a customer-level operation; multiple bank_account operations describe 'source' or 'card' operations due to copy-paste; POST /v1/terminal/configurations/{configuration} says 'Updates a new Configuration'. These documentation errors mislead developers and reduce the quality of generated SDK documentation.
findings.rationale: Empty descriptions and misleading summaries across 10+ operations undermine developer experience and indicate systemic copy-paste errors in the spec.
findings.patchSummary: Fix empty, missing, and copy-paste-incorrect descriptions and summaries across all affected operations.

findings.title: The `subscription_exposed_id` path parameter name leaks an internal implementation detail across multiple endpoints
findings.narration: The path parameter name subscription_exposed_id appears in at least four operations: GET, POST, and DELETE /v1/customers/{customer}/subscriptions/{subscription_exposed_id} and DELETE /v1/subscriptions/{subscription_exposed_id}/discount. The '_exposed_id' suffix is an internal Stripe naming convention that indicates a parameter name that was widened for public exposure but was never cleaned up before the spec was published. It is confusing to API consumers and SDK users who see this parameter name in generated code, breaking the abstraction. It should be renamed to subscription consistently with every other subscription-related path parameter in the spec (e.g., /v1/subscriptions/{subscription_exposed_id} vs /v1/subscription_schedules/{schedule}). Similarly the operationId values for these operations contain the same artifact.
findings.rationale: Internal naming artifacts in path parameters produce confusing generated SDK parameter names and break consistency with the rest of the spec.
findings.patchSummary: Rename all subscription_exposed_id path parameter occurrences to subscription for consistency and clarity.

findings.title: DELETE operations return HTTP 200 with a body instead of 204 No Content across the spec
findings.narration: All DELETE operations in the spec return HTTP 200 with a JSON response body (a deletion confirmation object following Stripe's tombstone pattern) rather than 204 No Content. This is a consistent Stripe-wide design choice, but it deviates from REST conventions where 204 is the standard for successful deletions. Affected endpoints include DELETE /v1/accounts/{account}, DELETE /v1/customers/{customer}, DELETE /v1/coupons/{coupon}, DELETE /v1/invoices/{invoice}, DELETE /v1/customers/{customer}/tax_ids/{id}, DELETE /v1/subscriptions/{subscription_exposed_id}/discount, and all other DELETEs in the spec. While Stripe intentionally returns the deleted object for audit trail purposes, this choice should be explicitly documented at the spec level (e.g., via an x-stripe-delete-returns-object extension or a spec-level description) so consumers understand the deliberate deviation from convention.
findings.rationale: Returning 200 with a body on DELETE is a consistent Stripe design decision but deviates from REST conventions across all ~40 DELETE operations without explicit documentation of the intentional choice.

value.delete-response: DELETE operations return HTTP 200 with the deleted object as a tombstone rather than 204 No Content. This is intentional.

findings.patchSummary: Document the intentional 200-with-body DELETE pattern at the spec info level via an extension field.

findings.title: No request body examples on any complex POST/PUT operation across the spec
findings.narration: Despite the presence of many extremely complex request bodies — POST /v1/checkout/sessions (50+ top-level parameters), POST /v1/payment_intents (40+ parameters with 50+ payment method types), POST /v1/subscriptions (deeply nested billing configuration), POST /v1/issuing/cardholders (conditional company/individual sub-objects), POST /v1/terminal/configurations (WiFi/cellular/device configs), POST /v1/tax/registrations (100-country discriminated union), POST /v1/billing_portal/configurations (nested feature flags), and many others — not a single operation in the 587-operation spec provides a request body example. The absence of examples is a universal pattern. Examples are the most effective way to communicate correct usage of complex, multi-conditional schemas and are particularly important for operations with mutually exclusive fields, discriminated unions, and conditional requirements that cannot be expressed in JSON Schema.
findings.rationale: Zero request body examples across all 587 operations, including many with extreme complexity, severely degrades developer experience and increases integration error rate.
findings.patchSummary: Add at least one request body example to every POST operation with a complex or conditional schema.

findings.title: Typos and minor documentation errors recur across multiple operations
findings.narration: Several typos and minor prose errors appear across the spec, suggesting a need for a spec-wide documentation pass: (1) 'overriden' should be 'overridden' in /v1/billing_portal/configurations POST and /v1/billing_portal/configurations/{configuration} POST (appears twice); (2) 'Zeland' should be 'Zealand' in nz_bank_account descriptions in /v1/payment_method_configurations POST and /v1/payment_method_configurations/{configuration} POST; (3) broken markdown link syntax (missing closing bracket) in payco descriptions in the same two operations; (4) 'an scheduled' should be 'a scheduled' in GET /v1/sigma/scheduled_query_runs/{scheduled_query_run}; (5) 'Retrieves a new' should be 'Retrieves a' in GET /v1/sources/{source}/mandate_notifications/{mandate_notification}; (6) stray period in reboot_window description in POST /v1/terminal/configurations; (7) copy-paste typo in canceled_at description in GET /v1/subscription_schedules; (8) preferred_locales enum inconsistency missing da/pl/sv in /v1/issuing/cardholders. These are individually minor but collectively indicate a documentation quality gap.
findings.rationale: Multiple typos and documentation inconsistencies across the spec degrade developer trust and indicate a need for a systematic documentation review pass.
findings.patchSummary: Fix all identified typos: overriden→overridden, Zeland→Zealand, broken markdown links, grammar errors, and copy-paste description errors.

findings.title: Bank account request/response body schemas conflate bank-account and card fields without discrimination across multiple update operations
findings.narration: A systematic copy-paste pattern exists across multiple external account and source update operations where the request body schema is a flat union of both bank-account-specific fields (account_holder_name, account_holder_type, account_type, routing_number) and card-specific fields (exp_month, exp_year, name, address_line1, address_line2, address_city, address_state, address_zip, address_country). Affected operations include: POST /v1/accounts/{account}/bank_accounts/{id}, POST /v1/accounts/{account}/external_accounts/{id}, POST /v1/customers/{customer}/bank_accounts/{id}, POST /v1/customers/{customer}/cards/{id}, POST /v1/customers/{customer}/sources/{id}, and POST /v1/external_accounts/{id}. This schema pollution means card fields appear on bank account update forms and vice versa, creating developer confusion and allowing logically invalid payloads to pass schema validation. The fix is to use oneOf or separate operation schemas conditioned on the resource type.
findings.rationale: Mixed bank-account/card schemas appear in at least 6 update operations as a copy-paste artifact, allowing invalid payloads and creating developer confusion.
findings.patchSummary: Separate bank-account and card update schemas using oneOf or discriminated sub-schemas to eliminate field cross-contamination.

findings.title: exp_month and exp_year are typed as string instead of integer in multiple card-related schemas
findings.narration: Card expiry fields exp_month and exp_year should be integers (1–12 and 4-digit year respectively) but are typed as type: string in at least four operations: POST /v1/accounts/{account}/external_accounts/{id}, POST /v1/customers/{customer}/sources/{id}, POST /v1/customers/{customer}/cards/{id}, and POST /v1/external_accounts/{id}. This inconsistency means string values like 'abc' and '99' will pass schema validation for month/year fields, and generated SDK types will use string instead of integer for these numeric fields. Other card-related operations in the spec use integer for these fields, making this an inconsistency.
findings.rationale: Type inconsistency on card expiry fields across 4+ operations allows invalid string values and produces incorrect SDK types.
findings.patchSummary: Change exp_month and exp_year from type: string to type: integer with minimum/maximum constraints in all affected card update schemas.

findings.title: Nationality, country, and ISO code fields consistently lack ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 pattern constraints
findings.narration: Fields that accept ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes appear throughout the spec — nationality in all person/people operations, country in tax registrations, country in addresses, rate_id in exchange rates — but none carry a pattern: '^[A-Z]{2}$' or maxLength: 2 constraint. Instead they use maxLength: 5000, making them effectively unconstrained strings. Affected operations include POST and GET on /v1/accounts/*/people, /v1/accounts/*/persons, /v1/tax/registrations, /v1/exchange_rates/{rate_id}, /v1/country_specs/{country}, and many address.country fields across the spec. A 2-character pattern would catch common errors (full country names, 3-letter codes, typos) at validation time.
findings.rationale: ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 fields without pattern constraints across 20+ operations allow invalid country codes that will only fail at runtime.
findings.patchSummary: Add pattern: '^[A-Z]{2}$' and maxLength: 2 to all ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code and nationality fields across the spec.

POST endpoints accept only `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`; not `application/json`
`x-stripeBypassValidation` vendor extension exposed on 538 enum fields signals non-authoritative enums
`expand` parameter declares `style: deepObject` but `schema.type: array` on 270 operations
5 unix-epoch integer fields lack `format: "unix-time"` despite 152 consistent usages elsewhere

Three operations have prose-only deprecation markers but `deprecated: true` is not set
Five operations are missing the `description` field entirely
24 operations missing the `summary` field, including high-traffic POST /v1/charges and POST /v1/accounts
Seven `/search` endpoints use page-based pagination while the rest of the spec uses cursor-based
`api_errors.code` is typed as a free-form string but is documented as an enumerated value
Error payloads expose full nested PaymentIntent / PaymentMethod / SetupIntent / Source schemas

Parameter-relationship rules embedded spec-wide in prose only, not in JSON-Schema constraints

Integer and number properties have zero range constraints across the entire spec
`operationId` values are excessively verbose machine-generated names rather than human-readable identifiers
Zero operations carry `requestBody` examples; codegen and documentation render without sample payloads
Rate-limit response headers are not declared on any operation
79 % of component schemas carry empty-string `description`
